EU Eyes €20 Billion Surge to Fuel Joint Defense Operations With Ukraine
The European Commission is preparing a tender for defense initiatives aiming to secure approximately €20 billion ($22.2 billion) in unallocated capital from the SAFE program, opening participation to joint ventures between European Union member states and Ukraine.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius stated that the initiative focuses on expanding defense collaboration by executing shared projects both on Ukrainian soil and within EU territories, leveraging Ukraine’s leading position in defense innovation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Kubilius noted that Ukraine faces a €23 billion ($25.5 billion) defense budget shortfall this year, underscoring the requirement for continuous aid from global partners.
He explained that this deficit stems from unfulfilled commitments by individual nations that previously pledged over €40 billion ($44.4 billion) during the NATO summit in Ankara.
Additionally, the European Commission recently directed €325 million ($360 million) toward five European Defense Projects of Common Interest, with Ukraine taking part in four of those initiatives.
The new commitments come as individual European countries continue to strengthen Ukraine’s air defenses through bilateral support.
Germany, in particular, is expected to deliver additional air defense packages to Ukraine later this month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced following talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukrainian and German officials are also finalizing a bilateral Drone Deal aimed at strengthening the defense capabilities of both countries.

Ukraine Successfully Uses Domestic FP-7 Ballistic Missile for the First Time, Zelenskyy Says

- Category

Ukraine Successfully Uses Domestic FP-7 Ballistic Missile for the First Time, Zelenskyy Says
Ukrainian forces have marked the first successful operational deployment of the domestically developed FP-7 tactical ballistic missile during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on October 1.
Footage shared on official social channels captured the launch from an undisclosed firing position.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Ukrainian tactical ballistics. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next is production. Glory to Ukraine!” Zelenskyy stated in a message accompanying the video.
The deployment marks a significant transition for Ukraine’s defense industry as it expands domestic production of long-range strike systems.
Ukrainian missile maker Fire Point updated its FP-7.x Freyja interceptor with a combined infrared and radar seeker, replacing the missile's previous infrared-only design.
The dual-mode seeker allowed the system to track targets using both heat signatures and radar reflections during its final flight phase, helping maintain lock-on even through bad weather or decoys.
Developed as part of a joint initiative with nine other European nations, the 7.25-meter-long interceptor was designed to reach speeds up to 7,200 kilometers per hour to counter short-range ballistic threats during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Fire Point made significant progress on its domestic missile program during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, aiming to complete its 850-kilometer FP-9 ballistic missile by late 2026.
Company CEO Iryna Terekh revealed in a September interview that the shorter-range FP-7 had already entered codification after roughly two years of rapid development, costing approximately $200 million for research and initial production setup.
The company worked to finish testing the long-range FP-9—designed to potentially reach distant targets, including Moscow—while overcoming tight international export controls by engineering critical components internally.

Taiwan Cabinet rejects claims supplementary budget breaks rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:41:30 UTC
16:41:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) on Friday defended the legality of the government's NT$607.6 billion (US$19 billion) supplementary budget after the Legislative Yuan Budget Center raised concerns that the proposal could break budget rules.
The center said Thursday that the Cabinet's proposal to submit a supplementary budget before the 2026 central government budget takes effect could violate the Budget Act, per Mirror Daily. It noted that agencies may apply for supplementary funding when a major event requires spending beyond their allocated budgets.
The center also questioned the Cabinet's inclusion of increases to national pension and elderly farmers' welfare allowances in the supplementary budget. It said changes to benefit levels require authorization.
The Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics responded that the benefit increases are being pursued in parallel with legislative work, per Rti. It said the move was intended to allow recipients to receive the increased benefits as soon as the relevant amendments are passed by the legislature.
Responding to the Budget Center, Lee cited Article 51 of the Budget Act, which stipulates that the legislature should receive the central government budget one month before the start of the fiscal year, per CNA. She noted that the 2026 budget was instead passed on Aug. 14.
Lee said the Cabinet submitted the supplementary budget after the 2026 budget completed its third reading to prevent further delays, stressing that the move complies with Article 79 of the Budget Act.
The review of the 2026 budget was delayed after the Cabinet refused to implement laws concerning pay raises for military personnel, pension increases for retired police officers and firefighters, and a halt to cuts to civil servant and teacher pensions. The legislature eventually agreed to send the budget to committees after the Cabinet promised to implement previously passed funding for new initiatives and submit bills related to the pay and pension increases.
The Budget Center has repeatedly criticized the Cabinet's budget decisions. It previously questioned the government's use of supplementary budgets to increase defense spending as a share of GDP, warning that repeated use could normalize employing flexible measures for defense needs, per China Times.
More recently, the center raised concerns about the inclusion of NT$10,000 cash handouts in the 2027 budget, per UDN. It argued that major policies require new legislation or authorization under existing laws to be implemented.
The center also said the fluctuating nature of securities transaction tax revenue makes it an unstable funding source for the handouts.

Cho says proposed NT$20,000 cash payment would require government borrowing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said Friday that doubling the government's planned universal cash payment to NT$20,000 (US$627) per person would require borrowing, CNA reported.
President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) announced the government plans to distribute NT$10,000 per person before Lunar New Year in 2027. KMT Legislative Caucus Convener Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁) later proposed doubling the payment to NT$20,000 during legislative questioning, claiming it would help people cope with rising prices and the wealth gap.
The government has budgeted NT$235.7 billion for the program as part of the 2027 central government budget. It says the payment is intended to let the public share the benefits of economic growth and higher tax revenue linked to the AI sector.
Cho said additional tax revenue is already being used for welfare, economic development, key industries, and disaster response. Increasing the cash payment would therefore require the government to borrow money, he said.
He added the government must also reserve funds for research, innovation, and industrial development. The government needs to plan for the country's needs over the next five, 10, and 20 years, he said.
Fu argued that stronger tax revenue gives the government room to increase the payment. He cited figures showing tax revenue rose by NT$487.1 billion through June and NT$619.1 billion through August from a year earlier, per Economic Daily News.
Fu said distributing about NT$460 billion would support households and boost domestic spending. Cho said the government must balance cash payments with other spending needed for Taiwan's long-term development.
The Cabinet has said the planned NT$10,000 payment would not require additional borrowing or reduce funding for welfare, defense, health care, education, and other government programs. It has argued that a larger payment would make those conditions harder to meet, per CTS News.

Taiwan optical suppliers eye orders as US moves to restrict Chinese-made transceivers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:40:55 UTC
16:40:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s optical communications industry could benefit from potential order shifts as the US moves to restrict Chinese-made components used in AI infrastructure, CTEE reported Friday.
A Morgan Stanley report said the US could add Chinese-made optical transceiver modules to its list of controlled products as early as October. The move would not initially amount to a blanket ban, with restrictions potentially starting with next-generation 3.2-terabit products.
The policy could create opportunities for Taiwanese suppliers as US customers seek to diversify their supply chains. Industry sources said local optical communications companies could become second-source suppliers as orders shift away from Chinese manufacturers.
Potential beneficiaries include LandMark Optoelectronics Corp., Elite Advanced Laser Corp., Fiber Optic Communications Inc., LuxNet Corp., Browave Corp., and Ezconn Corp.
LandMark and Elite Advanced Laser are developing components for high-speed optical communications. Fiber Optic Communications and Browave, meanwhile, have expanded into optical fiber components for AI data centers and co-packaged optics.
LuxNet has been developing high-speed optical transceivers. Ezconn is targeting high-speed fiber-optic connectivity products.
As AI data centers handle growing volumes of data, conventional electrical signals face greater signal loss and power consumption at higher transmission speeds. Optical communications address these limitations by using light-based signals to transmit data, enabling higher bandwidth and lower losses over long distances, according to Pocket Securities.
Optical transceivers are key components in data centers and AI infrastructure. They convert electrical signals into optical signals for high-speed, long-distance data transmission, using lasers to transmit signals and photodetectors to receive them, according to Moomoo.
As AI computing requirements grow, optical transceivers have advanced from 100G to 400G and 800G, with 1.6T products increasingly being deployed. Morgan Stanley said the proposed rules would have limited near-term impact on widely used 800G products and the growing 1.6T segment, as they would primarily target 3.2T products.
The 3.2T products are expected to begin ramping up in 2028 and see broader adoption in 2029, suggesting any impact on orders and revenue would emerge gradually.

‘I knew these were the final seconds’: Flydubai captain speaks from hospital after cockpit attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:38:20 UTC
16:38:20 KST

Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot of the Flydubai flight who was transferred Thursday to a hospital in the United Arab Emirates, appeared publicly for the first time Friday in footage from the hospital, speaking by video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
“I had so many injuries that I collapsed. I’ve been a captain for 11 years. I know, even with my eyes closed, what is happening with the aircraft. When I fell, I felt the plane descending, the nose going down, and I knew these were the final seconds. I tried to crawl. I opened the door, and everything else happened immediately after that. People in Saudi Arabia and here in the UAE took care of me, and I could not have received better treatment or medical attention,” Machchhar said.
He added: “I realized that if I didn’t show courage, 170 passengers would lose their lives.”
Modi praised the captain, telling him: “The entire country is praying for you. The courage, composure and calm you showed saved many lives. The country can proudly say Indians are not people who take lives, but people who are prepared to risk their lives to save others.”
Machchhar replied: “I never thought I would have the opportunity to speak with you.”
Indian media reported Thursday that Machchhar, who was stabbed by his Omani co-pilot, underwent emergency surgery at a hospital in the Saudi city of Tabuk, where the aircraft landed. His family was making its way from Mumbai to Dubai.
The government of the Indian state of Gujarat said it would honor Machchhar with an award. Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel praised the pilot’s “unwavering courage,” saying his actions saved the passengers’ lives.
Israeli investigators have still found no link between the Omani co-pilot and Iran, despite U.S. President Donald Trump suggesting Thursday that there could be a connection. The Omani co-pilot was also transferred Thursday from Saudi Arabia to the UAE.
Israel is seeking to send a team to the UAE in the coming days, though the move requires prior coordination. Emirati officials have conveyed anger to Israel over what they viewed as a premature Israeli conclusion that the co-pilot acted out of terrorist motives aimed at undermining the Abraham Accords, before the investigation had been completed.
An Israeli official said the word “terror” is particularly sensitive for the Emiratis because it could suggest a lack of control. Abu Dhabi therefore prefers not to get ahead of the investigation and, for now, is being cautious in drawing conclusions about the Omani pilot’s motives.
A senior Israeli official said the pilot most likely acted alone. After Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News that the Omani had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination,” the official said Israel was examining the suspect’s activity on social media. At the same time, Israeli assessments are increasingly leaning toward a nationalist and religious motive rather than a suicide attempt.
Israel had asked to participate as an observer in the investigation in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, but Riyadh did not agree. Now that the co-pilot has been transferred to the UAE, Israel is counting on its close ties and cooperation with Abu Dhabi to become as involved as possible in the investigation, even if only as an observer.

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 646 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov overnight, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
Ukrainian drones attempted to attack industrial infrastructure in Russia’s southern Volgograd Region. As a result of the attack, a fire broke out in an apartment building in the city of Volgograd. One person was injured and taken to hospital.
TASS has compiled key details on the aftermath.
Attack scale
- On-duty air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 646 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over Russian regions between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time (5:00 p.m. GMT) on October 1 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time (5:00 a.m. GMT) on October 2, the Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, drones were downed over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Kursk, Voronezh, Kaluga, Tula, Oryol, Rostov, Saratov, Volgograd, Ulyanovsk, Samara and Astrakhan Regions, the Republic of Crimea, the waters of the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
- More than 110 UAVs were destroyed in 24 hours over the town of Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, the Verkhnedonskoy, Kamensky, Millerovsky, Sovetsky, Tarasovsky, Ust-Donetsky, Chertkovsky, Sholokhovsky and Bokovsky Districts of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar said on his Max channel.
- Air defense systems shot down 62 Ukrainian drones over the Voronezh Region, Governor Alexander Gusev wrote in a post on his Max channel.
- Air defense forces intercepted 18 Ukrainian UAVs over the Kaluga Region, Governor Vladislav Shapsha reported on his Max channel.
- According to Shapsha, drones were shot down over the Babyninsky, Duminichsky, Kirovsky, Kozelsky, Lyudinovsky, Maloyaroslavetsky, Peremyshlsky, Sukhinichsky and Ferzikovksy municipal districts, on the outskirts of the towns of Kaluga and Obninsk.
Aftermath
- Ukrainian drones attempted to attack industrial infrastructure in the Volgograd Region, Governor Andrey Bocharov said.
- As a result of the attack, a fire broke out in an apartment building on Udmurtskaya Street in the Krasnoarmeysky District of Volgograd.
- One person was injured and taken to hospital.
- The blaze has been contained.
- Emergency services are working on site, with cleanup efforts underway.
- The governor instructed officials to conduct damage assessments and cleanup work and to prepare temporary shelters.
- A temporary shelter has been opened for residents at school No. 31, the city administration’s press service said.
- Beds and hot meals have been provided there.

Taiwan Coast Guard hoses Chinese fishing boat off Dongsha
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:35:59 UTC
16:35:59 KST

- Taiwan's Coast Guard used a water cannon on the Chinese fishing boat Jin Sha after it refused to leave waters near Dongsha Island.
- The patrol vessel Yunlin later gave the crew 35 hot meals and towed the boat out, handing it to a Chinese vessel early Oct. 2.
Taiwan’s Coast Guard used a water cannon on a Chinese fishing boat that refused to leave waters near Dongsha Island in the South China Sea, then warned its crew they would be arrested and their boat seized before finally towing it out of the area.
The Coast Guard Administration said its Dongsha-Nansha Branch spotted an unidentified boat around 11 a.m. on Oct. 1, about 15.5 nautical miles (29 km) northeast of Dongsha. It sent the 4,000-ton patrol vessel Yunlin (CG-5003), which around 3 p.m. found two Chinese fishing boats, the Yue Hui Dong Yu 75066 and the Jin Sha, fishing about 27 nautical miles (50 km) east of the island inside waters Taiwan controls, Taiwan’s Central News Agency reported.
The Yue Hui Dong Yu 75066 left after the Yunlin’s warnings. The Jin Sha did not. After three radio warnings went unanswered, the Yunlin fired its water cannon for 30 seconds from about 200 meters (660 feet) away, and when that failed it moved closer and sprayed the boat for another 90 seconds.
Coast Guard personnel then approached the fishing boat again and told the crew to leave or face arrest on the spot and seizure of the vessel. Footage released by the agency shows one Coast Guard officer holding a firearm at the ready during the encounter.
The standoff ended without arrests. At the crew’s request, the Yunlin gave the Jin Sha’s crew 35 hot meals, then towed the boat out of Taiwan’s restricted waters and handed it over to a Chinese work vessel early on Oct. 2. The Coast Guard said its use of the water cannon followed standard procedures, and urged Beijing to stop illegal fishing in the area.
Dongsha, also known as Pratas Island, lies about 450 km (280 miles) southwest of Kaohsiung and is one of two island groups Taiwan controls in the South China Sea, along with Taiping Island in the Spratlys. About 300 Coast Guard personnel are stationed there, and the surrounding atoll is a marine national park where all fishing is banned.
Taiwan defines two zones around its territory. Its prohibited waters are its territorial sea, normally 12 nautical miles from shore, and its restricted waters are a contiguous zone extending to 24 nautical miles. Around Dongsha, the lines can reach farther because they are measured from surrounding reefs.
The waters around Dongsha have seen repeated encounters this year. In May, the 5,500-ton Chinese coast guard ship CCG-3501 entered Taiwan’s restricted waters there and spent more than a day in a standoff with the Taiwanese patrol vessel Taichung, with each side radioing the other to leave. The Coast Guard said at the time it was the sixth time this year a Chinese coast guard ship had approached the island. In June, Taiwan reported the first entry by a Chinese government vessel into the restricted waters around Taiping Island.

Five years under the Taliban: Meduza reports from Afghanistan, where a war on drugs and greater security have come with mass poverty, unemployment, and the loss of women’s rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:33:21 UTC
16:33:21 KST

Five years under the Taliban: Meduza reports from Afghanistan, where a war on drugs and greater security have come with mass poverty, unemployment, and the loss of women’s rights
In August 2021, after the withdrawal of U.S. troops, the Taliban, an armed religious and political movement, seized power in Afghanistan. Active fighting has since ended, but life has hardly improved for many Afghans. The Taliban established a Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice and severely curtailed women’s rights. The authorities also tried to block internet access nationwide and ban officials from using smartphones. At the same time, the Taliban declared war on drugs, specifically opium, and it appears to be waging that war quite successfully.
In August 2026, Middle East scholar Ruslan Suleymanov traveled to Afghanistan to see how the country had changed over the past five years. He visited three cities and had dozens of conversations. Meduza has translated his report.
‘Russia? Welcome!’
“Get out of the car!” a Taliban fighter dressed entirely in camouflage tells me firmly, but without aggression, at one of the many checkpoints on the Herat–Kandahar highway. He asks me to follow him.
A local Taliban commander sits on the grass near the highway, surrounded by his aides. He takes his time examining my documents. When he realizes I have a Russian passport, his face lights up with joy, almost elation.
“Oh, Russia! Welcome!” the commander says in Pashto. Only a moment later do I notice that his left leg is missing. A prosthetic leg lies beside him.
He invites me to join him for tea from a thermos and even to stay the night. Hospitality is central to the culture of the Pashtuns, who make up Afghanistan’s ethnic majority and the backbone of the Taliban.
The roughly 500-kilometer (310-mile) journey from Herat in the north, considered Afghanistan’s cultural capital, to Kandahar in the south, where the Taliban movement originated in the mid-1990s, is much the same throughout: poor pavement — in places, very poor — document checks almost every hour, and enthusiasm at the mere mention of Russia.
That enthusiasm is understandable. Russia remains the only country in the world to officially recognize the Afghan government the Taliban formed in September 2021, shortly after seizing power.
For more than 40 years before the Taliban took power, Afghanistan’s roads were the scene of fighting, ambushes, and kidnappings. Today, long-distance travel around the country is relatively safe. Foreigners, however, are still better off traveling with someone local.
In 2026, Afghanistan ranks 11th in the world for terrorism risk, according to Australia’s Institute for Economics and Peace, which compiles the Global Terrorism Index. This is the first time it has fallen outside the top 10 since the ranking began.
In the first years after the Taliban took power, the main source of terrorism in Afghanistan was the Taliban’s bitter enemy, the Islamic State group — specifically its Afghan affiliate, Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISIS-K).
The group became known in Russia in March 2024 following the terrorist attack at Crocus City Hall in Krasnogorsk, outside Moscow, which killed 145 people. U.N. experts estimate that ISIS-K still has around 2,000 fighters. Afghans dissatisfied with the current authorities and people from Central Asia, mainly Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, periodically join its ranks. Over the past five years, ISIS-K has recruited at least 600 volunteers from those countries.
In any case, improved security is one of the few achievements the Taliban can claim over the past five years. That is partly because, before August 2021, the Taliban itself carried out most of Afghanistan’s major terrorist attacks.
How popular is Taliban rule?
In nearly 300 years of statehood, Afghanistan has yet to develop a shared national identity. “We remain a deeply divided community, but we are not yet a nation. Everyone understands the word ‘Afghan’ differently,” Amin, a 31-year-old employee of the nationwide radio station Salam Watandar, tells Meduza.
The main divide is ethnic. Broadly speaking, the country can be divided into Pashtuns in the south and Tajiks, Uzbeks, Hazaras, and others in the north. The government formed by the Taliban is almost 100% Pashtun. The Taliban’s reasoning is simple: the country is led by those who contributed most to the fight against foreign forces from 2001 to 2021. That means exclusively Taliban members and allied groups that fought most actively against the U.S. and its allies.
“Claims that our government supposedly isn’t inclusive are part of an agenda imposed by the West. Afghans are happy with their government,” an ethnic Pashtun employee of the Ministry of Information and Culture told Meduza, asking not to be named. But in private conversations with Meduza, members of six minority groups — Baloch, Qizilbash, Sikhs, Tajiks, Uzbeks, and Hazaras — said they lacked equal rights and equal opportunities to pursue their ambitions in Afghanistan.
Ethnicity, however, is far from the country’s only dividing line. At least 74% of Afghans live in rural areas or are nomads; only 26% live in cities. In rural areas and mountain valleys isolated from the outside world, ways of life have remained unchanged for centuries. The village elder or mullah commands the greatest respect and generally has ties to the Taliban.
That is why, under the previous government, most Afghans heeded Taliban calls to boycott elections. The militants called the elections illegitimate and threatened to cut off the fingers of anyone who went to a polling station. Turnout in Afghanistan’s last presidential election, in September 2019, was less than 20%.
The Taliban’s propaganda about defending Islamic values or fighting foreign invaders, meanwhile, met with understanding, if not approval, among local people.
“The front line used to run through here. Shells were exploding. Today I can grow potatoes and fruit,” Najib, 57, who lives on the outskirts of Lashkar Gah, the capital of Helmand province in southern Afghanistan, tells Meduza.
Najib’s father was killed in the mid-1980s during the Soviet invasion. In the late 1990s, he lost his older brother, who fought for the Taliban against the Northern Alliance — a coalition of northern warlords led by Ahmad Shah Massoud. In 2006, during the U.S. military presence in Afghanistan, his eldest son was killed after accidentally stepping on a mine on the road into Lashkar Gah.
“The war is over. For the first time in more than 40 years, we’re living in peace. That’s all I’ve asked the Almighty for in recent years,” he says. Like Najib, many Afghans are willing to forgive the Taliban for everything else because it has brought long-awaited peace.
‘We have to find a way to survive’
Before the Taliban took power, Helmand was known as Afghanistan’s leading producer of opium poppies. The province accounted for more than half of the country’s opium production.
In April 2022, Taliban supreme leader Hibatullah Akhundzada ordered a crackdown on the drug trade. His decree said offenders would be punished under Sharia, or Islamic law. It did not specify how.
Over four years, the Taliban has achieved impressive results: the area planted with poppies in Afghanistan has fallen by roughly 95%, according to the U.N. In our conversation, Afghan Interior Ministry spokesperson Mufti Abdel Matin Qani went further, insisting that the figure was 98%.
As a result, around five million Afghans across the country have lost a steady source of income. So far, the Taliban has been unable to offer them another way to earn a living legally. Unemployment stands at no less than 75%. More than 90% of the population now lives below the poverty line, and more than 70% of Afghans depend on humanitarian aid.
“We all used to grow poppies. The Taliban themselves controlled the sales and made huge amounts of money from them. We just got what was left over. But we could survive on that,” Ahmad, 62, who also lives in Helmand, near the city of Gereshk, tells Meduza.
He says that now, like many former poppy growers, he has to grow fruit and vegetables and take them into town to sell. “I used to earn up to 20,000 afghanis a month [about $300 at the current exchange rate]. Now I barely make 10,000 [about $150],” Ahmad says.
For many Afghans, that is a substantial amount of money. The U.N. estimates that the country’s average salary is now around $100. Meanwhile, prices keep rising, and inflation had already exceeded 7.5% at the beginning of the year.
Gasoline in Afghanistan now costs around 84 afghanis ($1.20) per liter, liquefied gas costs 66 afghanis ($1) per liter, and beef costs 500 afghanis ($7.60) per kilogram (2.2 pounds). Monthly electricity bills come to nearly 1,000 afghanis ($15.30).
The huge influx of Afghan refugees and migrants from neighboring countries, primarily Iran and Pakistan, has made the situation worse. Over the past three years, more than five million people have been forced to return to Afghanistan at those countries’ insistence, increasing its population by 10%.
Two of Ahmad’s sons, ages 23 and 26, spent several years working in construction in neighboring Pakistan. But Islamabad’s tighter immigration policy forced them to return home in late 2024. They now help their father harvest his crops and sell them at the market in Gereshk.
“Life isn’t getting any easier. We have to find a way to survive. What matters most is that there’s no war,” Ahmad says, alluding to the periodic armed clashes between Afghanistan and Pakistan, which have become more frequent over the past couple of years.
How has the Taliban changed
When the first Afghan state emerged in the 18th century, Kandahar was its first capital. It was also here, in 1994, that graduates of religious schools known as madrasas, mostly from neighboring Pakistan, founded the armed Taliban movement. By 1996, it controlled most of Afghanistan, including Kabul.
Kandahar, now often called the country’s political capital, is home to the headquarters of Taliban supreme leader Hibatullah Akhundzada, who also holds the title amir al-mu’minin, or “commander of the faithful.” He is consolidating his power, which rests on his high standing in the Taliban’s religious hierarchy.
Akhundzada relies on his own military guard and the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, effectively the morality police. The ministry was reestablished in September 2021 in place of the Ministry of Women’s Affairs. It enforces his draconian laws and restrictions, including those imposed on women.
Over the past five years, girls in Afghanistan have been barred from attending school beyond the sixth grade and from pursuing higher education. Women are also banned from beauty salons, fitness centers, parks, and other recreational spaces. The Taliban’s supreme leader has prohibited women from working in government institutions, nongovernmental organizations, and U.N. agencies.
Some Taliban members, mostly in Kabul, do not share the rigid conservatism of their leader, who once turned his own son into a suicide bomber. During the movement’s 20 years underground, some militant leaders lived in countries such as Pakistan and Qatar. They saw that life in a Muslim country could be very different — certainly different from Afghanistan under Taliban rule in 1996–2001.
Some militant leaders are known to have sent their daughters to schools and universities in those countries. These experiences changed Taliban leaders, who became less radical than their predecessors. This is especially true of the movement’s younger generation, those born in the 1980s and 1990s.
In February 2023, for example, Taliban Interior Minister Sirajuddin Haqqani sharply criticized the supreme leader over the ban on education for girls, accusing him of “usurping power.” He later had to leave the country for several months, reportedly because he faced the threat of arrest.
Another member of the Kabul-based Taliban leadership, Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammad Abbas Stanikzai, also repeatedly called for girls to be allowed to return to school and young women to university. As a result, he was dismissed in May 2024 and later left Afghanistan altogether.
Kandahar itself is more conservative than Kabul. Most women here wear dull purple burqas that cover their faces completely. Boutiques and malls are rare, and most commerce takes place informally at simple stalls or carts on the streets.
Over the past five years, many of the movement’s members most loyal to the supreme leader have moved to this birthplace of the Taliban. Among them is Zabihullah Mujahid, spokesperson for the “Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan” and the Taliban’s public face.
Three years ago, we met in Kabul at the Ministry of Information and Culture, where he is deputy minister. This year, we met at a hotel in Kandahar.
“Education authorities are continuing their efforts. They are trying to create the conditions needed to resolve this issue, which is strictly an internal matter,” Mujahid says when I ask when girls in Afghanistan will be able to return to school beyond the sixth grade.
He says attempts to pressure the Taliban or force it to change any of its restrictions will never succeed. “We urge all countries not to concern themselves with Afghanistan. These are matters for our nation, and they do not concern other states,” Mujahid says, making his reluctance to discuss the subject clear.
He has more to say when asked about the “Islamic Emirate’s” relations with Moscow. “Russia has a very important role in Afghanistan. Russia also plays a very important role in our region, especially economically. You could say that Russia is needed,” Mujahid says. “Moreover, Russia’s recognition of the ‘Islamic Emirate’ government is a very important step that sets an example for everyone else. It shows Western countries in particular that there is no need to be afraid of taking such a step.”
The distance from Kandahar to Kabul is also roughly 500 kilometers (310 miles), but the journey takes a couple of hours less. The pavement is much better here, probably because Taliban officials themselves regularly use this highway.
There was once heavy fighting here, too, and kidnappings were frequent. In July 2007, for example, the Taliban abducted 23 Christian missionaries from South Korea on this road. Two were executed; the others were released more than a month later in exchange for Seoul’s commitment to withdraw its roughly 200 troops from Afghanistan by the end of the year.
Now, the only reminders of the war are the burned-out wrecks of cars and military vehicles occasionally visible beside the highway.
There are checkpoints roughly every 100 kilometers (60 miles), as well as at the entrance to Kabul. At the final checkpoint before entering the Afghan capital, security officers thoroughly inspect the car and record detailed information about every foreigner in a logbook.
As one might expect of a capital, Kabul is different from the rest of Afghanistan. Modern malls, fitness clubs, and fashionable coffee shops from before the Taliban’s return to power are still open. Before the Taliban’s return, those coffee shops were gathering places for Kabul’s cosmopolitan young people, hipsters, and LGBTQ people.
Strangely enough, the Taliban itself no longer shuns the trappings of Western civilization. This sets its members apart from their older comrades who controlled Afghanistan in 1996–2001. Back then, the militants banned music, confiscated photographic equipment and video recorders, forced people to follow a strict dress code, and held public executions in stadiums.
Today’s Taliban members happily take selfies, set up Facebook and Instagram accounts, watch the national cricket team’s matches, and order cappuccinos or lattes at coffee shops.
When Hibatullah Akhundzada ordered Afghanistan’s internet blocked in the fall of 2025 to “prevent immorality,” Taliban leaders in Kabul opposed the move, and service was restored after just three days. In June this year, the supreme leader ordered a ban on smartphones for government employees because, in his view, modern technology threatens Islamic norms and leads to “the destruction of the next generation.” From what I have seen, most officials, and not just in Kabul, still have smartphones.
Unlike in Kandahar, cafes and ordinary eateries in the capital also often show broadcasts from London-based Afghanistan International, the leading anti-Taliban TV channel run by Afghan exiles.
The militants in the Afghan capital also turn a blind eye to many of the restrictions on women imposed by the leadership in Kandahar. Roughly half the women in Kabul, for example, leave their faces uncovered and disregard the requirement to be accompanied in public by a male relative, known as a mahram.
Since August 2024, women in Afghanistan have officially been forbidden even to speak loudly in the street: the supreme leader ruled that “a woman’s voice is a source of impurity.” But this unrealistic rule is barely enforced either.
Perhaps the only thing women really cannot do in the streets is protest against Taliban rule. Immediately after seizing power in August 2021, the militants were shocked by the many protests by young women. Demonstrations took place in all of Afghanistan’s major cities, including Kabul, Herat, Mazar-i-Sharif, and Jalalabad. Typically, each drew between 100 and 300 young women.
This was largely a result of higher levels of education in the country. According to the U.N., primary school attendance among girls in Afghanistan rose from 0% to more than 80% between 2001 and 2021.
Now, at least 80% of the country’s 2.5 million women and girls of school age receive no education. In May and June this year, Afghanistan held entrance exams for public universities. A total of 120,000 applicants took them, without a single woman among them.
Nevertheless, an entire generation has grown up in the country with ideas about freedom, rights, and personal space that are completely different from those of the conservative Taliban. The Taliban, in turn, sees all of this as an intrusion by Western culture.
Can outside pressure influence the authorities?
“My life ended three and a half years ago. I’ll never forget that day. We were on our way to university classes, as usual, but people in uniform with assault rifles stopped us,” Shukriya, 24, tells Meduza, recalling the introduction of Afghanistan’s ban on university education for women in December 2022.
At the time, she was in her third year at Abu Ali ibn Sina (Avicenna) Medical University in Kabul. By now, she could have been working and supporting her loved ones. During decades of unrelenting war, it became commonplace for girls and women to support an entire family financially. But the Taliban’s return to power has made life much harder for women.
“For the first year, I was deeply depressed and thought about killing myself. I couldn’t imagine how to go on living. Even now, I don’t know what will happen to me tomorrow or how to build a life for myself,” Shukriya says. Women now account for up to 80% of all suicides in Afghanistan. Every day, at least one or two Afghan women take their own lives.
She says what kept her from suicide was knowing that she needed to care for her sick father and help raise her two younger brothers. At first, she wanted to work in a beauty salon, but the Taliban banned those, too, in July 2023. These were places where many young Afghan women found work, met, and spent time together.
Only men’s salons now operate openly in Afghanistan. Even the men’s faces on posters advertising these businesses have been painted over. Women’s salons continue to operate only in private homes, and their customers visit in secret, afraid of the “morality police.”
Shukriya now makes dresses to order and sells them through social media. “The money I make barely covers food for the family. But I’m getting more and more orders, and I hope to save as much as I can so I can leave and bring my loved ones with me,” she says.
Education for women and girls is one of the clearest examples of the conflict between urban and rural Afghanistan. Even before the Taliban returned to power, women in rural areas wore burqas, and girls were often kept out of school beyond the sixth grade. While primary school attendance improved dramatically in 2001–2021, average secondary school attendance among girls across Afghanistan never exceeded 40%.
Another source of tension is the Taliban’s particular understanding of Islam. Officially, the Taliban professes Sunni Islam, but its interpretation also incorporates the rules of the Pashtun ethical code, Pashtunwali. Under that code, a woman’s place is “either in the home or in the grave.”
Despite their extraordinary hospitality, Pashtuns fiercely guard their culture against foreign influence. Graffiti on a fence outside the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice in Kabul reads: “The hijab is a shield against the intrusion of foreign culture.”
The Taliban’s draconian laws have baffled even the Muslim world. In January 2023, for example, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said the ban on university education for women “has nothing to do with Islam.”
During the Taliban’s first period in power, in 1996–2001, three Muslim countries recognized its government: the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan. Today, even those countries do not. Nor does Qatar, which has hosted the movement’s political office since 2013.
At the U.N., Afghanistan is still represented by a diplomat from a state that no longer exists: the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan. Taliban spokesperson Mujahid told me this was because “the countries that waged wars in Afghanistan, the countries that occupied Afghanistan, have political influence over the U.N.”
Further isolation appears likely to make life even harder for Afghanistan’s population. Five years of ultimatums and attempts to pressure the Taliban have failed and instead led to a sharp reduction in international humanitarian aid, from $4 billion to $1 billion.
“We want the international community to cooperate with the authorities in Afghanistan, who have ensured security and eradicated corruption, drug trafficking, and other forms of crime,” Afghan Interior Ministry spokesperson Mufti Abdel Matin Qani tells Meduza.
For ordinary Afghans, particularly women and Kabul residents, all the Taliban’s achievements pale beside the restrictions imposed over the past five years. But they, too, see little point in trying to pressure the Taliban from abroad.
“The West was traumatized by its experience in Afghanistan and would rather forget about the country. All it does is try to lecture the Taliban. But they’ll never change. We need some other way to talk to them,” Shukriya says firmly.
“All I want is for people not to forget us or put all the responsibility on the Taliban. The world is responsible for us, too. Otherwise, our lives will become even more hellish,” she says.

louvre-lens turns cuteness into an art history of pink, plush toys and kawaii

so cute! louvre-lens exhibition unpacks the art of happiness from ancient times until today
through more than 300 works, from ancient cats to rebellious soft toys and the history of pink and glitter, the show examines art's ability to bring us joy and comfort.
LOUVRE-LENS TRACES THE ART AND AESTHETICS OF CUTENESS
Cuteness gets the museum treatment at Louvre-Lens with So Cute! The Art of Happiness, an exhibition tracing how artists and cultures have produced — and occasionally weaponized — the feeling of ‘aww’ from antiquity to the present. Bringing together around 300 paintings, sculptures, photographs, films, objects and installations, the show moves between animals, babies, the color pink, soft toys, glitter and kawaii culture to ask why certain shapes, gestures and materials trigger affection, comfort and the instinct to protect. In other words, the museum is taking cute seriously, without pretending it has always behaved itself.
Curated by Annabelle Ténèze, director of Louvre-Lens, and Émilie Girard, director of the Musées de la Ville de Strasbourg, the exhibition places works from radically different periods into deliberately unlikely conversations. Egyptian cats and ancient babies meet Théodore Géricault, Auguste Renoir, Nicolas Poussin, Jeff Koons and Philippe Katerine, while Cindy Sherman, Rosa Bonheur, Agnès Varda, William Wegman and Pierre et Gilles expand the story through portraits, pets and pop culture. Rather than defining cuteness as a fixed aesthetic, the exhibition treats it as something that shifts with time, geography and whoever happens to be doing the looking.
FROM KAWAII AND PINK TO CUTENESS WITH A DARKER SIDE
One section follows kawaii back well beyond its contemporary overload of mascots and merchandise. The Japanese term emerged centuries ago before developing into the visual vocabulary of rounded forms, oversized heads, large eyes and soft colors now embedded in manga, fashion and advertising. Takashi Murakami appears among the artists extending that language into contemporary art, while an adjacent chapter looks at South Korea’s own culture of cuteness. Elsewhere, pink gets its historical due, alongside works by Cindy Sherman and Ettore Sottsass, whose Ultrafragola mirror makes a fairly convincing case that a color can be both sweet and spectacularly self-aware.
The sugar rush does not last uninterrupted. So Cute! also examines the relationship between adorableness, consumer culture, propaganda, war imagery and social critique, showing how supposedly innocent visual codes can comfort, persuade or unsettle depending on their context. Soft toys move from childhood companions to artistic tools for addressing memory and vulnerability, while the mischievous expressions of characters such as Labubu complicate the idea of the perfectly behaved plushie. The exhibition ends this line of thinking with Pascal Lièvre’s glitter-covered reinterpretations of Louvre icons, where sequins and drag aesthetics turn familiar masterpieces into something brighter, stranger and considerably less reverential.
MATHIS BOUCHER BUILDS A PINK, INTERACTIVE DREAMWORLD
Architect-scenographer Mathis Boucher translates the theme into an environment conceived somewhere between a story and a video game. Visitors pass through a rounded pink entrance into a sequence of dreamlike rooms linked by curves, soft edges and tactile materials including fur, mirrors, bouclé and carpet. Rabbit-shaped magnifying glasses and other ‘treasure objects’ are tucked into the route, while a chapter dedicated to cuteness’ darker side interrupts the fantasy before the exhibition heads towards what the museum describes as a happy ending in a puff of glitter. Argile developed a custom powder tone, dubbed Louvre-Lens Pink, specifically for the scenography.
The visitor is not expected to remain entirely passive in all this softness. A 2.7-meter-wide wheel of emotions greets the public before entry, while interactive labels, a kawaii guide character named Momo, a manga library and a multisensory ‘Symphony of Emotions’ room invite different ways of moving through the show. At the end, visitors can even vote for the work that affected them most. The cheerful scenography also hides a pragmatic layer: almost 90% of its display cases and 80% of its hanging system come from the museum’s reuse program. So Cute! The Art of Happiness runs at Louvre-Lens through January 18, 2027.

name: Trop mignon! L’art du bonheur
 curators: Annabelle Ténèze and Émilie Girard
 location: Louvre-Lens, Lens, France | @louvrelens
 when: September 23, 2026 – January 18, 2027

‘I have not lost my dreams’: Refugee education funding cuts threaten millions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:30:36 UTC
16:30:36 KST

‘I have not lost my dreams’: Refugee education funding cuts threaten millions
A teenage girl who fled war-torn Sudan for neighbouring Egypt and hopes to pursue a technology degree is an example of why countries must ensure that young refugees can continue to learn.
“When we left Sudan, I was worried that my education would stop,” said Jamila Mostafa, 19, one of the estimated 13.1 million refugee children of school age worldwide in 2025.
Yet nearly half – 5.8 million – remain out of school as funding cuts threaten to roll back years of progress in educating children and adolescents forced to flee their homelands due to war, conflict, violence or persecution.
A generation at risk
The warning comes in a new report by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR.
“At a time of severe pressure on humanitarian and development financing, cuts to education risk reversing decades of collective investment and closing opportunities for a generation of young people,” said UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih, a former refugee from Iraq.
The transition to secondary education remains one of the biggest challenges for refugee children, according to the report. Only 32 per cent were enrolled in high school in 2025, compared to 65 per cent at the primary level.
However, many young refugees arrive at primary school unprepared. Two in three lack the foundational learning that prepares them for the classroom.
Gender gap, enrollment goals
Even though refugee girls and boys attend primary school at similar rates, the gap widens sharply in secondary education. Increasing numbers of adolescent girls leave school due to poverty, early marriage, safety concerns and other pressures.
Meanwhile, progress in higher education underscores the value of sustained investment. Refugee enrollment at the tertiary level reached a record 11 per cent in 2025, with more than 450,000 students attending university or undertaking technical and vocational training.
This means UNHCR and partners are on track to ensure that 15 per cent of refugee youth can access higher education by the end of the decade, known as the 15x30 pledge.
Faiza Qudrati from Afghanistan grew up in Kazakhstan and studied medicine before switching to psychology.
“For me, higher education gives me a chance to grow, learn and one day help other people in the same way that support was once provided to me,” she said.
Unequal access
Although higher education can significantly improve the lives of refugee women and girls, providing them with access to skills, qualifications, employment and greater financial independence, access is still deeply unequal.
Refugee enrollment remains below the national average in more than 80 per cent of reporting countries. In low-income and conflict-affected countries, only two per cent of refugees were enrolled in higher education, compared to 13 per cent of nationals.
UNHCR stressed that improving refugee education also means strengthening national education systems by investing more in teachers, classrooms, learning materials and financing to benefit both refugees and host communities.
Shaping their own future
UNHCR called for the international community and development partners to safeguard education funding and invest in the national systems of countries hosting refugees.
“Education gives young people the tools to shape their own future,” said Mr. Salih. “Our responsibility is to make sure they have that chance.”
Jamila, the young Sudanese woman in Egypt, is continuing her high school education through UNHCR-backed support. She has developed a particular interest in artificial intelligence (AI) and how it can help address social and economic challenges. She hopes to study technology at university.
“School gives me confidence,” she said. “It reminds me that even though I lost my home because of the war, I have not lost my dreams.”

Hungary welcomes Ukraine's bill strengthening Hungarian minority rights
BUDAPEST, Oct 2 - Hungary welcomed on Friday Ukraine's move to submit draft legislation to parliament that strengthens the education rights of its ethnic Hungarian minority.
A long-running dispute over minority rights had strained ties between Budapest and Kyiv and complicated Hungary’s support for Ukraine’s ambition to join the European Union.
"The bill strengthens the legal guarantees of education in the Hungarian language, and the network of educational institutions," Prime Minister Peter Magyar said in a Facebook post.
Magyar has taken a less confrontational stance towards Kyiv than his predecessor Viktor Orban, but he too has said that progress on boosting the rights of some 100,000 ethnic Hungarians in Ukraine is a prerequisite for Budapest's backing of Ukraine's EU accession.
Hungary's Foreign Minister Anita Orban - no relation of the former prime minister - said on Friday that Ukraine's Deputy Prime Minister Vsevolod Chentsov had informed her that the bill on education rights would be submitted to the Ukrainian parliament with a decision expected this month.
"We welcome this step, which was preceded by bilateral Hungarian-Ukrainian expert-level talks in recent weeks and consultations with representatives of the Transcarpathian Hungarian community," Orban wrote in a Facebook post.
This step follows a June announcement from Magyar that Hungary and Ukraine had reached an agreement on the language, cultural and educational rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine.
At the time Magyar said that once Ukraine enshrines the terms of that agreement in legislation, as well as its action plan for its EU accession talks, Hungary would support the opening of the first cluster of Ukraine's accession talks.
Magyar has repeatedly said his government does not support accelerated membership talks for Ukraine. REUTERS

Captain Smit Machchhar: A steady hand, in and out of the cockpit

Long before he was the captain who held a cockpit together despite stab wounds, Capt Smit Machchhar was the pilot who interacted with loaders, engineers, ground staff, catering people, all with equal respect.“Smit is the most calm, composed and down-to-earth person you could ever meet,” said Capt Dharav Gosalia, a friend since his flying school days.On Wednesday, that steadiness was tested at altitude. flydubai flight FZ1073 was carrying 174 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv when, according to Israeli officials, Machchhar’s co-pilot stabbed him and tried to crash the aircraft. The jet reportedly dropped nearly 14,000 feet in under 30 seconds. Seriously wounded, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, letting passengers and crew overpower the attacker. The plane landed in Saudi Arabia.Those who know Machchhar, 39, are not surprised by how he behaved. What shocks them is that it was ever required. “He is one of the calmest and most fun guys possible,” said a friend, a B737 pilot who requested anonymity. “Maybe it is his upbringing. He is always in fun mode, but he is family-oriented too.”
.
Machchhar earned his commercial pilot licence at Mainland Aviation College in New Zealand in the late 2000s, where he became the classmates’ go-to person for hard subjects. “Anyone with a problem in air navigation, aircraft technical or any subject went to him,” the pilot said. “Becoming a line trainer at flydubai was the best thing that could have happened to him.”The instinct to help was visible earlier, too. At M D Bhatia School, where he passed Class 10 in 2003, school friend Bhavin Jethva remembers him as “straightforward, bindass”. “He didn’t like to lie,” Jethva said. “He was never fake and he couldn’t pretend.” Amit Soni, a childhood friend who played cricket with him, called him cheerful and lively.At Swastik Heights in Mumbai’s Tilak Nagar, where Machchhar lived until about 2022, neighbour Laxmikanth Joshi remembers practical kindnesses. After returning from Kenya, Joshi realised he had bought too little coffee to share with friends. Machchhar arranged for a pilot colleague to bring back more. Joshi also remembers Machchhar going straight to the hospital after landing in India when his father underwent bypass surgery about six months ago. He stayed through the treatment. Then there were the Independence Day and Republic Day celebrations. He recalls Capt Machchhar taught them to tie the rope into a knot just right. “One pull and the flag unfurled,” recalled Joshi.
Akshay Joshi, his immediate neighbour, recalls tense moments at his place when his parents learned about the attack. Late in the evening, though, Machchhar’s parents informed the society’s WhatsApp group that their son was recovering.Capt Machchhar moved to Dubai around 2022 after leaving SpiceJet, and flies the Boeing 737 as a captain and line trainer at flydubai. He and his wife, Sonal, have two children: Krishay, 2, and Ziva, 9.Friends and colleagues tried to reconstruct the sequence. A B737 commander said the co-pilot would most likely have used the ‘crash axe’, which is carried on the flight deck for use during emergencies, such as cutting through panels and debris, or the cockpit window to exit the aircraft after an accident. “At the Dubai airport, even shoes and belts are removed at security,” he said. “There’s no way the co-pilot could have got onboard with a pocket knife.”
Another colleague said the co-pilot “apparently stood up and hit Machchhar on the side of the head”. This colleague added that the captain was also struck in the chest, before he regained control after the dive. A third pilot said Machchhar appeared to have squawked ‘7500’, the hijack transponder code. A B737 commander also pointed to a gap: “We have SOPs for a hijack scenario, but not for a cockpit where the aggressor is inside.
” He noted that Capt Machchhar’s bravery boils down to two acts: first, he managed to get the aircraft straight and level after that precarious dive, despite being attacked; second, though he had lost a lot of blood, he managed to open the cockpit door before he passed out.At M D Bhatia School, former classmates have been posting prayers for his recovery on their WhatsApp group. “We are proud of him,” Jethva said.

U.S. anti-ship missiles head to Japan’s westernmost island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:26:16 UTC
16:26:16 KST

- The U.S. military will deploy its NMESIS anti-ship missile launcher to Japan's Yonaguni Island during the Keen Sword exercise, Kyodo News reported.
- Keen Sword is set to begin Oct. 19 and run 11 days, NHK reported, marking NMESIS's first deployment on Yonaguni.
The U.S. military will deploy its NMESIS anti-ship missile launcher to Yonaguni, Japan’s westernmost inhabited island and about 107 km (66 miles) from Taiwan, during a major U.S.-Japanese exercise this month, Japan’s Kyodo News reported on Oct. 2, citing the Yonaguni town government.
The launcher will take part in Keen Sword, a large joint exercise held every two years. Japan’s public broadcaster NHK reported that this year’s live field training will start on Oct. 19 and run for 11 days, with both countries bringing their newest ground-based anti-ship missiles, and that it will be the first time NMESIS is deployed on Yonaguni, SBS reported.
Neither government has said how many launchers will go to the island, how long they will stay, or whether any missiles will be fired.
NMESIS, short for Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System, is a U.S. Marine Corps weapon built on an unmanned Joint Light Tactical Vehicle that carries two Naval Strike Missiles. The missiles can hit ships at ranges of more than 185 km (115 miles), and the remotely driven launcher is designed to move between islands and hide, so it can threaten enemy warships from shore while staying hard to find.
The system belongs to the 12th Marine Littoral Regiment, a unit based on Okinawa that the U.S. Marine Corps reorganized to defend and hold key islands in a conflict. The regiment formally received NMESIS, along with the MADIS counter-drone system, in June 2026. Its Hawaii-based sister unit, the 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment, was the first to field NMESIS in late 2024 and took it to the Philippines for the Balikatan exercise.
NMESIS first arrived in Japan in July 2025. During the Resolute Dragon exercise that September, Marines moved a launcher to Ishigaki, about 240 km (150 miles) from Taiwan, and displayed it alongside Japan’s Type 12 anti-ship missile at the Japanese base there, though no missiles were fired. Yonaguni is closer to Taiwan still.
Japan has stationed troops on Yonaguni since 2016, when a Ground Self-Defense Force coastal surveillance unit and radar began operating there. Tokyo announced in February 2026 that it plans to place surface-to-air missiles on the island by 2031. The 12th Marine Littoral Regiment has also used the island before, deploying its AN/TPS-80 G/ATOR radar to the Japanese base there during Resolute Dragon in 2024.

Russia and Ukraine exchanged overnight strikes Friday, with at least one person killed and three others injured, according to officials from both sides.
A Russian drone struck a residential building in the capital Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district, killing one person and injuring two others, Kyiv prosecutors said on Telegram.
Another Russian attack targeted the Pivdennyi Bridge in Kyiv, prompting authorities to close it to traffic in both directions, the city’s Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces continued to strike Ukrainian port and energy infrastructure, as well as maritime vessels allegedly used by the Ukrainian armed forces.
It said targets included a combined road and rail bridge across the Dnieper River in Kyiv "facilitating the movement of troops and the logistical delivery of military supplies" to support Ukraine's troops in the eastern province of Donbas, an electrical substation near Nalyvaikivka, Kyiv "serving the transmission and distribution of power to military-industrial facilities," and an industrial complex at the port of Izmail, Odesa "used to receive, store and transport military cargo and fuel."
The ministry also said a cargo ship was struck in the Black Sea, alleging it was carrying military equipment and dual-use cargo to Odesa for the Ukrainian armed forces.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 108 attack drones overnight, with 88 shot down or suppressed.
Strikes on Russia
In Russia, meanwhile, Ukrainian drones targeted industrial infrastructure in the Volgograd region, causing a fire at an apartment building, regional Gov. Andrey Bocharov said. One person was hospitalized and the fire was contained, he said.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses intercepted or destroyed 646 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over several Russian regions, as well as occupied Crimea and the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
Independent verification of the claims from both sides remains difficult due to the ongoing war.

Taiwan: first new F-16V fighters arrive amid China threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:25:00 UTC
16:25:00 KST

Taiwan: first new F-16V fighters arrive amid China threat
October 2, 2026
Two new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets landed in Taiwan on Friday, the first of a batch of 66 US-made planes ordered back in 2019 as the island nation looks to bolster its defenses in the face of threats posed by neighboring China.
The aircraft, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at Chihhang Air Base near Taitung on Taiwan's mountainous east coast at midday local time (0400 GMT).
The arrival of the fighter jets was delayed by several months due to reported software issues, and Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo said more were on the way.
"Of course we won't only have delivered these two by year-end," he told reporters in the capital, Taipei, without providing further details.
"At present, I think aircraft are gradually moving through the production line, and there are also aircraft that have passed tests," he said.
Taiwan fears drop in US support
The delivery comes amid growing concern in Taiwan regarding the United States' commitment to arming Taiwan – and a week after US President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.
The US insists that there has been no change in policy towards China and Taiwan but Trump has stalled signing off on a new $14 billion package for Taipei. In May, he called it a "very good negotiating chip" in dealings with Beijing, raising fears that Taiwan's security could be traded away.
"We continue standing with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan," said a US State Department spokesperson when asked about the new F-16Vs.
The jets, made by US defense contractor Lockheed Martin as part of an $8 billion sale agreed seven years ago, are equipped with advanced avionics, and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its stealthy J-20 fighters — but Washington has been unwilling to provide its most advanced fighters like the F-22 or F-35.
The Taiwanese air force, which scrambles on an almost daily basis in response to aggressive Chinese maneuvers, is expected to have over 200 F-16Vs once deliveries are completed.
"China's intention to annex Taiwan by force has never changed," said Defense Minister Koo, referring to Beijing's claims that the democratically governed island belongs to China.
The Chinese foreign ministry has not commented on the arrival of the F-16s but US officials told the Reuters news agency that a Chinese invasion before 2028 is considered increasingly unlikely in Washington.
Taiwan: locals welcome arrival of F-16Vs
That assessment didn't stop dozens of locals – some equipped with binoculars and long-lensed cameras – gathering near the air base's perimeter fence to watch the highly anticipated arrival of the jets.
"The threat from the CCP has always been there so we definitely need to strengthen our defense capabilities," Eric Chan, a 57-year-old former air force servicemen, told the AFP news agency, referring to the Chinese Communist Party and stating that the F-16Vs will "play a very important defensive role."
"In terms of hardware capabilities, there will definitely be an improvement," added Kimi Chi, a 37-year-old salesman from the central city of Taichung who had travelled through the night to be able to photograph the aircraft.
"But what we are actually lacking the most right now is pilots. Of course, I hope the government can provide better additional allowances for these military pilots."

Protesters in Denmark rally against last EU shipyard servicing Russia-linked tankers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

16:22:53 KST

Protesters in Denmark rally against last EU shipyard servicing Russia-linked tankers
A coalition of civil society organizations protested against Danish shipyard Fayard's continued servicing of vessels transporting Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG), at a rally held in Copenhagen on Oct. 1.
Fayard is the last known EU shipyard that is still maintaining a fleet of specialized Arc7 tankers that export LNG from Russia's Arctic north.
"Fayard's service of the LNG fleet is a blemish on Danish support for Ukraine. We will continue to pressure Fayard to stop," Jens Alstrup, the chairman of the NGO Freedom for Ukraine, said in a statement shared with the Kyiv Independent.
Fayard has faced scrutiny from NGOs, European lawmakers, and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen for servicing Russian-linked tankers. Critics say that aiding Russian energy trade contradicts Denmark's support for Ukraine.
The shipyard has serviced four Russian-linked LNG tankers since late June, with the fourth, Nikolay Yevgenov, undergoing service at the yard on Sept. 24, according to the sanctions-monitoring NGO Urgewald.
An EU-wide ban on Russian LNG imports will take effect from Jan. 1, 2027, and countries are already weaning themselves off Moscow.
However, sanctions pressure began to slacken when the bloc decided to grant an exemption to Greek shipping company Dynagas, which will allow it to keep transporting Russian LNG to third countries even after 2027.
Likewise, the EU has repeatedly failed to agree on a maritime services ban, which would make it illegal for Fayard to provide maintenance services to Russian vessels. The bloc has instead said such a move should be done with the agreement of the G7.
"Enough is enough. Denmark faces a growing security threat from Russia, yet Fayard continues to repair tankers that keep Russian Arctic LNG moving while also servicing Danish naval vessels," said Alexander Kirk, a protest organizer and a sanctions campaigner at Urgewald.
"That is a glaring security contradiction. Fayard should stop servicing the Arc7 fleet now."

Saudi Arabia says Houthis attempted to target Mecca, Medina 3 times over 9 years: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:20:28 UTC
16:20:28 KST

Hussien Elkabany and Lina Altawell
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
- Houthis have denied targeting Mecca, while Iran dismissed one Saudi accusation as an unsubstantiated claim
Saudi Arabia has reported three Houthi attempts to target the holy cities of Mecca and Medina over the past nine years, including two incidents in September, drawing condemnation from Arab and Muslim countries.
The Yemeni group has denied some of the accusations.
According to an Anadolu review of official Saudi statements, the latest alleged attacks targeted Medina and an area south of Mecca, while the first reported attempt occurred in July 2017.
Mecca and Medina are home to Islam’s holiest sites, the Grand Mosque and the Kaaba in Mecca and the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis since March 2015. The Yemeni group has controlled the capital Sanaa and several provinces since September 2014.
Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia intensified in September after the group announced what it called a “maritime blockade” on the kingdom in July and later claimed ballistic missile and drone attacks on Saudi sites and vessels.
2 incidents in September 2026
On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said a drone attack it attributed to the Houthis had targeted a power station in Medina.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said the attack occurred early Tuesday and knocked a transformer out of service without affecting the electricity grid.
Maliki accused the Houthis of targeting civilian infrastructure providing electricity services to the Prophet’s Mosque, describing the incident as an “extension of this extremist militia’s approach in attempts to target the Two Holy Mosques.”
“Investigation findings, operational data and examination of debris from the drone used in the attack proved the Houthi militia’s involvement in planning and carrying out this act,” he said.
The coalition would continue taking measures to deter the Houthis and protect the Two Holy Mosques and pilgrims in Mecca and Medina, he added.
On Sept. 16, Maliki said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered the city’s restricted airspace.
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry said at the time that it was the second alleged Houthi attempt to target Mecca after an earlier incident in July 2017.
Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz condemned the Houthi militia’s attempt to again target Mecca, saying the incident had drawn international condemnation because violating the sanctity of holy sites provoked the feelings of Muslims around the world.
Abdul Mohsen al-Qasim, an imam at the Prophet’s Mosque, also said during a Friday sermon that attacking Mecca and Medina was “a grave offense before God.”
2017 allegation
On July 27, 2017, the Saudi-led coalition announced that it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Mecca over Taif province, around 69 kilometers (43 miles) from the holy city, without causing damage.
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry accused the Houthis at the time of violating the sanctity of Mecca in “a desperate attempt to disrupt the Hajj season.”
Houthi denials
The Houthis did not immediately deny the latest accusation involving Medina.
The group, however, swiftly rejected the Saudi accusation concerning the Sept. 16 incident near Mecca.
Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi and Hizam al-Assad, a member of the group’s political bureau, denied the allegation.
The Houthis also rejected the July 2017 accusation, saying their missile forces had targeted only the Taif military base, and had not targeted Mecca.
In September, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said on US social media company X that any attack targeting Mecca should be condemned, but described reports of an intercepted drone over the city as “merely a claim” that could not serve as a basis for accusing any party.
Arab, Muslim condemnation
Saudi announcements concerning the alleged attempts to target Mecca in July 2017 and September 2026 prompted condemnation from a number of Arab and Muslim countries and organizations.
According to an Anadolu review, statements condemning the Houthis were issued by Türkiye, Qatar, Egypt, Yemen, Jordan, Morocco, Palestine, Syria, Bahrain, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Sudan, the United Arab Emirates and Somalia.
The Gulf Cooperation Council, Arab League and Organization of Islamic Cooperation also issued condemnations, with several statements warning that attacks involving Mecca would offend Muslims around the world.

Lithuanian lawmakers seek new ways to preserve citizenship after referendum efforts fail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:16:00 UTC
16:16:00 KST

Lithuanian lawmakers are seeking new ways to allow more people to retain their citizenship after two referendums failed to secure the constitutional changes needed to expand dual citizenship.
Three amendments to the Citizenship Law have been registered in the Lithuanian parliament, Seimas. The proposals would tighten the procedure for stripping people of Lithuanian citizenship, expand eligibility for citizenship for people whose relatives suffered under occupation and repression, and allow some Lithuanians who acquire citizenship in other “friendly countries” to retain their Lithuanian citizenship.
Under current laws, Lithuania does not allow holding multiple citizenships. Exceptions apply to people who left the country before 1990 and children of mixed families – but most Lithuanians who acquire citizenship of another country automatically lose their Lithuanian passport.
This has been a sore issue for the new diaspora that swelled during the 1990s and 2000s. And since the regulation is underpinned by an article in the constitution, the Constitutional Court has so far maintained that changes require a referendum.
So far, referendums on retaining Lithuanian citizenship have been held twice. In the latest vote, in 2024, nearly 74% of voters supported changing the rules, but the result fell short of the constitutional threshold required to amend the constitution.
One of the new proposals would broaden the legal definition of a person deported or persecuted during the Soviet occupations and repressions. Under current rules, certain citizenship exceptions apply to people who were deported from Lithuania – and the proposed changes would also cover people who were included on deportation lists but avoided deportation by going into hiding, as well as people imprisoned in Lithuania without being deported.
Conservative lawmaker Dalia Asanavičiūtė-Gružauskienė, one of the proposal’s initiators, said the changes would align the Citizenship Law with legislation that expands the definition of people considered victims of deportation and repression.
The proposed change could affect Lithuanians whose families avoided deportation by hiding.
Gediminas Ramanauskas, a member of the Lithuanian-American community in New York, said his grandparents were included on a list of people scheduled to be deported to Siberia but left their home after a neighbour warned them.
“They hid for more than 10 years, changing where they lived, staying on different farms and sometimes in forests and remote homesteads,” Ramanauskas said.
He said his grandparents had remained in Lithuania because they wanted to raise their family there, rather than leave the country.
Lawmakers also want to change the procedure for revoking Lithuanian citizenship. Under the proposal, authorities would have to conduct a more extensive assessment of the consequences for both the state and the individual, with the person whose citizenship is at issue taking part in the process.
Asanavičiūtė-Gružauskienė said some people currently learn that their citizenship has been revoked through an email notification.
A third proposal would allow Lithuanians who acquire citizenship in NATO countries to retain Lithuanian citizenship. The proposal also mentions countries such as Malta and Ireland, non-NATO countries that “closely cooperate” with the alliance.
Social Democrat Kęstutis Vilkauskas said lawmakers could consider extending the arrangement to other friendly countries with which Lithuania has normal diplomatic relations.
The Seimas is expected to consider the proposals during its autumn session.
The debate comes amid renewed concerns about emigration. Lithuania has recorded more returning citizens than departures since 2020, but preliminary data for this year suggest that trend may be shifting.
During the first eight months of the year, about 3,500 more Lithuanians left the country than during the same period last year.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
