The Sudan connection: Is Ethiopia at risk of a proxy war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:52:00 UTC
14:52:00 KST

The Sudan connection: Is Ethiopia at risk of a proxy war?
October 2, 2026
Over the past week, three militias from a new alliance, led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), have been fighting the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) in northern Ethiopia.
The heterogeneous alliance that calls itself the "Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival" brings together seven armed domestic groups that oppose Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.
However, the ENDF has painted a picture of an alliance that extends far beyond Ethiopia's borders: Its commander-in-chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting the TPLF.
Sudan dismissed the allegation as "baseless." Its military government countered with accusations that Ethiopia was supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia that has been fighting Sudan's army for over three years.
Eritrea said Ethiopia was attempting to shift responsibility for its own internal conflicts onto its neighbors. Cairo, meanwhile, issued a flat denial.
A domestic conflict with "external actors"
Viewing developments in northern Ethiopia as a domestic affair is not the full picture, according to experts.
"While it is primarily a domestic conflict, it certainly has a foreign policy dimension due to the many external actors directly or indirectly involved," said Susanne Stollreiter, the head of the Ethiopia office of the Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation.
Stollreiter told DW that these actors have their own interests in the region — interests that could potentially be advanced by the conflict.
"If this conflict escalates, I would even assume that it could truly lead to a kind of conflagration across the region, given the various conflict dynamics here in the Horn of Africa."
Mirroring alliances between Ethiopia and Sudan
Egypt and Sudan have long harbored grievances against Ethiopia because the source country of the Blue Nile dammed the river just before the border.
Sudan has been caught up in a brutal civil war since April 2023. Both sides to the conflict — the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF militia — are believed to have ties to partners that are now fighting on opposing sides in Ethiopia.
On one hand there's the Sudanese government and the TPLF, which was largely defeated in the 2020–22 Tigray War in Ethiopia. Many Tigrayan fighters went into exile in Sudan where they organized as "Army 70" and fought alongside the SAF against the RSF.
"They played quite an important role in the Sudan Armed Forces pushing back against the RSF in eastern Sudan and even into Khartoum. And then that relationship continued," said Magnus Taylor, Deputy Project Manager, Horn of Africa at the think tank International Crisis Group (ICG).
"The issue that the federal government of Ethiopia has is that it appears that Sudan is in a kind of alignment or an alliance with one of the strongest opposition groups in the country."
Tigrayan fighters in Sudan and training camp for Sudan militia in Ethiopia
In May, the Sudanese government hosted high-ranking representatives of the TPLF and leaders of other Ethiopian groups that are critical of Abiy. Some of those groups are now part of the new seven-member alliance.
On the other hand, there's the Ethiopia's central government and the former Sudanese special unit, the RSF.
In February, the news agency Reuters reported on a secret training camp for RSF fighters in the Ethiopian border region of Benishangul-Gumuz. According to the report, the United Arab Emirates provided instructors, funding, and logistical support — claims the UAE denied.
The UAE is closely allied with Ethiopia and, despite denials, is considered the RSF's most important backer.
Is Eritrea involved in the latest conflict?
So far, there are no signs of direct involvement by the Sudanese army or the RSF in the conflict in Ethiopia. There is no evidence of Eritrea's role in the latest escalation either. But there's no shortage of wild speculation.
Eritrea fought alongside Abiy's forces in the Tigray War but the leaders of the two countries had had a falling out by the time the Pretoria peace agreement was signed in November 2022.
Experts have long suggested that Eritrea — despite denials — is now supporting the TPLF. Distrust of Abiy runs deep, given his stated ambitions to secure Ethiopia access to the open sea — by force if necessary, such as by seizing the Eritrean port of Assab on the Red Sea.
ICG analyst Magnus Taylor told DW that Eritrean involvement in the latest fighting is plausible.
"I think the Eritreans have used the TPLF and other opposition groups to deter the perceived risk of Ethiopian aggression, whether that's for access to the port or other reasons," Taylor said.
"Having a large physical presence within Tigray or within Afar even would be, I guess, a justification for the Ethiopians to carry out more extensive military operations on Eritrea. The Eritrean tactic is to deter military action, not to invite it."
Asmara has strengthened relations with Cairo this year, and the United States has just let sanctions against Eritrea expire.
Is there a risk of a wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa?
The Horn of Africa borders the Gulf region in the north, which has lost stability due to the Iran war. Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are also disrupting the Bab al-Mandab Strait. .
In Somalia, Al-Shabab is regaining ground, cooperating with the Houthis despite wide ideological differences.
"These are important trade routes that are being disputed and fought over and everyone is trying to profit from the unstable situation," Stollreiter, the head of the Ethiopia office of the Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation, said.
"In this respect, it is no real coincidence that so many actors are now becoming particularly strong again, also because of the absence of the actors who were otherwise protective powers in the region."
The US in particular, but also the Europeans tied down by Russia's war in Ukraine, have less of an eye on the Horn of Africa than before, Stollreiter said.
Have Gulf powers taken sides in Ethiopia?
The UAE and Saudi Arabia, which are accused of supporting different warring parties in Sudan and Yemen, and have polarized the entire region in recent years, are all the more present.
However, ICG's Magnus Taylor does not think that the situation in Ethiopia is at risk of escalating into a proxy war between the Gulf powers.
"While the UAE is a strong backer of Addis Ababa, the Saudis are not strongly backing the TPLF or any other opposition group."
Whether from the Arabian Peninsula, Sudan, or Eritrea — one week after the outbreak of war in Ethiopia, there are no clear signs that the internal conflict is becoming internationalized. However, in the unstable Horn of Africa, that risk is particularly high.

Queensland police seize 558 e-mobility devices in three months

2026-10-02
05:47:58 UTC
14:47:58 KST

Police across Queensland have given out more than 2,400 traffic infringement notices to e-mobility device users in the last three months, seizing 558 non-compliant vehicles.
Of the fines issued, more than 60 per cent were for riders failing to wear a helmet, while 157 users were caught speeding.
What's next?
Queensland Police are urging the community to review new e-mobility laws on their website, including changes that came into effect at the end of August.
Queensland Police are seizing an average of six illegal e-mobility devices every day, as officers crack down on non-compliant e-bikes and e-scooters.
More than 27 infringement notices are also being issued each day.
In the first three months of the statewide Operation Yankee Surety, police seized 558 devices and handed out more than 2,400 traffic infringement notices to riders.
Emergency Response and Coordination Command Acting Assistant Commissioner, Tim Partrige, said the misuse of one of Australia's fastest-growing forms of transportation had "life-threatening consequences".
"Electric power assisted cycles, e-scooter and other e-mobility devices are vehicles, and like any other vehicle, dangerous behaviours like speeding, drink riding or using non-compliant devices can have life-threatening consequences — not only for the rider," Acting Assistant Commissioner Partrige said.
"Non-compliant devices and dangerous riding have no place in our communities, and police will continue to take enforcement action against those disregarding the law."
Since the operation began at the start of July, police conducted targeted enforcement to seize non-compliant devices, ensure age and licensing requirements are adhered to, and deter dangerous behaviour such as speeding, drink riding and riding without a helmet.
Of the 2,400 fines issued, about 1,500 — more than 60 per cent — were for riders failing to wear a helmet, while a further 157 users were caught speeding.
As police conducted 878 roadside breath tests on e-mobility riders over the three months, some 68 drink riders were prosecuted.
"As with any road safety operation, our goal under Operation Yankee Surety is to protect all road and pathway users, including those on e-mobility devices," Acting Assistant Commissioner Partrige said.
Since licensing restrictions for e-bikes and e-scooter came into effect at the end of August, 64 tickets have been issued for non-compliance.
Brisbane, the Sunshine Coast and Capricornia have emerged as the hot spots for illegal e-mobility activity, according to Queensland Police data for the first three months of the campaign.
The Sunshine Coast led the state in terms of non-compliant bikes seized by police, with 146 compared to 88 on the Gold Coast. Brisbane's northside saw the most traffic infringement notices issued.
North Brisbane saw 511 notices given out, while South Brisbane users received 433. Capricornia reported 254 notices issued over the same period, almost twice of neighbouring Mackay Whitsunday (133).
The Queensland capital city recorded the highest number of positive RBTs for e-mobility users with a combined 38.

Where in Europe is data centre hiring growing fastest – and why do these jobs pay more?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:46:03 UTC
14:46:03 KST

Several European countries have seen a significant rise in data centre job postings in recent months. Euronews Business takes a closer look at the reasons behind the growth, including why these roles offer higher pay.
AI is rapidly becoming part of daily life, and demand for data centres is rising too. As of 2025, the US remained the clear global leader in data centres, with more than twice the EU total. At the same time, the European Commission aims to strengthen Europe’s sovereignty and competitiveness in the AI and cloud ecosystem.
Data from global hiring platform Indeed show that data centre job postings are rising in Europe. As of August 2026, they were above pre-pandemic levels across 10 European economies, while postings for other tech roles and overall job postings were lagging behind data centre postings.
So, which countries saw the biggest rise in data centre job postings? How much more do these jobs pay than the same occupations in other sectors? And why is there a pay premium?
The recent rise is most striking in Spain, Italy and Ireland. When data centre job postings on Indeed are indexed at 100 for the average between December 2019 and February 2020, the index exceeded 200 points in all three countries as of August 2026.
This means postings more than doubled compared with pre-pandemic levels. The index stood at 260 in Spain, 237 in Italy and 210 in Ireland.
Aubrey Woessner, an economist at Indeed, and Pawel Adrjan, director of research at Indeed, said that Spain and Italy had more room to grow as both started from a low base.
“They are seeing major new AI-focused build-outs, such as campuses in Aragón and projects around Milan, rather than legacy sites clustered around major population hubs such as Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, and Dublin,” they told Euronews Business.
The rise is also more than 30% in the Netherlands (138), Poland (134) and Switzerland (133).
Belgium recorded the lowest increase at 9%, followed by France at 13%. The rise is 25% in Germany and 24% in the UK.
As of August 2026, tech job postings excluding data centre roles were below pre-pandemic levels in nine of the 10 countries. Spain was the only exception, with the index just one point above its pre-pandemic level.
Data centre job postings significantly outpaced other tech job postings, with the widest gaps in Italy (173 points), Spain (159 points) and Ireland (141 points).
The chart below shows this trend as of August 2026.
Europe’s data centre hiring is spread across more companies
Compared with the US, where just 10 big tech companies account for 71% of data centre postings, data centre hiring in Europe is spread across many companies, according to Indeed.
“Across the ten European countries we analysed, it takes over 500 firms to account for 70% of data centre postings,” Woessner and Adrjan said.
Data centre jobs offer higher pay for the same roles
Advertised salaries for data centre roles are generally higher than for similar jobs in other sectors in the same country.
The pay premium is clear: in 28 of the 29 country-occupation pairs, data centre jobs offer higher salaries. The only exception is very small, at -1% for IT infrastructure, operations and support roles in France.
Data centre employers in Italy offer significantly higher pay than other sectors. For example, management roles in data centres pay 65% more, while installation and maintenance roles offer 50% higher advertised pay.
In the UK, management roles in data centres offer 49% higher pay. In Germany, installation and maintenance roles pay 36% more.
Why do data centre employers pay more for the same job?
Woessner and Adrjan noted that data centres may be a small slice of the overall labour market, but they are competing for the same technicians and infrastructure specialists as other industries going through the digital and green transitions in Europe.
“Postings related to data centre roles ask for more skills, on average, than other postings in the same field,” Woessner and Adrjan said.
“Concrete technical and digital skills – including knowledge of IT systems, software, and cybersecurity – as well as English language requirements are also over-represented in data centre-related roles compared with other roles in the same occupation.”
They noted that higher pay also helps attract workers quickly to keep projects on schedule.
Which jobs dominate data centre hiring?
Woessner and Adrjan explained that the mix of occupations in data centre hiring across Europe points to two trends happening at the same time: continued staffing of existing data storage and cloud facilities, and an emerging boom in new AI-related construction.
Five occupations account for between 50% and 60% of data centre job postings in Europe: IT infrastructure, operations and support; software development; management; installation and maintenance; and project management.
While demand for workers in data centre-related jobs is rising, these roles still make up only a small share of total job postings in each country. In most of the countries analysed, the share is around 1% or less.
Ireland is the exception, where nearly 5% of all job postings on Indeed now mention a data centre.
Is there a skills shortage in data centres?
Indeed economists expect the growth phase to continue for some time, as the EU aims to triple its data centre capacity within five to seven years.
“One concern for employers is that data centres are competing for workers with technical skills that were already in short supply even before the data centre boom,” Woessner and Adrjan said.
As of 2025, Germany (529) and the UK (523) had the highest numbers of data centres in Europe, followed by France (322) and the Netherlands (298). Italy had 168, Spain and Poland each had 144, and Switzerland had 121.
Western Europe dominates the region’s data centre infrastructure, while Northern Europe has a smaller but strategically important presence. Central and Eastern Europe’s infrastructure is more fragmented and less developed.

Lithuania tests Ukrainian-developed drone detection system SkyFortress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:31:00 UTC
16:31:00 KST

Lithuania is testing a Ukrainian-developed airspace monitoring system designed to detect low-flying drones and other threats by analysing acoustic and radio signals, the Defence Ministry said Friday.
The pilot deployment of the SkyFortress system is intended to strengthen the first stage of Lithuania’s air defene network – detecting and tracking potential threats before they can be intercepted.
“Air threats are changing rapidly, so we are adapting our solutions accordingly,” Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said in a statement. “Instead of developing everything from scratch, we are adapting systems that are already operating in Ukraine.”
SkyFortress uses artificial intelligence to detect and track low-flying drones and cruise missiles based on acoustic or electromagnetic signatures, the ministry said. The system can classify detected objects in real time.
Under a contract signed this summer, the project also includes processing data collected by the system’s sensors, using libraries of digital acoustic and radio-frequency signatures based on unclassified data, and training personnel, according to the ministry.
Testing will assess the system’s ability to detect and identify low-flying unmanned aircraft in Lithuania.
The deployment comes as Lithuania and its Baltic neighbours have strengthened airspace security amid Russia’s war against Ukraine and an increase in reports of potential air threats in the region.
A drone that entered Lithuania from Belarus was shot down over Lithuanian territory in September by Italian fighter jets stationed in Šiauliai. It was the first time a drone had been shot down over Lithuania. Similar incidents had previously occurred in Latvia and Estonia.
The Defence Ministry said SkyFortress will contribute to strengthening Lithuania’s broader air defence capabilities, from surveillance and identification to the interception and neutralisation of aerial threats.

Lula and Bolsonaro’s mudslinging heats up ahead of weekend vote
The mudslinging between Brazil’s incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his election rival, Flavio Bolsonaro, has heated up ahead of what is expected to be an extremely close vote this weekend. From stating loose rumours as facts, to taking comments completely out of their context, they are both doing everything they can to win a few more votes.
Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his election rival Flavio Bolsonaro are leaving no controversy unturned in their last-ditch efforts to discredit each other and win over voters ahead of Sunday's nail-biter election.
A campaign dominated by scandals and insults has done little to ease the deep political polarisation in Latin America's biggest economy – one of the last major leftist bastions in the region.
The tight race pits Lula, 80, against the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of US President Donald Trump who has backed a wave of victorious right-wing candidates in Latin America.
Trump said Thursday he was watching Brazil's election "very closely".
Opinion polls predict the vote will go to a run-off on October 25, with Lula and Flavio in a dead heat.
Read moreFlavio Bolsonaro probed for corruption as Brazil election tightens
"The race is tied but not at a standstill: the final week will determine where the voters who can still be swayed will go," Felipe Nunes, director of the Quaest polling institute, told AFP.
Many of the nation's 160 million registered voters are disenchanted with their options and were deprived of a debate between the leading candidates when both declined to attend a televised programme on Thursday evening.
Marcelo Vilanova, 32, a fish market manager in the southeastern city of Juiz de Fora, said he was voting for Lula as the "lesser of two evils".
"He did good things for me, for my family," he said, referring to Lula's social welfare programmes. "I have criticisms of him too."
Lucas Sales, 38, a cell phone shop owner in the city, is voting for Flavio Bolsonaro even if "he himself isn't the best option," citing his promise to be tough on crime – a key concern for many Brazilians in this election.
A saintly spat and gynecological gaffe
The race for undecided voters has had both sides on alert for anything they can twist to their advantage.
In recent days, Brazil's beloved patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, depicted as a Black Madonna, became the focus as rumours erupted that Flavio Bolsonaro planned to strip her of her post if elected.
Flavio issued fierce denials as Lula took to the campaign trail clutching a statue of the saint, declaring that "messing" with her was "unacceptable".
The electoral court ordered Thursday that posts with the "untrue" claims be taken down.
Lula tends to have more support among Catholics while Bolsonaro has the backing of a booming Evangelical population.
Next, Flavio Bolsonaro and his supporters pounced when Lula said that men were "cowards" when it comes to getting their prostates examined, while "women learn to receive a touch from a young age," referring to gynecological exams.
Clips of his comment circulated widely on social media as if it were an allusion to abuse, and Flavio Bolsonaro accused Lula of being "sexist".
"It's really turned into a circus...my vote won't go to any of them," said Gisele Sousa, 45, a clothing shop employee.
In another jab during a podcast Thursday, Lula said he was sure he would win in the first round, over a rival he said was not even qualified "to serve as a building manager".
Lula's political clout
Veteran leftist Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, boasting he is fitter than ever despite his advanced age.
The former union leader has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment while massively curbing deforestation in the Amazon rainforest.
Nevertheless, voters complain about a high cost of living and are fed up with violence and crime.
Lula unveiled a flurry of measures in the run-up to the election to win over voters, increasing social welfare payments and banning sports betting that has ensnared many in gambling addiction.
"Only Lula has the political clout and credibility to carry out reforms," Edinho Silva, president of Lula's Workers' Party, said.
Lula made Brazilian sovereignty a central plank of his campaign, warning Trump not to "meddle" in his country's elections.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has remained a tough foe for Lula, even as it emerged he was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic, "Dark Horse", about his father.
He was forced during the campaign to admit he had asked jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro – at the heart of one of Brazil's largest financial fraud cases – to bankroll the film.
Bolsonaro was also confident of a first-round win, vowing that Lula would be "ousted from the presidency" on Sunday.

US Marines deploy to Baltic Sea region for NATO's Baltic Sentry mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:36:00 UTC
14:36:00 KST

US Marines deploy to Baltic Sea region for NATO's Baltic Sentry mission
Personnel from the United States Marine Corps are being redirected to the Baltic Sea region as part of NATO's enhanced vigilance activity Baltic Sentry.
The marines will number around 50 and will aid in supporting and protecting critical undersea infrastructure, the Pentagon has announced.
The personnel come from the 2nd Reconnaissance Battalion, 2nd Marine Division, II Marine Expeditionary Force Information Group, based at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina. They are to operate alongside Finland's Coastal Brigade, providing advanced expeditionary surveillance and tactical reconnaissance capabilities.
The deployment comes as Estonia, Finland and other allied nations continue to grapple with a series of cable damage incidents in the region. Most recently, in December 2024, the EstLink 2 power cable between Estonia and Finland and several communication cables were ruptured, with authorities suspecting deliberate sabotage. NATO launched Baltic Sentry in response to these incidents.
Baltic Sentry is a highly integrated collective defense effort, led by European allies under Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum and Allied Maritime Command, with the U.S. Marine Corps serving in a supportive, enabling capacity.
Marine Corps Maj. Gen. Daniel Shipley, commander of U.S. Marine Corps Forces Europe and Africa, said the operational design was a premium example of European allies leading regional maritime security while the US provides specialized capabilities.
"Our participation in Baltic Sentry demonstrates the dynamic agility of the Marine Corps to rapidly project specialized capabilities where they are most effective," he said. "Working side by side with our Finnish allies strengthens our collective readiness, ensuring we can operate seamlessly as a cohesive, lethal team to deter hybrid threats in the Baltic littoral."
The rotation will use reconnaissance Marines' capabilities, including small unmanned aerial systems and littoral sensors, to feed data into NATO's shared operational picture.
"The experience, skills and systems of the US Marine Corps are perfectly suited for supplementing our situation picture and supporting our monitoring of the Baltic Sea," noted Finnish Navy Capt. Johan Tillander, Finland Navy Command chief of operations.
What is Baltic Sentry?
NATO launched Baltic Sentry in January 2025 to protect critical undersea infrastructure in the Baltic Sea, including power and data cables, following a series of suspected suspected sabotage incidents. The mission incorporates naval vessels such as frigates, maritime patrol aircraft, naval drones and new sensor technology. Allies are integrating national surveillance assets to improve detection and response. It is led by Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum, based in the Netherlands, with Allied Maritime Command playing a central role in its maritime operations.
Founded in 1775, the U.S. Marine Corps is the the U.S. military's amphibious and expeditionary force, and has been deployed in the Baltic region in various capacities since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

South Korea warns of 'further measures' if Ukraine refuses public apology over POW transfer disclosure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:34:26 UTC
14:34:26 KST

The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said on Friday that Seoul would take "further measures" if Ukraine refuses to publicly apologise over what he called its unilateral disclosure of North Korean POWs being sent to South Korea.
Seoul has taken a hard stance on Ukraine disclosing the transfer of two soldiers captured fighting for Russia, warning that their families could be targeted by Pyongyang.
North Korea is known to retaliate against defectors and their families.
Both POWs are identifiable as they had been photographed by South Korean media before their arrival to the South.
The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine, in exchange for economic and military assistance to Pyongyang.
Hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed last week the transfer in remarks at the United Nations, Lee expressed his dismay, with Seoul claiming confidentiality was key to protecting the POWs' relatives.
Seoul later demanded an official apology from Ukraine, saying that both sides had reached a "clear understanding" during consultations to keep the transfer confidential.
"If Ukraine continues to refuse to acknowledge the facts and publicly apologise, we will take further measures," the South Korean president said on Friday, accusing Kyiv of making him out to be a "liar."
"This is a matter concerning the dignity of the Republic of Korea and its people and cannot be overlooked," Lee posted on X.
Analysts say that from South Korea's perspective, keeping the transfer of the POWs confidential may have partly been for Ukraine's sake, as making it public could have complicated Kyiv's own prisoner exchanges with Russia.
In domestic South Korean politics, however, Seoul's approach "could prove problematic," Shin Yul, a political science professor at Myongji University, said given the current administration's dovish approach to the nuclear-armed North.
"The government has acted swiftly in this case involving Ukraine, while exercising extreme caution over the North Korean landmine incident (that injured South Korean soldiers). That contrast could leave the public deeply dissatisfied."
Diplomatic misunderstanding
Lee referred on Friday to an interview with Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha published by RBC-Ukraine and other Ukrainian outlets on Thursday.
Sybiha said he would "not like to call it an incident," describing it instead as a "diplomatic misunderstanding."
"South Korea is an important country for us. And I very much hope for momentum, continued cooperation, and concrete results that we are indeed achieving with them," he said.
Seoul's spy agency said that Zelenskyy may have disclosed the transfer of the North Korean soldiers to boost public support in South Korea for Seoul providing arms to Ukraine, a lawmaker said on Wednesday.
South Korea has in recent years emerged as a major arms exporter, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, including through a multibillion-dollar arms deal with Poland.
But it has refrained from supplying Kyiv with lethal weapons, citing its longstanding policy of not arming countries engaged in active conflicts.

EC launches special drive to restore names dropped during SIR, BLOs to trace left-out voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:30:54 UTC
14:30:54 KST

SIR fallout: EC orders house-to-house drive to trace voters dropped from rolls
NEW DELHI: The Election Commission has directed state poll officials to launch a special drive to immediately enrol “left-out” and new voters in areas where the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) has been completed. The move comes amid allegations by the opposition parties that the electoral roll revision exercise disenfranchised crores of eligible citizens.The instructions were conveyed in an official communication issued on Thursday, following a virtual meeting with state chief electoral officers (CEOs), as cited by PTI.The drive aims to re-enrol eligible voters who were omitted or deleted during the intensive revision, while also registering first-time and “young voters”.The Commission stressed that voter registration is an ongoing process and that no eligible citizen should be disenfranchised for not being included during the SIR enumeration.Booth Level Officers (BLOs) have been instructed to cross-check the current electoral rolls with pre-SIR lists to identify electors whose names were included earlier but dropped from the final roll.BLOs will conduct house-to-house verification of all identified missing electors.
Each officer will be tasked with covering 20 to 25 electors a week, with the verification drive targeted for completion within a month.BLOs will also collect Form 6 applications on the spot from newly eligible young electors and genuine left-out voters. The lists will subsequently be shared directly with Booth Level Agents (BLAs) of recognised political parties to ensure transparency.The move follows a September 26 meeting of the full Commission, comprising Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi. After the meeting, the poll panel said the declaration attached to Form 6 was meant “specifically for SIR” and that “for non-SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used.”The Election Commission has withdrawn the additional SIR-related declaration attached to Form 6 in states where the electoral roll revision exercise has been completed.
The declaration has been removed from the ECINET app and portal, as well as the respective Chief Electoral Officer portals. New applicants in these states will now only have to submit the regular statutory Form 6 for voter enrolment.In states and Union territories where the SIR exercise is still underway, the additional declaration remains available on the ECINET portal. Under the declaration, new applicants are required to provide details linking themselves, their parents or grandparents to electoral rolls prepared during an earlier SIR.

‘A life mission’: Omri Miran to lead Oct. 7 testimony gathering after 738 days in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:28:55 UTC
14:28:55 KST

Omri Miran, who was released after 738 days in captivity in Gaza, will lead one of more than 450 gatherings planned across Israel in early October where people directly affected by the October 7 massacre will tell their stories.
The gatherings are part of “Salon Otef,” an initiative launched in 2024 that brings returned hostages, hostage relatives, massacre survivors, bereaved families and members of the security and rescue forces into homes, community centers, workplaces and other venues to speak about what they experienced.
“To understand what happened to us on October 7 and what the hostages and their families have endured since then, we need to hear the stories firsthand from those who lived through them,” Miran said.
“The hundreds of gatherings taking place across the country allow these stories to pass from person to person and from home to home,” he added. “I see passing these stories on to the public as a whole and to the younger generation as an immensely important national mission, a life mission.”
Thousands of people are expected to attend this year’s events. Alongside testimony about October 7 itself, speakers will also discuss the years that followed, including bereavement, rehabilitation, returning home and efforts to rebuild their lives.
At each gathering, the speaker tells his or her story at their own pace before an open discussion with those attending. Some events also include music or singing.
Mor Peretz, CEO of 255, the Hostages and Families Organization, which is leading the initiative, said the accounts should remain in the hands of those who experienced the events themselves.
“The story of October 7 should first and foremost be told by those who were there and experienced it firsthand,” Peretz said. “They are the ones who should make their voices heard, describe what they saw and endured, and ensure that the story is written through their testimony.”
“The more these testimonies are heard and resonate in more homes and among more people, the better we can preserve the story as it was experienced by those who were there,” she said.
The project also includes participation from Atid LaOtef, the Nova Tribe Community Association, Edut 710, Kumu, the Kibbutz Movement and other organizations. Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund and the Konrad Adenauer Foundation are supporting the initiative.
Eyal Ostrinsky, chairman of KKL-JNF, said the anniversary should focus not only on what happened on October 7 but also on those still living with its consequences.
“Three years after October 7, our responsibility is not only to remember what happened that day, but also to listen to the people who carry with them what they experienced on that terrible day and what they have endured ever since,” he said.
“The direct encounters created through ‘Salon Otef’ provide an opportunity to hear their testimonies and understand the ongoing challenges involved in recovery and rebuilding.”

SINGAPORE, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's overall private residential property price index rose 1.4 percent quarter-on-quarter in the third quarter of 2026, accelerating from a 0.5 percent increase in the second quarter, the flash estimate released by the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) showed on Thursday.
For the first three quarters of 2026, the index increased by an average of 0.9 percent per quarter, unchanged from the average quarterly increase over the same period in 2025, the URA said in a statement.
To meet housing demand and maintain market stability, the government is sustaining a high level of private housing supply through the Government Land Sales Program.
A total of 4,745 private residential units will be launched under the Confirmed List in the second half of 2026, bringing the full-year Confirmed List supply to 9,320 units, more than 50 percent above the annual average over the past ten years, according to the URA.
This will bring the total supply of private residential units expected to be completed over the next few years to about 60,600 units. ■

Multiple Indian payloads reach orbit aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:19:34 UTC
14:19:34 KST

SpaceX Falcon 9 launches multiple Indian payloads into orbit (representational image)
BENGALURU: Multiple Indian payloads, representing four space startups, reached orbit aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket, which lifted off at 12:02 am IST on Friday (October 2) as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission.The mission carried satellites developed by Dhruva Space and TakeMe2Space, along with payloads from SatLeo Labs and EON Space Labs. The payloads will demonstrate technologies for thermal imaging, Earth observation and artificial intelligence (AI)-based data processing in orbit.Dhruva’s LEAP-2 satellite, its second commercial mission using the P-30 satellite platform, was successfully deployed into orbit at 1 am IST. It hosts two in-orbit demonstration payloads: a star tracker developed by France-based Sodern, part of ArianeGroup, and TAPAS-1, developed by SatLeo Labs.SatLeo describes TAPAS-1, or Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions, as India’s first dedicated commercial thermal payload. The CubeSat-category payload uses thermal infrared sensing to capture temperature information that conventional optical satellite imagery cannot directly provide.
The mission will validate its thermal sensing technology, payload performance and data-processing capabilities in orbit.“Most satellites show us what the Earth looks like, TAPAS-1 will show us how it behaves by revealing temperature patterns that ordinary payloads cannot see,” said Shravan Bhati, co-founder and CEO, SatLeo Labs.Dhruva Space also undertook the end-to-end integration of LEAP-2 with the Falcon 9 launch vehicle. The company said this builds on its work on LEAP-1, through which it became the first Indian private company to undertake the launch vehicle integration of its satellite in-house.“This extends our role beyond satellite manufacturing into launch integration and end-to-end mission delivery, reinforcing its full-stack Space engineering approach. LEAP-2 will also be supported by our growing global ground infrastructure, including its owned and operated ground station in Luleå, Sweden; the first non-govt entity owned and operated ground station outside India, authorised by the GoI to provide Ground-Station-as-a-Service,” the firm added.TakeMe2Space’s 14-kg MOI-1A satellite is designed to allow customers to run AI models on Earth-observation data directly in orbit. It carries onboard computing capacity of 117 trillion operations per second (TOPS), 2 TB of storage and a nine-band multispectral imager. Processing imagery in space could reduce the need to transmit large volumes of raw data to Earth, with potential applications in agriculture, mining and supply-chain intelligence.MOI-1A follows TakeMe2Space’s 2024 MOI-TD technology demonstration, which validated onboard AI inference and data processing. The company said it had signed up 23 customers for its in-orbit inference services.MOI-1A also carried MIRA, a 502-g optical telescope developed by EON Space Labs. “A compact optical telescope engineered for space imaging. It delivers high-resolution Earth observation with exceptional stability and thermal robustness,” EON describes the payload.
MIRA is a pathfinder for a planned small satellite constellation. Its flight comes after the loss of the PSLV-C62 mission on Jan 12, which had affected the company’s earlier launch plans.“Satellites collect vast amounts of data, but much of it still has to reach the ground before it can be turned into useful information. With MOI-1A, customers will be able to run their AI models directly in orbit and receive the insights they need, without downloading all the raw imagery. This mission is an important step towards making computing in space a service that businesses can use,” Ronak Kumar Samantray, founder and CEO, TakeMe2Space, said.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

On Friday and Saturday, sunny spells will frequently alternate with clouds, while the weather will remain dry. Light winds will prevail on both days, meaning fog will thicken in some areas overnight and during the early morning hours, reducing visibility, according to the Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Centre.
Across most of Latvia, overnight temperatures will fall to between +3°C and +8°C, while coastal areas will remain warmer at +8°C to +12°C. During the day, sunshine will warm the air to between +15°C and +20°C.
Sunday will also bring variable cloud cover, although clouds will bring rain to some western areas in the afternoon.
Light to moderate south-westerly and westerly winds will prevail.

Burgas welcomes international COP31 Bike Ride
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:16:26 UTC
14:16:26 KST

Friday 2 October 2026 07:20
Friday, 2 October 2026, 07:20
PHOTO burgas.bg
Font size
Burgas will welcome the international COP31 Bike Ride on 4 and 5 October as the cycling relay makes its way towards the UN Climate Change Conference COP31 in Antalya, Turkey. This year’s route covers more than 22,000 km across three continents and over 20 countries, the Municipality of Burgas said.
In Bulgaria, the relay follows two routes. One starts in Sofia and continues via Plovdiv to Burgas, while the main international group enters the country through Silistra and follows the Black Sea coast. The two groups will meet in Burgas on 4 October before setting off together for Turkey the following morning.
The COP Bike Ride was launched in 2024, when nearly 200 participants covered 6,500 km between Paris and Baku. Participation grew to more than 1,000 people a year later, while thousands of cyclists are expected to join different stages in 2026. This year’s riders will also take part in an attempt to set a world record for the largest number of participants in a cycling relay.

Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 drones - how many were destroyed
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of October 2, Russia launched 108 drones at Ukraine. Air defense shot down or suppressed 88 of them; hits were recorded at 11 locations.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 drones during the night of October 2. A total of 88 of them were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What the enemy attacked with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 2 (from 18:00 on October 1), the enemy attacked with 108 Shahed-type attack UAVs (47 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Bryansk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russian Federation, the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk region and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiyske.
How the air defense performed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 88 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types
Hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 11 locations, as well as the falls of downed objects (debris) at 5 locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy UAVs in the airspace.

Ukraine's General Staff reports 207 combat clashes on front over past 24 hours
A total of 207 combat clashes were reported on the front line on 1 October. Russian forces attacked 30 times on the Pokrovsk front and 27 times on the Kostiantynivka front.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on X (Twitter), information as of 08:00 on 2 October
Details: A total of 207 combat clashes were reported over the past 24 hours.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, no Russian assault operations were reported. The Russians carried out five airstrikes, dropping 10 glide bombs, and conducted 151 strikes on Ukrainian troops' positions and settlements, including four from multiple-launch rocket systems.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukrainian units repelled 11 Russian attacks. The Russian forces attempted to advance near Lyman, Vovchansk and Chaikivka and towards the settlements of Mala Vovcha and Radkivka.

On the Kramatorsk front, the Russian forces did not carry out any assault operations.
On the Kostiantynivka front, a total of 27 attacks were reported. The Russians carried out assault operations in the areas of Kostiantynivka, Novoselivka, Illinivka, Mykolaipillia, Sofiivka and Vilne and towards Osykove and Hruzke.
On the Pokrovsk front, 30 Russian attacks were reported. The Russians attempted to advance in the areas around the settlements of Krasnopodillia, Novyi Donbas, Bilytske, Svitle, Vodianske and Molodetske and towards Hannivka, Dobropillia, Novohryshyne and Serhiivka.
On the Oleksandrivka front, the Russians attacked once in the vicinity of Ternove.
On the Huliaipole front, the Russian forces attacked Ukrainian defenders' positions five times. They attempted to advance in the area of Huliaipilske and towards Rizdvianka, Dolynka and Yehorivka.
On the Orikhiv front, the Russians made three attempts to improve their positions by attacking Pavlivka and Prymorske.
On the Prydniprovske front, the Russian forces did not carry out any assault operations.
On the Volyn and Polissia fronts, there is no evidence of any offensive Russian groups being formed in the area.

Swedish researchers create an ‘AI scientist’ that designs and runs its own experiments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:15:17 UTC
14:15:17 KST

Swedes created an AI system that can carry out the full scientific process from hypothesis to results interpretation with minimal human input.
Researchers in Sweden have developed an AI scientist capable of generating scientific hypotheses, designing experiments and interpreting results.
The team combined multiple Large Language Models (LLMs), large databases and physical laboratory robotics into a closed-loop system that can run the full cycle of scientific discovery.
“It is too much information for a human to analyse, but our AI scientist could identify promising biological questions, recommend experiments to test them, evaluate experimental outcomes and iteratively refine its understanding based on new evidence,” said Ievgeniia Tiukova, a researcher at Chalmers University of Technology, and one of the authors of the new study that examined the AI scientist.
The AI scientist analysed a database of approximately 60,000 phenotypical, physiological and metabolic relations for S. cerevisiae — a species of yeast also called brewer’s yeast or baker’s yeast. Then the system formed nearly 2,000 testable predictions about how nutrients impact cell growth and stress resistance.
Then these hypotheses were evaluated, selected comparison controls and converted the ideas into step-by-step, machine-readable instructions for lab equipment.
Once tests were finished, the AI analysed the data, determined whether predictions were correct and automatically updated or refined refuted hypotheses for future cycles.
“Rather than serving solely as decision-supporting tools, the AI scientist actively generates new scientific knowledge,” Tiukova said.
The authors noted that the future of scientific research lies in automation; advances in robotics, AI and high-throughput technologies are transforming the scientific process.
“AI Scientists will collaborate with human scientists to accelerate discoveries across biology, medicine and biotechnology,” said Ross King, senior author of the study at the University of Gothenburg.
“Such AI systems have the potential to reduce the time required to explore complex scientific questions, and optimise the use of laboratory resources,” King said.
Humans will still be essential
Researchers said such AI solutions could minimise human bias, accelerate research cycles and reduce variation caused by human error, incomplete recording of experimental protocols, environmental conditions and other factors that can affect outcomes and reproducibility.
However, the authors stressed that humans will still be key in scientific research.
“Humans will remain essential for setting priorities, interpreting broader contexts, developing research programmes and ensuring compliance with ethical rules,” King said.
“Future generations of autonomous laboratories will become increasingly capable of collaborating with humans and will be valuable partners in efforts to solve the most challenging questions in biology and medicine”.
As AI use in research advances, international bodies are moving to set out how it should be governed.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recently published a report with recommendations for researchers, ethics committees, regulators, funders and policymakers “to help ensure that AI-enabled health research is conducted responsibly and for the benefit of all”.
"Artificial intelligence is creating unprecedented opportunities to accelerate health research and improve people's lives,” said Meg Doherty, director at WHO’s Department of Science for Health.
“At the same time, innovation must be guided by strong ethical safeguards that protect human dignity, rights and equity”.

Three former Taiwan service members indicted for spying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:08:52 UTC
14:08:52 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Prosecutors in Kaohsiung indicted three former military personnel Thursday for allegedly gathering intelligence for China since 2020.
The Kaohsiung branch of the Taiwan High Prosecutors’ Office said in a statement that the three were charged with violating the National Security Act, Anti-Corruption Act, Classified National Security Information Protection Act, and the Criminal Code of the Armed Forces.
According to prosecutors, a man surnamed Chen (陳), an Air Force retiree, reportedly has been receiving instructions and funding from an intelligence organization linked to the Chinese Communist Party since 2020.
During these years, Chen obtained military secrets, including information on tank specifications and details about the Han Kuang military exercises, through an enlisted Army member who was serving in the military at the time.
In 2024, Chen allegedly traveled to Zhuhai, China, with another retired officer to attend a banquet with Chinese intelligence officials. Prosecutors said he intended to “develop an organization for China.”
During the meeting, Chen allegedly encouraged the officer to approach active-duty service members in Taiwan to gather military information.
The National Security Bureau reported last year a “noticeable increase” in the number of people indicted on suspicion of spying for China, from 16 in 2021 to 64 in 2024. Of those indicted in 2024, 43 were current or former military personnel, according to the bureau.
Military personnel have become a target of Chinese efforts to gather intelligence in Taiwan, the bureau said.
In April, the Ciaotou District Prosecutors Office in Kaohsiung indicted nine active-duty and retired military personnel who were recruited through online networks to collect confidential military information for China. The case is set to be the first National Security Act case to be tried by citizen judges under the Citizen Judges Act.

Taiwan Coast Guard uses water cannon to drive Chinese fishing boat from Dongsha waters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:08:42 UTC
14:08:42 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Coast Guard said Friday it used a water cannon to drive one of two Chinese fishing boats out of restricted waters near Dongsha Island after its crew refused orders to leave.
The Coast Guard said its patrol vessel Yunlin detected two Chinese fishing boats, identified as Yue Hui Dong Yu 75066 and Jin Sha, on Thursday afternoon, about 8 nautical miles (15 km) inside restricted waters east of Dongsha Island. The Yunlin ordered both boats to leave, prompting Yue Hui Dong Yu 75066 to raise its anchor and depart, while Jin Sha refused to comply.
After three unsuccessful radio warnings, the Yunlin sprayed water from its water cannon into the air from about 200 meters away, then moved closer and directed the water at Jin Sha’s bridge. The vessel then raised its anchor and began moving away.
The Coast Guard said the operation followed standard procedures for driving away Chinese vessels and using less-lethal weapons, which require personnel to avoid striking vulnerable areas of the body or injuring bystanders. The Yunlin avoided directing water at crew members on deck throughout the operation.
Jin Sha lost power as it attempted to leave, prompting the Yunlin to remain alongside and deploy a small boat to check the crew, all of whom were safe. In the evening, the Yunlin delivered 35 hot meals to Jin Sha’s crew at their request before beginning a towing operation, accompanied by another Coast Guard patrol boat.
The vessel was towed beyond Taiwan’s restricted waters late Thursday and remained under Coast Guard escort while awaiting assistance from another Chinese vessel. On Friday morning, the Coast Guard transferred Jin Sha to the Chinese-flagged Hai Yang Shi You 681, an offshore oilfield support vessel, which took it under tow.
The agency also called on Chinese authorities to prevent their fishing boats from operating illegally in Taiwan’s waters, saying such incursions had recently intensified, with catches often reaching several tonnes. It said the activity seriously undermines maritime order and threatens valuable marine ecosystems around Dongsha.

Evacuated in an incubator, now back in Gaza getting to know mama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:08:11 UTC
14:08:11 KST

Evacuated in an incubator, now back in Gaza getting to know mama
CAIRO/GAZA, Oct 2 - Bissan was born because of an airstrike.
Two weeks into the war in Gaza in October 2023, an Israeli attack ripped through her family's home in Beit Lahiya near the Israeli border, killing a sister she never got to meet. The blast seriously injured her pregnant mother, who was forced to deliver Bissan six weeks early to save both their lives.
Weeks later, the baby was driven out to Egypt in an ambulance while still in an incubator, one of a group of 29 preterm infants evacuated from a neonatal hospital ward as Israel's invading forces drew close.
Seven of those babies died in Egypt, but Bissan survived. While she grew in Egyptian hospitals and a care home, her mother, Sundus al-Kurd, never lost hope that they would be reunited. Back in Gaza, as the war raged on, Sundus made video calls to speak to the baby whenever she had internet access.
In March this year, with a ceasefire ostensibly in place, Bissan was returned to Gaza to be reunited with her family in a mission assisted by the UN, along with 10 other children from the same group evacuated as preterm babies.
When they were finally reunited, Bissan didn't recognise her mother, Sundus said. The girl, now 2-1/2, would say "mama" to any woman who showed her kindness.
Reuters documented their reunion and visited with them and several of the other children in the months that followed as they built bonds with their mothers and fathers. Here are their stories.
GETTING USED TO EXPLOSIONS
Returning to Gaza as a toddler meant learning to live in a war zone, where Israeli airstrikes have continued despite the ceasefire agreed a year ago between Israel and Hamas.
When Bissan first heard the booms, she would freeze in a state of fear for several minutes, Sundus said. She still begins to panic if a balloon pops near her.
"Her life changed. Her life became sleeping and waking up to the sound of explosions, to the sound of the numerous attacks and missiles," said her mother.
On a sunny morning soon after their reunion, her mother took her to a small zoo in central Gaza. Bissan, who wears pink-framed glasses, gazed in awe as a blue parrot latched onto her mother's arm.
'HE WAS SUPPOSED TO CALL ME DAD'
Of the 11 preterm babies evacuated to Egypt in November 2023 and returned to Gaza this year, not all were able to meet their mothers. For baby Ibrahim it was already too late.
His mother, Israa Badr, fell into a deep state of depression after her son, born during her eighth month of pregnancy, was evacuated to Egypt. She died the following month. Her husband Jabri Badr said doctors "told us she died of sorrow, of sadness."
"Ever since he was in her womb, she thought about him, dreamed of holding him, playing with him, and feeling what it was like to be a mother," he said.
Ibrahim is now reunited with his father in Gaza, but Badr said they have struggled to connect.
"He was supposed to call me dad. Today he doesn't even say dad, or anything. I tell him to come, and he ignores me."
Arafat Abu Mashayikh, a Gaza-based mental health expert, said that after two years apart it was natural that it would take time for parents to connect with their children.
MOTHER'S MILK, AND HER EMBRACE
Bissan, Ibrahim and the others "were deprived not only of their mother's milk but also of her embrace and the emotional development that comes with it," Abu Mashayikh said.
Rebuilding the bond takes time. Some days, Bissan and Sundus walk down to Gaza's Mediterranean shore. On a recent afternoon, they held hands as they walked where the sand meets the sea. Bissan flashed a big smile as she gazed out to the horizon.
The evenings are more difficult, but still bring them closer together, Sundus said.
When explosions ring out in the middle of the night, Bissan wakes up and seeks out her mother's care.
"Bissan has begun to understand who mama really is, who her mother really is," Sundus said. "I am the only person present in her life. I am the one who feeds her, changes her clothes, combs her hair, and plays with her." REUTERS

Latvijas Banka grants crypto-asset and payment licences to three companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:06:01 UTC
14:06:01 KST

Latvijas Banka’s Supervision Committee granted four licences to three companies on 30 September: Noah LV SIA received authorisation to provide both crypto-asset and payment services, Neverless SIA obtained a payment institution licence, and Atrya Technologies SIA was authorised to provide crypto-asset services.
Noah LV SIA’s crypto-asset licence covers custody and administration of crypto-assets on behalf of clients, exchanging crypto-assets for funds, executing client orders and providing crypto-asset transfer services. Its payment institution licence authorises the execution of payment transactions, including credit transfers and standing orders.
Neverless SIA also received authorisation to execute credit transfers and standing orders. The company already holds a crypto-asset services licence from Latvijas Banka, which it obtained in May 2026.
Meanwhile, Atrya Technologies SIA’s licence allows it to provide custody and administration of crypto-assets on behalf of clients and to exchange crypto-assets for other crypto-assets.
The latest approvals bring the number of companies authorised by Latvijas Banka under the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) to 12, while 13 companies in Latvia hold payment institution licences. Crypto-asset service providers authorised under MiCA in one EU member state may offer their services across the bloc through the cross-border notification mechanism.
The list of authorised crypto-asset service providers is available in Latvijas Banka’s financial market participant register, while the European Securities and Markets Authority maintains an EU-wide register.
Latvijas Banka encourages businesses preparing licence applications to consult its licensing guides, which explain the requirements, supporting documents and application review deadlines. Crypto-asset businesses can also use the central bank’s guidance on classifying assets under MiCA and determining whether they fall within its scope or are governed by other legislation.
Companies can request pre-licensing consultations to discuss the applicable legal framework and obtain an initial assessment of their compliance with regulatory requirements. According to Latvijas Banka, this early cooperation helps businesses prepare stronger applications and supports a smoother licensing process.

How many birds are killed by offshore wind turbines? Scientists use thermal cameras to find out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:02:08 UTC
14:02:08 KST

A year-long study has observed millions of birds migrating across the North Sea to measure the threat of offshore wind farms.
Europe leads the world in offshore wind energy, with more than 30 gigawatts (GW) of installed capacity across the continent – enough to power more than 26 million homes annually.
Earlier this year, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway and the UK committed to deliver 100GW of joint offshore wind projects across shared North Sea waters by 2050.
The €9.5 billion plan, known as the Hamburg Declaration, aims to turn the North Sea into the world’s “largest clean energy reservoir” and mobilise €1 trillion of capital in Europe.
But is our path to a fossil fuel-free future jeopardising birds that are already plummeting in number due to human-caused climate change?
Are offshore wind turbines a threat to birds?
Most studies into bird collisions with turbines tend to focus on wind farms located on land. But every year, millions of songbirds cross the North Sea during spring and autumn migration, mostly at night.
Capturing collisions at sea can be difficult, due to a lack of light and the remote location.
However, a new year-long pilot study has allowed researchers to detect these small birds and bats during hours of darkness, as well as larger birds during daylight hours, using a combination of thermal cameras and artificial intelligence (AI).
The study, initiated by the energy company Vattenfall, was carried out at the Hollandse Kust Zuid offshore wind farm in collaboration with Wildlife Imaging Systems (WIS) and Wageningen University & Research (WUR).
WIS installed 16 thermal cameras on an offshore wind turbine, covering all angles and operating 24 hours a day. Combined with AI, the system detected and interpreted bird movements day and night, including in poor visibility such as fog or rain.
“Safeguarding biodiversity is an important part of the energy transition,” says Karen Krijgsveld, a bird ecology researcher at Wageningen University & Research.
“On land, we already know quite a lot about when and why birds collide with turbines, and which species are most at risk. As offshore wind energy continues to expand, we need to develop that same understanding at sea.”
Over almost a year of monitoring, covering both a spring and an autumn migration season, 22 possible bird collisions were identified – two of which were confirmed and one considered highly probable.
“Until now, estimates of offshore bird collisions were mainly based on theoretical models,” says Jesper Kyed Larsen, a bioscience expert at Vattenfall.
“At sea, it’s extremely difficult to verify fatalities because there are no remains to recover. This study demonstrates how we can get the empirical data needed to improve collision estimates and secure efficient mitigation measures.”
The study does not claim that collisions are rare or that these initial results from one turbine can be applied everywhere. The primary aim was to test the technology’s performance under real offshore conditions.
But a previous study by the German Offshore Wind Energy Association (BWO) also yielded similar results.
Researchers analysed more than four million bird movements over one and a half years, using radar and AI-based cameras. They found that more than 99.8 per cent of migratory birds reliably avoided the wind turbines.
Vattenfall previously conducted another study on an offshore wind farm near Aberdeen, Scotland. Over a period of 19 months – from June 2023 to December 2024 – video recordings of a wind turbine were made with the help of AI-supported analyses.
A total of 2,007 bird flight paths near the monitored turbine were examined and no collisions were found.
How can Europe protect its endangered birds?
Despite all three studies suggesting a minimal impact of offshore wind farms on birds, conservationists warn that measures must still be put in place to help protect endangered species.
Of the 26 seabirds that breed on the UK’s coastlines and islands, 10 are already on the endangered list.
Back in 2020, the land-based Smola wind farm in Norway, which consists of 68 turbines, painted one blade on each turbine black to make them stand out to birds. They found the initiative reduced avian fatalities by a staggering 70 per cent, from 11 recorded bird carcasses before painting to six afterwards.
Some critics argue that making wind farms more visible could impact birds’ migration patterns, forcing them to fly longer routes around a turbine. This means they will use up more energy, and it will take them longer to get back to their chicks.
Other measures include placing turbines far away from sensitive habitats and avoiding migration paths in the first place. Thermal cameras and radar can also be used to further investigate the risk these turbines pose to our flying friends.

How India's classrooms are coping in the age  of instant gratification &amp; low attention spans?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:01:56 UTC
14:01:56 KST

Classrooms in parts of India are grappling with an underlying problem that no curriculum revision can easily fix. Students raised on on-demand food delivery, constant social media reels and instant AI answers are finding it harder to sustain attention, tolerate boredom, or work toward rewards that don't arrive at once.Teachers, as a result, are increasingly engaging a generation that is much less attentive than before. A recent nationwide survey by the National Council of CBSE Schools found that almost 70% of teachers across the country have observed a sharp decline in their students' focus and classroom attention.The survey, which covered around 6.3 lakh respondents -- teachers, under 18 students and their parents -- also found that 74% of students spend more than two hours a day on screen for non-academic purposes. And teachers reported rising anxiety, irritability and reduced face-to-face interaction among children.Parmeshwar Dattarao Bhurke, a teacher, says the trend is evident in everyday classroom experiences. "Many children no longer have the focus needed to sit through an hour-long lesson or read a passage without their minds wandering," he said. This has prompted many teachers to experiment with newer learning methods, he added.
"Earlier, one student could read a chapter aloud while the rest of the class listened. That no longer works... The idea now is to keep their minds actively engaged through the session."Priya, another middle school teacher, says she has noticed a decline in students' retention levels. "Even when children appear to be listening, their minds are elsewhere. They are also less willing to struggle through any difficult task. This affects their performance in school as well as their behaviour, as they become averse to any kind of challenges or discomfort."For 15-year-old student Chinmayee Sonna, the shift is visible in the way her classmates now study. "Instead of sitting with textbooks or working through ideas, many of my classmates look for the easier option, whether that is AI-generated summaries or explainer videos. They are able to retain less through this method but it helps revise quickly and saves time," she said.Psychologists say such habits reflect a behavioural shift driven by constant access to instant rewards. "They trigger dopamine, giving us a brief rush of joy that reinforces the behaviour and makes us want to repeat it. This is different from the real-life feats, where satisfaction comes only after much effort and patience," Rashi Bhatnagar, a psychologist, said.It is these consequences that extend into the classroom. "When rewards come with almost no effort, the brain begins to prefer them. Like an unused muscle, our ability to wait, tolerate boredom and sustain attention gradually weakens, leaving us restless when tasks demand patience," Bhatnagar said.This is why there is a downside to schools trying to make every lesson entertaining, she adds. "Education cannot always provide instant pleasure if it is to encourage deep thinking. Schools need to consciously create opportunities for children to reflect and generate new ideas."The habit of expecting immediate outcomes also affects resilience. "Because children have not developed the ability to wait for results, many give up too quickly. We need to teach them not to quit at the first sign of difficulty," Bhatnagar said.Psychiatrist Nisha Singla, talking about the digital ecosystem, says it is deliberately designed to reinforce instant gratification. "Social media apps, notifications and quick commerce applications are addictive and the brain begins to crave them. Reading or learning something new also gives us a sense of achievement, but the reward is delayed. That is where all the difference lies."Rebuilding patience, she says, begins with allowing children to slow down. "We need to let them get bored... There is a tendency to fill every moment of their day with something or the other, but boredom is equally important. Parents and schools should consciously encourage delayed gratification."
Another challenge to consider in adapting classrooms is large class sizes and poor teacher-student ratios. "This leaves little room for us to nurture each child's curiosity and individual learning needs. At the same time, schools remain under pressure to deliver high marks and pass percentages, leaving us focused on examination outcomes rather than redesigning learning around children's changing needs," Priya said.As educators wait for the national mental health and well-being policy for schools, they say it should help students find meaning in a learning process whose greatest rewards cannot be a sprint and a quick fix.
A Dehradun-based journalist focused on human-interest stories that link local issues to wider national conversations. She covers developments across genres, with a special interest in civic issues, education, and the environment.

Would a gambling tax rise in the budget really shut shops and cost jobs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
05:00:11 UTC
14:00:11 KST

Would a gambling tax rise in the budget really shut shops and cost jobs?
Most of the betting industry is urging the chancellor not to double slot machine duty to raise up to £460m more a year
Gambling industry kingpins are fuming about reports that the chancellor, John Healey, is considering increasing taxes on high-street slot machines in his first budget.
The billionaire owner of Betfred, Fred Done, is among industry bosses who say such a policy would force shop closures, cost jobs and ultimately fail in its objective, depriving the Treasury of taxes.
But not every figure in the gambling world agrees. Stewart Kenny, the co-founder of Paddy Power who has become a critic of his erstwhile industry, accused Done of “scaremongering”.
So who’s right? It’s complicated …
What does the industry say?
Bookies might be best known for bets on horses or football but they make big money from slot machines. The Betting and Gaming Council, an industry lobby group, commissioned a report from the accounting firm EY that estimated a duty rise to 40% could close up to 1,470 betting shops (nearly a third of the total 5,617), resulting in 15,900 job losses and a net loss to the exchequer of about £120m. Horse racing, which receives a levy from bookies’ profits, would also take a hit.
Done said he alone would be forced to close about 495 betting shops, nearly half of Betfred’s estate, with the loss of 2,475 jobs and £67m in taxes.
Entain, the owner of Ladbrokes and Coral, has written to Burnham saying it would have to make job cuts across its nationwide estate of 2,300 shops, were the policy to go ahead. Casinos and bingo halls are in the firing line too. Rank Group, which owns Mecca Bingo and Grosvenor Casinos, cautioned that a third of its venues could close, affecting 2,000 staff.
Are they crying wolf?
When dealing with bookmakers, it is wise to be sceptical.
Back in 2019, Betfred had about 1,620 shops. Since then, the company has threatened to close nearly 1,000 in response to tougher regulation or taxes. While most of the policies it objected to have come to pass, the number of shops has decreased by only about 330. Some of that is down to a broader shift to the web that has led to soaring online gambling revenues.
In one Betfred TV ad, Done encourages punters to “come and see me”. In your neighbourhood bookies? No, at Betfred.com. Meanwhile, the Done family has taken out tens of millions of pounds in dividends, including £50m in 2022 alone.
What it failed to mention is that it has been increasing its use of AI within the business since well before the tax rise. Some staff at Bet365’s Stoke HQ are understood to feel that government policy is a convenient smokescreen for good old-fashioned corporate cost-cutting.
A spokesperson said Bet365 was responding to a “highly competitive trading environment, plus increased regulatory and tax-related costs”.
So it’s all a bluff?
Well, no. The UK’s biggest gambling companies, including Betfred, Entain, Flutter and more, have all announced cuts since Reeves’s duty rise. It is impossible to say how much of this retrenchment might have happened anyway, given economic worries and structural shifts within the sector. However, it makes sense that any further increase in costs, in the form of higher taxes on slot machines, will negatively affect the gambling sector.
Simon Thomas, the chief executive of the Hippodrome Casino in London, says that fear of the tax is already hurting investment.
“We have a £6m rooftop expansion plan with full planning permission, ready to go. With MGD up in the air, we’ve had to shelve it,” he said, adding that if MGD goes up to 40%, a third of bingo halls and a third of casinos could close.
Does the government want a smaller gambling sector?
Burnham has already moved to limit the opening of new gambling premises. He has voiced particular concerns about 24-hour adult gaming centres (AGCs), high street venues packed with the sort of machines that would be more heavily taxed by an MGD increase. The rise of these “slot farms” is understood to be the main driver for any such move.
But there are question marks over whether AGCs would actually take the hit. They already have much lower overheads and looser regulation than casinos and bingo halls, which have experienced negligible growth. Last year, AGCs managed to increase their takings from £528m to £613m by packing more machines into larger venues.
So if slot machines taxes go up, in theory AGCs are best placed to survive the impact. The AGC operator Merkur has already offered to buy some of the 132 shops that Betfred put up for sale, indicating it is unruffled by the prospect of a tax rise. If others follow suit, just as bookies retrench, an MGD rise could simply lead to bookies being replaced by 24-hour slot farms.
As Treasury officials weigh up duty rises, they will have to consider the law of unintended consequences.
