AI is ‘better informed’ than doctors, US health secretary Kennedy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:10:00 UTC
09:10:00 KST

AI is ‘better informed’ than doctors, US health secretary Kennedy says
Sheryl Gay Stolberg
US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has frequently advised Americans not to trust medical experts, said this week that artificial intelligence could offer patients “a second opinion that is much better informed than any doctor in the country” and had the power to “free us from medical tyranny”.
Kennedy made the comments on Sept 29 during a “fireside chat” with Vice-President J.D. Vance at a Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) conference sponsored by companies that have business before his department, as well as AI companies, such as Anthropic and OpenAI.
Kennedy said OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman told him during a recent visit to his office that it would be “malpractice for a doctor to make a diagnosis or to make a prescription without at least checking AI”. Kennedy apparently agreed.
The health secretary’s wholehearted endorsement of AI comes as the Trump administration is facing mounting pressure to do more to regulate the technology. Kennedy’s own department has faced some criticism for moving too rapidly to fund AI projects in healthcare.
“One of the things that is going to change is that we’re never ever again going to be able to be dominated by public officials who tell us, ‘Trust the experts,’” Kennedy said during the Sept 29 session.
“If somebody tells you, ‘Masks work, trust the experts,’ AI may tell you otherwise,” he added. “If somebody tells you, ‘Social distancing works, trust the experts,’ AI may correct that. And if somebody tells you that a vaccine will prevent transmission and infection, or you need to take it to protect your grandmother, AI may say it actually doesn’t do that.”
When it was finally Vance’s turn to speak, he cracked a joke: “I guess I’m in the wrong summit. I thought this was about weight loss and acid, not AI.”
The MAHA Summit, at the Waldorf Astoria in Washington, did indeed address other topics, including some of Kennedy’s core issues: the promise of psychedelic drugs, healthy eating and chronic disease prevention.
Kennedy and other administration officials were not involved in planning the conference; they were invited speakers. But so many appeared – including Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins; Lee Zeldin, who heads the Environmental Protection Agency; and Mehmet Oz, who runs Medicare and Medicaid – that at times it looked like a corporate advertisement with a government imprimatur.
The conference’s tilt towards business, and its sponsorship by companies such as Walmart and Grail, which has an application for a cancer screening blood test pending before the Food and Drug Administration, generated a backlash from some longtime Kennedy supporters.
“It’s all a grift,” said Dr Robert Malone, a critic of mRNA Covid-19 vaccines. Malone served briefly as vice-chair of a vaccine advisory committee appointed by Kennedy, but resigned in March after a judge ruled that he and other committee members lacked essential qualifications.
“Why were none of the founding women of the movement involved?” asked Alex Clark, a podcaster with the conservative group Turning Point USA, referring to the so-called MAHA Moms. One of them, Vani Hari, who calls herself “the Food Babe” and has worked closely with Kennedy, attended as a guest but was not on the programme.
Stefanie Spear, Kennedy’s closest adviser, moderated a session that included Jonathan Neman, a founder of the salad chain Sweetgreen, who marvelled at how Kennedy has changed the conversation around food. Neman said that in 2015, his company briefly promoted an initiative it called Make America Healthy Again.
Coming just five weeks before the midterm elections, the conference shed light on how the MAHA movement has fractured since 2024, when it rallied behind Kennedy and helped power US President Donald Trump’s election victory.
In effect, there are now two MAHAs: corporate, Trump-aligned MAHA, including the conference organisers, and grassroots unaffiliated MAHA, which Democrats are now trying to court. In Michigan on Sept 29, Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Senate, announced a Build a Healthier America agenda.
“Any MAHA anything that is brought to you by Walmart Corporation and the health insurance companies tells you everything you need to know,” El-Sayed, a former public health official in Detroit, said in an interview Monday night.
El-Sayed’s agenda includes plans to address many of the issues that have galvanized MAHA followers: getting toxic substances out of foods, clean water, improving the health of school meals and eliminating pesticides from farming. But he said he did not support Kennedy’s push to discourage childhood vaccination.
The topic of vaccines, central to Kennedy’s work for decades, was conspicuously absent from the conference agenda. So was Dr Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health, who has been tangling with the White House over its plan to assert political control over his agency’s grant-making decisions.
Bhattacharya, who was initially scheduled to moderate a panel discussion, disappeared from the final agenda. A spokesperson would not say why.
Journalists were excluded from the conference for the most part, although it was streamed online. Major news outlets that applied for press credentials, including The New York Times, were denied them. In an e-mail, conference organisers said they had “limited space”. But the press section inside the hotel ballroom was empty.
“I cannot understand why the MAHA Summit denied so many press credentials, especially with so many US govt officials on stage,” Helena Bottemiller Evich, founder of an influential newsletter, Food Fix, wrote on the social platform X. She added that while she was granted credentials, “the press area was largely empty and our movement was restricted so I left”.
Reporters and conference guests instead mingled in the grand lobby and restaurant of the hotel, which Trump owned from 2012 to 2022. Among those spotted there was entrepreneur Mark Cuban, whose company Cost Plus Drugs teamed up with Trump on TrumpRx, the president’s plan to reduce the cost of drugs.
Cuban, dressed in a teal T-shirt and dining alone, said he had no idea the MAHA Summit was taking place and had no interest in attending. He was in town for another meeting.
Kennedy’s supporters, including Tony Lyons, who oversees a constellation of MAHA-themed non-profits, including the organiser of the conference, defended the secretary. The MAHA Center, which hosted the conference, said on its website that it did not “coordinate with any government entity” in planning the event.
“People have been going after Bobby Kennedy for many, many years now,” Lyons said during a conversation that included Calley Means, a top Kennedy adviser; Zeldin; and Kyle Diamantas, the acting FDA commissioner.
“They’re going after Bobby Kennedy because they say he’s dangerous,” Lyons added, “and we know what he’s a danger to. He’s a danger to the people who are roadblocks: The people, the companies, the deep-state actors who are roadblocks to real progress.”
The Sept 29 conference came on the heels of another MAHA event, focused on healthcare data, hosted on Sept 28 by the MAHA Institute, another organisation affiliated with Lyons. Kennedy mingled with guests at a private reception Monday night.
One of them, Jeffrey Tucker, who runs the Brownstone Institute, a free-market policy organisation that grew out of a backlash to Covid-19 restrictions, described the scene on X. “Guy at reception last night in DC, confusing me with someone important, started pitching his new medical product that is being considered by the FDA,” Tucker wrote.
“The conversation was not particularly welcomed by me,” he added, “so I said the following: ‘It doesn’t matter if it works or not. All that matters is whether you have the money. Pay the needed millions and it is approved. Pay nothing and it is not approved. That’s how it works.’ To my amazement he said: ‘Yes, that’s it exactly.’” NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times

Nic Maddinson and Sam Harper have been called into the Australian men's Test squad for the series against South Africa.
Cam Green is in doubt after suffering an abdominal strain, while Josh Inglis has a fractured finger.
What's next?
The first of three Test matches between Australia and South Africa begins on October 9 in Durban.
Nic Maddinson is within touching distance of a remarkable return to the Test team, after Cameron Green's abdominal strain left him in doubt for the series opener against South Africa.
Selectors confirmed on Thursday night that Maddinson had been called into the Test squad after not featuring in Australia's red-ball side for almost 10 years.
Sam Harper has also been drafted in as a back-up wicketkeeper, with a finger fracture now officially ruling Josh Inglis out of the first Test in Durban starting next Friday.
Inglis was hurt while playing in the series-opening ODI against South Africa last week, with further scans back home in Perth revealing a fracture.
There are now similar concerns around Green following the third ODI in Potchefstroom on Wednesday after he hurt his abdomen trying to pull a ball while batting in Australia's dead-rubber win.
Australian medical staff will now keep close watch on the allrounder, who will be "assessed further" in the coming week.
Regardless, the latest abdominal injury will raise question marks over Green's ability to bowl, after having not done so yet in a game on this tour.
The one bit of good news for Australia is opener Matt Renshaw has been cleared of a wrist injury after being hurt while fielding in the final ODI.
But the injuries do leave Australia's line-up for the first Test largely up in the air with up to two spots in the top-six unclear if Green is not fit.
Inglis had stood a chance of coming into the side for Marnus Labuschagne if selectors had opted to drop the Queenslander for the series opener.
Maddinson could now fill one of those roles, with Cooper Connolly the other reserve batter in the Test squad.
Maddinson last played a Test on Boxing Day in 2016, and has since overcome a battle with testicular cancer to restart his cricket career.
The 34-year-old did not play a first-class match last summer, but struck 126 for NSW in a one-day match against Victoria last week.
Harper looms as another option, after being called into his first Australian squad at age 29.
The Victorian was the second-leading run-scorer in last summer's Sheffield Shield with 677 at 35.63 and is fresh off hitting a century for Australia A against India A in Pudcherry.
"Sam gives us wicketkeeping cover as Josh continues his recovery, while Nic provides flexibility throughout the batting order," chief selector George Bailey said.
Australia will play an intra-squad warm-up match in Potchefstroom this weekend, before moving to Durban on Monday to commence preparations for the first of three Tests.

OpenAI says three employees fired for mishandling ‘sensitive’ info
- OpenAI fired three researchers for mishandling sensitive information and violating company policies, particularly involving work with an external AI evaluation organisation.
- The fired employees, including Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni, had publicly expressed concerns about AI safety and risks on social media.
- US tech leaders, including OpenAI, signed a voluntary safety pledge with President Trump to regulate AI development and ensure proper safeguards for the technology's rapid advancement.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – ChatGPT maker OpenAI said on Oct 1 that it has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling “sensitive information” and violating company policies, including work that involved an external organisation that evaluates artificial intelligence models.
The San Francisco-based AI lab did not confirm the identities of the employees involved, but at least two of them had worked on safety and alignment, according to the Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg.
“We have parted ways with three individuals,” OpenAI told AFP in a statement.
“Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work.”
The firings come amid a tense debate about AI safety and whether the technology presents an existential risk to humanity.
In September, a 27-year-old researcher named Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic with a stark warning that the leading AI labs, including OpenAI where he had worked, were “gaming with our lives” by racing towards developing ever more powerful models.
The three researchers fired by OpenAI are Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, according to the WSJ.
All three have in recent weeks regularly posted about AI safety-related issues on X.
“I am at OpenAI and I think AI is >10% likely to kill all humans,” Balesni posted on Sept 10, echoing statements made by other AI employees in recent weeks.
As speculation swirled about why employees at OpenAI and Anthropic were speaking so freely about their personal beliefs, Korbak jumped into the public discourse.
“I’m quite unhappy with much of what OpenAI does. I am very happy that I’m allowed to say ‘I’m quite unhappy with much of what OpenAI does’,” Korbak wrote on Sept 11.
“It’s hard to overstate how dangerous speeding towards RSI is,” Wang posted in response to Coxon’s resignation, referring to recursive self-improvement, which is a technique where software is designed to continuously teach itself.
Leading US tech companies signed a voluntary pledge this week to regulate themselves on safety after meeting with President Donald Trump at the White House.
Trump called it a “morally binding” commitment to build adequate safeguards on the fast-moving technology.
Executives from Nvidia, Google, Meta, XAI, OpenAI and Anthropic signed the agreement.
Safety concerns
Concerns about the safety of advanced AI models have escalated in recent months.
OpenAI cancelled the release of a new model, Astra 6.1, because it deemed the model unreliable and found that it frequently ignored instructions.
Instead, the company launched GPT-6.1 Sol, an updated version of a different model, during its annual DevDay conference on Sept 29 from San Francisco. OpenAI said Sol would cost one-fifth the price of Astra.
In July, AI agents developed by OpenAI attacked Hugging Face, an AI model and application library, during an incident where the autonomous software escaped its confined testing environment.
Since then, additional security incidents have been reported that involved models developed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
On Oct 1, cybersecurity firm Asymmetric Security said in a report that agents developed by OpenAI covered up their own tracks after gaining unauthorised access to government websites.
The US Federal Trade Commission launched a broad investigation into artificial intelligence safety practices at Anthropic and OpenAI, the Washington Post reported on Sept 30, though the scope of the inquiry is unclear. AFP

'Gang work to do': Deportee convicted over Comancheros bid in Tonga
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:04:02 UTC
09:04:02 KST

Tongan man deported from Australia convicted over bid to set up Comancheros gang branch
A Tongan man deported from Australia has been convicted over his role in establishing a branch of the feared Comancheros outlaw motorcycle gang in the Pacific Island nation, the ABC can reveal.
In a landmark case, Eneasi Taumoefolau was found guilty by a judge in Tonga of participating in an organised criminal group under the Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crimes Act. It is the first time the law has been tested in court.
He is facing a maximum sentence of 25 years and will be sentenced at a later date.
Taumoefolau is currently serving a life sentence in Tonga's main prison over separate charges, having been convicted in 2025 of importing more than 2 kilograms of methamphetamine into Tonga from the United States.
Three other men were charged over the Comancheros case and put on trial. Tevita Shoji, a deportee from New Zealand, was found guilty, while two other deportees from Australia, Lolomana'ia Tilini and Sione Tafokitau, were found not guilty.
Court documents revealed Taumoefolau was the president of the chapter in Tonga.
"Taumoefolau was regularly seen wearing Comanchero vests, riding a bike with the Comanchero label clearly displayed on it, and had a storage unit containing a significant amount of Comanchero uniforms and badges," Justice Elisapeti Langi wrote.
In an exclusive prison interview earlier this year with the ABC's Foreign Correspondent program, Taumoefolau denied having set up a Comancheros chapter in Tonga, saying he had plans to do so but abandoned them when he realised prospective members may not be criminally savvy enough to follow the gang's strict codes.
Speaking on the phone from prison this week, Taumoefolau told the ABC he stands by that explanation.
"I don't know how they've come up with that decision to say it's been set up," he said.
"We have no clubhouse. We have no set-ups."
'We got gang work to do'
Justice Langi said she was satisfied the defendants had formed a group based in part on "the physical evidence of a storage unit containing a significant number of Comanchero clothing and regalia together with telephone messages and conversations between all four defendants".
Messages tendered as evidence show Taumoefolau saying to one of his co-accused, "We got gang work to do."
Evidence submitted to the court also revealed Taumoefolau was in regular communication with Shoji, who was a "nom", a term given to a nominee or prospective member of the gang.
In one text exchange, Taumoefolau described Shoji as "the best nom eva (sic)".
Police also submitted evidence Taumoefolau said he would provide a "nom" T-shirt to a drug offender serving time in a Tongan prison.
Court documents also referred to text messages from July 2024 between Taumoefolau and a number in New Zealand.
They showed the New Zealand contact asking Taumoefolau to send photos to an individual in Auckland Prison.
The contact then warned Taumoefolau "not to post gang colors because gang flicks are not permitted" in prison.
It is understood the individual in Auckland Prison was Pasilika Naufahu, the president of the Comancheros New Zealand branch.
About the same time, Taumoefolau and the New Zealand contact also discuss organising an annual "National Run" in Tonga, an event where club members gather for a motorcycle ride on a pre-determined route.
The contact urged Taumoefolau to arrange food, drinks, accommodation and "taahines" (girls).
Speaking to the ABC, Taumoefolau said he does not remember either of these conversations and said Naufahu had nothing to do with trying to set up the chapter in Tonga.
Photos show search for gang paraphernalia
Taumoefolau and Shoji were the subject of a dramatic arrest in the Tongan capital in August 2024 that saw heavily armed officers from the tactical response group shoot into the engine block of Shoji's car. Police found a bag containing methamphetamine inside.
Loading...
The ABC has obtained photos tendered as evidence in the trial that show Taumoefolau being taken by police as they search various locations for gang paraphernalia after his arrest.
They show him being taken to a storage unit, rented in the name of his partner, where police discovered "bags of T-shirts with comanchero logo (sic) and signs", and "suitcases containing vests and labels of ranks".
There is also a photo of him with police in the Nuku'alofa airport parking lot where police found more gang paraphernalia in a car that had previously been driven by Shoji, including a vest marked "Commander".
Taumoefolau said earlier this year his motivation for trying to establish a branch in Tonga was to "piss off the Australian government" who deported him in 2022 after a string of drug convictions.
"It was just stupid," he said. "I was reckless, and I was very ambitious in the way I thought, 'I'll do it because it'll really, really piss them off,'" he told Foreign Correspondent earlier this year.
Taumoefolau has been in an isolation cell in Tonga's main prison since March.
"It's 23 hour lockdown," he told the ABC this week.
Neither he nor prison officials could confirm why he's been removed from the general prison population.
He says he plans to appeal the verdict in this case and his drug conviction.
Are tides turning on Pacific drug scourge?
South Pacific nations have been grappling with a devastating surge in drug smuggling due to what the Australian Federal Police commissioner has described as Australia's "insatiable appetite" for meth and cocaine, with customers willing to pay some of the highest prices in the world for illicit drugs.
The Australian government recently announced $600 million for a new Pacific scheme designed to tackle the surge of drug smuggling into the region.
Tonga's police commissioner, Geoff Turner, says his force's efforts to combat drug crime in the Kingdom of Tonga are paying off. He says the price of a gram of methamphetamine has increased fivefold in 18 months, meaning supply has dropped significantly.
"There is a great shortage of methamphetamine in the Kingdom at the moment. Having said that, with the increased prices, it also makes it more attractive," he says.
"So it's that balance between, you know, stopping supply, but also then making it more attractive because of the prices that are attractive."
He says about six to eight weeks ago several blocks of cocaine washed up on the beach in the tourist hotspot of Vava'u, with similar markings as some that washed up in Fiji, which is 800 kilometres away.
"I'd say it's probably being carried on the tide and probably some part of a load that's fallen over the side or a semi-submersible that may have lost something," he said.
"Or, alternatively, it's been a raft type or something that's maybe dropped off and a few blocks have gone over the side.
"So now at this point in time, we don't have any evidence of a cocaine market here in Tonga, but it's certainly something we're monitoring at the moment," he said.

Call centers that funneled money through &quot;money mules&quot; exposed in Dnipro
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
03:03:08 EEST
09:03:08 KST

Call centers that funneled money through "money mules" exposed in Dnipro
Kyiv • UNN
Fraudulent call centers sending out messages about fake winnings were shut down in Dnipro. Police seized money, weapons, and equipment.
In Dnipro, law enforcement officers shut down the operations of fraudulent call centers whose participants, according to the investigation, transferred funds obtained through fraud via the bank cards of “drops” and converted them into cryptocurrency. This was reported by the Department of Strategic Investigations of the National Police, according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that the call centers were organized by a group of individuals with a clear distribution of roles. To facilitate their activities, the suspects rented two premises in the city.
Some participants controlled the work of the “operators” and the movement of funds, while others were responsible for registering bank cards in the names of nominees, converting money into cash and cryptocurrency. To seize citizens’ funds, the fraudsters sent out mass messages via Telegram and Viber announcing purported winnings
It is reported that the suspects posted advertisements on social media seeking to purchase people’s personal and identification data needed to open bank accounts and gain access to remote banking systems.
The scheme involved both so-called “professional drops” and students, pensioners, and unemployed people. Bank accounts and payment cards were registered using their data, while actual control over them was obtained by the group’s participants. Subsequently, the victims’ funds were deposited into these accounts
They added that during the investigative actions, more than 40,000 euros, 18,000 dollars, 113,000 hryvnias, weapons, ammunition, 158 mobile phones, 35 pieces of computer equipment, 13 data storage devices, 25 SIM cards, 153 SIM card holders, 10 bank cards, and two Starlink kits were seized.
Background
The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine supported tougher liability for electronic communications fraud and the operation of fraudulent call centers. The relevant Law No. 10190 was adopted in its entirety on September 16.

Philippines’ jeepney drivers ‘stuck between a rock and a hard place’ despite fare increase
Drivers say the overdue fare increase of 1 peso ‘barely makes a dent’ as the sector battles the massive loss of livelihoods
Reggie Manlapig, 46, has been driving jeepneys for nearly 25 years and has weathered rising fuel prices – but with costs spiking amid the global energy crunch, he is now wrestling bigger demons.
“The impact has been huge. Before, in a 16-hour shift of driving, I could take home 400 to 500 pesos [US$6.30 to US$8] – now there’s a big cut to that income,” said Manlapig, who plies a two-hour daily round route from Malolos in Bulacan, north of Manila, to San Fernando, Pampanga.
“Doing the full route five times straight in a day really pushes you. Before, three round trips alone would already give you decent earnings – especially on days with no classes, holidays, or student holiday periods; those are especially hard.”

If Moscow Is Not Stopped in Ukraine, NATO Itself Could Be Next, Merz Warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
23:59:49 UTC
08:59:49 KST

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned Thursday that any weakening of Germany’s commitment to Ukraine could trigger consequences across Europe, arguing that European unity has become essential both to Ukraine’s survival and the continent’s own security.
“The security of Europe, our security, is at stake in Ukraine,” Merz said at a ceremony in Münster awarding NATO the International Award of the Peace of Westphalia. “If we fail to halt Moscow, the Russian war machine will sooner or later turn against us, against NATO itself.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Merz said Russia’s full-scale invasion had shown that Ukraine’s survival and Europe’s security could no longer be separated.
Russia, he said, was violating the most fundamental principles of international law and the European order, while its missiles and drones continued to strike Ukrainian homes, bridges, power plants, schools, hospitals and other civilian infrastructure.
Merz warned Europeans against assuming the threat would remain confined to Ukraine.
He asked whether the Baltic states could eventually become a drone battlefield like Ukraine’s Donbas, or which European cities might one day face the ballistic missiles Russia currently launches against Kyiv and Kharkiv.
“Three generations after 1945, war would return to our part of Europe,” he warned.
‘Unity and strength’ against Moscow
Merz said NATO’s experience had shown that unity and military strength were prerequisites not only for deterrence but also for successful diplomacy with Moscow.
CCTV Captures Russian Drone Slamming Into Kyiv School With 104 Children Inside – Warhead Fails to Detonate
“Unity and strength remain prerequisites for successful negotiations with Moscow,” he said.
He stressed that maintaining US involvement remained vital.
“This can only encourage us to keep the United States of America by our side in our policy regarding Ukraine.”
Merz pointed to continued transatlantic coordination and argued that sustained pressure on Washington had helped preserve US involvement in European security and Ukraine policy.
Europe, meanwhile, had undergone what Merz described as a security awakening.
For the past two years, he said, European states have provided the largest share of assistance to Ukraine.
“Europe is waking up to what is required in terms of security policy,” Merz said. “For Ukraine, this European awakening today is its salvation in an hour of great need.”
“This struggle for unity is hard work. But it is crucial on the path towards peace in Ukraine and security in Europe.”
He warned that the war must not be allowed to fracture Europe.
“If Germany falters, Europe falters. If Europe falters, Ukraine falters,” Merz said.
“If we stand firm, then Europe stands firm. And if Europe stands firm, then Ukraine also stands firm.”
Merz takes aim at AfD and its Russia policy
Merz also turned the focus inward, warning that Germany itself faced pressure to weaken support for Ukraine.
“In Germany, too, we will not let ourselves be divided – not by hybrid attacks, not by hate speech in social media driven by Moscow’s bots, and not by the sound bites of the AfD and their Russian puppeteers,” he said.
The Alternative for Germany has opposed extensive German military assistance to Ukraine and advocated restoring closer relations with Moscow and easing sanctions against Russia.
The party has also made dramatic electoral gains in recent weeks. It won roughly 44% in Saxony-Anhalt in September and later finished first in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while recording its strongest-ever result in Berlin.
Merz rejected arguments that Germany’s support for Ukraine was damaging Germans economically.
“Our support for Ukraine is not an end in itself,” he said. “We are, first and foremost, providing this support in order to protect the freedom and security of the people in our country. Freedom and security are prerequisites for our prosperity.”
He also pushed back against claims that NATO enlargement had effectively forced Russia into acting defensively.
Merz said Moscow’s perceptions should be taken seriously but added that Europe must “speak out when perpetrators portray themselves as victims.”
‘Dictated peace’ would leave Europe less secure
Merz stressed that Germany ultimately seeks stable and predictable relations with Russia.
But he said those relations could not be restored while Moscow continues its war against Ukraine and hybrid attacks across Europe.
Western military support for Kyiv, he argued, was therefore necessary to create the conditions for genuine negotiations rather than prolonging the war.
“Our assistance for Ukraine is laying the groundwork to enable serious peace negotiations with Moscow to get under way in the first place,” Merz said.
He warned that without continued Western backing, the war risked ending not in a negotiated settlement but in a peace “dictated” by Russia.
That, he said, could destabilize the Ukrainian state, trigger large-scale migration toward Western Europe and reward Russia’s aggression.
“Europe would become an insecure continent,” Merz said.
Any settlement, he added, must preserve Ukrainian sovereignty, leave territorial decisions to Ukraine itself and provide Kyiv with credible security guarantees and the freedom to continue its European path.
Ukraine faces its hardest winter
Merz warned that Ukraine was approaching what could be its most difficult winter since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Residents of Ukrainian cities, he said, were preparing for further ballistic missile attacks and Russian strikes against heating and electricity infrastructure, schools, apartment buildings and churches.
“Ukraine has to survive this winter,” Merz said.
“I am convinced: Ukraine will survive it.”
Germany would continue helping, he said, including through repairs to destroyed energy facilities and development of new air-defense systems designed to intercept jet-powered drones.
Those German systems are expected to enter mass production, according to the chancellor.
Merz said Germany was also drawing directly on battlefield lessons from Ukraine in drone defense, military command systems and defense-industrial innovation.
He argued that such cooperation was strengthening Germany’s own security as well.
NATO chief: ‘Support Ukraine’
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, accepting the Westphalian Peace Prize on behalf of the alliance, echoed Merz’s call to continue backing Kyiv.
“Keep calm, carry on, and support Ukraine,” Rutte said. “Putin wants to intimidate and divide us. But he will fail.”
Rutte said Russia’s hybrid campaign across Europe – including cyberattacks, sabotage, arson, drone incidents and airspace violations – was aimed in part at distracting NATO countries from Ukraine and weakening their willingness to support Kyiv.
“Our response to his hostile actions is to support Ukraine even more,” he said.
Rutte also urged NATO members to accelerate defense investment and weapons production, warning that Russia’s military-industrial base would not weaken quickly.
“Increased defense production is not about warmongering,” he said. “It’s about making sure we keep our people safe and Ukrainians strong in their fight for freedom.”
The NATO chief said Ukraine’s fight had become inseparable from the alliance’s own security.
“Ukraine’s fight is our fight, their security is our security, and our support is unwavering,” Rutte said.
For Merz, the coming months would test whether Germany and Europe could sustain that unity.
“The coming months will be critical for the fate of Ukraine and for security in Europe,” he said. “If we waver or falter, then this could have fateful consequences. But if we stand firm, then, together, we can achieve peace for Ukraine and freedom in security for all of Europe.”

Ukrainian minister hopes to heal ‘misunderstanding’ with South Korea: Reports
Ukraine is working to heal a spat with South Korea over Kyiv’s publicly announced transfer of two North Korean servicemen taken prisoner in the war against Russia, Ukrainian media reported on Oct 1, quoting Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky revealed while he was addressing the UN General Assembly last week that the prisoners had been sent to South Korea, angering Seoul which expected the transfer to remain secret.
“I would not like to call this an incident. Let’s say, it’s a diplomatic misunderstanding,” Sybiha told journalists at an event, according to a report in news website nv.ua and other media.
“I really hope that this situation will be resolved in the very near future and we are working on it. For us, South Korea is an important country. And I really hope for momentum, continuation, and concrete results that we are truly achieving with them.”
South Korea’s presidential office this week demanded an explanation and apology from Ukraine for disclosing the transfer, and said Ukraine had also falsely denied that the two sides had agreed to keep the move confidential.
South Korea had sought to keep the transfer confidential given security, diplomatic and humanitarian concerns, including the safety of the prisoners and their families, a senior official in Seoul said.
Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in January 2025, the first soldiers to be captured alive since Pyongyang entered the war in 2024, assisting Russia.
North Korea has signed a strategic partnership agreement with Russia, including a mutual defence pact, and dispatched an estimated 14,000 troops to help Moscow evict Ukrainian troops from its Kursk region.

Third aircraft carrier, thousands of troops head to Mideast as Trump weighs new Iran strikes
The U.S. military is dispatching roughly 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the Middle East, a U.S. official said Thursday. The bolstering of the American military presence comes as President Donald Trump warned anew that new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon.
The troop movement, which includes a third aircraft carrier, underscores the rapidly evolving dynamic of Trump's war against Iran as he ponders his next move, with midterm elections in the United States looming large and new signs that the nature of the conflict may be becoming more complex.
Trump has threatened that a post-midterm election escalation — despite his initial promises to Americans of a campaign that would last a matter of weeks — remains a viable option. Further complicating matters, Trump told reporters Thursday that early indications suggest that Iran is linked to the flydubai co-pilot who stabbed his captain and tried to crash an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday.
In an exchange with reporters at the White House, Trump raised the connection when asked by a reporter if there were any links between the pilot behind the attack and Tehran.
"I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is 'yes,' but we’re working on it right now," Trump said, without offering details.
Trump added that if the link to Iran is established, the United States would retaliate. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed in a Fox News interview earlier Thursday that investigators believe the flydubai suspect underwent "Islamist, radical indoctrination" but did not provide further details.
"Oh, they’ll be hit very hard, don’t worry," Trump said. "You just ask them. They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard."
Thousands of US sailors and Marines head to the Middle East 
Meanwhile, the group of ships now en route to the Middle East together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines.
It includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, which recently deployed with the cruiser USS Chosin, and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships.
It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October, according to the U.S. official, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the U.S. naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft. The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
The carriers USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington are in the region now, along with the USS Boxer amphibious readiness group. The Washington is typically deployed to the Pacific Ocean, but it was moved to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose arduous deployment resulted in the crew being at sea for more than 260 days straight.
Trump explains why he rejected Iran's latest truce proposal 
Trump, in a Time magazine interview published Thursday, also raised the prospects of new strikes, saying it is "possible" that he will ramp up bombing in Iran after the 3 November elections in the United States.
When pressed, Trump said he could not go into further detail about his strategy.
"I can’t tell you that because look, you know, you’re asking, where are you going to bomb?" Trump said.
He said in the interview, conducted on Monday, that he rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Iran because "things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today."
Trump cited as an example an offer from Iran to "open up" the Strait of Hormuz, the key energy shipping corridor, but said the overall proposal was "not good enough."
The war shows signs of getting more complicated 
Asked if the increasingly unpopular war would threaten Republican Party chances in November, Trump at first responded, "It’s possible." But then he added, "It should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon."
The president said "100% of the people" oppose Iran having nuclear attack capabilities "including worldwide."
"So, when you say it that way, it would help," Trump added. "If you don’t say that, it could hurt."
Yet, there's also growing concern that Tehran might be turning to asymmetrical tactics following the flydubai attack and another suspicious incident in the U.K.
Authorities believe that Iran might be looking to shift strategy just as the U.S. finds greater success in loosening Iran’s grip over the Strait of Hormuz and getting Gulf allies' oil to market, while a Navy blockade is shutting down Iran’s own oil exports.
British authorities announced on Thursday the arrest of a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran.

Putin vows Russia will respond with 'all weapons at our disposal' if attacked by NATO
Speaking at the annual Valdai Discussion Club forum on Oct. 1, Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that Russia may respond with nuclear weapons in the event of a military conflict with NATO.
"We understand that we'll be facing an adversary twice our size," Putin said about a potential conflict with NATO. "The point is that we have competitive advantages in our means of self-defense. Yes, of course, France and Great Britain are nuclear powers; we understand this perfectly well and are fully aware of it. But no one else has the weapons that Russia has today."
Putin's comments echoed warnings Russia issued to NATO on Sept. 30, saying that it would be ready to use nuclear weapons if alliance members attempt to isolate the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
"Can we be sure this weapon will never be used? Of course not," Putin said about nuclear weapons in his speech. "We're all familiar with the saying: If a gun is hanging somewhere on the stage at the beginning of a performance, on the wall, it's bound to go off eventually."
Russia has repeatedly used nuclear rhetoric in its confrontation with Western countries over its full-scale war against Ukraine. The U.K. has previously condemned Moscow's nuclear signaling as destabilizing and warned that such rhetoric increases the risk of miscalculation.
Putin went on to say that Russia has "no intention of attacking anyone," despite Russian drones increasingly violating NATO airspace, the Kremlin being accused of multiple attempts of sabotage, and Moscow launching near non-stop attacks across Ukraine.
On Sept. 28, Putin signed a decree raising the total personnel of Russia's armed forces, days after it was reported that Moscow plans to raise military spending to record levels.
Putin also echoed threats from Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova that European factories manufacturing weapons for Ukraine could become military targets for Moscow.
For months, European leaders have raised concerns over what they describe as growing Russian hybrid operations against NATO members, particularly countries on the alliance's eastern flank and those supporting Ukraine.
At the Discussion Club, Putin reiterated his familiar gripes with the West and demanded Ukrainian land in exchange for ending the war. The Russian president also effectively rejected proposals for a mutual halt to attacks on energy infrastructure with Ukraine, and for the restoration of safe shipping in the Black Sea.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu allegedly planned a “false flag” hijacking operation involving an Emirati aircraft in an effort to draw the United States into a new war with Iran, Iranian state-run Press TV reported Thursday
The broadcaster based the report on an unnamed “well-informed regional source” who alleged that an incident involving a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday was part of the purported plan.
According to the source, the operation was discussed and finalized during a secret visit by Netanyahu to the United Arab Emirates three days before the flight incident.
The source claimed Netanyahu was accompanied by several senior military and intelligence officials and that discussions involving officials from several Arab countries focused on devising an operation that could subsequently be attributed to Iran.
Press TV’s source alleged that the objective was to draw US President Donald Trump into another war against Iran.
The source also linked the alleged plan to Netanyahu’s domestic political situation, claiming that the Israeli prime minister was concerned about his coalition’s prospects in upcoming parliamentary elections.
Press TV did not identify its source or present evidence in its report to substantiate the allegations.
There was no immediate comment from Israel, the UAE or the US regarding the allegations.
The claims came a day after flydubai flight FZ1073, carrying 174 passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv, made an emergency landing at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in the Saudi city of Tabuk.
Flydubai said Wednesday that “an altercation occurred in the flight deck” and that crew members aboard secured the aircraft before it was safely diverted to Saudi Arabia.
Saudi airport authorities said both the captain and first officer were injured and taken to a hospital. All passengers and crew were reported safe.
Saudi Arabia’s National Transport Safety Center subsequently opened an investigation into the incident.
Flydubai later announced that flights to and from Israel would be temporarily suspended while the investigation continues, saying the measure would allow authorities to “establish all the facts surrounding the incident.”

Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:42:33 BST
08:42:33 KST

On the streets of Barcelona, fiery red and gold Chinese dragons (presumably with very sweaty people inside the costumes) danced among delighted crowds, while Chinese acrobats elicited gasps of amazement as they rolled, tossed and threw spherical lanterns in the air, keeping - as if by magic - the candle inside them upright at all times.
Shanghai made history this week: the first Asian metropolis to be invited as the city of honour to Barcelona's famously rambunctious cultural festival, La Merce. Vast street processions here are overwhelmingly aimed at celebrating centuries-old Catalan traditions. So it was quite something to witness velvet-clad Catalan pipers, sashaying down Barcelona's main boulevards, their medieval tunes intermingling with lilting music that accompanied flocks of brightly dressed Chinese performers.
Shanghai Vice Mayor Lu Shan flew to Barcelona to speak at La Merce's opening ceremony. Chinese and Catalan cultural traditions differ in form, he remarked, but they share "a common spirit".
Spain and China are experiencing a period of mutual appreciation. But that sense of bonhomie is far from shared across the EU.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited China's President Xi Jinping four times in as many years. He's urged the EU as a whole to improve relations with China since Donald Trump's re-election two years ago.
Sanchez's move has sparked resentment and disapproval among a number of Spain's European partners who view Beijing as a strategic rival and possible geopolitical threat to the EU. Privately, they ask if Madrid's welcoming stance - opening up its market to Chinese businesses - is enabling China to become the (economic) enemy within the bloc too.
Pedro Sanchez is not the only EU leader going off piste. Global volatility means other EU countries feel squeezed and exposed and unsure they can rely on America under President Trump. His policy on trade and defence is seen as unpredictable and, at times, aggressive. And so EU member states are selecting strategic partners that they believe suit their national needs, even if that alienates or irritates fellow member states.
So do these new-found alliances risk a permanent splintering of unity in the EU or even Nato?
Spain accused of self-interest
Germany and France - the EU's biggest powers - have just united around a more aggressive approach towards China. They want to give Brussels the muscle to shut subsidised Chinese competitors out of the EU market to address ballooning trade imbalances with Beijing that the European Commission claims have reached a whopping €1bn (£850m) a day.
Other EU countries fret about China's tight relationship with Russia. Beijing has denied helping Moscow's war effort in Ukraine but defence experts point to technological and economic support from China, which they say has enabled Russia to sustain its military assault.
That's why, as Spain enthusiastically courts Beijing, it stands accused of looking after its own, rather than wider European interests.
"It's a bit chicken and egg. Did Spain distance itself from European allies, or did they distance themselves from us?" asks Victor Cortizo, a lawyer and academic specialising in Sino-Spanish relations.
"I think it's more us. It's Spain. But legitimately so. Realpolitik is a thing. If I get closer to China because that attracts Chinese investment and bolsters my economy, then that is strategically more appealing than supporting allies who are also only looking out for themselves."
Cortizo and I were surrounded by towers of crates as we spoke, at the end of the longest freight rail link in the world. It runs over 13,000km (8,000 miles) between Yiwu in eastern China and Madrid, largely bringing car parts and electrical goods to Spain and transporting delicacies like Spanish ham and red wine back to China. The link is a symbol of the burgeoning relations between the two countries.
"Our prime minister has made the decision to pursue national gain over EU relations," Cortizo told me. "Chinese investment in Spain has doubled over the last year alone."
Rising Chinese investment
According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants.
Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe".
"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me.
The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around €1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.
Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally.
According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably.
China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran.
That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US.
And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro.
"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo.
But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market.
There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.
However, Miguel Otero, China specialist at Madrid's ElCano Royal Institute, accuses Spain's European allies of being condescending and hypocritical.
"France, Italy, Germany, they all have their own strategic relationship with China," he tells me. "Spain isn't going much further. It's been catching up with them." In fact, he says, now that Europe can no longer rely fully on the US, Spain's priority is to diversify. It wants to do business not just with China but also Canada, Brazil, India and Africa. Spain is not China-obsessed, he says.
But there's also the question of security.
On his latest trip to Beijing in April, Prime Minister Sanchez met the founder of Chinese wind turbine manufacturer Ming Yang, which had just had its plans to open the UK's largest wind turbine manufacturing plant in the Highlands blocked on national security grounds.
This followed uproar in the EU after Spain's Ministry of the Interior awarded Chinese tech giant Huawei a €12.3m contract to store and manage sensitive judicial wiretap data last year.
MEPs from several political groups in the European Parliament said Spain's contract could endanger the EU as a whole.
"When you introduce a high-risk vendor... we do not just risk a localised data breach, we risk poisoning the well of European intelligence sharing," said Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Pirate Party MEP, part of the Greens group back in February.
Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez, a member of Spain's centre-right opposition party, said the decision puts "the entirety of the EU at risk".
Spain's defence ministry continues to deny there is any risk, but former US Ambassador to Nato Julianne Smith, the co-founder of geostrategic advisory firm Clarion Strategies, warns the episode could really erode European cohesion.
"As EU countries seek ways to hedge against what some see as an unpredictable and unreliable America, they have to be careful not to rush towards alternatives that stand to weaken the EU's collective hand," she tells me.
"Some of those growing relationships, such as Canada's rapidly expanding relationship with the EU, could produce real dividends," she added. "But others, such as Spain's decision to deepen its relationship with China, could further derail the EU's ability to speak with one voice and create added security vulnerabilities for both Spain and wider Europe."
More emerging alliances
Spain is far from alone amongst EU countries in striking up controversial alliances.
Finland has a massive 1,300km-long land border with Russia. This has left it feeling exposed since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Finland already has the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership per capita in the EU. It has the largest reserve military force in both the EU and Nato. It has built cavities under bridges that can be packed with explosives, should Russian armoured vehicles enter its territory. This is a country that believes military preparedness is an existential necessity.
In 2022, it decided there was safety in numbers. Helsinki ditched its traditional strategic neutrality and rushed to join Nato.
Now though, there are fears that Washington might not respect the alliance's mutual defence clause in case of an attack on a member country.
No longer confident the US would come to the rescue if needed, Finland has turned to Israel to purchase advanced defence equipment, including the David's Sling air-defence system and Spike anti-tank missiles.
Finland renewed its contract with Israel at the height of the recent Gaza war despite its government having publicly expressed considerable reservations about Israeli activity in the occupied Palestinian territories and at a time when many other EU countries also feel deep unease about Israel's policies and activities in Gaza and the West Bank.
"There is a sense in Finland that we can't always afford [to have] a moral superiority. Survival comes at a price," says Minna Alander, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defence and Security Programme at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA).
"Finns and political opposition parties do question whether Israel is a country whose defence industry they want to support [because of its actions in Gaza and the West Bank] but the Finnish government has kept out of the debate, saying the deal with Israel fulfils Finland's needs," she tells me.
In the end, Alander says her fellow Finns have "a less sentimental mentality".
Greece's shift
Greece also feels threatened by a far bigger, immediate neighbour. It perceives Turkey as a "constant and significant danger to its national security and sovereignty", Nick Malkoutzis, co-founder of political analysis website MacroPolis, tells me.
In the past, the US mediated disputes between the two countries. Both are members of Nato. But under Donald Trump, Nato insiders say the US is increasingly perceived as missing in action politically and diplomatically, with Washington's focus very much elsewhere.
In late August, Greece and Israel signed one of the largest defence export deals in both countries' histories. The "Achilles Shield" agreement provides Athens with Israeli technology aimed at protecting Greece against a range of threats, including drones, aircraft and missiles.
There is a history of public sympathy with the Palestinian cause in Greece and many people have been sceptical about ever closer relations with Israel. But Malkoutsis says the public and political reaction to the "mega-deal" with Israel has been "more muted than might have been expected".
He says this is because there is a bottom line - a common understanding of the fundamental need for Greece to strengthen its security in relation to Turkey that takes priority over everything else.
With Israel a close ally of Washington, Greece hopes that "buying Israeli" will also help maintain decent relations with the US, even in these turbulent times.
But it's a delicate dance because Greece and Finland both very much want to be seen as "good Europeans", feeding into the European collective, according to Malkoutsis.
He says EU countries "scrambling in all directions" complicate everyone getting on the same page and speaking with one voice on defence and security which is the opposite of what Brussels and Nato say they want.
That said, European countries banding together in smaller groups to pursue common interests is nothing new. The E3 "gang", composed of the UK, Germany and France, was originally formed in 2003 to co-ordinate diplomatic negotiations with Iran in the hope of a nuclear deal. It's now a more ad hoc communication channel for Europe's three largest military and economic powers.
Nordic and Arctic nations have their own formats for working together to promote regional defence, while the "Visegrad Four" made up of Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia was for many years a well-known pressure group in EU circles.
However, Nato and the EU are convinced that the continent is under intense pressure, unprecedented since the end of the World War Two. Their leaders say it is time to form a united front. An aggressive Russia growls threateningly at the door, bolstered by Beijing, while the United States, Europe's former best friend abroad, seems, at best, distracted by other priorities.
Splintering, fracturing and rampant "mini-lateralism" will only be applauded by Europe's adversaries, they believe. China and Russia are watching closely.

US judge finds law criminalizing noncitizen voting unconstitutional
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
23:38:56 UTC
08:38:56 KST

A US judge dismissed a federal case on Thursday that accused a Jamaican national of illegally voting, finding the law criminalizing noncitizen voting was unconstitutional and delivering a blow to the Trump administration's campaign against alleged election fraud.
The ruling by Miami-based US District Judge David Leibowitz applies only to the case of Florida resident Chelsea Cox, who was charged in October 2025 with illegally voting in the 2020 election. It is not binding for judges in other cases.
It marks a setback for President Donald Trump's administration on noncitizen voting, a cornerstone of its push to highlight alleged election fraud ahead of November's midterm elections. Republicans are fighting to retain majorities in both houses of Congress.
The Justice Department has charged at least 60 people with noncitizen voting since Trump returned to office in January 2025.
The ruling by Leibowitz, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, appears to be the first time a federal court has found the 1996 law a violation of the US Constitution.
Leibowitz says voter qualification state issue not federal issue
Leibowitz wrote that under the US Constitution only states can set voter qualifications, not Congress. Every state requires US citizenship to vote, and Leibowitz said it was up to Florida, not the Department of Justice, to prosecute her for violating that requirement.
"Can the State of Florida prohibit and punish the exact conduct Defendant Cox allegedly engaged in here? This has already been decided elsewhere and is not addressed here: Florida can and does," Leibowitz wrote.
Trump, who falsely claims that fraud cost him the 2020 election, has said stricter enforcement of documented citizenship is needed for election integrity. His critics say the administration's highly publicized crackdown on noncitizen voting exaggerates a rare problem and could undermine confidence in election results.
Neither the White House nor the Justice Department immediately responded to requests for comment.
In a court filing, the Justice Department had said Congress, not the states, was best-equipped to handle immigration and foreign affairs.
"Foreign interference in elections is clearly within the purview of Congress," federal prosecutors wrote.
Other defendants have challenged law
Cox's attorney Bruce Udolf welcomed the ruling. "This is a situation that cries out for discretion by government officials and they'd be well-advised to walk away from this without further reprisal against her," he said.
Cox entered the United States as a tourist in 1999 and remained after her visa expired the next year, according to a court filing by the government. She used a fraudulent US Virgin Islands birth certificate to obtain a Florida driver's license and used those documents to register to vote in 2012.
Records show she voted in federal elections from 2012 to 2020, but only the 2020 election was within the statute of limitations.
There are about 45 pending noncitizen voting cases around the country and at least four other defendants have challenged the law on similar grounds. Judges in those cases may find Leibowitz's reasoning persuasive, but they are not bound by his decision.
Trump has portrayed noncitizen voting as part of a broad Democratic Party conspiracy to dilute Republican power. But Cox was one of just 129 people charged with violating the law known as "voting by an alien," according to a Reuters investigation published in July.
The investigation, published on July 19, found no defendant accused of conspiring to sway an election, backing a candidate or taking payment for a vote.
The Reuters investigation also showed that most of the people accused of noncitizen voting were lawful permanent residents who either registered by mistake or were encouraged to sign up to vote based on the misguided advice of an election worker or government clerk.
Illegal voting is grounds for deportation, and as Reuters has reported, the Trump administration has been investigating noncitizen voting and deporting defendants, sometimes years after their criminal cases were closed. Cox's attorney Udolf said he hoped the government would not move to deport her, citing her declining health.
On July 16, Trump said without evidence that 278,000 noncitizens were registered to vote in California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
Five days later, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, said about 400 noncitizens in her state voted after a software error mistakenly registered about 6,600 people in 2023-24. The Justice Department has demanded their names, nationalities, and addresses.

Reshet Gimel co-founder, Kol Yisrael veteran Gilad Ben-Shach passes away at 85
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
23:38:32 UTC
08:38:32 KST

Gilad Ben-Shach, a composer, music editor, and veteran of Kol Yisrael, has died at the age of 85.
Ben-Shach, one of the founders of Reshet Gimel who later served as the station's manager, was for decades one of the most influential figures behind the scenes of Israeli radio and music.
Ben-Shach joined Kol Yisrael in the late 1960s and went on to hold a number of positions within the Israel Broadcasting Authority, including music editor, head of the entertainment department, and manager of Reshet Gimel.
In his work, he helped shape the station's musical sound at a time when radio had an enormous influence on musical tastes in Israel and on how songs and artists became hits.
One of the decisions most closely associated with him was the creation of the program Mediterranean Basin. In the late 1970s, Ben-Shach tasked Shimon Parnas, then a young editor who specialized in rock and pop, with producing a program dedicated to Mediterranean music.
Ben-Shach's world was Hebrew music
The program, which aired on Reshet Gimel for years, eventually became one of the genre's most important platforms, at a time when Mediterranean music was still struggling to find a place at the heart of the Israeli mainstream.
Alongside his work in radio, Ben-Shach was also a composer and songwriter. Among the songs associated with him are Every Person Has a Star, performed by Ilan and Ilanit, as well as Violets.
For years, he was also involved in producing performances and events dedicated to Hebrew song, including shows held as part of the Ein Gev Festival. He devoted a significant part of his work to preserving and nurturing Hebrew song.
His family said that "Ben-Shach's world was Hebrew music, its preservation and its cultivation."

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Iran would be willing to restore inspectors' access to bombed nuclear facilities in exchange for sanctions relief in private talks, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the discussions.
Araghchi suggested the agreement in private meetings with European and Middle Eastern diplomats at the United Nations while in New York for the General Assembly, diplomats told Bloomberg.
The foreign minister also attempted to convince Europeans to reverse a UN decision to re-impose broad sanctions on Iran, which led to the sanctions 'snapback' last September, which the Europeans refused, diplomats said.
While Araghchi did not speak explicitly about the state of Iran's economy, the diplomats told Bloomberg that the suggestion that Iran would grant the access in exchange for sanctions relief signals the extent of the country's economic struggles.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told CBS last week that Iran would be willing to allow inspectors in, but Araghchi had not previously raised the possibility during the talks.
Iranian inflation rises as oil exports halt
According to the report, inflation is now almost 90% year over year, and the rial has weakened 30% against the dollar as the sanctions have taken effect.
US President Donald Trump said that Iran had 301% inflation on Thursday, adding that their money had become "valueless."
The US blockade of Iran has stopped Iran from loading any crude oil onto tankers last month, according to Bloomberg.
Negotiators reportedly pushing Iran for nuclear program concessions in exchange for US peace talks
On Sunday, negotiators between Iran and the United States told the Wall Street Journal that they are pushing for Iran to make concessions on its nuclear program in exchange for reviving peace talks.
One high-level Middle East government official involved in the talks told the WSJ that Iran had been close to compromising on its nuclear program earlier this year during negotiations with US Vice President JD Vance, but would need explicit assurance that it would not be attacked by Israel after making a deal with the US.
Other officials said that Iran is confident it could withstand a long-term US blockade or renewed bombing campaign.
Arab officials and mediators also told the WSJ that Iran has not compromised at all since US President Donald Trump rejected the recent ceasefire offer, and that it wants the US to offer concessions before continuing any negotiations.

Ukraine’s former defense minister, dismissed suddenly, has announced Army of Robots. He says target is $10,000 per unit and need is tens of thousands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
23:38:02 UTC
08:38:02 KST

The robots Ukraine wants to throw into its deadliest fights should cost as little as $10,000 each, Mykhailo Fedorov says. The former defense minister has set out the first stage of his Army of Robots: cheap, simple humanoid-like machines that would take over an infantry's most dangerous jobs, with tens of thousands needed, he said on Telegram, citing his own interview with Forbes.
On 26 September, Fedorov, who continues to work on military tech reforms despite his sudden and unexpected dismissal, announced the creation of the Army of Robots.
Humanoid robots would carry ammunition and pull out the wounded, lay and clear minefields, scout, hold positions, and strike, taking the roles that today cost soldiers their lives.
Potential need amounts to thousands
"Our main goal is to save lives. A human should not take risks where a machine can do the job," Fedorov says.
At the first stage, it will not be a classic humanoid but a simpler humanoid-like robot that can be produced quickly and scaled up, he adds.
Such a machine should perform some of an infantryman's tasks directly on the battlefield.
Today, such platforms cost $40–70 thousand on average. For mass use in war, Ukraine needs something much cheaper: the target is $10–20 thousand per unit, he believes.
"The potential need is tens of thousands of such machines," Fedorov continues.
Next come prototypes
The former defense minister adds that he and his team are already working with teams that have ready-made MVPs and are designing solutions.
"Next come prototypes, simulations, model training, and finding the right combination of hardware and software," he explains.
The Army of Robots is not a single product but an ecosystem that will unite companies, startups, engineers, R&D, and capital around the robotization of the front.
"Our task is to get from prototype to mass product as quickly as possible," he adds.

Saudi Arabia said two weeks ago it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered restricted airspace over the city. The coalition described that incident as the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca since 2017, while the Houthis denied targeting Mecca or any other Islamic holy site.
The coalition said the Medina attack was part of what it described as repeated Houthi attempts to target the Two Holy Mosques and “provoke” Muslims worldwide. It said it would continue taking measures to protect the holy sites and pilgrims.
The Houthis said later in the day that Saudi Arabia had carried out strikes on Sanaa and the provinces of Saada, Taiz and Amran, according to their news agency. Nuclear war, Ukraine, ‘AI totalitarianism’: Key takeaways from Putin’s Valdai speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
23:33:00 UTC
08:33:00 KST

Nuclear war, Ukraine, ‘AI totalitarianism’: Key takeaways from Putin’s Valdai speech
Russian President Vladimir Putin delivered his annual keynote address and answered audience questions at the Valdai Discussion Club’s international forum outside Moscow on Thursday.
During a more-than-three-hour session moderated by foreign affairs expert and RT contributor Fyodor Lukyanov, Putin spoke on a broad range of topics, including tensions with the West, the Ukraine conflict and artificial intelligence.
A world in turmoil and the emergence of a new global balance
The world has reached a pivotal moment shaped by profound transformations in global politics, the economy and demographics, as well as the rapid development of technology, including AI, Putin said.
“We are confident that, in the long term, as we move away from Western hegemony, the global situation will gradually change for the better – toward a more stable, democratic, and free multipolar international order,” he said.
The risk of new conflicts
Technological and social change is fueling a sense of uncertainty and greater international tensions, Putin said. Governments may seek to preserve stability at home by “exporting instability” abroad, while new opportunities “fuel ambitions” and encourage countries to take greater risks.
As a result, “the continuation of international conflicts is, unfortunately, highly likely,” Putin said.
AI could herald an era of ‘digital totalitarianism’
The proliferation of AI could lead to “digital totalitarianism,” shaping individuals and stripping away their individuality through the use of algorithms configured by others, Putin warned.
“Such digital totalitarianism would be just as much of a dead end – as bleak and inhumane – as the totalitarian societies of the past that we know so well,” he said.
Countries and communities must join forces to find broadly acceptable solutions to the challenges posed by AI and other technologies capable of influencing human behavior, identity and thought, Putin said.
While AI can be a useful tool, any final political decision must remain in human hands, he stressed.
Relations with the West
Russia’s current tensions with the West date back to the fall of the Soviet Union, when certain Western leaders sought to further weaken Russia instead of welcoming it into the European security system, Putin argued.
“Despite the many years – and I want to emphasize this, many years – of attempts by the new Russia to become part of so-called Western civilization, in practice they did everything they could to truly isolate and further break apart the Russian Federation itself,” the president said.
“They still say this at various events and gatherings even today: ‘We need to finish breaking up the empire,’” Putin added.
He pointed to NATO’s eastward expansion, which he claimed violated assurances given to Moscow. Putin further argued that European politicians were using escalatory rhetoric toward Moscow to draw attention away from political and economic problems at home.
No saber-rattling around Kaliningrad
The president reiterated that Russia would respond to any potential attack on its Kaliningrad Region, an exclave on the Baltic Sea sandwiched between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. Any assault on Russian territory would “inevitably” be viewed as grounds for using all the weaponry at Moscow’s disposal, he said.
Putin was referring to recent statements by Western officials, including Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys and Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, who have argued that NATO should be prepared for a potential conflict involving Kaliningrad.
Nuclear weapons as ‘Chekhov’s gun’
The president warned that a conventional war could escalate into a nuclear conflict.
“Today, when the world’s leading powers possess weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, bringing the Earth to a catastrophic state, can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Of course not,” Putin said.
Putin compared the risk posed by the continued existence of nuclear weapons to “Chekhov’s gun,” a dramatic principle attributed to Russian playwright Anton Chekhov that holds that a gun introduced early in a story should eventually be fired.
”We all know the famous saying: if a gun is hanging on the wall at the beginning of a play, by the end it is bound to go off,” the Russian leader said. “We must bear that in mind and prevent it from happening.”
“If we want to live – and everyone wants to live – then, as I once said in a public speech, let’s live in peace. Let’s work together to find ways to make that happen,” he said.
The Ukraine conflict and Russia’s goals
Putin said the Ukraine conflict, which is on track to enter its fifth year next February, is about Russia’s security rather than territorial ambitions. He reiterated Moscow’s demand that Ukraine abandon its plans to join NATO in favor of permanent neutrality.
Russia is ready to end the conflict, but only on terms acceptable to Moscow, he said.
