What is celebrated on October 2 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
02:32:29 EEST
08:32:29 KST

What is celebrated on October 2 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On October 2, international and national holidays are observed around the world, including the International Day of Non-Violence and Mahatma Gandhi's birthday. Believers commemorate Saints Cyprian, Justina, and Theoctistus.
On October 2, the world observes the UN-sponsored International Day of Non-Violence, World Farmed Animals Day, and World Smile Day. India celebrates Mahatma Gandhi's birthday, while Guinea celebrates Independence Day. According to the new-style church calendar, the hieromartyr Cyprian and the martyr Justina are commemorated, while according to the old style, the holy martyrs Trophimus, Sabbatius, and Dorimedon are remembered, reports UNN.
International Day of Non-Violence
An official international UN observance established by a resolution of the General Assembly in 2007. The day is timed to coincide with the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, the leader of India's independence movement and the founder of the philosophy and strategy of nonviolent resistance.
The event aims to promote the ideas of peace and tolerance, protect human rights, reject armed aggression, and resolve sociopolitical conflicts through dialogue, education, and civic awareness.
World Day for Farmed Animals (WDFA)
Established in 1983 by the Movement for the Rights of Farmed Animals, it is also timed to coincide with the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, who was a consistent advocate of humane treatment for all living things.
The event highlights the problem of the mass industrial raising, slaughter, and suffering of billions of farmed animals worldwide, calling for the humanization of animal husbandry standards, ethical consumption, and the promotion of plant-based food alternatives.
World Smile Day
An unofficial international holiday observed on the first Friday of October since 1999. The holiday was founded by American artist Harvey Ball, who created the famous graphic symbol—a smiling yellow face—in 1963.
The event is held under the motto "Do an act of kindness. Help at least one person smile!" and encourages people to show genuine kindness, engage in positive emotional exchange, and support those experiencing hardship.
Guinea Independence Day
The main national holiday of the West African country, commemorating the events of October 2, 1958, when Guinea became the first among the French colonies of Tropical Africa to reject the French Community project in a referendum and officially proclaim full state sovereignty under the leadership of Ahmed Sékou Touré.
Gandhi Jayanti in India
An official public holiday and one of India's three national days, established in honor of the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi—the "Father of the Nation."
On this day, ceremonial wreath-laying ceremonies, joint prayers by representatives of all the country's religious denominations, and cultural and educational events dedicated to preserving Gandhi's legacy take place near the Raj Ghat memorial in New Delhi.
Grandparents' Day in Italy (Festa dei Nonni)
An official holiday established by the Italian Parliament in 2005 to emphasize the exceptional role of the older generation in raising young people and preserving family values.
The date was chosen for a reason: in the Catholic tradition, October 2 is the feast of the Guardian Angels, symbolically emphasizing the protective and caregiving role of grandfathers and grandmothers in the family.
Day of Remembrance of the Hieromartyr Cyprian, the Martyr Justina, and the Martyr Theoctistus
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate the hieromartyr Cyprian, the martyr Justina, and the martyr Theoctistus. Cyprian was a renowned pagan magus and sorcerer in Antioch who, using pagan incantations, attempted to seduce the virtuous Christian maiden Justina at the request of a young man named Aglaias.
Seeing that all his magic was powerless against Justina's prayerful sign of the cross, Cyprian believed in Christ, burned his books of sorcery, was baptized, later became a bishop, and, together with Justina, suffered martyrdom under Diocletian in 304.
The blessed Andrew, the fool-for-Christ, is also remembered on this day.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate the holy martyrs Trophimus, Sabbatius, and Dorimedon, who suffered for their faith during the reign of Emperor Probus in the 3rd century in Antioch, displaying unshakable courage during torture.

Air Force Adjusting Plan for Maintenance Career Overhaul from Just 7 AFSCs to 14
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
23:30:27 UTC
08:30:27 KST

The Air Force will officially kick off a major overhaul of maintenance career field next year with a pilot program, but the plan for the revamp is still evolving—while officials once intended to condense 50 aircraft maintenance specialties down to just seven, now they are targeting 14 Air Force Specialty Codes, according to Lt. Gen. Kenyon K. Bell.
Bell, deputy chief of staff for logistics, engineering, and force protection, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview that the sweeping effort will be “a multiyear transformation” how the Air Force recruits, trains, and develops its maintenance force, suggesting it will be quite a while before that transformation is complete.
“The two-way career field strategy is on track to initiate [an 18-month] pilot test in mid- to late-2027,” said Bell, who added, “It’s going to be a yearslong effort for this to take place.”
The service first revealed its career field transformation plan for maintenance Airmen in January 2025. The strategy called for enlisted Airmen to start out on a generalist track—a single Air Force Specialty Code—where they will focus on applying the most common maintenance skills such as recovering and fueling across multiple airframes. Once Airmen reach the rank of Senior Airman and are preparing to become noncommissioned officers, they would become a specialist in one of six non-aircraft-specific areas:
- Avionics and Electrical, which combines avionics with the electrical side of the Environmental and Electrical (E&E) specialty
- Aerospace Ground Equipment, which will look the same as it does now
- Advanced Mechanical, which combines crew chiefs, fuels, hydraulics, and the flight line side of engine maintenance
- Crew Support Systems, which combines ejection seat systems with the environmental side of E&E
- Fabrication, which combines aircraft structural maintenance, aircraft metals technology, and nondestructive inspection.
- Intermediate-level engines, for maintainers dedicated to intermediate-level engine maintenance.
The New Plan
In the revised plan, the initial phase is similar. It will train maintainers entering the Air Force as aviation maintenance technicians, or AMTs, for their first 18 months of service, focusing on maintenance fundamentals for multiple airframes. The initial phase will also emphasize that the skills they are learning will ground them in the importance of aircraft sortie generation, which is a key focus of the service’s strategy to generate and sustain airpower even if under attack, Bell said.
“We’re an Air Force. We fly, fix, fight, and win. And the first thing that we want to be able to do is make sure that as all of our maintainers come in, they understand what sortie generation is about,” Bell said. “If you can’t get the aircraft off the ground, then what are we really here for?”
Maintenance Airmen will then transition into a specialty track where they will select from one of 14 different specialties, Bell said. The Air Force would not release the new specialty list because it is still refining how it will be organized, according to an Air Force spokesperson. There will be six specialties that are “aircraft-agnostic,” but it’s unclear how they will be different from the original six, the spokesperson said. Another eight specialties will be split among three different aircraft groups:
- Fighter/Atack
- Mobility/Strike
- Tactical Lift/Rotary
Air Force officials refined the plan to offer more specialties after meeting with maintenance Airmen as part of the effort’s feedback-gathering campaign that began in January.
“We stood up 10 different working groups; we brought in almost 280 different maintainers from across the Air Force to help us refine the strategy and the specifics,” Bell said. “It was long list of things that we went through.”
The revised plan offers maintenance Airmen the option to change their specialty, which is currently based on their score on the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery test that the majority of enlisted Airmen take while still in high school, Bell said.
“How well they did on that ASVAB test could probably determine what career field they went into and where they were going to spend the next 20 years of their life; something just doesn’t sit right about that,” Bell said. “And if we have the ability to now say, hey, ‘this may be where you scored and which you what you were selected for, but maybe now with a little more maturity, and now that we have shown you some other things, maybe there’s a different path still within the aircraft maintenance career field … maybe you want to choose this specialty over another.’ So, I’m really excited about that aspect of it. There is a little more optionality that also matches up with Air Force needs.”
Eventually, maintainers in the specialty track will have the opportunity to apply for the master aviation technician, or MAT, track—a more specialized pipeline designed to create a smaller force of highly skilled maintainers who will focus on fixing more complex problems on specific aircraft, Bell said.
But the highly selective pipeline is only designed for a “small percentage of maintenance force; that’s going to cultivate them into cross-functional technical experts on a specific aircraft.”
“That small percentage of folks will help us ensure that as people move around, that MAT group of folks will be that core group of folks that we lean on to be those very technical experts to solve some of the hard breaks, the hard problems that might go on the aircraft,” Bell said.
When it was first revealed, the new strategy sparked concerns among current and former Air Force maintainers that the new design could dilute expertise across the career field and reduce local leaders’ ability to solve complex maintenance problems.
“I’m not going to say that that is not a valid concern, but with any change, you’re going to have some amount of pushback to it,” Bell said, adding that that is why the service sought feedback from current maintainers.
“I take all input, and that’s the reason why we have asked the major commands to send me your brightest people who can represent you, who are going to be constructive disruptors,” Bell said.
“To the maintenance Airmen that said, ‘I’m a naysayer and I don’t believe you in this’: give me your input and then help us try to mitigate that,” Bell added. “We can’t continue to do what we’re doing now and think that we’re going to get a different result.”
Critics also question how the Air Force would switch to the new model amid a shortage in maintenance manning.
Bell said that a key benefit of the 2A career field transformation is it will instill in young maintainers the importance of aircraft sortie generation similar to the way Air Force is stressing “airmindedness” in Basic Military Training and tech school to ensure Airmen understand they have a role in generating combat airpower.
“This particular line of effort that we’re doing right now with the two-way career field strategy speaks to retention because we believe that as more maintainers come in and then we train them up in this way, this ability to be sortie generators up front is going to add to their motivation and their reason for being,” Bell said.
“People want to add value, and their ability to be sortie generators early will show that they can add value—that’s why this two-way career field strategy, I believe, is going to be a benefit for us in the retention area.”

"As they reach retirement, they deserve to understand what their fund can actually do to support them through the years ahead."
The push for better fund support comes as many Australians approach retirement facing significant savings shortfalls.
According to the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia, a single homeowner requires $630,000 and a couple $730,000 in super for a "comfortable" retirement.
However, Australian Taxation Office data reveal that the median super balance for those aged 60 to 64 is just over $200,000 — meaning retirees rely heavily on fund advice, tax strategies, and government pension integration to stretch their savings.
Wilson noted that the tick is not a product ranking or a directive to switch membership.
"The Tick is not a rating, ranking or recommendation of a super fund or financial product. There's no first place, second place or 'best fund'," she said.
Instead, it serves as a tool to help Australians "become a more informed super fund member and customer".
Which super funds received the Epic Retirement Tick?
Of 45 assessed regulated, defined-contribution funds, only eight met the benchmark for the 2026/2027 financial year.
Those were:
- AMP Super
- ART-Super Savings
- Aware Super
- Brighter Super
- Colonial First State - FirstChoice
- Hostplus
- UniSuper
- Vision Super
These funds performed well in several distinct categories, like tailored pension investment options, digital security, and advice access.
AMP, ART, Aware, Hostplus, and Vision Super were highlighted for allowing pension members to request ad-hoc payments and receive funds on the same day or via immediate OSKO transfers.
Funds like ART, AMP, and UniSuper also stood out for offering dedicated lifetime income options like annuities to provide members with guaranteed retirement income.
However, industry analysts note that the overall pass rate remains remarkably low.
Writing in Investment Magazine, Chant West general manager Ian Fryer highlighted that, to earn the badge, funds could no longer rely solely on offering specialised retirement products but also had to demonstrate meaningful member engagement.
For example, funds offering lifetime income options were assessed on whether their members were actually taking up those products.
What has changed this year?
Now in its second year, the Epic Retirement Tick has been awarded to three new funds in addition to last year's six — TelstraSuper having merged with Aware. AMP, Colonial, and Vision are all new additions to the benchmark.
The assessment framework has also been updated to target industry difficulties and raise consumer standards. The pass threshold was raised from 12 out of 18 to 14 out of 20, with a new requirement that funds have no outstanding regulatory enforcement actions.
The expanded 2026 criteria introduced tougher hurdles around digital service delivery, complaints management, and cybersecurity protections.
Investment performance criteria were refined to focus on a seven-year evaluation window, rather than 10 years, to allow a stronger emphasis on non-investment support features.
"Some have really stepped up to the plate," Wilson said. "Others are still working towards the standard, and there remains a meaningful gap between what some funds currently provide and what the criteria ask of them."
The Epic Retirement Tick is a proprietary badge issued by a private research firm, not a binding compliance benchmark.
It is separate to statutory government assessment through the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority.

Latvian parliament adopts amendments on minority languages, restricting use of Russian

Latvian parliament adopts amendments on minority languages, restricting use of Russian
According to Ukrinform, the Latvian public broadcaster LSM reported this in an article.
The Saeima of Latvia adopted the decision on Thursday, October 1. Fifty-five MPs voted in favor and 24 against.
Previously, public-service media were required to produce programs in the languages of national minorities. Following a ruling by Latvia's Constitutional Court on March 30, 2026, this framework had to be changed. The court ruled that content produced by the public broadcaster LSM should primarily be in Latvian.
According to the court, Russian is a self-sufficient minority language in Latvia, meaning the state is not required to provide additional support for it. At the same time, the court emphasized that support should be provided for minority languages that are not considered self-sufficient.
The court defines a self-sufficient minority language as one spoken by a significant proportion of the country's population and supported by a stable social structure, cultural organizations and media outlets. The court noted that Russian continues to be widely used in Latvia and that commercial broadcasters produce content in Russian.
According to the court, the previous obligation imposed on public-service media had contributed to the creation of a "parallel information space" and weakened the status of Latvian as the country's sole official language.
This summer, following a change of government, the Saeima began implementing the court's ruling, resulting in the amendments to the law.
Under the new rules, content in languages classified as self-sufficient, including Russian, may be produced in only three circumstances:
- in an emergency;
- in a state of emergency;
- when it is necessary to specifically refute only such information that is misleading, untrue and poses a threat to democracy and the Latvian state as a whole.
In the third case, the law requires public-service media, in accordance with the principle of proportionality, to take into account the intensity and nature of the threat to national security.
As Ukrinform reported, the Lithuanian parliament authorized the government to establish, from 2028, a Lithuanian-language proficiency requirement for taxi and ride-sharing service drivers.

Roundup: China provides practical pathway for Global South countries to seize opportunities in AI development -- experts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:20:01 CST
08:20:01 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- China's commitment to open source, openness, cooperation and sharing provides a practical pathway for Global South countries to seize opportunities in the development of artificial intelligence (AI) and bridge the North-South AI divide, experts have said.
At the 2026 Global South Modernization Forum, held Wednesday in Cairo, participants said modernization in the Global South is at an important stage of overcoming development constraints, bridging capability gaps and transforming growth drivers, stressing the need to make good use of AI to strengthen endogenous development momentum.
Former Egyptian Prime Minister Essam Sharaf said in his remarks that Global South countries face challenges related to resources, infrastructure and professional talent in developing AI.
AI could deepen the Global South's external dependence on software, algorithms, data, computing power and knowledge, thereby creating a new North-South divide, he said.
This requires Global South countries to strengthen cooperation, promote collaboration among research institutions and joint training, develop AI applications in local languages, and work together to build a responsible global AI governance system, Sharaf added.
Chen Zhimin, vice president of Fudan University, said that "the focus of the Global South is shifting from whether these countries can access and use technology to whether they can truly transform technology into their own development capacity."
These needs provide a clearer direction for deepening AI cooperation between China and Global South countries, he added.
Ezzat Saad, director of the Egyptian Council for Foreign Affairs, said AI cooperation between China and Global South countries could help better align China's experience with the development needs and priorities of the Global South.
Cai Fang, a member of the academic divisions of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, said China and other Global South countries face similar tasks in AI development, which makes experience sharing and mutual learning practically significant.
The experts and scholars said Global South countries should take a more active part in discussions and cooperation on AI ethics, security, data governance and standard-setting, thereby promoting a more inclusive international AI governance system.
Maged Botros, a political science professor at Capital University in Egypt, said AI development should take into account countries' different levels and stages of development and their specific needs.
Gustavo Lema, director of communication and information at the Latin American Council of Social Sciences, said China's promotion of open-source AI models and encouragement of AI applications tailored to local needs could help more Global South countries use and develop related technologies.
"Latin American countries have already begun using relevant Chinese technologies and tools to address climate change and improve production conditions, thereby better benefiting local people," he told Xinhua.
At a parallel forum titled "Advancing Mutual Learning Among Civilizations Through the Proper Use of AI," Yang Bojiang, president of the Institute of Global Civilizations, said the deeper integration of technological development and civilizational dialogue could make AI an important technological infrastructure for promoting exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations in the new era.
This could offer Global South countries a new path to modernization that both respects their cultural traditions and embraces the wave of modern technology, he added.
Yang Cheng, executive dean of the Shanghai Academy of Global Governance and Area Studies at Shanghai International Studies University, told Xinhua that AI cooperation between China and Arab countries should move beyond "technological cooperation" toward "joint civilizational development," with AI governance rules drawing more on the ethical resources embedded in the traditions of both sides and cooperation helping promote exchanges and mutual learning between civilizations.
AI is now being applied at an accelerating pace in specific sectors across the Global South.
The Egypt-based African Disaster Mitigation Research Center and Fudan University have jointly developed intelligent optoelectronic remote-sensing technology and established a research platform for disaster monitoring and early warning to meet Africa's disaster prevention and mitigation needs.
Mohamed ElGabry, director of the African Disaster Mitigation Research Center, told Xinhua that Chinese large AI models, characterized by open-source accessibility and inclusivity, provide more convenient technological conditions for Global South countries to leverage AI.
Joseph Olivier Mendo'o, executive director of the international exchange department of the China-Africa Business Council, told Xinhua that during visits to rural areas in China, he had seen firsthand the application of AI in agriculture.
"China seeks to demonstrate AI applications that can be adapted to local conditions. In the future, agriculture, healthcare and public services are expected to become important areas of China-Africa AI cooperation," he said.
Held under the theme "The Rise of Artificial Intelligence: Opportunities and Challenges for Modernization in the Global South," the forum drew more than 100 experts and scholars from nearly 30 countries and regions.
During the forum, "The Rise of the Global South: An Atlas of Academic Research on Modernization in the Global South" and "Top 10 Buzzwords in Global South Modernization Research of 2026" were released, and a session titled "Voices of Global South Youth" was held.
A series of youth exchange activities and think-tank seminars were organized before and after the forum. ■

News Analysis: EU tightens migration chain as return rules approved
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:19:58 CST
08:19:58 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- The European Union (EU) member states on Thursday gave final approval to a new regulation to accelerate the return of people with no legal right to stay, adding an enforcement mechanism to migration and asylum rules that took effect in June.
Under the new Return Regulation, EU countries will operate under common return procedures, including a new European Return Order, and gain the option of establishing so-called "return hubs" in non-EU countries.
According to the EU figure, around two in three people ordered to leave the bloc currently do not actually depart. The regulation complements the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which took effect on June 12.
The pact sets common rules for screening, asylum procedures, responsibility among member states and solidarity mechanisms, while the new regulation focuses on returning people found to have no right to stay.
The European Commission earlier described returns as the "missing piece" of the pact, while European Parliament rapporteur Malik Azmani called return the "final piece in Europe's migration system."
PRESSURE FOR GREATER CONTROL
The tougher return rules come after a turbulent summer that again pushed migration high up Europe's agenda.
On July 30 and 31, tens of thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta, prompting Madrid to deploy the military and triggering calls from several European governments for tighter border controls.
The crisis came only weeks after the migration pact entered into application and added urgency to a broader push for tougher enforcement.
Claire Kumar, head of policy and senior research fellow at ODI Europe, told Xinhua that public concern over irregular migration was strongly linked to a perceived "lack of control," with people expecting governments to demonstrate that borders and migration rules were effectively managed.
That pressure has become politically significant as mainstream parties face sustained pressure from right-wing and far-right forces advocating stricter migration controls, she added.
Pressure for further restrictions is also growing. Greece on Thursday proposed a mechanism that would allow EU countries to temporarily suspend asylum applications during large-scale arrivals deemed instrumentalized, with Germany, Austria, Denmark and Poland open to considering the idea.
These discussions suggest that the adoption of the Return Regulation may not mark the end of the EU's tightening migration agenda.
ENFORCEMENT MEETS REALITY
Yet passing a common return law does not guarantee a sharp rise in actual returns.
The German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) said in a recent analysis that return hubs are likely to remain limited in scale and heavily dependent on cooperation with third countries.
It said that persistent obstacles include establishing migrants' identities, obtaining travel documents, securing cooperation from countries of origin, and finding third countries willing to host return facilities. Such problems cannot simply be bypassed by moving parts of the return process outside Europe.
At the same time, Europe's aging economies still need migrant workers, Kumar said.
She said that beneath increasingly restrictive political rhetoric, labor demand remains a powerful driver of migration. If adequate legal pathways are unavailable, workers may still fill those jobs through irregular or informal channels, increasing risks of exploitation and labor-market informality.
The next test is implementation: whether the EU can turn its new legal powers into more effective returns while its aging economies continue to need migrant labor. ■

Canada lists Pacific Link oil pipeline project of national interest
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:19:38 CST
08:19:38 KST

OTTAWA, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Canadian government on Thursday designated a proposed West Coast oil pipeline, now named Pacific Link, as a project of national interest, a move aimed at reducing reliance on the United States and expanding energy exports to other markets.
The roughly 1,250-km pipeline would run from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a deepwater port near Delta, British Columbia, adding up to 1 million barrels per day of oil export capacity.
The project is the first to receive a national interest designation under the Building Canada Act. The designation allows it to undergo a streamlined federal regulatory review.
The pipeline would follow a southern route designed to avoid sensitive marine ecosystems along British Columbia's North Coast. The project is estimated to cost between 35.2 billion and 43.7 billion Canadian dollars (about 25.8 billion to 32 billion U.S. dollars).
Canada has the world's fourth largest proven oil reserves, but remains heavily dependent on the U.S. market. More than 90 percent of Canadian crude oil exports went to the United States in 2025.
The government said Pacific Link, together with improvements to the existing Trans Mountain pipeline system, could reduce Canada's dependence on U.S.-bound pipeline capacity from about 82-83 percent in 2025 to 65-70 percent.
The project is also expected to narrow the price differential between Western Canadian Select and West Texas Intermediate crude by 3 to 5 U.S. dollars per barrel, according to a government explanatory note. ■

Feature: Manneken-Pis dons Chinese attire for China's National Day
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:19:36 CST
08:19:36 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese national anthem echoed through Brussels' historic center on Thursday afternoon as Manneken-Pis - the Belgian capital's iconic little bronze statue - donned traditional Chinese attire to mark China's National Day.
Just a short walk from the Grand-Place, the unusual sight quickly drew a crowd. Tourists paused to take photos and videos of the tiny landmark in its Chinese outfit, while the sound of familiar Chinese melodies brought many Chinese visitors closer.
When a brass band struck up the Chinese national anthem, several Chinese visitors joined in singing. Some raised their phones to capture the moment; others quietly wiped away tears.
The Chinese Embassy in Belgium and the City of Brussels jointly held a dressing ceremony for Manneken-Pis to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China. More than 200 guests, local residents and tourists attended the event, including Li Yan, Charge d'Affaires a.i. of the Chinese Embassy in Belgium, and Brussels City Councillor Sevket Temiz.
The ceremony tapped into a tradition deeply woven into Brussels' identity. Manneken-Pis has a wardrobe of more than 1,200 costumes from around the world and is regularly dressed for festivals, commemorations and international occasions.
On Thursday, his traditional Chinese costume offered a distinctly Brussels way of marking China's National Day.
For Temiz, the small statue captured something larger about Brussels. "Seeing him dressed like this is a beautiful gesture of rapprochement between our countries and our cultures," he said.
Describing Brussels as an open city where languages, traditions and life stories intersect, Temiz said residents of Chinese origin, as well as Chinese merchants and entrepreneurs, have contributed to the city's diversity and the vitality of its neighborhoods.
"Beyond this day of celebration, it is encounters and exchanges that give all their strength to the ties between our peoples," he said.
Li said that Manneken-Pis has long been familiar to many Chinese people. This year's event also coincided with the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and Belgium.
She said China values openness, inclusiveness and friendship with people around the world, and stands ready to work with Belgium and other countries to write more chapters of friendship through mutual learning among civilizations.
Angelina Chan, a member of the Parliament of the Brussels-Capital Region, told Xinhua that China and Belgium share a strong friendship and should continue to build on it, noting that the two countries have complementary strengths and broad potential for cooperation.
Music provided another bridge between the two cultures. Belgium's Meyboom brass band performed both the Chinese national anthem and the traditional anthem of Manneken-Pis before turning to familiar Chinese melodies, including "Ode to the Motherland" and "Jasmine Flower."
For some Chinese tourists who happened upon the ceremony, the celebration was entirely unexpected. They had come to see one of Brussels' best-known landmarks, only to find Manneken-Pis dressed in Chinese attire on China's National Day. Some immediately sent videos of the scene to family and friends back home.
The ceremony also stirred memories for people in the crowd with their own connections to China.
A Belgian couple from Liege said they had visited Shanghai about a decade ago and still remembered the trip fondly. "We hope to take our children on a trip to China during next year's summer holidays," they told Xinhua. ■

Gulf oil exports rebound despite Iranian blockade on Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
23:10:44 UTC
08:10:44 KST

Breadcrumb
Gulf oil exports rebound despite Iranian blockade on Hormuz
Gulf oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz have rebounded to pre-war levels, according to a tracking platform, as more vessels prove willing to make the risky transit under US escort despite Iran's efforts to choke the waterway.
Before the Middle East war, around a fifth of the hydrocarbons consumed worldwide passed through the strategic chokepoint, which has become a major source of friction between Tehran and Washington.
Iran still claims control over the strait, and ships without its authorisation risk coming under attack, but more and more are making it out, and alternative routes meant to bypass the waterway are operating at full capacity.
Despite the rebound, experts stressed that the situation was far from normal, and Iran remains deprived of a large share of its own exports by a US counterblockade of its ports.
According to preliminary data from the commodity-tracking platform Kpler, non-Iranian crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz, from Gulf countries and Iraq, averaged 13.5 million barrels per day between 22 and 28 September - equivalent to pre-war levels.
"There are more players ready to try to get out of the Strait of Hormuz and succeed," TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanne told investors on Monday.
Saudi Arabia is benefiting from the reactivation of its East-West pipeline, which links the kingdom's main oil fields in the east to its Yanbu terminal on the Red Sea, allowing it to bypass Hormuz.
Shut down on 11 September after being hit by strikes launched from Iraq, the pipeline resumed operations on 22 September, according to Amena Bakr, an analyst at Kpler.
Based on data from the platform on Wednesday, at least 10 tankers left Yanbu loaded with crude over the weekend.
On Sunday, 9.5 million barrels were exported from the terminal area, a volume unseen since the start of the conflict.
The United Arab Emirates are also able to bypass the Hormuz thanks to their pipeline linking Abu Dhabi's fields to Fujairah, a terminal just outside the strait on the Gulf of Oman.
The resumption of traffic comes as negotiations have restarted between Washington and Tehran, focused on restoring freedom of navigation in the strait.
Iran has proposed to reopen it in exchange for the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade, among other conditions.
Washington has rejected the plan, but indirect talks are ongoing.
The current situation provides some respite for the oil monarchies, but it is not a lasting solution, said Sanam Vakil of the UK-based think tank Chatham House.
"The Gulf states all recognise that the current arrangement is not sustainable. They depend on the United States to secure the maritime routes and keep exports flowing but they also know that military protection is not a substitute for a political understanding with Tehran," she told AFP.
"The regional trajectory still points toward greater escalation rather than a durable status quo, so higher exports today should not be mistaken for a new normal."
In a sign of persistent market concerns, international benchmark Brent remains above $100 a barrel.
Traffic in the Strait of Hormuz - all goods combined - remains far below its pre-war level, and ships continue to face risks when transiting.
British maritime agency UKMTO said unknown projectiles struck three ships in the waterway on Tuesday and again on Thursday.
Last week, an attack on a cargo ship there killed an Indian sailor, according to Omani and Indian authorities.
And another sticking point has emerged.
The Iran-backed Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them seize Yemen's entire Red Sea coast, including the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital shipping lane.
The violence has disrupted exports from Saudi Arabia, the world's leading supplier of crude oil, as well as maritime traffic.

Falling glass and ‘decapitated’ plants: the race to protect Edinburgh botanic garden’s plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
23:01:03 UTC
08:01:03 KST

In the early autumn sunlight, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh’s extensive plant collection appears safe in their glass enclosures. But danger lurks from above for the tropical ferns, cycads and rare alpine heathers.
Soon the September sunshine will give way to the storms and gales of the Scottish winter, which can bring hundreds of glass panels crashing to the greenhouse floor on the windiest days. Nobody is allowed inside when the wind is above 30mph.
“We’ve had plants that have essentially been decapitated by falling bits of glass,” says Sadie Barber, the glasshouse curator at RBGE. “You go into one of these tropical spaces in winter and there’s icy air coming in. It’s traumatic for those of us who put decades into caring for these plants. A storm can literally just wipe them out.”
But this week, change is in the air for the creaking infrastructure at the 356-year-old botanic garden, the second oldest in Britain after Oxford. On Friday, the palm houses are reopening after five years of painstaking restoration work, complete with 5,750 panels of toughened glass to keep out the elements.
Before they closed for renovation works, the horticultural team had installed a net in case panels fell from the weathered structure. The new ones are not bulletproof – but they are strong enough to resist a bird strike.
Part-Georgian, part-Victorian, the £23.5m refurbishment has kept nearly all of the original sandstone and wrought iron shell. Inside, more than 600 temperate plants have returned to the building. The air is clean and crisp, purified by ferns that naturally remove toxins from the air. Its temperature and humidity is still controlled by the original pulleys and winches.
“We have made it one vast cathedral-like space for temperate plants,” says Prof Julia Knights, the garden’s regius Keeper and the royally appointed chief executive. She points out her favourite tree fern, which comes from Tasmania and has a Scottish liverwort growing on its woody stem. “They can grow outside in our botanic garden in Logan on the west coast of Scotland because of the oceanic climate,” she says.
Founded by two physicians in 1670 to teach doctors about medicinal plants, RBGE has morphed into one of the most important collections of plant biodiversity in the world. Its research glasshouses are stuffed with rare ginger species, bananas, blueberries and dozens of begonias.
It is a global authority on rhododendrons and ferns, houses rare plant species that have gone extinct in the wild, and its scientists have helped pioneer new technology, such as DNA barcoding which is used to identify plant species. Arthur Conan Doyle studied here, infusing Sherlock Holmes novels with his botanical knowledge. Today, conservation is its primary focus.
“Our conservation collections are so important to have. The threats are extreme in the wild,” said Prof Pete Hollingsworth, RBGE’s director of science. “The driver[s] for environmental damage are so strong, so having these ex situ safe sites is really important,” he said.
But the restored palm houses aside, many of the glasshouses used to care for the plants are decades past their originally intended lifespan and are waiting for upgrades. Leaks from Scottish rain rot the rootstock of plants, sometimes killing them. Last year, horticulturalists were not allowed inside the greenhouses for 20 days due to high winds. In 2026, they have been shut out 15 times. When they return, they have often worn hard hats and safety gear to pick out the broken glass.
“The glasshouses are the one thing we don’t want to break. It’s the plants inside that suffer,” said Barber. “I was looking at one of our records the other day of a plant we lost in the lowland tropical house. It just had ‘storm’ written next to it. It had either suffered from the cold, or even been cut by falling glass.”

"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work."
The San Francisco-based AI lab did not confirm their identities but at least two of the employees worked on safety and alignment, according to the Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg.
Rogue OpenAI agents covered up their tracks
Meanwhile, according to a report artificial intelligence agents developed by OpenAI tried to erase traces of their activity after gaining unauthorized access to government websites.
Cybersecurity firm Asymmetric Security analysed the activity of the agents — AI programmes capable of acting autonomously — which targeted Australian government websites and other public bodies between March and September.
Asymmetric said on Thursday that it could not determine whether the agents' cover-up was deliberate.
The report adds to investigations by OpenAI and independent researchers into a series of incidents disclosed since July, including the hacking of AI platform Hugging Face.
OpenAI itself described the attack on Hugging Face as the first of its kind.
These analyses aim to gauge the capabilities of autonomous AI tools, as their lapses fuel fears of losing control over the technology.
According to Asymmetric, the agents were able to refine their techniques in a matter of days, a process that typically takes traditional hackers months or even years.
The incidents reviewed in the report appear to have begun with "innocent tasks," such as gathering Australian health statistics, which then went off course.
"Most of the activity we've reviewed so far involved routine research tasks, such as accessing public web content to answer questions," an OpenAI spokesperson told AFP.
"Some involved government websites because our models often turn to them as authoritative sources of public information."
Calls to pace AI development
Asymmetric's report found, however, that the agents opened private accounts on a website analytics service, which concealed their searches, and created temporary email inboxes, one of which was set to self-delete after 48 hours.
OpenAI acknowledged in late August that its models had sometimes tried, unsuccessfully, to erase or modify their own activity logs during internal tests.
The incidents have amplified calls to slow AI development, most notably from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who wrote last month that he feared swarms of agents "taking over the entire internet."
But there is no consensus within the industry or among regulators on how to proceed.
The Trump administration opposes any binding regulation that could hinder innovation, amid fierce competition with China.
On Tuesday, President Donald Trump met with tech executives, who adopted a voluntary code of conduct.
No federal law specifically governs these models in the United States.

US Navy awards RTX’s Raytheon US$24.4b contract for Standard Missile-6 amid stockpile concerns
- RTX’s Raytheon unit won a US$24.4 billion contract to produce Standard Missile-6 interceptors for the US Navy to replenish depleted munitions stockpiles.
- The five-year contract aims to ensure a steady supply of SM-6 missiles, capable of offensive strikes and missile defence, supporting the Pentagon’s push for faster weapons production.
- RTX has invested in workforce expansion, partnerships, and automation to meet rising demand, while Congress has yet to approve funding for these large defence contracts.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – RTX’s Raytheon unit won a multiyear contract worth up to US$24.4 billion (S$31.2 billion) to produce Standard Missile-6 interceptors for the US Navy, the service said on Oct 1, as the Pentagon pushes to replenish munitions stockpiles depleted by conflicts in the Middle East.
The five-year contract, which includes two additional option years, the Navy said, is meant to provide a steady and reliable supply of the SM-6, a missile that can carry out both offensive strikes and missile defence missions.
The SM-6 award is the latest in a series of large munitions contracts the Pentagon has pursued in 2026 to pressure contractors into ramping up output faster. It follows a US$20.7 billion provisional multi-year deal for Raytheon’s AMRAAM air-to-air missiles in late September and a US$58.6 billion Patriot interceptor deal awarded to Lockheed Martin in July.
The production agreements are designed to entice contractors to move faster on increasing output. They are part of a broader push by the Trump administration to prioritise weapons production over shareholder returns.
Industry executives have warned that Congress has not yet appropriated funding for the deals, meaning contractors may be unable to invest at scale in components and facilities until lawmakers act.
RTX has said it has invested heavily to keep up with rising demand. It has expanded its skilled workforce, strengthened partnerships across the defence industrial base and automated production, with the aim of significantly increasing output for near- and long-term needs.
Raytheon says the SM-6 is the only combat-proven weapon that can perform anti-air warfare, anti-surface warfare and ballistic missile defence. It has been fired from a range of Navy ships as well as from land-based launchers. REUTERS

Spain housing protests continue as parliament prepares to vote on measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
22:54:39 UTC
07:54:39 KST

Şenhan Bolelli
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Protests over Spain's housing crisis continued in Madrid on Thursday, with more than 300 tents filling the capital's central Sol Square.
The demonstrations, which began Sept. 26, have been backed by left-wing and far-left civil society groups.
Protesters have held public meetings and called for neighborhood committees to be established to campaign for a general strike over housing.
Hundreds of protesters banged pots and pans, while smaller groups also demonstrated in cities including Barcelona, Seville and Las Palmas.
The protests come as Spain's parliament prepares to vote on two government decrees aimed at addressing the housing crisis.
The opposition People's Party and Vox have said they will vote against the measures. Their passage is expected to depend on smaller parties from the Basque Country and Catalonia.
One decree would introduce automatic, indefinite extensions for rental contracts, with rent increases linked to the consumer price index.
Landlords refusing the extensions would have to compensate tenants. The measure is expected to be rejected.
A second decree, which is expected to pass, would extend some rental contracts by two years, suspend forced evictions until 2030 and introduce new rules for seasonal and room rentals.
It would also prevent rent increases in contracts exceeding housing price index limits.
The decree would also ban certain high-risk investment funds, described as "vulture funds," from buying homes until 2028.
The government said the measures would benefit about 5 million people covered by 1.89 million rental contracts.
The housing crisis has become a major political issue in Spain.
The issue drew further attention last month when 87-year-old Mari Carmen was forcibly evicted from a Madrid home where she had lived for 70 years.
Following an agreement involving Madrid City Council and a property investment company, she is expected to return home under a new eight-year rental contract, paying 30% of her pension in rent.

Pilots of crashed Amazon cargo plane were unaware of wind conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
22:53:16 UTC
07:53:16 KST

Pilots of crashed Amazon cargo plane were unaware of wind conditions
- The Miami-based 21 Air cargo plane operating for Amazon crashed due to excessive speed, unused braking systems, and lack of wind information from air traffic control, killing five people.
- The NTSB report revealed the pilots were unaware of critical wind conditions as the FAA controller did not provide required wind data during landing clearance.
- Amazon paused use of 21 Air, and 21 Air's leadership is reviewing the report to improve safety and operational risk management following the crash investigation.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The pilots of a Miami-based 21 Air cargo plane operating for Amazon.com that crashed in Miami in September, killing five people, were unaware of wind conditions, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said on Oct 1.
The NTSB’s preliminary report is the first detailed account of the Sept 6 crash and points to a series of likely failures – from excessive speed and unused braking systems to missing wind information from an air traffic controller – that may have led to one of the deadliest US runway accidents in years.
The 21 Air-operated cargo flight for Amazon Air, which is Amazon’s cargo logistics network, overran a runway while landing at Miami International Airport and struck two vehicles on the ground. Amazon has since paused use of 21 Air.
The NTSB said a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) air traffic controller issued a landing clearance, but did not provide information on the wind as required by the FAA.
About four minutes before issuing the landing clearance, when asked by another flight for wind information, the controller stated winds were from 190 deg at 19 knots with gusts to 22 knots. The 21 Air flight was not on the radio frequency at the time, the NTSB said.
The FAA did not immediately comment.
The aircraft was a 32-year-old Boeing 767-300 freighter that had previously operated as a passenger jet for various airlines from 1994 to 2015.
The NTSB said the captain of the 21 Air-operated plane considered aborting the landing after the aircraft touched down, citing evidence from a flight data recorder.
The NTSB said the first officer cautioned the captain they were flying “too fast” just over a minute before touching down on the runway that they overran and made additional comments about the airplane’s excessive speed.
The NTSB said the captain did not verbally acknowledge all of the first officer’s comments about speed. The NTSB said data showed the speed brakes remained stowed and the thrust reversers did not deploy during the landing.
The airplane touched down about 1,143m past the start of the runway at a groundspeed of 160 knots.
The cargo plane was on its third flight of the day, coming from San Juan, Puerto Rico. It had flown from Cincinnati to Miami and from Miami to San Juan earlier before the crash.
Amazon said it remains committed to supporting the NTSB’s ongoing investigation.
21 Air said its “executive leadership team is actively engaged in managing operational risk and fostering a culture of accountability and continuous improvement”.
The company added it is reviewing the NTSB preliminary report and “will take all appropriate action to improve our safety based on the facts as they are established”. REUTERS

No uniform explanation for collegium decisions on compassionate transfers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
22:47:03 UTC
07:47:03 KST

The five-member collegium on Sept 28 recommended the repatriation of Justice T Vinod Kumar from Madras HC to his parent HC in Telangana 'in view of his ensuing retirement on Nov 16'
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court collegium's decisions to transfer judges from one HC to another are explained as being meant "for the better administration of justice". But the standard reasoning does not translate into a uniform explanation, with the collegium showing unusual compassion in approving requests from some for transfer or repatriation due to difficult family situations or health issues, while maintaining aloofness from others.There are many judges in HCs who have expressed resentment at the absence of any procedure or norm for transfer of HC judges. A member of the collegium, who will go on to become CJI, has mooted framing a transparent transfer policy. He told TOI that a judge under consideration for transfer should be warned first to mend his ways and be kept under watch for some time. Only when he does not improve should he be transferred, he said.The five-member collegium on Sept 28 recommended the repatriation of Justice T Vinod Kumar from Madras HC to his parent HC in Telangana "in view of his ensuing retirement on Nov 16". Justice Kumar was transferred from Telangana HC to Madras HC in May last year by the SC collegium headed by then CJI BR Gavai.In May last year, a complaint had reached the SC alleging that Justice Kumar, heading a division bench, had kept more than 50 judgments reserved.
Sitting as a single judge, he had reserved verdicts in over 170 cases since 2020. If Justice Kumar's imminent retirement was a ground for his repatriation, no such consideration was shown to Justice D Nagarjun, who was transferred from Telangana HC to Madras HC. Justice Nagarjun, a career judicial officer who was elevated as an HC judge in March 2022, was transferred to Madras HC in April 2023.
As he was due to retire on Aug 14, 2024, he sent a request to the CJI on July 25, 2024, for repatriation to his parent HC in Telangana, but the collegium remained aloof to the request and allowed him to retire in Madras HC.A Punjab and Haryana HC judge represented against his transfer to another HC, citing his wife's serious illness and disability of his child. But that evoked no compassion with the collegium, which remained firm on his transfer.Justice D V Ramana, who was only 13 years old when his railway gangman father died in an accident, rose from humble backgrounds to become a judge of Andhra Pradesh HC in Aug 2022. He was transferred to Madhya Pradesh HC in Nov 2023. On his retirement in May last year, he gave vent to his frustration. Abiy is facing an alliance of several rebel organizations opposed to his government in Ethiopia, a country made up of about 80 ethnic groups, four years after the end of the bloody civil war against Tigrayan rebels.
Alamata is an important supply hub for food and fuel and lies in southern Tigray along the border with neighboring Amhara, where fighting is also underway between rebels and government forces.
Another neighboring region where clashes have been reported in recent days is Afar. There, rebels were reported this week to have made gains by capturing the town of Arbati, about 60 kilometers south of Tigray.
Ethiopia’s civil war began in 2020 between the federal army and allied militias on one side and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front on the other.
Tigrayans had been the dominant force in national Ethiopian politics for decades, until Abiy came to power in 2018 following a broad wave of protests. They later felt increasingly marginalized and stripped of their former status.
The war that erupted after they rebelled against the federal government is estimated to have caused one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters in recent years, with at least 500,000 people killed, whether directly in fighting and violence or as a result of disease or hunger.
More than 1 million of Tigray’s roughly 6 million residents fled their homes, while the region’s economy suffered massive destruction and its health system collapsed.
The war ended in November 2022 with the Pretoria Agreement, which was intended to bring the conflict to a close. But some of its provisions were never implemented, and tensions gradually returned and intensified.
By the beginning of this year, a brief new round of fighting had already been reported in Tigray.
In May, the TPLF ousted the local administration that had been appointed to govern the northern region under the Pretoria Agreement. In June, the Tigrayan rebels, together with Ethiopia’s main opposition parties, boycotted national elections won by Abiy’s ruling party.
Both sides accused each other of violating the peace agreement, and since August there have also been reports of renewed airstrikes by Abiy’s military against Tigrayan forces.
Tensions peaked last Sunday, when the TPLF announced the formation of an alliance with six other armed groups waging their own insurgencies in Ethiopia, including the Oromo Liberation Army, or OLA, and the Fano militia from Amhara, with the declared goal of toppling Abiy’s government.
Three days after the alliance was formed, Tigrayan rebels launched a large-scale offensive against government forces and said they were waging a “total defensive war” against Abiy, a former Nobel Peace Prize laureate.

07:43:22 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia expects to seize the remaining Ukrainian-held areas of the Donetsk region much sooner than Ukraine and European countries anticipate.
Speaking at a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow, Putin said Kyiv and Europe believe the areas could be held for another one-and-a-half to two years.
"High-ranking officials in Ukraine say they will hold the remaining 11% of the territory of the Donetsk People’s Republic for another year and a half. In Europe, they say Ukraine will hold it for two years. We believe this (Russia’s seizure of the remaining areas) will happen much earlier, given the pace of our troops’ advance," he said.
According to Putin, Russian forces brought 1,301 square kilometers (502 square miles) under their control in September, which he said was two and a half times more than in previous months, adding the pace of their advance was increasing.
He reiterated Moscow's position about wishing to end the conflict as soon as possible through negotiations.
Putin conditioned the end of the conflict on receiving security guarantees from Western countries and creating conditions for a lasting peace.
Ukraine’s neutral status also remains among Russia’s goals, he said.
Putin said a settlement should address issues including the Russian language and the Orthodox Church in Ukraine, adding that it would be preferable to avoid further casualties on both sides and reach political solutions.
He also said that Russia had been ready to resume negotiations immediately after its Sept. 18-21 legislative elections but that Ukrainian strikes during the voting prevented this.
"They don't hold elections themselves, and they tried to stop us. From the evening of Sept. 19 to the morning of Sept. 20, more than 1,600 drones were launched in an attempt to breach Moscow’s air defenses and attack the capital and polling stations in other Russian regions," he said.
Putin said Russia was receiving calls to stop its strikes against Ukrainian vessels in the Black Sea but rejected the idea, saying Moscow had begun responding after Ukrainian attacks on Russian tankers and other vessels carrying civilian cargo.
"Now, from all sides, we are being told: 'Why don't you stop?' They started it. So get a grenade, fascist, from a Soviet soldier," he said.
He said Russian strikes in the Black Sea had been directed at military vessels or ships carrying military equipment while Moscow would respond to attempts to detain Russian vessels “symmetrically,” whether in the Baltic or the Atlantic.
Putin also linked the issue to Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, saying Moscow had responded by targeting facilities important to Ukraine’s economy.
He said that according to Russian estimates, the attacks on Russian refineries had cost the country about 1% of its GDP.
Commenting on proposals to stop strikes on Ukrainian vessels in exchange for an end to attacks on Russian refineries, he said such an arrangement could only be discussed on the basis of mutual interests.
"Let them stop hitting your refineries, and you stop hitting their ships. Let them export civilian goods and agricultural products, they say to us. What about our other civilian cargoes such as oil, petroleum products?" he said.
He emphasized that Russia oil and petroleum products will not enter the world markets in any case because there are bans and sanctions against them, and therefore, this step would only favor Ukraine.
Putin also thanked US first lady Melania Trump for assisting in humanitarian issues between Russia and Ukraine.
He also rejected statements that Russia was nationalizing European assets, calling them "a lie and a provocation," and said Western owners could regain their assets in Russia if conditions developed favorably.
"We are not taking anything from anyone and we are not nationalizing anything," he said, referring to Russian measures affecting foreign-owned assets.
Putin said Russia was closely monitoring where weapons supplied to Ukraine were coming from, distinguishing between arms deliveries and direct Western involvement in strikes deep inside Russian territory.
"When someone wants to fight us with someone else’s hands, in this case with the hands of the Ukrainian regime, which is effectively sending its people to be shot and killed, when someone starts fighting us with someone else’s hands, this is, of course, a threat," he noted.
He said Moscow had no plans to attack countries supplying weapons to Ukraine and generally has no plans to attack any Western country "neither in 2029, nor in 2030, nor in 2050" but argued that Western technical specialists involved in strikes deep inside Russia represented a different level of involvement.
On the Palestinian issue, he said it can be resolved only through the creation of a full-fledged Palestinian state. He also doubted the idea that US policy toward Palestine is dictated by Israel.

====================================================================================================

We Picked the Best AI Model Six Months Ago. So I Tested It Again.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
22:37:59 UTC
07:37:59 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
How a dozen images, a sealed answer key, and one blind grader settled a hunch
The hotspot that taught the wrong answer
In this article, I explain how we tested a Sage Studio system to improve one of our asset types. I think this methodology has broad application and may be applicable to work you’re doing.
One of the activity types we build in Sage Studio is an image hotspot. A learner sees an illustration, say a food wheel or a map of a park, and is able to click on (or keyboard to) parts of it to learn what each part is.
We generate the illustration with AI and then use a second AI model to examine the finished image and work out where each clickable label should go. For example, in the food wheel image, we’d want the “Proteins” hotspot to go on the fish and the eggs and the “Carbohydrates” hotspot over the bread and pasta.
Typically, this is done manually but because Sage Studio builds at scale, we worked out a way to automate this using AI.
Most of the time, it works quite well. When it doesn’t, the result is worse than a missing hotspot. A learner clicks on the bread and is told it’s protein. The activity doesn’t just fail to teach. It teaches the wrong thing. Thankfully, the tool has a way to hand edit the hotspots very easily so these can be caught in a test pass. But we continually work to improve the system’s accuracy.
We chose the model that reads those images months ago, when it was clearly the best at this kind of task. AI models don’t stand still, though. Newer models have arrived since then, and my experience confirmed that the technology had advanced to the point where it was worth another exploration to see if we could improve the subsystem for this type of asset.
So we tested it.
Keep the test small and real
The temptation with any evaluation is to build something big with a hundred images, a scoring rubric with twelve criteria, and a spreadsheet that ends up needing its own spreadsheet. You know the story.
We went the other way. We pulled 12 images that had already shipped in courses for a K-12 curriculum partner, spread across 11 different courses: a food wheel, a theatre stage, a park map, a market square, a kitchen, a set of geometric shapes, and so on. Together they had 53 hotspots to place across those images.
We made two choices that mattered more than the sample size.
- 
We used real work, not demo images. Demo images are clean. Real course images are whatever the image generator produced on some random Tuesday afternoon months ago. If the model has to cope with the messy ones in production, it should be tested on the messy ones from production.
- 
We changed one thing. Each model got the same image, the same instructions, and the same fallback steps the production system uses. The only thing that changed was the model. By changing just the one thing, we were able to clearly determine what we wanted: did accuracy improve?
We tested three models: the one we’d been using (Gemini 2.5 Flash) and two newer ones (GPT-5.4 and GPT-6 Sol). Note that the focus here is not the models themselves but the methodology we used for getting to our answer. This is not an argument about models.
Plan A for the answer key failed
To score anything, you need to know what would constitute success. That is, what is the goal you’re trying to reach and how do the individual tests measure up to that goal.
We thought we had a clever shortcut. Each target object in our illustrations is generated with a visual cue the model can look for. If the cue was there in the pixels, a short script could find each object and compute exactly where its label belonged. No human judgment required.
It didn’t work. The image generator got close to the cue, but not close enough to measure against. On most images the script couldn’t find the targets at all.
This is the part I’d underline for anyone running their own test: check that your answer key works before you trust it. If we hadn’t checked, we’d have scored the models against noise and drawn confident conclusions from it.
Plan B: grade it blind
So we graded by eye. To keep that honest, we borrowed a trick from taste tests.
For each image, every model’s hotspot placements were drawn on its own copy of the picture. The three copies were labelled A, B and C, in a different random order for each image. The key that said which letter stood for which model was set aside, unopened, until every hotspot had been graded.
The first grader was Claude, working with me on the research. It marked each hotspot as on the right object or not, image by image, without knowing which model had placed the hotspots for that image. Then I went through the images myself and did my own visual assessment. Finally, I checked sheets myself and checked Claude’s grading with my score and we generally agreed.
One of the twelve grading sheets. The graders saw only A, B and C.
We did one more thing that mattered. We threw out test items that had no right answer. One image, a living room, had labels for breakfast, a car, swimming and bedtime. None of those things were in the picture. You can’t score a model on finding an object that was never drawn. (Interestingly, one model declined to place those labels at all, which is arguably the correct response.) That left 44 hotspots we could fairly grade.
When the test item is broken, take it out of the score, and write down why.
What we found
- 
Gemini 2.5 Flash (our old pick): 26 of 44 (59%) completed in 17 seconds
- 
GPT 4.5: 42 of 44 (95%) completed in 4 seconds
- 
GPT-6 Sol: 42 of 44 (95%) completed in 8 seconds
The intuition that newer models would perform better was right and the gap was bigger than I expected.
Before you reads this as a vendor scorecard, it’s not. The Gemini model we tested is the one we happened to be running. It’s two generations behind Google’s current models, and we didn’t test the newer ones. This isn’t “OpenAI beats Google.” It’s “the model we picked months ago is no longer the best choice for this job.” That’s really what we were testing and it drove the entire exercise.
Further, the number that mattered most wasn’t the accuracy percentage, but how each model failed.
The older model’s misses were mostly swaps. On the food wheel it put “proteins” on the grains and “vitamins” on the dairy. On the park map, most of the labels landed on the path instead of the places they named. These aren’t near misses but wrong answers that a learner would trust.
Same image, same instructions. Only the models changed.
The newer models’s four misses were neighbors on the image. In the park image for instance, “pollen” was put on the bee instead of the pollen floating around it and “flower bed” on the bush beside it. One label was simply left unplaced. The model got it close but it’s placement was and in each case the right answer was right next to the incorrect one.
If you only count hits and misses, those look the same. For the learner, they can matter a lot as near neighbors can at least make sense where as wrong placement is just wrong.
Try it yourself
If you’ve picked an AI model for a specific job and haven’t looked at that decision since, here’s the short version of what worked for us:
- 
Re-test your defaults. Models change every few months. A choice that was right in the spring may not be right in the fall.
- 
Use a small sample of your real work. A dozen examples is enough to see a big gap. If the gap is small, then it’s time for a bigger test.
- 
Change one thing. Same inputs, same instructions, different model.
- 
Prove your answer key before you use it. If you can’t tell what “right” looks like, a score won’t mean much.
- 
Grade the results blind. Hide which model produced which results until the grading is done. An AI can do the grading if a person checks its work. If you use an AI tool to do the grading, try to use one not used to generate the results.
- 
Look at how it fails, not just how often. A near miss and a confident wrong answer are not the same mistake.
- 
Remove broken test items, and keep a note. A bad test item is often a clue about a problem somewhere else.
- 
Say what the test can’t tell you. Our tests involved 12 images, one style of illustration, and one grader. That’s enough for us to make this decision given that we’ve already run hundreds of these through production. It isn’t enough to rank the industry.
The whole exercise took an afternoon, and the model costs were small enough to justify them. The hunch was right, but now we know by how much, and why.
I’m curious: when was the last time you went back and re-tested a decision you made about an AI tool? Tell me in the comments.

Arab party chief quits Knesset race after Supreme Court signals ban over alleged terror support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
22:34:09 UTC
07:34:09 KST

Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh will not run in Israel’s upcoming election after his party decided Thursday night to withdraw his candidacy, following a Supreme Court hearing in which the court’s president told him that a majority of the nine-justice panel supported his disqualification.
Abu Shehadeh, No. 3 on the Joint List slate, had appealed a Central Elections Committee decision seeking to bar him from running. During Thursday’s hearing, Chief Justice Yitzhak Amit suggested that Abu Shehadeh withdraw his candidacy, which would spare the court from issuing a formal ruling on the matter.
“We recommend that Abu Shehadeh consider whether he wishes to maintain his candidacy or withdraw it, which would make a ruling unnecessary,” Amit told him, after informing him that a majority of the judges supported his disqualification. Following several strongly worded statements from Balad and the Joint List, the party decided to withdraw his candidacy.
The Supreme Court hearing on the Central Elections Committee’s decision regarding Abu Shehadeh was held before an expanded panel of nine justices. The judges also considered decisions concerning the Joint List, the Islamist Ra’am party and lawmaker Ofer Cassif. The Hebrew report said those disqualifications were widely expected to be overturned.
The case against Abu Shehadeh centered on an article he published on Oct. 8, 2023, one day after the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attack. In the article, he described the assault on communities near the Gaza border as “an important historic event from a military, political and strategic perspective.”
“If small, besieged Gaza managed to do this, others can do it more effectively and easily,” he wrote.
Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara and State Attorney Amit Aisman supported barring Abu Shehadeh from the election. In their submission, they argued that his statements amounted to support for armed struggle against Israel, one of the legal grounds cited in the effort to disqualify him. Abu Shehadeh denied supporting violence or terrorism.
“I advanced issues and legislation for people with disabilities in the Knesset,” Abu Shehadeh told the judges. “My entire life I have dealt with human rights, including together with Jewish Knesset members. I ask you to allow me to continue.”
Justice Alex Stein challenged him over his public record.
“You have a great many publications in English,” Stein said. “Perhaps show me one article in which you wrote in English that Hamas is a terrorist organization.”
“There is no such article,” Abu Shehadeh replied.
Stein responded: “What Abu Shehadeh is saying is cheap talk. When a person no longer has anything to lose, he will say anything. Show me one time when Abu Shehadeh, when he had something to lose, said something different. Show me one article in English in which he called Hamas a ‘terrorist organization.’ Show me one time when he said acts were ‘terrorism.’ He has dozens of articles. Is there anything like that?”
Balad said overnight that Abu Shehadeh’s withdrawal did not mark the end of his political activity.
“The withdrawal of the candidacy is not the end of Abu Shehadeh’s political struggle, nor is it the end of Balad’s struggle,” the party said. “Abu Shehadeh continues to lead the party, Balad continues its project, and the Joint List continues its struggle to strengthen Arab representation and contribute to bringing down the Netanyahu-Ben-Gvir government.”
The party said the decision was taken following the Supreme Court hearing and the judges’ proposal.
“After an in-depth and responsible discussion, and in full consultation with comrade Sami Abu Shehadeh and a broad team of Arab lawyers, the central committee decided to approve the withdrawal of his candidacy in the election, out of political responsibility toward our people, toward the Joint List and because of the serious implications for political and parliamentary activity as a whole,” Balad said.
Balad also argued that the case had broader implications for Arab political participation in Israel.
“The decision was made only after it became clear that serious harm could be caused to political parties in general and to national parliamentary work in particular,” the party said. “The issue has already gone beyond the question of Sami Abu Shehadeh’s personal candidacy and has become a matter involving serious questions about the limits of political legitimacy granted to Arab citizens, as well as the use of disqualification as a tool to restrict the scope of Arab political activity and persecute national positions that fall outside the Israeli consensus.”
Religious Zionism party chairman Bezalel Smotrich criticized Amit’s proposal, arguing that the Supreme Court president should have issued a formal ruling rather than offer Abu Shehadeh the opportunity to withdraw.
“Yitzhak Amit does not want and is incapable of writing a simple ruling saying that supporters of terrorism, who support armed struggle against the State of Israel, like this despicable Abu Shehadeh, who supported the worst massacre suffered by the Jewish people since the Holocaust, are barred from running for the Knesset,” Smotrich said, “and instead he begs him to withdraw.”
Smotrich later wrote: “Yitzhak Amit is laughing at us all the way to the ballot box.” These were Smotrich’s characterizations of Abu Shehadeh and the court’s handling of the case.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose Otzma Yehudit party sought Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification, also welcomed his withdrawal while criticizing the absence of a formal ruling.
“We promised, and we delivered,” Ben-Gvir said. “I am glad that the struggle we led resulted in Sami Abu Shehadeh’s departure from the Knesset, following what he wrote and his support for Hamas a day after Oct. 7. At the same time, it is regrettable that the Supreme Court allowed him to withdraw without issuing a ruling on the disqualification.”
“Otzma Yehudit will continue fighting with all its strength against supporters of terrorism and haters of Israel who seek to enter the Knesset,” he added. “Abu Shehadeh will watch the next Knesset on Channel 99. Out with Abu Shehadeh!” Ben-Gvir’s claim that Abu Shehadeh supported Hamas was part of the political and legal dispute surrounding the candidacy; Abu Shehadeh denied supporting violence or terrorism.
Yashar! party chairman Gadi Eisenkot responded by posting a video in which Abu Shehadeh discussed contacts between Balad and Likud.
“On behalf of the entire Yashar! party, I would like to express my condolences to Likud and Netanyahu over the disqualification of a true partner in the Likud-Balad alliance,” Eisenkot wrote sarcastically. “Everyone in the Knesset knows how deep the relationship runs. Now Israel’s citizens do too. Sending strength.”
