====================================================================================================

Christa Pike getting 'life-saving medical care' after surviving Tennessee execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:34:05 UTC
06:34:05 KST

Christa Pike was critically ill and receiving "life-saving medical care" in a Nashville hospital on Thursday hours after she survived two attempts by Tennessee to execute her with lethal injections, her lawyers said, renewing scrutiny of capital punishment in the US.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in the 1990s after being convicted of a murder she carried out as a teenager. Her botched execution on Wednesday at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, the second this year in Tennessee, highlights the difficulties US states face in carrying out lethal injections and finding suitable alternative methods of capital punishment.
"Christa is alive right now," Randall Spivey, one of Pike's lawyers who was a witness at the execution attempt, told reporters on Thursday afternoon. "We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now."
Her lawyers repeated their calls for Pike's sentence to be commuted to life in prison after enduring what they called "chemical torture." Tennessee has suspended all executions for the rest of the year while it investigates the incident.
Failed executions
While botched lethal injections are not rare, they usually involve difficulties at the first step: setting intravenous lines in the condemned prisoner's body. Pike's case is unusual in that prison officials appeared to succeed in injecting the drugs into her with two syringes, causing her right arm to "turn purple" and her skin to blister at the injection sites, Spivey said.
She appears to be the first person known to have survived after execution drugs entered her body, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a non-profit group in Washington.
"This failed attempt is the worst we've ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," Robin Maher, the center's director, said in a statement.
After the second injection, Pike said her arm hurt and felt like it was "about to explode," her lawyers said, suggesting to them that the execution drugs had gone into her arm tissue rather than directly into the bloodstream.
Pike, who would have been the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than two centuries, has a blood condition and feared that something would go wrong with lethal injections, her lawyers say.
Her lawyers unsuccessfully petitioned the state to consider alternative methods, such as death by hanging or firing squad.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, who denied Pike's clemency appeal to commute her sentence to life in prison on Monday, ordered a suspension of scheduled executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year and a third-party review of Wednesday's failed attempt.
"There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen," Lee, a Republican, told reporters. "It's a tragedy, and it's deeply disturbing to me that that has happened in this state. The people deserve better and we're going to make sure that happens."
Pike was 'kind' with her executioners
Pike's lawyers shared new details about her time in the execution chamber, saying her request to prison officials for an all-female execution team appeared to have been honored.
During the hour or so it took to set up intravenous lines, Pike gave the executioners guidance on how they might try to place the needle to get better access to her veins, Spivey said.
"Miss Pike was kind, and she was cooperative, and she was at peace the whole time," Spivey said. "She was ready."
Even after the first dose was injected, Pike was speaking with her spiritual adviser and her executioners, wishing them "loving kindness," Spivey said.
Because pharmaceutical companies are forbidden by European law from selling drugs for use in executions, US prison systems typically rely on small, lightly regulated compounding pharmacies in procurement processes that are shrouded in secrecy.
Tennessee switched to a one-drug lethal injection protocol using pentobarbital, a powerful barbiturate, in 2024. It was unclear where it procured the drugs for Wednesday's failed execution, information that Pike's lawyers say was also withheld from them.
Most countries in the world and 23 US states have abolished the death penalty, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said Pike's case showed the rest of the country should follow suit.
"The prolonged suffering – physical and mental – arising from multiple failed execution attempts is abhorrent, and cruel," Turk said in a statement.
Pike was 18 in January 1995 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, and a third companion lured Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate at their Knoxville Job Corps vocational center, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her. Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing, and both were convicted of first-degree murder.

====================================================================================================

The Thaci verdict exposes the West’s unresolved Kosovo double standard - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:33:58 UTC
06:33:58 KST

The first-instance judgment against Hashim Thaci, former prime minister and president of the so-called Kosovo and former commander of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), as well as its three other former members, came as a surprise to many. Thaci was sentenced to a single prison term of 25 years. Jakup Krasniqi, former KLA spokesman and member of the Directorate for Political Affairs, received the same sentence.
They were tried for war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the 1998-1999 conflict in Kosovo. “They are criminally responsible for war crimes involving the detention of 385 people, cruel treatment of 49, torture of 303 and murder of 96,” the court stated in its judgment. The court further explained that the victims were Kosovo Albanians regarded as political opponents and collaborators with the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time, as well as Serbs and Roma. The court dismissed the charges of crimes against humanity.
Why has the judgment come as a surprise to many within the Albanian community, but also around the world?
Previous judgments handed down by international courts dealing with the former Yugoslavia, along with one-sided and highly partisan reporting by the mass media during the ethnic and religious wars fought in the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s, created an oversimplified picture of good guys and bad guys. Despite the fact that serious war crimes were committed on all sides, biased and lopsided global media based in the West portrayed Serbia as a regional Israel and the Serbs as aggressors and intruders on someone else’s territory, much as Jews are portrayed in Palestine, as though they had absolutely no historical or spiritual ties to the land. Add to this the fact that they came into conflict with peoples of the Islamic faith, and Western powers at the time could hardly have found easier or more expedient collateral victims than the Serbs, as they sought an opportunity to demonstrate their balanced approach towards the Muslim world.
Consequently, 27 years after the armed conflict, the question inevitably arises: how can the leaders of the side that fought against the Serbs, who were invariably portrayed as liberators, victims of the gravest war crimes and favorites of the West, be convicted at all?
If anyone in the world has the capacity to understand what it means to be assigned the status of the eternal, a priori culprit, against whom an avalanche of hostility from much of the Islamic world and from Western circles, now caught up in “woke” self-negation, has descended, it is Israel, Israelis and most of the Jewish Diaspora.
However, the problem goes deeper than the observation that the impact of this judgment is too little and too late. The key issue is that this judgment does not call into question the activities of the terrorist KLA during the conflict in Kosovo and NATO’s aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The KLA’s political and military leaders were precisely the men now convicted: Hashim Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi, and Rexhep Selimi. In this way, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, commonly known as the Kosovo Special Court, effectively absolves the KLA.
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established in 2015 by the so-called Assembly of Kosovo under strong international pressure from both the European Union and the United States. The Specialist Chambers’ main task is to investigate and prosecute serious cross-border and international crimes, primarily war crimes and crimes against humanity, commenced or committed in Kosovo between 1 January 1998 and 31 December 2000. The immediate impetus was a 2011 Council of Europe report authored by Swiss senator Dick Marty, which pointed to the involvement of KLA members in abductions, murders and illegal trafficking in human organs. Given the high risk of intimidation and information leaks, the court was tasked with ensuring a secure environment for proceedings. Its seat was therefore moved to The Hague, and its staff and judges are exclusively international experts.
A trap for the world and public opinion
The judgment against Thaci and the others thus presents a kind of trap for the international community and public opinion. In practice, it defines the convicted group as a criminal organization found guilty at first instance of individual murders. In other words, they were not convicted of systematic persecution and killings, or crimes against humanity committed on ethnic and religious grounds. Although the KLA’s official political platform did not, of course, formally proclaim ethnic or religious persecution, its military strategy and activities on the ground did in practice involve large-scale ethnically motivated violence and the expulsion of the non-Albanian population. Although the sentences imposed are quite severe, the legal classification of the crimes continues the practice of previous courts, under which only war crimes against Serbs are not treated as crimes against humanity.
Today’s geopolitical upheavals, and President Trump’s administration in particular, create conditions in which this narrative could change. We hope that the “autopilot” policy pursued for decades will not be repeated as a reflex in this case. We expect a position grounded in the facts. Serbia expects the same from Israel, a country that has faced terrorist threats and attacks for decades to an extent unmatched by any other. These culminated in the massacre of October 7, 2023, the most devastating loss of Jewish life since the Holocaust, marked by bestial, pathological killings, sexual violence and the captivity of babies, children, pregnant women and civilians of every other category.
Serbia seeks nothing other than equal treatment and for what happened during the conflict in Kosovo and Metohija (KiM) to be called by its proper name. Belated justice, however, brings no comfort to the families of KLA victims or to the hundreds of thousands of Serbs who fled KiM after the war ended.
The nature of the organization is also illustrated by the fact that, of the 220,000 Serbs who fled KiM because of persecution, threats and intolerable living conditions, only 2% returned after the war and the establishment of civilian rule by former KLA commanders who had exchanged their military uniforms for civilian clothes.
The result of the KLA’s activities under Thaci and his associates was 2,187 Serbs killed, most of them civilians, including the harvesters in Staro Gracko, as well as people abducted and killed in post-war reprisals, attacks and kidnappings after 12 June 1999. The fate of another 570 non-Albanians remains unknown.
During the three-day pogrom against Serbs, from March 17 to 19 in 2004, 10 Serbs were killed, 35 churches and monasteries were demolished or set on fire, along with 935 Serbian buildings, including 738 houses and 10 public buildings, such as schools, post offices and health centers. A total of 4,012 Serbs were expelled from six towns and nine villages. Two villages, Slatina and Svinjare, were wiped out.
The religious dimension must also be taken into account, particularly given that today it is precisely the Serbian Orthodox Church (SOC) that remains one of the key institutions to have survived under almost impossible conditions in KiM. It represents a bulwark that neither the KLA nor the current extremist authorities in KiM have yet managed to eliminate. We are witnessing almost daily attempts by representatives of the provisional institutions in Priština to make the SOC’s continued presence in Serbia’s southern province impossible through various forms of pressure.
During 2021, the authorities in Priština intensified their diplomatic efforts to appropriate Serbian cultural heritage. These efforts were spearheaded by Albin Kurti, prime minister of the provisional institutions in Priština, who sent official letters to 54 world leaders and to UNESCO. In these letters and in public appearances, “arguments” were put forward that the Orthodox monasteries and churches in KiM constitute “Kosovo heritage,” accompanied by demands to change their formal status and remove Serbia’s responsibility for these monuments.
The four Serbian Orthodox religious sites: Visoki Dečani, the Patriarchate of Peć, Gračanica and Our Lady of Ljeviš would thereby be removed from the List of World Heritage in Danger, on the grounds that security conditions had changed and Kosovo’s institutions were capable of protecting them. The authorities particularly objected to the term “Serbian cultural heritage” in official documents, insisting that these cultural monuments and Orthodox churches belong to all citizens and the “state of Kosovo”, regardless of ethnicity. Kosovo is the cradle of Serbian nationhood, given its exceptional historical, spiritual and cultural importance in the collective identity and national mythology of the Serbs, particularly its association with the Middle Ages and the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, against the invading army of the Ottoman Empire under the command of Sultan Murad I, as well as its monasteries and churches dating from the 13th and 14th centuries.
Kosovo is the Serbian Jerusalem and, in formal legal terms, the Serbian Galilee: sovereign territory of the Republic of Serbia where the demographic battle has gradually been lost on several occasions.
Most EU countries have looked the other way for years in the face of this attempt to promote such radical historical revisionism and undermine religious and human rights.
The radical religious component, so often overlooked when discussing the activities of the KLA, whose ideology underpinned the attempt to secede from Serbia, is shown in its true light by the participation of a significant number of Albanians from KiM in Islamic State operations, some of whom even served as military commanders. One of the Islamic State’s most wanted members was an Albanian from Kosovo and Metohija, a jihadist Lavdrim Muhaxheri, also known as Abu Abdullah al-Kosovi. He appeared on the US list of most-wanted terrorists and played a key role in recruiting Albanians for terrorist operations in the Middle East.
In stark contrast to the systematic, organized propaganda conducted over several decades, portraying the Serbian side as solely responsible for everything that happened in Kosovo in the 1990s, Serbs and other non-Albanians have virtually disappeared from the territory. The commitments made to establish the Community of Serb Municipalities have not been honored. As in certain countries in the Middle East, the oppression and disappearance of Christian communities continue, with little concern shown by much of the international community.
What is particularly discouraging is that, following the first-instance judgment against the former KLA leaders on 16 September, demonstrators in KiM reacted violently, while protests by their supporters in The Hague descended into riots in which Dutch police had to use water cannons, pepper spray and batons. Unlike in other parts of the former Yugoslavia, where representatives of the authorities, intellectual elites and civil society organizations have emerged to condemn crimes committed in the names of their peoples, there is no such response in KiM today. Ultimately, it remains to be seen what the second-instance judgment on appeal will bring.
For Jewish readers, this inevitably brings to mind the skillful manipulation of historical facts from the Second World War and the Holocaust.
While Albanians in Albania played a noble and exceptional role in protecting the country’s small Jewish community and Jewish refugees, making Albania the only country in Europe where the Jewish population at the end of the war was larger than it had been before the Holocaust, the situation in the dismembered territory of Kosovo and Metohija was entirely different. Members of Balli Kombëtar, an Albanian nationalist and anti-communist organisation founded in 1942 with the aim of creating a Greater Albania, worked closely with Italian and later German forces during the Second World War, despite declaring themselves opposed to the occupiers.
In KiM, as well as parts of now days North Macedonia and Montenegro, they committed numerous crimes and mass killings against non-Albanians, particularly Serbs. The 21st Waffen Mountain Division of the SS “Skanderbeg” (1st Albanian) bears direct responsibility for the arrest and deportation of Jews from Kosovo and Metohija during the Second World War. Composed predominantly of Kosovo Albanians under German command, the unit was formed in the spring of 1944. The Grand Mufti of Jerusalem, Haj Amin al-Husseini, acted as a religious recruiter and propagandist for Heinrich Himmler's Muslim Waffen-SS units, helping lay the groundwork for Balkan divisions that included the core nucleus of the 21st Waffen Mountain Division of the SS “Skanderbeg.”
Immediately after its formation, it became a key instrument in the implementation of the Holocaust in the area. On 14 May 1944, members of the Skanderbeg Division carried out a mass raid on Jewish homes in Priština. They arrested 281 members of the community, looted their property and handed them over to the Gestapo. The arrested Jews were first taken to a temporary holding camp in Priština and then deported via the Staro Sajmište camp in Belgrade to the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp.
Of particular note is Xhafer Deva, interior minister in the collaborationist government, who actively recruited personnel and cooperated with German intelligence agencies. The respected Jerusalem Post also reported on initiatives to renovate his house in Kosovska Mitrovica.
War crimes during the 1990s in the former Yugoslavia were committed by all sides in the conflict. Sadly, heavy war crimes were also committed in the name of the Serbs. All victims of crimes motivated by ethnic and religious hatred deserve equal respect, and all perpetrators deserve equal punishment. Serbian victims deserve the same respect, and the wounds remain unhealed. This is also a warning to humanity; the only question is who will be next to be branded. Audiatur et altera pars, a Latin legal maxim, forms a cornerstone of fundamental equity and due process in legal and administrative systems worldwide.

In recent years, Canada’s Jewish community has changed profoundly. A country long regarded as one of the safest and most comfortable places for Jewish life in the Western world is now facing a significant rise in antisemitism, threats, and violence against Jews and Jewish institutions.
The numbers are stark. In 2025, 788 hate crimes targeting Jews were reported to police across Canada. Jews accounted for approximately 71 percent of all police reported hate crimes motivated by religion.
These figures reflect a growing sense of insecurity in everyday Jewish life. During the most recent Rosh Hashanah, mezuzahs were torn from the doors of Jewish students’ rooms at Wilfrid Laurier University in Ontario. Should Canadian Jews consider Aliyah?
These efforts are essential. The current reality also raises a broader leadership question.
Has the time come for the leaders of Jewish federations and organizations in Canada to place a serious and practical discussion about Aliyah on their agenda?
Federation leaders are responsible for building strong Jewish communities. They invest in schools, synagogues, welfare, culture, Jewish identity, and the next generation. Their work is measured in the strength, continuity and resilience of the local community. Jewish leadership also carries responsibility for the individual Jew and for the choices available to every Jewish family.
At a time when families are asking new questions about security, identity, their children’s future and their connection to Israel, Aliyah deserves a clear and respected place in the communal conversation.
That conversation should be practical. It should address employment, education, housing, professional recognition, Hebrew, community integration and the needs of young adults, families and older people.
A person considering Aliyah should be able to get reliable information, understand the available options, and seriously examine the possibility before making any decision.
This is precisely the role Ofek Israeli was created to play.
Encouraging Aliyah from around the world
Ofek Israeli was established by the Jewish Agency for Israel and the World Zionist Organization and operates under the leadership of Israel’s Ministry of Aliyah and Integration as part of the national initiative to encourage Aliyah from around the world.
Its role is to help turn interest in Aliyah into a practical and informed option through information, connections, guidance, and support.
This coming November, I will travel to Canada in my capacity as Chairman of Ofek Israeli, together with the company’s CEO, Aryeh Abitbol.
We will visit Montreal and Toronto and meet with leaders of Jewish federations and organizations, students and young adults, older members of the community, Israelis living in Canada, and Jews who were born and raised there.
We want to hear how they see the current reality, what concerns them, and what they expect from their community leadership and from the State of Israel.
We also intend to open a direct discussion with Jewish leaders about Aliyah.
Our message to them will be clear: put Aliyah on the agenda.
Talk about it in synagogues, at conferences, on university campuses, and in community institutions. Give families information and practical tools. Connect those who are interested with the relevant institutions in Israel.
Strengthening Jewish life in Canada remains a vital mission. Encouraging Aliyah should also become part of the Jewish and Zionist responsibility of community leadership.
The reality has changed. The conversation should change with it.
Aliyah should be a real, openly discussed, and accessible option for every Canadian Jew considering the future.
The writer is Chairman of Ofek Israeli.

Leder denounced Brody on Wednesday over recent comments in which the Jewish actor for the first time publicly expressed his views on Israel’s actions in Gaza. Brody told GQ, “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine.”

'Ignorant Jew' with limited Jewish education

Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law and one of the key mediators in Gaza ceasefire talks, has an indirect financial connection through his private investment firm to a series of companies supplying weapons and equipment to the IDF, according to a CNN investigation published on Thursday and based on Israeli financial documents and Israeli transparency regulations.
According to the investigation, Kushner-owned Affinity Partners is the largest shareholder in Phoenix Financial. Documents reviewed as part of the investigation indicate that Phoenix has investments in nine companies connected to Israeli military activity, including manufacturers of ammunition, drones, vessels, and engineering equipment.
The most significant investment is in Elbit Systems, valued at at least $265 million. Other investments include more than $68 million in NextVision, which manufactures cameras for drones, and at least $40 million in Reshef Technologies, which manufactures electronic fuzes for shells. The list also includes Israel Shipyards, Ashot Ashkelon, Boeing, and Caterpillar.
Kushner does not directly own shares in the nine companies, but Affinity may indirectly benefit from their profits through its investment in Phoenix. According to CNN, the company sold about a quarter of its holdings in July for more than $340 million, generating a return of more than five times the original purchase price of the shares it sold.
Following the sale, Affinity remained Phoenix's largest shareholder, with a 7.4% stake valued at more than $1 billion.
Questions arise over Kushner's conflicts of interest in Gaza ceasefire efforts after CNN report
The investigation raises questions about the intersection between Kushner's diplomatic activity and his private business interests. Kushner is carrying out his work on behalf of the president on a voluntary basis and does not hold an official government position. Alongside the diplomatic negotiations, he has presented a plan for Gaza's reconstruction that includes the development of tourism areas and opportunities for private investment.
CNN stressed, however, that it found no evidence that Kushner's diplomatic activity directly influenced the investments examined in the investigation.
Kushner's lawyer said his client had never been involved in Phoenix's decisions to buy, hold, or sell shares in the companies in question. The White House also rejected allegations of a conflict of interest. White House deputy press secretary Anna Kelly said Kushner's private business interests were unrelated to his diplomatic work, which he carries out voluntarily at the president's request.

Russia’s Putin rules out ceasefire with Ukraine during speech in Moscow
Putin warned the West he would deploy nuclear weapons if necessary to defend the Russian Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ruled out a ceasefire on long-range strikes with Ukraine as Moscow steps up its campaign of aerial attacks on Kyiv.
“We are told: ‘Let them stop striking your refineries, and you will stop striking their ships.’ It is simply ridiculous,” Putin said on Thursday at the Valdai political forum in Moscow.

The remarks followed a meeting between United States President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York on September 22, when Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow also stopped its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Speaking at the forum of the Moscow-based think tank, Putin said Ukraine had “partially achieved its objectives” with these strikes, with attacks on Russian oil refineries having cost the country 1 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP), but added that Russia was now responding in kind.
Russia has ramped up long-range strikes, targeting Ukraine’s steel companies as well as supply chains, notably in the rail sector. Ukraine accuses Moscow of deliberately hitting civilian targets and keeping Kyiv on a near-constant state of alert as it braces for another tough winter.
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday, according to city officials, as the Ukrainian capital endured relentless aerial attacks. No casualties were reported as children and staff at the school were in shelters when the drone hit.
Putin added that Russia would prefer to end the conflict in Ukraine through talks and wanted it to be a neutral country after the end of hostilities.
The nuclear option
He warned the West not to escalate the standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which is wedged between Poland and Lithuania, and pledged to defend it with nuclear weapons if necessary.
“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation – in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well – the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country’s disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda,” he said.
Putin’s comments followed a diplomatic note which NATO said this week it had received from Russia, warning the Western military alliance it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia’s Baltic exclave.
Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios. “We must realise that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return,” he said.
On the contrary, in the event of a “favourable scenario”, Putin said the assets of Western companies that Moscow had seized could potentially be returned. Putin last month ordered the seizure of businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestle, French retailer Auchan, the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain and German wholesaler and food retailer Metro.

Who wins your vote for the 2026 ABC Australian Insect of the Year?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:31:46 UTC
06:31:46 KST

Scutter or flutter? Who wins your vote for the 2026 ABC Australian Insect of the Year?
Two very different butterflies, a pair of cute beetles, the iconic Otway glow-worm and a super-fly guy with eyes on stalks.
These are the 2026 ABC Australian Insect of the Year finalists selected by experts ahead of a national vote to choose the nation's favourite small wonder.
The Australian Insect of the Year is an annual online poll run by the ABC in partnership with insect conservation organisations.
This year's top six were nominated by the CSIRO, Invertebrates Australia, Australian Entomological Society and Zoos Victoria, along with Gardening Australia magazine and A Naturalist's Guide to the Insects of Australia.
Their finalists:
- Gold Christmas beetle (Anoplognathus aureus)
- Mallee Bronze Azure butterfly (Ogyris subterrestris)
- Orchard swallowtail butterfly (Papilio aegeus)
- Otway glow-worm (Arachnocampa otwayensis)
- Stalk-eyed signal fly (Achias australis)
- Tortoise-shelled ladybird (Harmonia testudinaria)
Eminent entomologist Ken Walker, who nominated last year's champion, the graphic flutterer dragonfly, said each of this year's finalists represented an important story about insects.
He said that through charismatic creatures like butterflies and beetles, Australians could learn about insects, most of which remained unnamed and unknown.
"A review by the Academy of Science in 2018 looked at the state of our understanding of the Australian fauna of insects and estimated only 30 per cent of our insect fauna is named, which means 70 per cent of our insect fauna is unnamed," Dr Walker said.
"When you're used to things going along quite nicely, you don't notice something until it goes wrong. So much of that is due to insects doing things like pollination. It's easy to forget 90 per cent of crops rely on insect pollination.
"On the other hand, only 1 per cent of known insects are pest species, but we tend to know those quite well."
Dr Walker said it was vital that people protect insects for our environment.
"Through Insect of the Year, we can highlight the importance of conservation. Insects play an essential role in nature and agriculture," Dr Walker said.
"We need to protect them and to mitigate the things that reduce insect populations, because without them we are all stuffed."
This year's ABC Insect of the Year expert panellists were:
- CSIRO entomologist Keith Bayless
- Australian Entomological Society president Mark Schutze
- Invertebrates Australia founding managing director Kate Umbers
- Gardening Australia magazine horticultural editor AB Bishop
- Zoos Victoria invertebrate conservation coordinator Jessie Sinclair
- Author and nature photographer Peter Rowland
The blue-banded bee (Amegilla cingulata) was the inaugural ABC Insect of the Year, with the graphic flutterer dragonfly (Rhyothemis graphiptera) winning last year's popular vote.
You can cast your vote for the 2026 Australian Insect of the Year until the end of October.
Dr Walker said much of the public awareness of insects centred on the adult life stage, which included familiar butterflies, beetles, flies and ants.
He said the nomination of the Otway glow-worm, the larval stage of a gnat, highlighted the complex life cycle of many insects.
"People might only think about the adult stage, but they've got eggs, larvae and pupae," Dr Walker said.
"So much of their life we don't notice them because they're out of sight.
"It's great then, with the Otway glow-worm, we have one of the contenders as the grub or larval stage."
Two finalists, the Mallee Bronze Azure butterfly and the gold Christmas beetle, are currently subjects of conservation programs at Zoos Victoria and Invertebrates Australia, respectively.
Dr Walker said countless insect species could be subjects of conservation programs if more was known about their plight.
"There are myriads of other insects that deserve similar conservation but they just haven't been studied,"
"They do need our conservation and protection."
You can cast your vote for the 2026 Australian Insect of the Year until the end of October.
The 2026 ABC Australian Insect of the Year will be announced on November 9, coinciding with the start of Australian Pollinator Week.
Your 2026 Australian Insect of the Year finalists
Gold Christmas beetle (Anoplognathus aureus)
"These iconic and much-loved beetles emerge over the festive season and were once a common fixture of summer nights.
"However, sightings of this species, and many others, have become rare.
"That's why scientists are gathering data via the Christmas Beetle Count to learn more about these beetles to help protect them."
– Dr Kate Umbers, Invertebrates Australia
Mallee Bronze Azure butterfly (Ogyris subterrestris)
"The critically endangered Mallee Bronze Azure butterfly embodies everything that makes Australian insects extraordinary — striking in appearance and ecologically remarkable.
"By celebrating this insect, we celebrate the importance of protecting entire ecosystems and the overlooked invertebrates that keep them functioning."
– Jessie Sinclair, Zoos Victoria
Orchard swallowtail butterfly (Papilio aegeus)
"The orchard swallowtail, also known as the Australian citrus butterfly, is one of our largest and most spectacular butterflies.
"While the larvae occasionally nibble the leaves of backyard citrus, they rarely cause lasting damage and are well worth accommodating because the adult butterflies are important pollinators."
– AB Bishop, horticulture editor, Gardening Australia Magazine
Otway glow-worm (Arachnocampa otwayensis)
"Glow-worms are mysterious, ethereal, and beautiful … and they're not worms at all! They are juvenile flies: fungus gnat 'maggots', to be precise, which become bioluminescent to attract prey.
"This species (otwayensis) is unique to south-west Victoria and a magnificent tourist drawcard yet is highly susceptible to ecological disturbance."
– Mark Schutze, Australian Entomological Society
Stalk-eyed signal fly (Achias australis)
"It's weird but beautiful. As its name suggests, it has eyes on stalks. Their purpose is to attract females and compete with rival males. The females have much smaller heads.
"This species is largest stalk-eyed fly in Australia, and is found in north Queensland, where it feeds on rotting fruit and animal faeces, helping to clean up the environment."
– Keith Bayless, CSIRO
Tortoise-shelled ladybird (Harmonia testudinaria)
"Beyond their spectacular appearance, these striking but tiny (about 6 millimetres) ladybirds are the mighty unsung heroes of our backyards and ecosystems.
"Both the adults and their larvae are voracious predators, eating soft-bodied pests like aphids. The tortoise-shelled ladybird proves Australia's most beautiful insects are often its hardest workers."
– Peter Rowland, nature writer and photographer

The occupiers in the Kherson region have admitted a shortage of water tankers - CNS
Kyiv • UNN
The occupation administration of the Kherson region does not have enough water tankers during power outages. Some of the tankers require repairs.
The occupation administration of Kherson region itself acknowledges a shortage of water tanker trucks for water deliveries. The Special Operations Forces’ National Resistance Center of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (NRC) reports this, according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that the problem becomes particularly acute during prolonged power outages, when populated areas are left without a centralized water supply. Thus, instead of systematically repairing the infrastructure, the occupiers are forced to address the problem with water tankers.
At the same time, a question arises: where is the occupation administration directing budget funds if there are not even enough resources to deal with unforeseen problems with the water supply? Either the necessary expenses were not provided for at all, or the allocated resources are not reaching the people. According to the NRC, some of the available water tankers require major repairs and replacement of their tanks
It is indicated that residents of remote villages and people with limited mobility suffer the most from this.
"Even when water is delivered, there is not enough for everyone, and the quality of the water may not meet drinking-water standards. As a result, people who have no other source are forced to use non-potable water for household needs and, in some cases, even for drinking. The occupation authorities once again demonstrate that money can be found for propaganda and showcase projects, but not for the basic needs of the population," the NRC concludes.
To remind you
According to the NRC, Russia is failing to cope with the water crisis in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. The occupation administration is unable to repair the water-supply systems in time, putting people at risk of being left without a stable water supply as early as winter.

New Russian Mobilization Could Leave Low-Skill Workers Poorer, KSE Institute Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:30:00 UTC
06:30:00 KST

KSE Institute has released a new paper, “Fewer Bodies or Cheaper Bodies? What a New Wave of Russian Mobilization Would Do to the Wages of Those Who Stay Behind.” Drawing on 16 months of Russian vacancy data, regional decrees, and casualty records, the study estimates how a new call-up could affect civilian wages. Mobilization would remove more men from civilian employment, but it would also allow the state to replace costly contract recruitment with compulsory service. The study finds that the loss of contract payments would likely outweigh the wage gains from greater labor scarcity.
Russia’s military industry has cut hiring sharply. Over the past year, weapons and aviation manufacturers reduced advertised positions by 37%, other military industries by 14%, and drone makers by 13%, while civilian vacancies rose by 7%. At the same time, 94% of advertised military positions require neither experience nor qualifications, compared with 46% of civilian vacancies, meaning the army largely recruits from the same low-skill segment of the labor market.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Sign-on bonuses have become a major recruitment tool. The median payment rose from RUB 1.5 million to RUB 2.5 million over two years, while sign-on payments now total around RUB 1 trillion a year. Contract pay alone is about five times the civilian wage available to the workers the military targets; including the bonus, one year of service is worth a median of about nine years of local income.
‘A Deliberate Tactic’: Zelensky Condemns Russian Drone Strike on Kyiv School
Removing men from the civilian workforce raises wages, but only modestly. The study estimates an additional 0.1–0.2 percentage points of real wage growth for every 100,000 men removed from civilian employment. Because mobilization would largely replace the roughly 400,000 men a year already recruited under contracts, a call-up of 500,000 would add only about 0.1–0.2 points to real wage growth, while one million would add 0.6–1.2 points.
The resulting wage gain is estimated at RUB 20–200 billion, far below the roughly RUB 1 trillion in annual sign-on bonuses that mobilization could eliminate. The losses would fall most heavily on the men and regions that currently receive contract payments, especially where local wages are lowest. According to the study, wage gains from labor scarcity would only catch up with the withdrawn payments at a call-up of roughly 3.5–6.5 million men — well beyond the scenarios considered.

'Right to access to justice equal for all': SC frowns at out-of-turn hearings
Unknown

'When we grant early hearing to one litigant who has the resources to approach the SC, we do injustice to millions of litigants who are waiting for a hearing on their petitions,' the bench said.
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Thursday said a bus conductor's right to access to justice is equal to that of a top bureaucrat, and granting out-of-turn hearing to a litigant having the wherewithal to approach the SC would violate the right to speedy justice of millions languishing in the queue.A bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana refused to entertain a plea for expeditious hearing of a petition by an additional district judge challenging his dismissal from service for corruption in 2022. His petition has been pending in Allahabad HC since 2022.
Sacked for taking bribe, can’t allow early hearing: SC
"When we grant early hearing to one litigant who has the resources to approach the SC, we do injustice to millions of litigants who are waiting for a hearing on their petitions," the bench said.In his plea for a direction to HC for expeditious disposal of his plea, the judge said he has suffered a lot in the last four years and that since his retirement is due on Nov 30, he would like to leave service with dignity.Referring to the pendency of more than 12 lakh cases in Allahabad HC, the bench told the counsel: "You are making a submission which is against the equal right to access to justice of every litigant, be it a bus conductor or a principal secretary.
We will not request HC to grant out-of-turn hearing unless we are convinced about egregious circumstances in the case that warrant urgent hearing."The petitioner is one of the three additional district judges - Ashok Kumar Singh, Himanshu Bhatnagar and Rakesh Kumar Nain - who were dismissed from service on corruption charges through a full court resolution passed by Allahabad HC in May 2022.
He complained that "no show-cause notice was ever issued to the petitioner and no opportunity was ever afforded to give any representation against the major penalty so imposed upon the petitioner, therefore, the resolution dated May 12, 2022, and the order dated May 17, 2022, by which the services of the petitioner were terminated, was passed in violation of principles of natural justice".The bench said that as the petitioner has been dismissed from service on charges of acceptance of bribe, it is not a fit case for requesting the HC to grant an out-of-turn hearing.The petitioner, who joined judicial service in Aug 1999 and was promoted as additional district judge in 2013, was accused of taking a Rs 6 lakh bribe to acquit a person in 2015. The inquiry and disciplinary proceedings were concluded in 2022, following which his services were terminated.

Spanish housing decree imperilled by opposition of Junts party
MADRID, Oct 1 - Chances that Spain's Congress would pass a decree aimed at curbing the housing crisis grew dimmer on Thursday after Catalan kingmaker party Junts raised last-minute issues and requested the government devise a new proposal on the eve of a scheduled vote.
Junts, a separatist centre-right party with seven MPs, argued that the proposed measures would make matters worse by reducing housing supply. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's minority leftist government has only 147 seats in the 350-seat chamber and relies on the support of a patchwork of smaller parties to pass legislation.
Opposition parties have already signalled that they will not support the decree, one of two crafted by Spain's Socialist government after protests sparked by the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal last week.
Thousands of mostly young activists camped out in Madrid's main square and other Spanish cities to protest the eviction and call for major reforms.
A second decree, which would permit automatic and indefinite renewal of rental contracts, was already expected not to pass, failing to secure the minimum support required from Spain's fractured Congress.
"I already thought the measures were insufficient and only temporary, but vetoing them is selfish and abandoning the people," Aidan, a 26-year-old wildfire firefighter, said of Junts' decision not to back the measures. "We'll keep up the encampment," he added. REUTERS

ASX top and bottom movers, and best and worst sectors
The market closed for the day with Elsight, a company that provides hardware and software for uncrewed systems like drones and ground robots, at the time, up by 13%.
Cloud infrastructure form Megaport Limited also crept into second place with a day gain of 10% after financial firm Bell Potter recommended to "buy" the stock.
IT services company Data#3 slipped to third place by day's end after leading the pack for most of Friday and all of Thursday, but was still up by 8% by market close.
And on the opposite end of the spectrum, Cochlear was the worst performer, after receiving a shareholder class action filing against it in the Victorian Supreme Court earlier this week. Down nearly -4%, its worst week since April.
Property juggernaut Lendlease also had a bad day, trading down by nearly -4%, off the back of news that it is extending its costly exit out of a development in Milan.
And with the best three stocks all being tech, perhaps it comes as no surprise that technology was the standout sector for the day, finishing up with 2% gains. Energy and Consumer Non-Cyclicals followed close behind.
Real estate dragged down the list, ending the day at -1.66%, and Healthcare wasn't much better, trading at -0.83%.
Qld government to take over data centre planning applications
The Queensland government says it will take the planning and assessment of data centre applications away from local councils.
It comes as Australia's largest proposed data centre is planned for the Western Downs, 200 kilometres west of Brisbane.
International developer Zerra DC lodged plans for the hyper-scale computing project in August. Anthropic has since signed on to lease the first of four planned buildings at the site.
Developers are increasingly eyeing sites across Queensland as locations for data centres due to the state's available land and capacity to connect to the energy grid.
The state government said the changes would ensure a "consistent and transparent framework across the state".
NAB 'strikes twice' on mortgage holders with another round of rate hikes
While the RBA hiked the cash rate by 25%, NAB has gone a step further, increasing its fixed rate offerings by up to 0.32 percentage points.
On Friday afternoon, NAB announced it would be increasing its fixed rate loans, ranging from 0.20 to 0.32 percentage points.
Consumer comparison site Canstar noted that the 0.32 percentage point figure was "more" than what was "standard" for a 0.25 RBA hike on the bank's lowest 2-year fixed rate.
And it's actually the second time in two weeks NAB has moved to up its fixed rates. On September 17, NAB hiked each of its lowest fixed rates by 0.15.
“The ink was barely dry on NAB’s last fixed-rate hike announcement and it’s already served up another one," said Canstar data insights director, Sally Tindall.
“As a result, NAB’s lowest 2-year fixed rate has risen by 0.47 in just over two weeks, suggesting the bank is now factoring in yet another rate hike in the months ahead."
CBA, Westpac and ANZ have also hiked their fixed rates last few weeks - CBA hiking by up to 0.48 percentage points while Westpac hiked by up to 0.45.
The lowest fixed rate you can get from one of the big four bank is now 6.49% at ANZ for either a 1 or 2-year term.
In a statement to the ABC, NAB said: “Fixed home loan rates are influenced by a range of factors, including wholesale funding costs and market conditions. Like other lenders, NAB regularly reviews its pricing and adjusts rates when required.”
September EV sales skyrocket on-year
The EVC’s Vehicle Sales Report for September 2026 reported almost 6,000 Tesla or Polestar vehicles sold last month. That takes the total to over 43, 000 so far this year.
The majority of sales are from the Tesla Model Y family.
On a year-to-date basis, all states and territories have recorded significant increases in sales ranging from 45.7% to 113.3%.
You can access the State of EVs 2026 report here.
Regional Queensland businesses facing tough decisions in face of latest rates rise
A nice feature here from Olivia Nunes-Malek on the decisions businesses are facing when it comes to passing on rising costs.
One business owner described the rising price of inputs as a "snowballing effect", with a "balancing act" to make sure they don't alienate customers.
ASX-listed money transfer business hacked, 'some' data of clients at risk
An ASX-listed international money transfer provider has been hacked and some of its client data may have been accessed.
OFX Group released a statement to the ASX on Friday which revealed the firm was investigating a cybersecurity incident that involved "unauthorised access to data, including data related to some clients".
The international payment provider said it had not identified any cases where client accounts or funds had been compromised, and did not believe any clients had suffered financial loss as a result of the hack.
Hackers had accessed identity documents but did not seem to have made copies, according to the firm.
And of the information they did obtain, it couldn't be used to make payments on OFX's platform, the business also said.
They warned that some non-clients' data had also been breached, such as job applicants.
OFX said its security teams "responded immediately" once they learned of the breach and that their investigations are continuing "as a matter of urgency" and the relevant authorities have been notified.
Jetstar strike this weekend
This is set to be a busy weekend of travel, with a long weekend in many states as well as the NRL Grand Final. But for some travellers, it could be impacted as thousands of Jetstar workers strike over pay.
The Services Union says Jetstar travellers will have their fees waived for things like excess baggage and seat changes and that there will be no admin staff working.
They say the plan is to have differently timed strikes at different airports.
The airline says there will be delays as it has continency plans in place and that it is disappointed the union has taken this action this weekend as it's a busy one. Jetstar also defended pay increases, saying staff will recieve a 2.1% bump this year and a 3% rise next year.
The union says it's not good enough and will be going ahead with its industrial action.

CBA predicting rates will remain on hold, mostly.
The CBA says following the Reserve Bank of Australia's decision to raise interest rates on Tuesday they expect for the RBA to be "on hold from here".
In an economic note out today the bank says "risks are heavily skewed to another hike" and the November meeting "remains live".
"Following [RBA Governor Michele] Bullock's comments, we view the hurdle for another hike is now higher, given somewhat dovish comments centered on monetary policy already being somewhat restrictive and the full impact of recent increases is still to come."
They expect the Board to remain on hold in November. They continue to expect two rate cuts in late 2027.
"The key risk however is that inflation remains sticky and further tightening is required."

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has reportedly fired three staff over their alleged mishandling of sensitive information.
"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson confirmed to the BBC.
The controversial AI juggernaut did not share any more details on the nature of the alleged breach, but at least two of the employees worked on safety and alignment, according to reports from the Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg.

USD at 17-month high
The US dollar is heading for its third straight week of gains as a bond market rout pushes borrowing costs to multi-decade peaks.
Yields on benchmark US 10-year Treasuries hit 5.344 per cent yesterday, their highest since 2002, ahead of a US jobs report that could influence the near-term policy outlook.
The dollar index, which measures the US currency against six rivals, was at 102.08, set for a 1 per cent gain this week, its third consecutive weekly gain, a run it last had in May 2025.
Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, says investors are confronting the uncomfortable mix of sticky inflation, heavy government borrowing and large bond supply.
"The fact that long-end yields are pushing higher even as expectations for an immediate Fed hike have eased suggests this is increasingly about the term premium and fiscal risk, not just the next Fed decision," she said.
Data on Wednesday showed US consumer prices rose less than expected in August, along with downward revisions to July's figure, leading traders to rein in wagers of a rate hike from the Federal Reserve later this month.
Two of the Fed’s top policymakers this week staked out an unusually clear case for taking in more data before deciding about another hike.
That has sharpened the focus on the US payroll report due later in the day, with data likely to show that job growth slowed in September, and that the unemployment rate is forecast to have been 4.1 per cent for a third straight month.
"With the Fed now myopically focused on inflation and price pressures, a hot wages print could prove particularly influential for US rates, Treasuries and the USD," said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone.
Brent crude futures were back above $100 per barrel as traders kept an eye on the stalled talks between the US and Iran to end the conflict in the Middle East.
Sterling was at $1.3187 while the Australian dollar was 0.18 per cent softer at $0.6918, as both hovered around their three-month lows.

The KPMG audits scandal that rocked the corporate world
ANZ cutting ties with its long-time auditor KPMG after nearly 60 years working together is just the latest consequence the firm has faced since its dirty laundry was aired earlier this year.
In March, Senator Deborah O'Neill exposed in a speech to parliament allegations from a whistleblower that KPMG had used confidential client data to win corporate audit contracts for two years.
The whistleblower alleged that for two years, KPMG had batted away accusations that information obtained during an audit of Lendlease accounts was used to win work elsewhere.
It was also alleged the auditors had been expressly forbidden by the company to access the confidential board documents.
In the six months since, KPMG has been in almost constant upheaval.
Some of the allegations were substantiated and chief executive Andrew Yates and audit boss Julian McPherson left the firm.
KPMG was also referred to the National Anti-Corruption Commission.
The firm apologised and admitted its internal investigations were conducted without the "necessary rigour required".
KPMG agreed to a three-month freeze on new Commonwealth government contract bids that ran until September 30.
This prompted KPMG to lay off about 5% of its staff, which was about 400 people.
The firm's revenue fell from $2.28 billion the previous year to $2.26 billion in the 2026 financial year, and KPMG Australia chief executive John Sams expected more revenue falls.
Lendlease unsurprisingly cut ties with the big four accounting firm.
In August, so did Macquarie Bank.
The ABC has contacted KPMG for comment in the wake of ANZ ending their business relationship. A call was returned by veteran crisis communicator David Luff, who said the firm declined to comment.
You can read more on the context of this scandal-plagued firm from a piece my colleague Ian Verrender wrote a few months ago.

Another one bites the dust: More on ANZ dropping KPMG
The new auditor will not commence until FY2029.
KPMG has reportedly made $24 million a year from its ANZ business.
Macquarie Bank and Lendlease have also recently dumped the auditor.
The ABC has contacted KPMG for comment.
Major bank drops KPMG in wake of audit leaks scandal
After 57 years, ANZ is ending its relationship with KPMG, making it the latest client to sever ties with the firm amid its audit leaks scandal.
In a statement to the ASX, the bank says:
"The board of ANZ Group today announced it will commence a competitive tender process to select the next provider of ANZ Group external audit services."
ANZ has used KPMG for its external audit since 1969 but says "a tenure of this length is no longer considered appropriate and has been under consideration by the board for some time".
KPMG is accused of misusing client data and then mishandling a whistleblower's complaint about it.
ANZ says it will find a new auditor through a tender process and that:
"KPMG will not be eligible to participate."

Nike's share price savaged amid poor results, job cuts on horizon
Nike's share price has dropped almost 9% in after-hours trading following disappointing results and revelations that job cuts are in the works.
Overnight, the sportswear juggernaut released its results for the first fiscal quarter, showing it made revenue of $US11.21 billion, representing a 4% decline from the same reporting period in the previous year.
Nike also warned that revenues are expected to keep declining, largely blaming its flailing China arm — which reported a drop of 26% in revenue — for the poor results.
The brand revealed plans to start a major restructure, which will involve layoffs from next year.
Nike chief executive Ellliot Hill has told analysts that the company is "moving with urgency".
Key Event
Disney announces layoffs as part of restructure
Disney shares dropped 3.5% in US trade after the Wall Street Journal reported the entertainment giant is expected to lay off hundreds of workers as part of its restructuring process.
Since Josh D'Amaro got the top job in March, there have been sweeping changes with layoffs across marketing, Pixar, ABC News and ESPN. He used to lead Disney's parks division — which has kept the company afloat in recent years as it struggled to make a profit from its streaming and movie businesses.
The WSJ reports D'Amaro's goal is to consolidate Disney's "fiefdoms" so the company starts thinking of itself as a unified digital entertainment operation.
One interesting move has been to launch a voluntary early-retirement initiative open to executives over 50 with at least 10 years of experience.

Sudan's ousted president Bashir sent to Khartoum for treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01

Breadcrumb
Sudan's ousted president Bashir sent to Khartoum for treatment, lawyer says
Ousted Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir has been transferred to a military-run hospital in Khartoum for medical treatment and requires further care outside the country, his lawyer said on Thursday.
Bashir, 82, was toppled by the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in April 2019, following a months-long popular uprising.
The RSF and army later fell out over plans to integrate their forces during a planned transition to civilian rule and have been fighting a civil war that has laid waste to much of the country over the past three-and-a-half years.
Bashir had been moved from prison to hospital prior to the outbreak of war, and later transferred to the town of Merowe in northern Sudan, where he had been put under military guard.
Bashir was sent to Khartoum for medical tests and he had symptoms that required diagnosis and treatment outside Sudan, his lawyer, Mohamed Alhassan Alameen, told Reuters.
In a statement on Wednesday, Bashir's family said his need for medical treatment outside Sudan "has become critical and urgent, and cannot be delayed any longer", but they had not received official permission to send him abroad.
It was unclear precisely what condition Bashir was suffering. Sudan's military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Several prominent Sudanese Islamist figures also called for his transfer out of the country on social media.
Any such move would likely cause discord within Sudan and could draw international condemnation since Bashir is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges including genocide and also has open cases against him in Sudan.
During Bashir's three decades in power, Sudan was listed by the US as a state sponsor of terrorism and was subject to wide-ranging sanctions. Protesters during the popular uprising accused him and his Islamist National Congress Party of widespread corruption and repression.
After his ouster, Bashir was tried on various charges and convicted of corruption and illicit financing, for which he was serving prison time at the start of the war.

Trump could target three Fed governors. Removing them may be harder than it looks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:14:49 UTC
06:14:49 KST

President Donald Trump has new ammunition he can use in his campaign against his perceived opponents at the Federal Reserve, although a watchdog report released Wednesday found no basis for criminal charges stemming from the Fed's costly renovations to its headquarters.
Combined with separate disputes involving governors Lisa Cook and Michael Barr, Trump's decision to pin the headquarters spending issues on former Chair Jerome Powell means the president could potentially seek the removal of as many as three of the Fed's seven board members. But recent court rulings suggest any attempt would face significant legal hurdles.
Any legal maneuvers could take months to play out and may have the effect of persuading his targets to postpone any plans to leave the Fed, as Powell has already done. Trump's ability to force the Fed off its recent decision to raise interest rates appears limited, despite the institutional damage he could do if he took further legal action.
Trump appears to be weighing his options for how to proceed. The Fed is scheduled to announce its latest interest-rate decision on Oct. 28, only days before the Nov. 3 midterm election. The administration faces a deadline in the Cook case shortly after the election.
If the administration does move against any of the three governors, it may backfire for Trump, said Scott Alvarez, a former Fed general counsel.
"All have an incentive to litigate and stay," Alvarez said.
"The Supreme Court said that Lisa Cook can stay while the litigation goes on. If they all stay while he goes on, then all he's done is hurt his own agenda," Alvarez said of Trump.
Trump fumed in the wake of Wednesday's report from the Fed's inspector general. "Powell is a disaster," the president said Wednesday when asked by reporters about the findings. Powell "should not be sitting on the Federal Reserve Board."
Trump appointed Powell during his first term, then quickly soured on him.
Trump asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to review the IG report. A spokesman for Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia said her office was also reviewing the report.
The Department of Justice didn't respond to emailed questions about its plans and how Blanche's review might differ from Pirro's. Pirro previously oversaw a criminal investigation into Powell. A judge quashed her subpoenas in the matter, saying their "dominant (if not sole) purpose is to harass and pressure Powell."
The Fed declined to comment on Trump's remarks about Powell.
The long-awaited IG report found a raft of managerial problems had allowed construction costs to jump by about a billion dollars as the Fed renovated its Washington office space. But the report found no evidence of administrative misconduct and saw nothing meriting a criminal referral to prosecutors.
"I personally don't think the renovation report would be enough for a court to remove Jay for cause," Alvarez said. "It exonerates him on the criminal side, but it also says they didn't identify any administrative misconduct."
The report details how bureaucratic disorganization left the Fed vulnerable to overspending on a project to renovate and connect a pair of historical federal buildings in Washington. The IG's office faults the Fed for failing to enforce a guaranteed maximum price for the project, among other issues.
But the backward-looking report can't directly prove the Fed would have saved money had it operated better. It acknowledges in a footnote that better management "does not necessarily mean the project's overall cost will be lower."
Nor does the report pin the cost overruns on Powell or any individual governor, instead describing failures in project management, contracting and the board's governance and oversight systems. The IG's office notes that the board delegated responsibility to the staff, as it would have expected for a construction project at a large organization.
Powell can stay on the Fed as a governor through January 2028. He said in March he would remain until the legal threat was "well and truly over, with transparency and finality."
The Supreme Court in June blocked Trump's attempt to remove Cook over allegations that she had lied on a mortgage application. The court said she was owed notice of the allegations and a chance to respond, and issued guidance for what a later finding of cause might entail.
As of August, Cook has received the notice and opportunity to respond, removing one obstacle to her potential removal. The administration would still need to show courts it has met the threshold for cause, which would likely require another Supreme Court review.
The White House hasn't publicly addressed the issue since Cook's response, though in an interview published by Time on Thursday Trump complained about Cook. The White House declined to comment on how the president might respond further to the IG report's findings.
Newly confirmed Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is "controlled to a certain extent" by the board, Trump said. "We have Lisa on there," he said.
For now, the Cook case is pending before U.S. District Court Judge Jia Cobb. She has asked the parties for a joint status report by Nov. 6 on how the litigation should proceed.
Meanwhile, an outside investigation into the Fed's handling of the 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank is ongoing. A preliminary report by the investigative firm Starling Advisory Group faulted the Fed's bank supervisors, whom it said should have known about the risks to the bank as much as a year ahead of its failure.
The preliminary review doesn't assign responsibility to Barr personally. But the White House heaped the blame for the episode at Barr's feet, while stopping short of calling for his firing.
There may not be evidence enough in that report to justify his removal to a skeptical judiciary.
But some in the Fed believe Trump has already proved the administration is willing to act on thin evidence.
Powell issued an extraordinary statement in January after subpoenas for evidence involving the renovation.
"This new threat is not about my testimony last June or about the renovation of the Federal Reserve buildings," Powell said. "Those are pretexts."

Finland’s prime minister says ‘foreign forces’ could be behind a string of intrusions at lawmakers’ homes
Several Finnish lawmakers have said someone entered their homes while they were away, Yle reported.
The incidents took place over the past year. Nothing was stolen during the suspected intrusions, but lawmakers reported noticeable signs that someone had been there — for example, doors left open or lights turned on. Parliament Speaker Jussi Halla-aho said this may have been deliberate.
The exact number of lawmakers affected has not been reported, but Yle puts it at “fewer than 20.” Halla-aho said they did not belong to the same party or share any other common characteristics.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said foreign actors could be behind the incidents. “If someone is trying to destabilize Finland, undermine our sense of security, or weaken our support for Ukraine, for example, it has the opposite effect,” he said.
Orpo also said Russia had previously tried to interfere in European elections. Finland’s next parliamentary election will be held in April 2027.

Russia’s Rostec Claims Cheaper Jet Drones Can Deliver Cruise Missile-Level Performance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:12:12 UTC
06:12:12 KST

- Category
- World
Russia’s Rostec Claims Cheaper Jet Drones Can Deliver Cruise Missile-Level Performance
On September 30, Russian state defense conglomerate Rostec presented the S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T as lower-cost jet-powered substitutes for cruise missiles, claiming all three are already being used against Ukraine, Defence Blog reported on October 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Rostec made the claims in comments to the Russian Defense Ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda, according to the outlet, describing the weapons as a new category between attack drones and missiles.
Defence Blog noted that the company provided no prices, production numbers or performance figures. It added that the figures and Rostec's claims about accuracy and combat results could not be independently verified.
Rostec argued that a classic cruise missile is already a fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle, though not every such drone qualifies as one. Its statement, as quoted by Defence Blog, claimed that “in the new S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, this line is being erased.”
The report described Rostec's assertion that the drones combine the accuracy, maneuverability and range of cruise missiles at a significantly lower price. Rostec also expects the gap between the two kinds of weapons to keep narrowing as drone production matures.
The company anticipates that the drones will become standard weapons for Russian frontline aviation in the near future, alongside glide-bomb kits that Russian jets have dropped on Ukrainian front lines in large numbers since 2023, the outlet wrote.
Rostec told the state news agency TASS that the S-71M and S-71K are designed for launch from fifth-generation fighters, including the Su-57, Defence Blog stated. Both are sized to fit inside the Su-57's internal weapons bay, allowing the jet to carry them without compromising its radar-evading shape.
Russia's arms exporter Rosoboronexport displayed them next to a Su-57E at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt in September, the report noted.
Ukrainian military intelligence has examined debris from both, Militarnyi reported, as cited by Defence Blog. According to those findings, the S-71K, known as Kovyor, carries a 250-kg (550-pound) OFAB-250-270 high-explosive bomb as its warhead and lacks terminal guidance.
The S-71M, called Monokhrom, reportedly contains an NVIDIA Jetson Orin computing module, a small US-made computer built to run artificial intelligence software on board. The outlet cautioned that some published reports have swapped the two designations, so details tied to each name should be treated with caution.
Rostec also told TASS that the smaller Dan-T has been confirmed in hundreds of launches against Ukrainian targets, a claim that Defence Blog did not independently verify. The company stated that the weapon can be fired from aircraft and helicopters, including foreign-made ones. Based on the outlet's reading, this suggests Rostec is targeting the Dan-T at export buyers.
Defence Blog described conflicting accounts of the weapon's origin. Some analysts present it as the export name for the S8000 Banderol, a small jet-powered cruise missile built by Russian drone maker Kronshtadt. Ukrainian experts, by contrast, have described it as a strike version of the Dan-M jet target drone that Russia used for air defense training.
Ukrainian estimates put the Dan-T's range at roughly 500 km (310 miles) with a 135-kg (298-pound) warhead, The New Voice of Ukraine reported, per the Defence Blog account. The outlet cited Ukrainian intelligence officials, who noted that Moscow wants the weapon built entirely from Russian components.
That goal follows Ukrainian findings about the Banderol, which first appeared over Ukraine in spring 2025, the report explained. It is launched mainly from Su-30/34 combat aircraft, Orion drones and Mi-28 attack helicopters, often from occupied Crimea toward the Odesa region.
Ukraine's military intelligence found a Chinese-made jet engine, a Japanese battery and mostly US-made electronics inside the weapon, Euronews reported, as relayed by Defence Blog.
The outlet emphasized that cheap jet-powered weapons that fly like missiles force Ukraine to spend scarce and expensive air defense interceptors on targets that cost Russia far less to build. That logic mirrors Russia's mass use of Shahed-type drones.
Defence Blog added that Rostec placed the new drones in a wider family of guided weapons. That family includes the Iskander ballistic missile system, Tornado-S rocket launchers with guided rockets, Krasnopol guided artillery shells and the Kalashnikov Group's KUB loitering munitions.
The pitch comes as jet-powered munitions already make up a growing share of Russian salvos.
During the large-scale attack on August 21–22, Russia launched 217 attack drones, including Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and decoys, of which more than 50 were jet-powered.
Ukrainian defenses destroyed or suppressed 191 aerial targets that night, among them six Banderol munitions. Several Banderol weapons strayed into Belarus, with at least one reportedly flying around 75 miles into Belarusian territory before running out of fuel and crashing in a field.

Putin warns Russia will use ‘all weapons’ in arsenal if any of its territory is attacked

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday reiterated Moscow’s long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries but will respond to aggression with “all weapons” in its arsenal.
In remarks at a foreign policy forum, Putin accused the West and Europe of escalating tensions by talking about preparing for a war with Moscow in the coming years, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea, and seizing Russian vessels.
His remarks followed Moscow’s warning to Nato that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad should any members of the military alliance try to cut off the Baltic exclave from the rest of Russia.

U.S. designates Russia-linked sanctions-evasion payment network A7 a ‘significant transnational criminal organization’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
21:05:18 UTC
06:05:18 KST

U.S. designates Russia-linked sanctions-evasion payment network A7 a ‘significant transnational criminal organization’
The U.S. Treasury Department has designated A7, a Russia-linked payment network created to evade sanctions, a “significant transnational criminal organization.”
The designation will make it possible to bar U.S. financial institutions from making any transfers involving A7’s “Sub-Agents,” foreign shell companies through which the network processes payments for clients in Russia.
The restrictions on A7 were formally imposed as part of sanctions targeting Iran. The Treasury Department said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and central bank used the network’s services.
Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor launched A7 in 2024, with Russia’s Promsvyazbank also taking part. The network consists of hundreds of companies in third countries that process payments for clients in Russia. By Promsvyazbank’s own estimate, A7 processed 7.5 billion rubles in payments in the first half of 2025.
The Russian company A7 itself and A7A5, the ruble-denominated stablecoin it created, have been under U.S. sanctions since August 2025.
