Dual U.K.-Iranian national arrested over security incident at U.S.-run air base in England
Police on Thursday arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at the U.S.-run RAF Fairford air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran.
The 27-year-old man was arrested in London on Thursday, and police have searched two properties in the U.K. capital, Counter Terrorism Policing said in a statement.
A 26-year-old British national was interviewed by police "under caution," which means the interview was recorded and can be used in future prosecutions.
On Sunday, five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. The suspects have since been released on bail.
Their quick release drew criticism from President Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But it also prompted questions in the U.K. as to whether the authorities had overreacted.
Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant – gasoline – in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said the investigation "is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry."
"As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles - including possible foreign state involvement," she said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the U.K. sees "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. Iran denies involvement.
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," the prime minister told the BBC.
The base 100 miles west of London has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year's war with Iran.
Iranian authorities have warned that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets, but the Iranian Embassy in London said in a statement shared Monday on social media that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Burnham said authorities have the investigation under "the strongest grip and the closest control," and British officials had been "talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done."
 U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

French student protesters started fires at two schools, while teachers were inadvertently splashed with petrol at a third, officials have said.
The demonstrations over staff shortages and deteriorating school buildings grew increasingly violent on Thursday.
At Marseille's Victor Hugo high school, teachers were inadvertently splashed when a student attempted to throw petrol into a rubbish bin, local authorities said. The prosecutor's office had initially said teachers were assaulted and “doused in petrol”.
At another Marseille school, Saint-Exupery high school, hundreds of young people surrounded a fire truck responding to a blaze, police said. The group forced firefighters to leave the vehicle before setting it alight.
Another fire broke out at Nelson Mandela high school in the western city of Nantes, where no injuries were reported. The building was evacuated and students arriving for classes were turned away.

The protests and school blockades, which began last week, have become a political flashpoint as the government unveiled unpopular spending cuts in its 2027 budget on Thursday.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office held a crisis meeting on the protests, which officials said have left dozens injured and led to hundreds of arrests, most involving teenagers.
In the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, crowds gathered in front of police lines, with one student holding a sign reading: “Can we explain ourselves without being tear-gassed?”
Students have accused police of using heavy-handed tactics, including tear gas. The government has condemned violence during some protests while acknowledging concerns over conditions in high schools.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said troublemakers were moving between schools to incite violence.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said he would meet staff unions, parent groups and student associations on Friday. He also called on schools to switch to remote classes if protesters blocked access.
“Violence will not keep our students from their fundamental right to an education,” Geffray said on X.

Luca Sabbatucci is the new Italian ambassador to Bern

02:41:21 KST

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs announces that Luca Sabbatucci has taken up his post today as Italy’s Ambassador to Bern. He was born in Rome on March 5, 1963. He graduated with honors in Political Science with a concentration in international relations from La Sapienza University of Rome in 1988 and completed his military service in the Carabinieri.
                                    
                                       
				   He joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in February 1990; during the early years of his career, he served in the Diplomatic Protocol Office and the Minister’s Office. In 1992, he was assigned to the embassy in Seoul, where he remained until 1996, when he was appointed Consul in Athens. In April 2000, he returned to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and served as Chief of Staff of the Directorate General for Human Resources. From 2004 to 2008, he served in Ankara as Deputy Chief of Mission. In 2008, he returned to the Ministry and once again oversaw the management of human and financial resources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, first as Deputy Director General and later as Director General for Resources and Innovation. In this role, he completed the process of reorienting Italy’s diplomatic and consular network launched by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, supported reforms aimed at increasing the emphasis on merit in human resources management policies, and promoted the adoption of innovative work methods to ensure their effective implementation. 
   In January 2019, he was appointed Director General for Global Affairs. In this capacity, he was responsible for a wide range of issues, both bilateral and multilateral: from relations with Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and Latin America, to Italy’s membership in the G7, the G20, the OECD, the IEA, and other global forums on energy, climate, the economy, and finance.
                                    
                                       
				   In 2022, he served as Chief of Staff to the Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, a position he retained following a change in government. On November 15, 2022, in Paris, he served as Permanent Representative to International Organizations, where, among other duties, he chaired the OECD’s External Relations Committee. Since October 1, 2026, he has been Italy’s ambassador to Switzerland.

Ukraine deploys FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for first time, Zelensky says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:33:19 UTC
02:33:19 KST

Ukraine deploys FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for first time, Zelensky says
- Ukraine has deployed its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, as confirmed by President Zelensky on October 1.
- The FP-7 is a short-range missile with about 200km range, developed to enhance Ukraine's defence against Russian missile strikes.
- Ukraine aims to integrate the FP-7 into the European Freyja missile defence system, with a prototype expected by mid-2027.
AI generated
KYIV - Ukraine deployed its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 1.
“Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile FP-7. First combat use,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
“Thank you for the result. Next - production.”
He did not say where the FP-7 had been used in combat or against what target.
Russia frequently uses ballistic missiles in strikes on Ukrainian targets, and Ukraine has viewed development of its own tactical ballistic missiles as an important element in ensuring its defence needs after four and a half years of conflict with Moscow.
The need for effective interception of ballistic missiles has intensified as Kyiv prepares for an expected sustained Russian assault in the coming winter. Ukraine’s missile production is well behind that of Russia.
Zelensky praised the test results of tactical ballistic missiles earlier in 2026, saying they showed good potential for their use by the military.
Ukrainian military analysts describe the FP-7 as a short-range missile with a range of about 200km.
The missile’s manufacturer, Fire Point, says it is being developed as a ballistic interceptor within the European missile defence programme Freyja launched in 2026.
Military analysts have likened the FP-7 to the US Army Tactical Missile System, or ATACMS, some of which have already been transferred to Ukraine. But the FP-7, which has undergone accelerated development to counter the Russian threat, is considerably cheaper.
Fire Point is also developing a FP-9 missile with a range of up to 850km, which company officials say should be ready by the end of 2026.
Analysts suggest that deployment of both missiles would enable Ukraine to strike Russian missile launch and production sites and apply pressure on Moscow’s war infrastructure.
Ukraine and key Western allies announced an air defence coalition in July to proceed with the Freyja project that aims to jointly develop a cheaper alternative to the US Patriot system.
Ukraine wants a prototype for the Freyja European anti-ballistic system to be ready in the first half of 2027, Davyd Aloian, deputy secretary of Ukraine’s National Security and Defence Council said in July. REUTERS

Failed Christa Pike execution ‘a tragedy’, says Tennessee governor, as she survives two lethal injections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:23:32 UTC

Failed Christa Pike execution ‘a tragedy’, says Tennessee governor, as inmate survives two lethal injections
- Tennessee Governor Bill Lee called the failed execution of Christa Pike a tragedy and ordered a suspension of executions with a third-party review after she survived two lethal injections.
- Pike, sentenced for a 1995 murder committed as a teenager, endured "unnecessary agony" during the botched execution using a new one-drug protocol, highlighting issues with lethal injections.
- The incident sparked criticism from the UN and renewed debate on the death penalty, as most countries have abolished it due to its cruel and inhumane nature.
AI generated
NASHVILLE - Tennessee Governor Bill Lee called the failed execution of Christa Pike a tragedy on Oct 1, hours after she survived two lethal injection attempts at a Nashville prison and was taken to a hospital.
“There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen,” Lee, a Republican, told reporters.
“It’s a tragedy, and it’s deeply disturbing to me that that has happened in this state. The people deserve better, and we’re going to make sure that happens.”
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in the 1990s after a jury convicted her of a murder she carried out as a teenager.
Her botched execution on Sept 30 at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, the second this year in Tennessee, highlights the difficulties US states face in carrying out lethal injections.
Tennessee switched to a one-drug lethal injection protocol using pentobarbital, a powerful barbiturate, in 2024. Prison officials injected two syringes into Pike, her lawyers said in a late-night court filing, causing her “unnecessary agony” but not killing her.
The Tennessee Department of Corrections said the execution was halted, and she was taken away in an ambulance, but her condition was unclear on Oct 1.
She would have been the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than two centuries.
Lee told reporters that it was unclear what went wrong. He said he had no update on Pike’s condition and had not spoken with her family.
After the botched execution, he ordered a suspension of scheduled executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year and a third-party review of the Sept 30 failed attempt.
Most countries in the world have abolished the death penalty, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said Pike’s case showed that the US should follow suit.
“The prolonged suffering – physical and mental – arising from multiple failed execution attempts is abhorrent, and cruel,” Turk said, in a statement on X.
Pike was 18 in January 1995 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and a third companion lured Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate at their Knoxville Job Corps vocational centre, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her.
Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing, and both were convicted of first-degree murder.
Pike’s lawyers and supporters tried unsuccessfully to halt Pike’s execution by pointing to her young age at the time of the crime, her history of childhood sexual abuse and untreated mental illness.
The US Supreme Court threw out an 11th-hour stay on Sept 30 issued by a lower court.
Tennessee halted the execution of convicted murderer Tony Carruthers in May after prison officials were unable to set up intravenous lines to administer the lethal drugs. REUTERS

02:23:17 KST

The Third Army Corps has released a video showing a mass surrender of Russian soldiers, in which the occupiers explain their decision to surrender by citing hunger, exhaustion, administrative chaos, and threats from their own commanders; it is also noted that it is increasingly not infantrymen but specialized personnel of the Russian Armed Forces who are being taken prisoner.
"The Third Army Corps has released a video showing the mass surrender of Russian soldiers and their interaction with Brigadier General Andriy Biletsky. During the three phases of Operation 'Vivaldi,' more than 250 enemy soldiers were captured alive, including dozens of officers. The occupiers attribute their decision to surrender to hunger, exhaustion, administrative chaos, and threats from their own commanders, who, under pressure from the Third Corps, are losing control of the situation," according to a statement from the corps' press service received by Interfax-Ukraine.
In a video released by the corps, the prisoners claim that due to a lack of provisions at their positions, they are forced to eat nettles and tree bark and hunt wild animals. To stave off dehydration, the Russians resort to rainwater and, at times, their own urine. The wounded are not being evacuated from their positions: their only chance of survival is to crawl to the evacuation point on their own. During a conversation with Biletsky, the commander of the Third Army Corps, one of the Russian officers confirmed that troops are dying en masse from exhaustion and starvation. Another reason for capture is the administrative chaos in Russian headquarters, which, under pressure from the Third Corps, have begun to lose control of the battlefield.
It is increasingly not infantrymen but specialized personnel who are being taken prisoner. "Several Russian regiments are now falling apart. That is precisely why it is not even infantrymen who are being taken prisoner, but UAV pilots, mortar gunners, and electronic warfare specialists. We encounter infantry in the trenches less often than specialists," Corps Commander Biletsky said.
Captured Russian officers report that eight months ago, the situation on the front changed dramatically – the advance halted, and it became impossible to carry out orders from the command. Addressing the Russians, Biletsky said: "Capture is the best thing that could have happened to you, because in the near future your troops will face an even worse hell."
As previously reported, over the course of three phases of operation "Vivaldi," the Third Army Corps liberated 176 square kilometers in Lyman sector, eliminated over 5,000 enemy troops, and captured 250 Russian servicemen.
As part of this operation, the Third Army Corps is facing off against the forces of three Russian armies: Russia's 20th Combined Arms Army, Russia's 25th Combined Arms Army, and Russia's first Guards Tank Army. As a result, the offensive by the West Troop Group – formed from troops of the Moscow Military District – was halted, and the enemy was exhausted, defeated, and pushed back.
The 20th Combined Arms Army of Russia has been the main adversary of the third Assault Corps ever since a unit of the third Assault Brigade shifted its operations from Avdiivka to Borivka sector.
"Throughout its participation in the full-scale invasion, the 20th Army under Yurchenko's command has been responsible for numerous crimes against the Ukrainian people. In Ukrainian human rights databases and projects documenting war crimes, Yurchenko has been included in the relevant registries. Among other things, there is a documented case in which Ukrainian prisoners of war were executed using shovels. The execution was captured on thermal imaging. "The army commander at the time reported this incident to higher command, and those who carried out the execution were awarded (by the previous army commander, Alek Mityaev)," according to the reference section of the third Army Corps' statement.
It is noted that personnel of Russia's 25th Combined Arms Army were involved in mass war crimes on the territory of Ukraine, including the torture of civilians, the execution of prisoners of war, and the terrorization of the civilian population in Kharkiv region in 2022, while occupiers from Russia's first Guards Tank Army have committed numerous war crimes against the civilian population and infrastructure in Kyiv, Sumy, and Kharkiv regions.

PACE declares Russian State Duma illegitimate – MP Kravchuk
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
20:21:36 EEST
02:21:36 KST

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has declared the new composition of the Russian State Duma illegitimate, according to Yevhenia Kravchuk, a member of the Ukrainian parliamentary delegation to PACE (Servant of the People faction).
"PACE has declared the 'new' Russian State Duma illegitimate and called for restrictions on the issuance of tourist visas to Russians!" Kravchuk announced on Facebook on Wednesday.
According to her, the PACE resolution regarding the sham "elections" in Russia was adopted unanimously (59 votes in favor) during the Assembly's plenary session in Strasbourg on Wednesday.
"The Assembly clearly states: the so-called 'elections' to the State Duma held on September 18–20 did not meet the fundamental conditions for free and fair elections and cannot be considered a genuine expression of the will of Russian citizens. Consequently, the new State Duma cannot be recognized as democratically elected or as a legitimate representative body," the MP noted.
Kravchuk stated that three amendments were incorporated into the resolution's text at her proposal.
"Principles of international humanitarian law regarding occupation were enshrined: occupation is temporary in nature and does not transfer sovereignty to the occupying state. The occupying state must respect the existing legal order of the occupied territory, and temporary control cannot be used to alter its legal status," Kravchuk noted. She also emphasized that the resolution condemned the coercion of Ukrainian citizens in temporarily occupied territories into participating in Russian "electoral" processes.
"Participation [in the elections] obtained under conditions of occupation, coercion, or pressure cannot be interpreted as a free expression of political will or used to legitimize the attempted illegal annexation. Calls were also made for immediate sanctions against those who attempt to 'represent' the temporarily occupied territories," Kravchuk stressed.
According to Kravchuk, the resolution’s key calls include rejecting the sham elections to the Russian State Duma and refusing to recognize any legal or political consequences of holding them in Ukraine's temporarily occupied territories. The document also proposes refraining from any engagement with the new Russian State Duma, continuing the political and diplomatic isolation of the Russian authorities, and preventing the normalization of Russia's participation in international forums.
She noted that the resolution proposes imposing sanctions against the Russian Central Election Commission (CEC), including its leadership and members, as well as regional election commissions and individuals who organized or administered these so-called "elections," ran as candidates, or acted as "observers" in the temporarily occupied territory of Ukraine.

Ethiopia: Embassy shut in Eritrea, 10 diplomats expelled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:57:00 UTC
01:57:00 KST

Ethiopia and Eritrea sever ties amid Tigray fighting
October 1, 2026
Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties on Thursday after Ethiopia accused its northern neighbor of involvement in renewed fighting in the Tigray region.
The Ethiopian Foreign Ministry was the first to announce that it was shutting its embassy in Eritrea "in response to Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia."
The Ethiopian embassy in Eritrea had been reopened in 2018 as part of the rapprochement that culminated in Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed receiving the Nobel Peace Prize.
Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry also declared ten Eritrean diplomats "persona non grata", accusing them of "involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security." The Eritrean diplomats were given 48 hours to leave the country.
Hours later, Eritrea's Foreign Ministry called the move "absurd" and said the expulsion of ten of its diplomats from Addis Ababa had effectively shuttered its embassy there.
Eritrea said it therefore had "no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia with all the negative corollaries that this entails."
Reports of earlier blast at Ethiopian military headquarters
The measures came following reports of an explosion overnight at Ethiopian military headquarters in Addis Ababa.
The AFP news agency reported that the explosion took place at the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) headquarters between midnight and 1:00am local time, citing diplomatic and security sources with the information.
The sources could not provide further information relating to the nature of the blast or who was responsible, or if there had been any casualties.
The Associated Press, citing security sources, reported that there had been three blasts that came after the government banned the use of drones in the capital.
It's not clear whether the blasts were related to any attack or whether they had been part of training exercises.
Eritrea has denied allegations that it supports an armed alliance — which includes the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) — currently fighting Ethiopian government forces. The coalition is named Alliance for Survival.
Hundreds have been killed and wounded since last week's resumption of heavy fighting in northern Ethiopia.
Clashes have been ongoing and have have taken place along several fronts.
The United Nations has called for de-escalation of the fighting and for talks between the government and the recently formed alliance.

====================================================================================================

Google’s dream of AI data centers in space gets its first off-world test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:56:41 UTC
01:56:41 KST

When Elon Musk took SpaceX public in June, a big part of its value proposition came from promises of data centers in space. Skeptics were quick to list all of the hurdles. This afternoon Google’s Project Suncatcher is scheduled to launch hardware in pursuit of the same idea: it will send artificial intelligence processors into orbit onboard—of all things—a SpaceX rocket.
That doesn’t mean Musk’s pitch will become reality anytime soon. If anything, the gulf between Suncatcher and a working data center in orbit suggests how far off that future still is. But as AI’s appetite for electricity tests the patience of communities being asked to feed it, some of the richest tech companies are racing to source their energy needs from space instead.
The test satellite will carry just four processors, which will be used to run Google’s Gemini AI models for 15 minutes at a stretch before they need to shut down and cool off. The ultimate goal is to establish a full-fledged orbital data center, built from constellations of thousands of satellites that will share the work of running AI models and beam their responses back to Earth.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The whole effort has less to do with what could be accomplished out in space than with what’s getting harder to achieve down here on Earth. Data centers are projected to use around 3 percent of the world’s electricity by 2030, roughly double their share today, according to an International Energy Agency report. In orbit, sunlight is abundant and free, and Google says a solar panel there generates up to eight times as much power as it would on the ground. “We have direct access to a wonderful renewable source of energy,” says Alexander Wyglinski, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at Worcester Polytechnic Institute.
There’s a political incentive to look beyond U.S. soil, too. As the data-center buildout grows more divisive, blasting that infrastructure into space and away from people’s backyards holds obvious appeal.
But scale is the main question, Google readily admits. The biggest AI data centers that are being built now pack in hundreds of thousands of chips and draw up to a gigawatt of power, several thousand times the output of the International Space Station’s solar arrays. Even getting enough solar panels into orbit would be a massive undertaking at that scale. “It’s going from arrays that are several meters on a side to arrays that are a couple of kilometers on a side,” says Kerri Cahoy, a professor of astronautics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “Launching enough mass to generate the power is huge.”
The problems don’t end once everything is up there, either. Though space is cold, its vacuum is a lousy place to dissipate heat, which is why Suncatcher’s chips must clock out to cool down and why the satellites require specialized radiators. The whole satellite network needs to be resilient to space debris. And the cosmic radiation that Earth’s atmosphere filters out can scramble calculations, forcing systems to catch and correct errors on the fly. “When we talk about satellite platforms, and you put a computer into them, you don’t put [in] a computer like the one you have on your desk,” Wyglinski says.
For months before today’s launch, Google has been anticipating those problems on Earth, shaking spacecraft to simulate the launch and bombarding its chips with proton beams to test their response to radiation. “It's about seeing what works, identifying points of failure and applying those findings to future missions,” says Travis Beals, a senior director at Google, who leads Project Suncatcher.
Even so, scaling up could force Google and SpaceX to confront some stubborn physics. Every chip and solar panel has to be hauled into orbit, and every answer those chips produce has to come back down.
Satellites can transmit data to Earth, but doing so at scale is expensive and difficult. “We don’t have the convenient, easy way to get that data back to the ground,” says Alan George, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Pittsburgh, who heads a National Science Foundation center focused on space computing. During the Cold War, the problem was bad enough that U.S. spy satellites parachuted exposed film back to Earth.
Computers on Earth relay information easily, and lasers have made it possible to do the same between spacecraft. But getting information between Earth and space is another story entirely, so it is best to process some of the information gathered on satellites before it is sent down to Earth. “I like to tell my students the best data compression is answers,” George says. While that logic could apply to AI responses, too, his work putting computers in space tells him that the resource constraints make it hard to match what “you would put down the street in a building.”
Google’s engineers say they began from a similarly skeptical premise. “As a first step, we tried to find reasons that it was impossible,” Beals says, “but we gradually became convinced that it might actually work.”
And then there’s the question that may ultimately decide the whole thing: How will the limited bandwidth and energy savings make up the maintenance costs?
The cost of launching data center satellites and replacing them as they wear out, along with the bottleneck of getting data back down, may eat up whatever the free sunshine saves. The competitors in the first space race were nations jockeying for scientific dominance. Orbital data centers are mainly being pitched by corporations, which tend to prefer profitable ventures. So even if Project Suncatcher solves its technical challenges, those physical limitations could still kill the idea before Google gets anywhere close to a full-blown data center in space.
More often than not, space throws up more challenges than early movers expect. “It’s usually the late entrants who finally figured out how to do it effectively,” Cahoy says. SpaceX itself didn’t reach orbit until half a century after Sputnik.
If she’s right, the company that eventually gets data centers in space to scale may not even have booked its ride to orbit yet.

AI generated
BERLIN - Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned on Oct 1 that Germany faced more hybrid attacks from Russia, as he pledged to continue support for Ukraine ahead of what is likely to be its harshest winter since the start of Russia’s invasion in 2022.
German authorities have warned repeatedly that Russia is conducting a hybrid campaign of drone and cyber attacks, accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in August.
“We are preparing for further hybrid attacks, including serious ones,” Merz said, in a speech marking the award of the 2026 Westphalian Peace Prize to the NATO alliance.
Moscow has rejected the accusations from Western governments and intelligence services.
Speaking to a forum of Russia experts on Oct 1, President Vladimir Putin said Moscow was not about to attack foreign factories that produce weapons for Ukraine but that this was something Russian intelligence services needed to track closely.
Merz and his conservatives have been badly weakened by elections in two eastern German states in September in which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) triumphed.
The AfD has criticised Germany and its Western allies for supporting Ukraine with billions of euros in military aid. It wants to repair ties with Moscow and restore the flow of cheap oil and gas cut off since 2022.
‘Russia must end the war’
Merz said Germany wanted to re-establish “stable, predictable relations with Russia” at an appropriate time, adding that there was no sign that Moscow was ready to end the war in Ukraine.
“We do not wish to humiliate the Russian people or destabilise the Russian state. But Russia must end the war and refrain from hybrid attacks on Europe,” he said.
Merz, who has set aside hundreds of billions of euros to rebuild Germany’s armed forces, said Ukraine was probably facing its harshest winter since the Russian invasion four years ago and that Germany, as the most powerful state in central Europe, had a particular responsibility to help.
“We are not mediators; we stand on the side of freedom, and that is why we stand on the side of Ukraine.”
Merz said Germany and its allies could not allow themselves to be divided by hybrid attacks, social media campaigns or “the slogans of the AfD and its Russian backers”. REUTERS

‘15,000 voters targeted’: Rahul Gandhi’s fresh attack on EC over Karnataka rolls

NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi on Thursday launched a scathing attack on the Election Commission and accused it of erasing nearly 15,000 voters from electoral rolls in Karnataka’s Belagavi region.In a social media post on X, Rahul said that a massive “flood” of Form 7 applications was filed in bulk over three days to remove targeted groups from the voter list.“In just three days - September 22, 23, and 24 - there was a flood of Form 7 applications to remove nearly 15,000 voters... Muslims, SCs, STs, and OBCs are being systematically targeted because they do not vote for the BJP,” Rahul said.“I had already exposed this method of vote theft - votes are deleted through software in a centralised manner. ‘Select’ people are targeted as BJP and EC officials collude to fill out Form 7 in bulk through automated means - and in the blink of an eye, millions vanish from the voter list. And all of this is controlled from the top,” he added.The Congress leader also demanded that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar immediately take action or step down, alleging that refusal to register an FIR undermines democratic institutions.
“Karnataka Congress leaders are at this moment demanding an FIR against the culprits at the Karnataka CEO’s office. Why is the CEO refusing this FIR? In this way, Modi, Shah, and Gyanesh are collectively destroying democracy through SIR. This is treason. That's why I'm saying Gyanesh Kumar should resign and become an approver, and there should be an investigation against Modi and Shah,” he added.Form 7 is the official document prescribed by the Election Commission for objecting to the inclusion of or seeking the deletion of a name from an existing electoral roll.In Belagavi, local election officials reportedly received thousands of such applications over a span of 72 hours, triggering alarm among local Congress workers and booth-level officers (BLOs).Meanwhile, the poll panel and regional authorities clarified the procedural safeguards surrounding Form 7 filings. Election officials stressed that no voter’s name can be deleted automatically or solely based on the submission of a Form 7.Every application requires physical field verification, notices to be issued to the affected voter, and due process to be conducted by Booth Level Officers (BLOs) before any deletion is finalised, the panel said.Election officials instructed local BLOs to halt the immediate processing of suspected bulk filings and initiated internal inquiries to trace the origin of the submissions and verify whether the signatures were genuine.
Earlier on Wednesday, INDIA bloc leaders held a coordination meeting in New Delhi and announced a series of protests against the EC.Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge said Opposition parties would organise a nationwide “Save Democracy March” at the district level from October 2 to October 8.

After 2 years in office, how has Claudia Sheinbaum changed Mexico?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:48:00 UTC
01:48:00 KST

After 2 years, Sheinbaum's Mexico sees incremental change
October 1, 2026
Since Claudia Sheinbaum first took office in 2024 as Mexico's first female president, she has largely adhered to the political agenda of her mentor and predecessor, Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador.
But she has also had to contend with several problems that go far beyond Mexico's borders: violence inflicted by drug cartels, tens of thousands of missing persons and the growing political pressure from US President Donald Trump.
Fewer murders — but more missing persons
Sheinbaum has been able to report some progress when it comes to the security situation in Mexico. In her second government report, presented in September, she touted a 51% drop in the daily homicide rate since 2024.
To what extent this progress can be attributed to Sheinbaum's administration is, however, a matter of debate. While the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy has also noted progress in the effort to reduce homicides, the Mexico Evalua think tank has said there isn't enough statistical evidence to attribute the decline directly to measures taken by Sheinbaum.
And other indicators highlight a problematic trend. Mexico Evalua, referring to the government's own figures, pointed out that the number of recorded cases of kidnapping and enforced disappearances has surged by 127% over the last decade, "crimes against life" by 197% and femicide by 53%.
As of June 2026, the national register recorded a total of 135,271 missing persons. At the start of Sheinbaum's time in office in October 2024, that figure stood at around 115,000, according to an analysis by Red Lupa, a citizen-led network dedicated to monitoring disappearances.
"There is a lack of political will [to address the issue]," said Edgar Cortez, a project coordinator at the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy in Mexico City. On the one hand, he said, the government sees little political benefit, while at the same time it's lacking the technical expertise to coordinate the varied measures implemented at the state and federal levels.
Displacement — another consequence of violence — is also disrupting the lives of millions across the country. According to the National Institute of Statistics and Geography, violence or crime forced at least one member in 510,000 households — some 1.6 million people — to change their place of residence between October 2020 and October 2025.
Selective crackdown on corruption
Eduardo Bohorquez, director of civil society organization Transparencia Mexicana, told DW he has noted a shift in the government's strategy when it comes to fighting corruption. Two years on, he said the government is now focusing on the links between federal employees and organized crime.
As example he gave Operacion Enjambre, during which more than 100 public officials of varying political affiliation were arrested — including mayors, former mayors and police commanders, according to Mexico's security chief Omar Garcia Harfuch.
Critics, however, have accused the government of taking a selective approach. To date, no incumbent or former governor of Sheinbaum's ruling Morena party has been either prosecuted or detained for corruption or alleged links to organized crime.
Shienbaum has announced a package of reforms to tackle corruption, and Bohorquez said that will show whether or not her administration will actually chart a different course than that of her predecessor.
Placating Trump a top priority
Domestic and foreign policy have been closely linked during Sheinbaum's two years in office. Most of that time has been shaped by Donald Trump's return to the White House in January 2025, and his administration's increasing pressure on drug cartels, migration and trade.
Trump has accused Mexico of not doing enough to tackle the cartels, with Washington classifying several Mexican criminal organizations as terrorist groups. The US president has repeatedly threatened to take unilateral action against the cartels. Sheinbaum, however, has opposed any US military actions on Mexican territory, calling instead for "cooperation without subordination."
At the same time, Mexico and the US have been cooperating closely — especially when it comes to migration. Between 2024 and 2025, the number of migrant contacts registered by US authorities along the US-Mexico border dropped by more than 84%, from 1.5 million to around 238,000.
Economic cooperation is also key to the cross-border relationship. Mexico and the US are currently negotiating several trade issues, including the future of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, known as USMCA. For its part, Mexico is hoping to reduce Trump's tariffs on steel, aluminum and automobiles.
After talks with Trump in September, Sheinbaum said both sides were working toward a trade deal. It remains a tricky balancing act for the Mexican president — developing the closest possible trading relationship with her country's most important economic partner, while at the same time not giving the impression that Mexico is giving up its political sovereignty under pressure from Washington.
Progress on social rights
The outlook is brighter when it comes to economic and social rights, with Cortez of the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy singling out the increase in minimum wage and government benefits for older people and those living with disabilities.
When it comes to other human rights concerns, however, he hasn't seen "any progress or setbacks." Alongside the staggering number of missing persons, Cortez also pointed out attacks on human rights defenders and journalists, along with a failure to sufficiently consult with Indigenous groups and rural communities when it came to major construction projects.
Sheinbaum has announced a plan to introduce a nationwide law against femicide that would align the various regulations on the local and state level, said Cortez. "That could end up being a positive, but the problem will be to put it into practice," he added.
Transparency without 'accountability'
The government's record on transparency remains problematic, according to observers, with Sheinbaum doing away with the National Institute for Transparency, Access to Information and Protection of Personal Data, or INAI. The responsibilities of the independent agency, which had been in place for two decades, have since been divided among several state entities.
"Instead of making things easier, everything has become fragmented," said Bohorquez of Transparencia Mexicana. Anyone looking for information from Congress, the judiciary, the military or local authorities now needs to go directly to the source.
Bohorquez also gave a mixed reaction to Sheinbaum's daily press conference, saying that while it was "a very effective political communication tool it didn't provide accountability."
For Cortez, that reflects a fundamental question of Sheinbaum's political priorities. New social programs bring "instant political benefits," he said, while advancing on civil and political rights required long-term effort and didn't allow the government to "immediately capitalize on political gains."

Türkiye to gradually hand over Bashiqa-Zilkan base to Iraq: ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:43:46 UTC
01:43:46 KST

The Turkish National Defence Ministry has said that the Turkish Armed Forces will gradually hand over a military base in the northern Iraqi region of Bashiqa-Zilkan to Iraqi authorities.
“Bashiqa-Zilkan Base, which has been used by the Turkish Armed Forces since 2015 as part of the fight against the Daesh terrorist group at the request of Iraqi authorities, will be gradually handed over to Iraqi authorities,” the ministry noted in response to questions following its weekly media briefing in Türkiye’s central Kayseri province on Thursday.
It would be in line with the agreed mechanism and timeline, taking into account the progress made by the central Iraqi government in its security efforts in Sinjar, the ministry added.
It underlined that Türkiye welcomes the central Iraqi government's recent steps to establish state authority in Sinjar.
“We believe these steps will contribute to the normalisation of the region, the establishment of an environment of security and stability, and the creation of a terror-free area,” the ministry noted.
“As in the past, Türkiye stands by its neighbour Iraq today in ensuring security and stability in the region,” it added.
The ministry stressed that steps are planned to further advance military and security cooperation between Türkiye and Iraq.
“We will continue to support the Iraqi Armed Forces under bilateral agreements in the areas of enhancing military capabilities, sharing experience and expertise in counterterrorism, military training, and defence industry cooperation,” it added.
Military parade in Greek-administered southern Cyprus
On the military parade held by the Greek Cypriot Administration, the ministry said, “We once again emphasise that the Greek Cypriot Administration’s ongoing arms buildup and its military cooperation with third countries negatively affect the delicate balance and security environment on the island.”
The ministry noted that the provocative actions carried out by the Greek Cypriot Administration and Greece do not contribute to efforts to establish mutual trust on the island, but only increase tensions and undermine stability.
“As a guarantor country, we reiterate that a fair, lasting and sustainable solution on the island of Cyprus can only be achieved through the recognition of the sovereign equality and equal international status of the Turkish Cypriot people,” it said.
Türkiye will continue to take the necessary measures, in cooperation with the authorities of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, to safeguard the security, peace and well-being of the Turkish Cypriot people, it added.
Procurement of C-130J aircraft
Asked about the status of the agreement to procure 12 C-130J aircraft from the UK, the ministry said that “the aircraft are planned to be gradually brought to Türkiye following ongoing maintenance activities in the UK.”
“In this context, the first two aircraft are scheduled to be delivered in December, while training activities for our personnel are continuing simultaneously,” it noted.
The training of six pilots and six technicians in the US, as well as 29 maintenance personnel in the UK, is continuing as planned and in line with the established schedule, it added.

Tainan underground station unveiled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:15 UTC
01:41:15 KST

The new underground Tainan Railway Station was unveiled to the public for the first time yesterday ahead of its official opening next month.
The Tainan City Government said that train operations are scheduled to officially move to the new underground station on Oct. 18.
The Railway Bureau said that the existing Tainan Railway Station, a designated national heritage site, would be closed for restoration once the new underground station becomes operational.
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
Train passengers would access the new underground facility through a different entrance while the train station is being restored, it said.
The bureau invited news media to see the facilities inside the newly built station, including the train control room, central monitoring room, telecommunications equipment room, tunnel ventilation plant room and ballastless tracks.
The station would be equipped with the Taiwan Railway Corp’s fourth-generation ticketing machines, which have eliminated the function for processing magnetic-stripe tickets and would be equipped with QR code scanners.
The Tainan underground railway station is equipped with a range of new rail, signaling and safety systems designed to improve train operations and passenger safety, the bureau’s Southern Region Engineering Branch said in its briefing.
The underground railway has 10 ventilation rooms equipped with 19 tunnel ventilation fans, silencers, control dampers and power-supply equipment. The systems provide routine air circulation and can be switched to emergency ventilation mode during fires to remove smoke and maintain airflow, making it possible for personnel to evacuate within 900 seconds of critical period.
The station’s train control room is equipped with signaling control units, control panels, train information displays, overhead power control switches, closed-circuit television cameras, and wired and wireless dispatch communications.
The equipment enables dispatchers to monitor train locations, track conditions and switch status in real time, and adjust train operations or respond to incidents as needed, the bureau said.
A central monitoring room serves as the control hub for the underground railway tunnels and station.
It monitors tunnel ventilation, power supplies, access control, lighting, fire alarms, elevators and escalators, while CCTV provide views of the station concourse, platforms and underground tunnels.
The train control room and central monitoring room are considered the “brains” of the new underground railway station.
Railway Bureau Deputy Director-General Liu Yun-sheng (劉雲生) said the station combines architectural elements reflecting Tainan’s history with rail, electrical and safety technologies to support safe and stable operations.
The bureau said that it is to hold open-house tours for the public this weekend and on Tuesday next week, led by professionals.

US Congress ought to fix the flawed Saudi nuclear deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:15 UTC
01:41:15 KST

The confusion surrounding a proposed civil nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia has not exactly disappeared: The White House is still claiming it depends on the country normalizing relations with Israel, even if that is not part of the written agreement. At least the US Congress now has the text for review. Having seen its flaws, legislators should demand changes.
The 30-year nuclear cooperation pact would allow US companies not only to build new reactors in the kingdom, but possibly also a uranium enrichment facility — needed to produce the fissile material for a bomb. The two governments would have up to two years to decide whether an indigenous enrichment program makes sense, both commercially and in terms of US national interests. If so, the US would introduce, but restrict the sensitive technology, keeping it in a metaphorical “black box” to prevent transfer to the Saudis. Congress has 90 days in session to decide whether to oppose the deal; otherwise, it will go into effect automatically.
Proceeding on such terms would be risky. For decades, the US and other nuclear suppliers have refused to provide customers with the technology to enrich uranium or reprocess spent fuel, precisely so they could not assemble the working materials for a bomb. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman has already said his nation would “have to” match Iran if it develops a nuclear weapon; the mere possibility that the Saudis might do so would encourage other countries in the region to pursue one as well. Any restricted facilities would be vulnerable to leakage, if not outright seizure.
It is unclear why the US even needs to offer such a concession. Other suppliers are not threatening to provide the same access to enrichment technology; Russia and China compete mainly on cost. Besides, the Saudis have been pursuing access to US nuclear technology for nearly two decades. They have had plenty of time to seek alternatives if they wished. Breaking with precedent, on the other hand, could liberate US rivals to do the same. (Russia is already leading major reactor projects in Egypt and Turkey.) It would also dramatically weaken the US case against allowing Iran a domestic enrichment program.
While a joint resolution opposing the agreement seems unlikely to muster a veto-proof majority, Congress should still use this chance to press for greater clarity and stronger safeguards against proliferation.
At minimum, lawmakers should thoroughly scrutinize the classified documents linked to the deal, including two secret side letters, and insist on answers to unresolved questions such as whether the Saudis would be allowed to pursue an independent enrichment program if the joint study decides against one. Congress should insist on input into that study, to ensure the arguments against allowing nuclear fuel-making are fully absorbed.
Legislators should continue to push for the Saudis to sign an Additional Protocol with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), allowing for expanded international inspections. Failing that, they should press the administration to work with the IAEA on expedited procedures to investigate any suspicions that the Saudis might be pursuing a hidden enrichment or weapons program. Perhaps most important, Congress should lay out severe consequences for such cheating — including asset freezes and cutting off access to other US technology.
The administration should be commended for looking for ways to boost US nuclear exports, but that goal should not be pursued at any cost — and Congress should say so clearly.

Manufacturing PMI rises to five-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:14 UTC
01:41:14 KST

Taiwan’s manufacturing sector expanded at its fastest pace in more than five years last month, as robust demand for artificial intelligence (AI) hardware continued to drive growth, despite easing new orders and mounting supply and cost pressures, the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research (CIER, 中華經濟研究院) said yesterday.
The manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) climbed to 63.4 from 61.7 in August, its highest level since August 2021, with all six major industries reporting improved business conditions, the institute said.
A reading above 50 indicates expansion.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
“AI demand continues to drive manufacturing growth, with the benefits gradually extending to nonmanufacturing sectors,” CIER president Lien Hsien-ming (連賢明) told a news conference in Taipei.
The expansion remained particularly strong in technology-related industries, although its pace moderated somewhat, Lien said.
The new orders index, a leading indicator of future activity, fell 2.9 points to 63.6. Manufacturers reported shortages of some materials, excess inventories of others and longer delivery times, all of which were complicating production schedules, the institute said.
The combination suggests manufacturers are shifting some focus from expanding output to managing inventory and supply-chain pressures, it said.
AI-related demand remains the main support for manufacturing, while rising energy costs amid heightened tensions in the Middle East have sharply increased raw material prices and prompted companies to reallocate orders, Supply Management Institute in Taiwan (中華採購與供應管理協會) adviser Jerry Pai (白宗城) said.
Petrochemical producers are facing higher raw material and transportation costs, while demand remains relatively firm for advanced semiconductor materials, specialty chemicals and materials used in precision medical products, Pai said.
Manufacturers are also reviewing products and production plans for next year, while new product trials and testing are competing for capacity already strained by long lead times, potentially weighing on some short-term PMI readings, he said.
Still, the six-month business outlook remained firmly in expansion territory at 59.5 last month, the highest reading since May 2024, with all six major industries expecting growth, the institute said.
Meanwhile, the nonmanufacturing index rose for a 19th consecutive month to 56.9, indicating that the manufacturing boom is gradually extending into services, including stock-related and tourism businesses, the CIER said.
Service sector companies also became more optimistic about fourth-quarter activity, although persistent cost and delivery pressures remained a concern, it said.
Lien cautioned that the expansion remains uneven, with a pronounced gap between technology and non-technology industries.
“We hope other industries can gradually catch up as the tech sector expands, narrowing the gap across the economy, but so far, the tech sector remains exceptionally strong,” Lien said.

Woman hospitalized after surviving execution twice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:13 UTC
01:41:13 KST

A Tennessee woman convicted of murder yesterday survived two lethal injection doses and was hospitalized, her lawyers said, marking the state’s second failed execution in months and prompting it to halt capital punishment this year.
Hours earlier on Wednesday, the Supreme Court cleared the way for Christa Pike, 50, to become the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in 200 years — but the attempt failed.
“This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” Death Penalty Information Center executive director Robin Maher said. “There is no precedent.”
Photo: Tennessee Department of Correction via REUTERS
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it “followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol.”
Her attorneys said she was transported to a nearby hospital, adding they have not been informed as to her condition.
“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” the attorneys said in a statement.
Tennessee halted the execution by lethal injection of Tony Carruthers in May after medical staff were unable to tap a vein.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee called for a “comprehensive, third-party review” after Pike’s failed execution.
“The remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year,” Lee said — apparently referencing the execution of convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton scheduled for Dec. 3.
The case has sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer’s body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Pike’s lawyers said she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of the killing.
“She was 18 when she committed her crime, and she was deeply mentally ill,” they said.
The US Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected an application for a stay of execution, which said that Pike’s history as a victim of sexual assault, post-traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant a lethal injection would cause “needless suffering.”

Advocates call for research into owls at Shalun park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:13 UTC
01:41:13 KST

Environmental advocates called for an investigation into the pre-breeding population size of eastern grass owls, the population density of rodents and the preservation of habitats for the critically endangered bird species in the Shalun Science Park development project.
Based in the Shalun (沙崙) area around Tainan High Speed Rail Station in the city’s Gueiren District (歸仁), the 507-hectare project is part of the government’s Southern Taiwan Silicon Valley Program, which aims to build a semiconductor industry S-corridor in southern Taiwan.
The project’s second scoping meeting was held at the Ministry of Environment in Taipei yesterday.
Photo: CNA
Environmental groups focusing on different fields yesterday attended the meeting to express concerns over the project’s public health risks, carbon emissions, water usage plan and biodiversity preservation plan.
Of all the discussed issues, the habitat conservation for eastern grass owls was at center of debate.
The critically endangered bird species has an estimated population size of 200 to 500 nationwide, with its population highly restricted to southern Taiwan.
Apple Bird Satoyama Conservation Foundation representative Tseng Lung-yung (曾瀧永) said that roadkill is the leading cause of eastern grass owl deaths while rodenticides are a sublethal factor for the rodent-eating raptor.
Eastern grass owls need large, undivided grassland covering at least 200 hectares for habitat and an area of 20 hectares to 70 hectares for nest range, he said.
“Micro shelters” planted with white cogongrass and covering only 10 hectares or less might not help preserve eastern grass owls at the project site, Tseng said.
Tseng also called for a rodent population density survey to ensure that eastern grass owls have sufficient food without excessive rodenticide intake.
“Eastern grass owl conservation does not conflict with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co setting up fabs at the science park,” he said, adding that the disagreement lies in different conservation thinking.
Tseng said that owl habitat preservation should be established before the project started construction, which could happen in 18 months.
“Creating an eastern grass owl habitat requires two years,” he said, adding the habitat preservation effort is falling behind.
Tainan City Wildlife Conservation Association executive director Tseng I-shuo (曾翌碩) said it might be difficult to establish the causal link between rodenticide intake from the project site and eastern grass owl deaths.
While wildlife could have trace elements accumulating in their body just like humans, eastern grass owls have an activity range of up to 300 hectares, making it difficult to identify their exact forage locations, he said.
Tseng Lung-yung said that if a causal link cannot be established between the project’s rodenticide use and its eastern grass owl population size, then it cannot be built between the government’s regional eco-friendly farming practices and the bird species’ population growth.
He called for an investigation to ensure eastern grass owls have a pre-breeding population size of at least 100 adult birds.
Taiwan People’s Party Legislator Chen Gao-tzu (陳昭姿), who also attended the meeting, asked the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency to designate major wildlife habitats for eastern grass owls at the project site.
She said she would list the issue as a resolution for review by the legislature.

Old masters, wider worlds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:11 UTC
01:41:11 KST

Van Gogh once said that he would starve himself to spend time with Rembrandt’s The Jewish Bride.
“I should be happy to give 10 years of my life if I could go on sitting here in front of this picture for a fortnight, with only a crust of dry bread for food,” van Gogh said.
The quote can be found at “Old Masters From Rembrandt to Goya,” an exhibition of 52 masterpieces from the Toledo Museum of Arts at the Fubon Museum in Taipei.
Photo: Bonnie White, Taipei Times
Rembrandt’s deep influence on van Gogh is a central theme to the exhibition which shows how European artists not only influenced each other, but were also influenced by their society and foreign cultures.
It is Rembrandt’s mastery of chiaroscuro and his unmatched ability to portray the emotional depth of his subjects that inspired van Gogh to spend hours looking at his paintings in Dutch museums.
In the section titled “Painting and Power”, monastic depictions and Napoleonic propaganda show how royal patrons and wealthy elites sought influence by wielding artistic commissions.
In The Oath of the Horatii (1786) commissioned by King Louis XVI, Jacques-Louis David contrasts determined male postures with women slumped in desperation to frame militaristic ambition as a moral virtue.
Seventeenth-century Dutch painters fractured this dynamic. Bypassing church and royal patrons, artists catered to a rising middle class.
Rembrandt embraced this shift to paint uncommissioned character studies. Two of his tronies displayed by van Gogh’s commendation, portray anonymous characters in theatrically flamboyant costumes.
The portraits, from his early and late period, offer a transfixing repertoire of his ability to grasp evocative facial expressions and capture light and shadow.
Yet, this emancipated merchant market still demanded structure. Thomas de Keyser’s portrait of authoritative Dutch guild officers debunks the lone genius trope to reveal how production markets actually sustained painters such as Rembrandt.
This new market based on a flourishing colonial economy also brought new artistic focus, introducing painters to imported commodities and turning bustling ports into landscape studios.
In the “European Art in a Global Context” section, Chinese porcelain, rare Turkish tulips and shells from the Indonesian archipelago in van der Astat’s Fruits, Flowers and Shells (1620s) reveal the Dutch East India company’s vast colonial expeditions.
Across the room, van Goyen’s View of Dordrecht (1649) shows billowing clouds above fleets of boats in the bustling Dutch port, capturing the momentum of a nation securing dominance over trade routes.
By the eighteenth century, artistic influence spread beyond colonial conquests and stolen luxuries. Genre work was popularized as painters elevated as subject matter ordinary people and everyday life.
In the “Everyday Beauty” section, Jean-Simeon Chardin paints textured surfaces and light effects in The Washerwoman and The Woman Drawing Water at the Cistern (1733-39), to transform laborious domestic settings into harmonious scenes.
“We have learned from Chardin that a pear is as living as a woman, that an ordinary piece of pottery is as beautiful as a precious stone,” said French writer Marcel Proust.
This elevation of feeling over form laid the groundwork for nineteenth-century Romanticism, during which artists rejected the order, logic and classical restraint of the Enlightenment to portray emotions.
In the “Capturing Nature” section, Theodore Rousseau’s Under the Birches, Evening (1842-43), shows an idyllic summer evening in the countryside by contrasting a darkening dusk sky with colorful autumn trees set ablaze by fading light.
Using impressionist-like brushstrokes and dabbed highlights John Constable brings movement to his landscape Arundel Mill and Castle (1837). Shifting clouds, the rustle of trees and dappling sunlight seemingly extend beyond the canvas.
While Rousseau and Constable searched for emotional resonance, Francisco Goya was inspired by the human condition.
Often remembered for his work consumed by the dark, psychological depths of his permanent deafness and the brutal French invasion of Spain, the exhibition anchors Goya in an earlier, unshadowed chapter of his life.
In his tapestry cartoon Children in a Cart (1778), Goya captures an optimistic world with playful and smiling youth before the political and personal upheavals that would eventually shatter his life and alter European art.
For art enthusiasts, this is a unique opportunity to map the societal shifts and cultural revolutions that transformed European painting from the Renaissance to Neoclassicism.
Sept. 28 to Oct. 4 Opening in 1971, Singapore’s Wisma Theatre (海燕歌劇院) was entirely modeled after Taiwanese live variety shows, combining singing, dancing and drama. Even its performers were recruited from Taiwan. The formula was an instant hit, selling out on the third night with the crowd fighting outside for tickets. Among its key figures was 31-year-old Chi Li-nan (紀利男), an acclaimed saxophonist and band leader who had entered Taiwan’s live entertainment scene at age 19 with zero musical training. Chi wasn’t even supposed to be there. He had accompanied his girlfriend, pop singer Shang Kuan Ping (上官萍), to negotiations with Wisma’s agent.
In 1951, the Central Propaganda Department of the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) Central Reform Committee launched an English-language magazine, which, for the next 75 years, would serve as a mouthpiece for Taiwan’s government. Initially titled the Free China Review, and later rechristened as the Taiwan Review, the magazine published its final issue in March. Former editor Richard Vuylsteke has described the magazine as Taiwan’s “landmark foreign language publication going abroad.” The magazine was not universally respected. Some international scholars, including a few contacted for this article, dismissed it as a “propaganda rag.” But others, including Shelley Rigger, a top US researcher at

His odds later fell, illustrating the highly speculative nature of the wagering. There is no public evidence Carney is on the Nobel Committee’s secret shortlist for the prize

Cabinet proposes extending bond, bond ETF tax exemption for 10 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:10 UTC
01:41:10 KST

The Executive Yuan yesterday approved a draft amendment to the Securities Transaction Tax Act (證券交易稅條例) that would extend a tax exemption on corporate bonds, financial bonds and passive bond exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for another 10 years, through Dec. 31, 2036, while expanding the exemption to actively managed bond ETFs.
The proposal came amid robust growth in Taiwan’s domestic bond market following the introduction of the exemption in 2017, the Taxation Administration said.
The outstanding value of corporate and financial bonds totaled NT$4.66 trillion last year, up from NT$2.66 trillion in 2017, while their total trading value reached NT$19.73 trillion, an increase from NT$17.23 trillion in 2017, administration data showed.
Photo: CNA
Meanwhile, the outstanding value of passive bond ETFs totaled NT$3.02 trillion last year, up from NT$40 billion in 2017, while their total trading value reached NT$2.16 trillion, compared with NT$70 billion in 2017, the data showed.
The tax exemption for bonds and passive bond ETFs is set to expire on Dec. 31.
The Ministry of Finance said the exemption has helped stimulate Taiwan’s capital market and promote its development.
Under the draft, the exemption for active bond ETFs would take effect on Jan. 1 next year and remain in place through Dec. 31, 2036.
The outstanding value of corporate and financial bonds could reach NT$17.96 trillion by 2036, while annual trading value could amount to NT $93.19 trillion, the ministry said.
The combined value of bond ETFs, including passive and active ETFs, could reach NT$12.75 trillion in 2036, while annual trading value could hit NT$7.65 trillion, it said.
Active bond ETFs were included to ensure tax neutrality between financial products with similar characteristics, the ministry said.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) believes the amendment would boost asset management activity, support the government’s goal of developing Taiwan into an “Asian asset management center” and promote the development of the capital market, Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said.
The ministry is still assessing the effect on tax revenue, but the extension would benefit companies and the financial industry, Deputy Minister of Finance Chen Yong-sheng (陳勇勝) said.
The proposal must pass legislative review before it can become law.

The Philippine Coast Guard yesterday said it has deployed its largest vessel and an aircraft to challenge a Chinese research ship operating off northern Batanes near Taiwan, adding that a Chinese coast guard vessel had also moved in.
The Philippine operation “disrupted the vessel’s unauthorized marine scientific research and compelled it to leave its loitering position,” said Jay Tarriela, Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson on South China Sea issues.
The Philippine Coast Guard said the BRP Teresa Magbanua and an aircraft were deployed to counter the Chinese vessel, which it said had remained about 37 nautical miles northwest of Itbayat Island since Monday.
Photo: Reuters
The Chinese vessel Jia Hai Ke 7 is the same Chinese-flagged survey ship that the coast guard said was spoofing its location while loitering off Batanes.
The Teresa Magbanua moved within 100 yards of the Jia Hai Ke 7 and deployed a rigid-hull inflatable boat that circled the research vessel several times as personnel issued radio challenges, the coast guard said.
The research vessel repeatedly maneuvered to evade Philippine boats during the operation, it added.
Photo: AFP
A China Coast Guard vessel then arrived to try to shield the survey ship and issued its own radio challenges to the Philippine ship.
The involvement of a China Coast Guard vessel was “significant,” because Jia Hai Ke 7 is privately owned, raising questions about its links to the Chinese government and the purpose of the data it might have collected near undersea cable corridors off Batanes and the Luzon Strait, the Philippine Coast Guard said.
The research vessel was forced to leave its loitering position, with Teresa Magbanua continuing to monitor it to ensure it exited the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone.
The Chinese embassy in Manila said the research vessel was “conducting normal operations in waters under China’s jurisdiction” and accused the Philippines of harassment.
It urged Manila to stop interfering with Beijing’s scientific research activities.

Ministry launches phone recycling event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:05 UTC
01:41:05 KST

The Ministry of Environment’s Resource Circulation Administration has launched a mobile phone recycling event open to locals and international residents in Taiwan, with an iPhone and an Apple Watch being offered as lucky draw prizes.
The event has about 2,700 recycling sites nationwide and would run through this month — the “Mobile Phone Recycling Month of October.”
Chen Yen-nan (陳彥男), head of the Sustainable Consumption and Recycling Division at the administration, yesterday said that all people in Taiwan can participate in the event and the lucky draw regardless of their nationality.
Photo: Screen grab from the ministry’s Web site
Anyone can enter the raffle by recycling a mobile phone at the designated sites, he said, adding that there is no limit on the number of mobile phones recycled or number of raffle entries.
The administration would offer raffle prizes such as an iPhone, an Apple Watch and convenience store gift vouchers, while some participating organizations would offer conditional gifts to participants, Chen said.
The annual recycling of mobile phones in Taiwan ranged from 80,000 to 100,000 phones over the past three years, he said, adding that more than 90,000 mobile phones were recycled nationwide last year.
The ministry set up the Mobile Phone Recycling Month in 2019 and continued to hold the event to encourage people to properly recycle unused mobile phones, the administration said.
Given that mobile phones are made of materials such as metals and plastics, recycling mobile phones helps facilitate reuse or circulation of such resources, it said.
The administration called on people to back up phone data, delete all personal information and restore their phones to factory settings before handing them to recycling site operators or local governments’ cleaning squads, to ensure personal data protection.
Those who need assistance with personal data protection on a phone that cannot be turned on can seek help from the event’s designated service sites to destroy the phone’s charging port within the event period, it said.
Such service sites include Acer Inc’s Sijhih (汐止) and Guanghua (光華) service centers in New Taipei City, Wenxin (文心) service center in Taichung, and Jiouru (九如) service center in Kaohsiung, as well as Asus’ Royal Club Yingcai store in Taichung, it added.
More detailed information on the event can be found at the event Web site (https://phonereca.com).

Tainan cultural items found during project displayed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:04 UTC
01:41:04 KST

Cultural heritage remains discovered during the completion of the Tainan underground railway project are on display at the Tainan Cultural and Creative Park, the Railway Bureau said yesterday.
The project’s construction team found 20 archeological sites along the 8.23km-long underground railway route, with historic objects dating back to prehistoric times, China’s Qing Dynasty, the Japanese colonial era and the post-World War II era.
Among the most significant discoveries, the archaeological site at Sheng Kung Girls’ High School yielded prehistoric pottery and stone artifacts, including deep-bellied bowls, pottery spindle whorls and stone tools used for fishing.
Photo: CNA
Remains of the Tainan city walls dating back to the reign of Qing Emperor Qianlong provide evidence of the city’s historic defense system, the bureau said.
A former underground military arsenal yielded a dense concentration of military artifacts, including more than 2,000 cannonballs, as well as firearms, cannon barrels and helmets.
Near the former Sin Lau Hospital, archaeologists uncovered remains associated with the traditional sugar industry, including a 5.1m-long arrangement of sugar molds used in white-sugar refining and layers of a compacted-earth road believed to have been used by ox carts. The remains shed light on Tainan’s sugar production during the Qing Dynasty.
Other discoveries include north and south railway turntables dating to the early Japanese colonial period, which were used to turn locomotives around, as well as the remains of Guyuan (固園), a residence and garden associated with a prominent family.
Railway Bureau director-general Yang Cheng-chun (楊正君) said construction of the underground railway project was postponed for about two years because of the discoveries of these archeological sites.
“Through the project, not only do the residents in Tainan get a new underground railway line, but they also discover valuable cultural assets that tell stories of their ancestors,” Yang said.
The exhibition is open to the public free of charge until Nov. 22, the bureau said.
