====================================================================================================

The resilient roots of a quaint west coast town
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:03 UTC
01:41:03 KST

Fangyuan Township (芳苑) in Changhua County is a quiet, unassuming setting, known for its wetlands, eco tours and trained sea-ox that transport the oyster harvest in carts. Topographically speaking, it’s also enormously diverse, boasting a proud tradition of aquaculture and an ecologically rich coastline.
Fertile fields abound with an abundance of crops from green onions to dragon fruit, with vineyards to the east in neighboring Erlin Township (二林鎮).
WANGGONG FISHING PORT
Photo: Shane O’Reilly
To the northwest of the township, flanked by the Wanggong Fishing Port (王功漁港) and harbor, stands the tall two-tone lighthouse. Built in 1983, this popular landmark is still fully operational.
The Wanggong Fishing Port has itself become synonymous with the region. Though small in stature, it has held on tight to its legendary status as Taiwan’s epicenter for oyster fishing.
Disruption by offshore wind farms means reduced yields, and as such, locals have had to adapt, introducing guided eco-tours and ox cart rides around the intertidal zone with optional clam digging or oyster grilling.
The modernization of a world looking toward a cleaner, more efficient planet may put an end to the old ways of life one day, but for now the deep-rooted heritage remains.
A food court nearby sells watermelon smoothies to be paired with soft-shell crab and fish tempura.
It’s all flash-fried with fresh basil leaves and doused in a generous helping of salt to be carried away in little brown bags and eaten elsewhere.
Dining al fresco, there’s usually a light breeze; everything’s so still, so quiet, the water surface shimmering under the glaring sun.
There’s a slight rhythmic swell outward from the moored boats of the harbor to the pelagic expanse around the legs and blue arches of the King’s Bow Bridge (王者之弓橋).
FANGYUAN PUTIAN TEMPLE
A short drive away is one of the country’s largest Mazu Temples, the Fangyuan Putian Temple (芳苑白馬峰普天宮).
A commanding presence flanked by two bell and drum towers, its grounds cover some 6 hectares, and it stands 35 meters tall at its highest point.
The ground floor acts as an expansive welcoming plaza, while the opulent halls, side altar rooms, and main sanctuary spaces can be found on the second and third floors.
When visitors have finished their prayer route (參拜順序), it’s a short 3-minute walk to the central entrance of the Fangyuan Wetlands Trail (芳苑海空步道).
The trail is a mere 2.1km, winding through a thick, variegated mangrove fringe, heavy with the scent of sea salt in the air.
From the walkway, the mangroves are half-submerged, but as the path curls away to shallower waters, you’ll be able to view the local wildlife in the pockmarked mudflats below on either side.
The anoxic, black, viscous mud supports a flourishing benthic life of red-hued Taiwanese bowed fiddler crabs, the males distinguishable by their one oversized claw as they potter in and out of their makeshift mud tunnels.
Alongside the crabs, skittish mudskippers, similar in appearance to lengthy tadpoles, are leapfrogging one another. It’s a wonderful setting for the whole family to spot unique coastal wildlife.

====================================================================================================

Sheinbaum is just another Trump appeaser
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:03 UTC
01:41:03 KST

Yesterday marked the end of the second year of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum’s six-year term. Her economic record is mediocre, as my colleague and former Mexican secretary of finance Guillermo Ortiz has demonstrated, and her performance on security, law enforcement, and fighting organized crime and corruption is questionable, too. Perhaps most worryingly, Sheinbaum is leading the country down an authoritarian path.
However, that has not stopped Sheinbaum from being widely praised at home and abroad for her handling of US President Donald Trump. Seen as firm and flexible, as avoiding confrontation without kowtowing, Sheinbaum is often compared to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney or Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who have defied Trump (albeit to limited effect).
Sheinbaum has skillfully — and cynically —disguised the extent to which she has deferred to Trump on almost every issue. She has been helped in this by the international press, which tends to give her the benefit of the doubt, and by the increasingly government-controlled Mexican media, which is always searching for reasons to praise her.
Consider Sheinbaum’s approach to immigration enforcement. Early last year, following Trump’s tariff threats, she dispatched 10,000 troops to the border with the US. To stop migrants from Central and South America and the Caribbean from transiting through Mexico, Sheinbaum also beefed up security on the southern border, added checkpoints on highways from the southern state of Chiapas to the rest of the country, and intensified patrols on rural migrant routes. The result was that migrant encounters at the US-Mexico border, which had already begun to fall during Joe Biden’s presidency, dropped precipitously.
However, she did not stop there. Last year, Mexico accepted about 12,000 deported non-Mexicans, mostly Cubans and Venezuelans, from the US, despite not being legally bound to take any of them — a practice that began during the first Trump administration, but intensified in recent years. Worse, although clearly indicating that Mexico accepts the return of all its nationals, Sheinbaum has been unable to stop the deportation of Mexican migrants to third countries, mainly Guatemala and Honduras. This particularly cruel move seeks to discourage Mexicans from migrating north, by flying them to dangerous places far from home.
On drug enforcement, Sheinbaum quickly acquiesced to Trump’s demands when he began to revoke US visas for Mexican officials, make strident claims about collusion between cartels and the Mexican political class, and designate those cartels as foreign terrorist organizations. When Sheinbaum transferred 92 cartel figures to the US, waiving extradition procedures and due process, the Americans were entranced. US authorities have expanded drone surveillance and undercover operations in the country, and engaged in more intelligence gathering and sharing with Mexican security forces, leading to the killing of drug cartel boss “El Mencho” and the capture or death of other high-value targets.
Sheinbaum is praised for rebuffing Trump’s “offers” of US “boots on the ground” in Mexico. It remains unclear if those “offers” have become demands or threats, and if “boots on the ground” refers only to uniformed US military openly participating in joint operations on Mexican territory. However, rejecting an overt US military presence in Mexico is something every Mexican president has done for a century. As for the number of clandestine, non-military US officials operating in the country today, that is, by definition, unknown to the public. Sheinbaum can publicly refuse “boots on the ground” while quietly accepting a more covert arrangement.
On trade, the other major item on the bilateral agenda, Sheinbaum has largely catered to Trump’s desires. Even before the scheduled review of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) began, Mexico unilaterally slapped a 50 percent tariff on key goods imported from China (with which it runs a trade deficit of about US$123 billion), as Trump complained that many Chinese products exported to Mexico end up in the US.
Sheinbaum has also failed to retaliate against US tariffs or restrictions on a wide range of Mexican exports, from steel and vehicles to cattle and avocados. When Trump refused to renew the USMCA for another 16 years, preferring annual reviews and only between the US and Mexico, the Mexican government went along grudgingly. Sheinbaum has accepted most of the US negotiators’ demands, although the true extent of her concessions will be revealed only when a new agreement is announced.
Even on more symbolic matters, such as support for Cuba, long an ideological lodestar for the Mexican left, Sheinbaum caved. When Trump announced a fuel blockade on the island in January, Mexico immediately suspended oil and petroleum shipments. They have not been renewed.
To be fair, Sheinbaum has had little choice but to placate Trump. Mexico is bound to the US economy, making it all but impossible to push back against tariffs or take any other action that might prompt US reprisals. This is not new, nor is it likely to change.
Moreover, with the economy she inherited, Sheinbaum can hardly afford to stand up to one of the world’s most powerful leaders, a man who is widely derided, but seldom confronted. Sheinbaum’s predecessor, Andre Manuel Lopez Obrador, secured her landslide victory, but left the country in shambles. He allowed the drug cartels to thrive and built “white elephant” infrastructure projects that required massive subsidies and discouraged private investment. The result was a stagnant economy, huge budget deficits and extreme vulnerability to US pressure. Income distribution has improved and poverty has dropped, but the Mexican economy refuses to grow.
The Mexican president’s dealings with Trump have largely been portrayed in a positive light. While she cannot necessarily be blamed for appeasing him, her policies should be seen for what they are.
Jorge G. Castaneda, a former secretary of foreign affairs of Mexico, is a visiting professor at Sciences Po.

Flu epidemic expected to peak this week at up to 150,000 visits: CDC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:03 UTC
01:41:03 KST

The nation’s influenza epidemic is expected to peak this week, with 140,000 to 150,000 weekly outpatient and emergency visits for flu-like illnesses expected, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday.
The elevated activity could continue until the middle of next month, although the epidemic is expected to decline significantly after the middle of this month as the publicly funded influenza and COVID-19 vaccination program gets under way, CDC Director-General Philip Lo (羅一鈞) told a vaccination program launch event.
Autumn and winter are the peak seasons for influenza and COVID-19, with older people, young children and those with high-risk chronic conditions at greater risk of severe illness and death, said Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良), who also attended the event.
Photo: CNA
Taiwan purchased 7.05 million doses of influenza vaccines for the publicly funded vaccination program this year, the first time the number has exceeded 7 million, Shih said.
Enhanced influenza vaccine shots would be prioritized for people aged 65 or older living in long-term care and nursing facilities.
Outpatient visits were affected by the recent Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, but have since begun to rebound, Lo said.
The CDC estimated that there would be 140,000 to 150,000 visits for flu-like illnesses this week.
Vaccination could help bring the epidemic under control more quickly, with a noticeable decline expected after the middle of this month if vaccination uptake is strong, Lo said.
The publicly funded influenza and COVID-19 vaccination program is being rolled out in two stages.
The first stage, which began yesterday, covers people aged 65 or older, indigenous people aged 55 or older, preschool children and pregnant women, among others.
The second stage would begin on Nov. 2, when publicly funded influenza and COVID-19 vaccines would also be available to adults aged 50 or older who do not have high-risk chronic conditions.

Xi’s rhetoric on Taiwan not new: official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:03 UTC
01:41:03 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) phrasing to “combat Taiwanese independence forces” is not new despite a perceived escalation in Beijing’s rhetoric, Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Chairman Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) yesterday said.
Xi yesterday reiterated his firm opposition to Taiwanese independence and external interference in a speech marking the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China.
He called for efforts “to resolutely fight secessionist forces seeking ‘Taiwanese independence,’ oppose external interference and promote the peaceful development of cross-strait relations to advance national reunification,” the state-run Xinhua news agency reported.
Photo: Taipei Times
Xi called on China to “take solid steps to achieve the great national rejuvenation” in remarks made at a reception at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, Xinhua reported.
Some observers have interpreted Xi’s remarks on Taiwan as an escalation in rhetoric, pointing to him replacing the term “oppose” Taiwanese independence, which had been commonly used in the past, with a pledge to “resolutely fight Taiwanese independence separatist forces.”
Liang said the phrase was not new.
Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference Chairman Wang Huning (王滬寧) used the phrase at a Central Committee Taiwan Affairs Work Conference in February 2024, and the wording was subsequently included in a Chinese government work report issued in March 2024, Liang said.
Xi also used the same wording at a ceremony marking the 103rd anniversary of the founding of the Chinese Communist Party on July 1 that year, he added.
After the phrase was used at the Taiwan Affairs Work Conference, China began taking a series of concrete actions, including holding regular military exercises, sending military aircraft across the Taiwan Strait median line, deploying coast guard vessels to harass ships in waters around Kinmen County, and labeling Taiwanese politicians, prosecutors and judicial officials as “Taiwanese independence elements,” Liang said.

Unknown

Shares of Vigor Kobo (維格餅家), a bakery specializing in pineapple cakes and traditional pastries, yesterday plunged 53 percent after announcing that it would delist from the Emerging Stock Board, as the company restructures its business and pursues optimal resource allocation.
At one point, the stock fell to NT$4.88, a record low since its debut on the preparatory board for the nation’s two main bourses in 2012. It closed at NT$4.98, compared with NT$10.64 a day earlier.
Vigor Kobo said in a statement on Wednesday that it decided to delist from the market as its business has largely been impacted by Taiwan’s tourism policy, especially for Chinese tourists, and the overall market environment.
Photo: Chen Wei-chung, Taipei Times
Established in 2003, the company once thrived on an influx of Chinese tourists, with its factory in New Taipei City’s Wugu District (五股) a must-see destination for Chinese tourists visiting Taiwan.
Chinese shareholder Fosun Group (復星集團) acquired a 20 percent stake in the company in 2012, making it the first Chinese firm to receive approval to invest in the nation’s food sector as Vigor Kobo sought to expand its footprint in China.
That boosted Vigor Kobo’s revenue to NT$1.24 billion (US$38.9 million) and earnings per share of NT$7.9 in 2013 and further to NT$1.34 billion and NT$8 respectively in 2014. Its stock soared as high as NT$152 during its heyday.
However, a sharp drop in Chinese visitors to Taiwan due to government policy and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic caused the company to suffer losses for six consecutive years since 2020, while its market capitalization and trading volume on the Emerging Stock Board declined over the period.
Even with the reopening of Taiwan’s borders and the return of foreign tourists following the pandemic, Vigor Kobo’s operations have not recovered to their previous peak.
Last year, the company reported revenue of NT$336 million and net losses of NT$49.21 million, or losses per share of NT$2.05. In the first half of this year, revenue was nearly NT$154 million, and its net loss came in at NT$24.93 million or losses per share of NT$1.04, company data showed.
Vigor Kobo will focus on transforming its operations, expanding its sales channels and developing new businesses, the statement said.
The company would reapply for listing on the Emerging Stock Board once its performance improves, it added.

McDonald’s features ‘Classic Spectrum’ décor at new Ruiguang Road location
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

Along Ruiguang Road, a major main road that runs through the heart of Taipei’s Neihu Technology Park (內湖科技園區), a new restaurant with counter seats and small hanging pendant lights by the windows has opened on the first floor of a glass-mirrored office building.
As one walks closer and the automatic sliding glass doors open, a modern restaurant comes into view. It has clean lines, but without a sterile corporate feel. Warm wood-textured furniture and soft lighting create a comfortable atmosphere that invites visitors to step inside.
As soon as one walks in, it becomes clear that the space is about more than coziness. Pops of vibrant red, golden yellow and bright green emerge from different corners of the airy room, adding a sense of fresh, playful energy without overwhelming visitors.
Photo courtesy of McDonald’s
An instantly eye-catching red bench sofa sits in the center of the open-space room, serving as the visual focal point of the restaurant, while two cheerful golden-yellow benches with vertical channel-tufted backrests sit next to it.
Both seating areas are paired with wood-textured tables with gently rounded corners and accented with brightly colored edging. Above some of the tables, oval or rectangular pendant lights cast a warm glow, painted in either golden yellow or classic red.
A dynamic mixture of high and low communal tables, bench seating, counter seating and booth seating areas, mostly in warm mid-tones, fill the remaining space, while the wood-texture tables and chairs create an overall cohesive, balanced and relaxed atmosphere.
Most of the walls are painted in warm mid-tones, but one prominent wall stands out, decorated with simple geometric-shaped wall lights and layers of green in varying shades, creating a distinct, multi-layered contrast that adds depth and visual interest to the overall space.
This is McDonald’s first restaurant in Taiwan that introduces its latest global décor called the “Classic Spectrum,” created in collaboration with FutureBrand. It officially opened to the public on Sept. 21.
The “Classic Spectrum” is a bold and modern take on the global fast-food chain leader’s distinctive branding identity — iconic yellow Golden Arches set against a vibrant red background — tied together with inspiration that comes straight from the signature colors of its core products — golden yellow French fries, the brown mid-tones of a Big Mac, the rich red of ketchup and fresh green of lettuce.
Two partitions creating privacy between the restaurant’s seating area and the ordering and queuing area are a quintessential example of the restaurant’s functional and thoughtful design.
The semi-transparent partitions are accented with horizontal lines in shades of tan and brown, creating a warm and inviting earthy palette. Looking closer, one may experience an “ah-ha moment” upon noticing a rugged line of green and a line of golden yellow with an inverted triangular dip caught in the middle of the shades, and the vivid image of a classic Big Mac — with its flavorful beef patties, melting cheese and crisp lettuce — comes to mind.
The clean geometric lines and color balance — overall subtle cozy shades and layers, fused with hints of the playful vibrant colors of the brand’s signature foods — create a sophisticated, yet relaxing and refreshing environment, inviting customers to “taste” the deliciousness visually before even taking a bite.
Office workers in the surrounding Neihu Technology Park can order ahead using the McDonald’s mobile app to skip lines and pick up their food fast. They can also easily order using the digital self-service kiosks or at the counters. If dining in, they can freely find a seat that suits their needs for the day, whether it be a discussion with colleagues at the communal tables or enjoying a quiet “me moment” at the counter seats by the window.
During the evenings and weekends, local residents from nearby apartments can enjoy the relaxing and playful atmosphere with friends and family, sitting around the red sofa or dining booths, sharing simple good moments together. The specially designed lighting throughout the restaurant also allows customers to clearly see how delicious their meal looks while eating, and ensures food looks great in photographs without light shining straight in their face or casting weird shadows.
In addition to the overall comfortable décor, the “Classic Spectrum” still sneaks subtle fun surprises and practical design details waiting to be explored and uncovered, including a few lively illustrations on tabletops.
Brenda Kou (寇碧茹), vice president of restaurant development group of McDonald’s Taiwan, said although there are different layouts and décor throughout the brand’s restaurants around the world, and local specialty items, such as the popular corn soup in Taiwan, every McDonald’s still feels instantly familiar.
Beneath those differences lie shared core elements, which include “delicious” – enjoyable, satisfying and trustworthy food backed by strict food safety and quality standards, creating simple “feel-good moments” for customers and crew alike, and making the experience convenient and accessible for all, she said.
To keep up with modern lifestyles, McDonald’s has streamlined its ordering, payment and pickup methods, providing flexible options and offering walk-in customers with a welcoming, comfortable and accessible brand experience through carefully designed spatial layouts and décor, Kou said.
As “Classic Spectrum” has plenty of thoughtful touches here and there, everyone who visits the first McDonald’s restaurant in Taiwan with the new décor, located at 208 Ruiguang Rd in Taipei, can easily find a space to relax and enjoy their food.

Chinese invasion unlikely to occur next year: sources
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

US officials believe a Chinese invasion of Taiwan before 2028 is increasingly unlikely despite Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) instructions for his military to be ready by 2027 to take Taiwan by force, if needed, people familiar with US thinking said.
The main reasons for the belief include delays in military readiness amid the Chinese Communist Party’s anti-corruption campaign, as well as Beijing’s eagerness to see the results of Taiwan’s 2028 presidential election, which some Chinese officials hope could usher in a government more amenable to bringing the nation under Chinese control, according to two US officials, one former US official and a person familiar with the matter.
Beijing might increasingly look to use force in 2028 and beyond if Taiwanese elect a Democratic Progressive Party candidate for a fourth consecutive term, and in particular if President William Lai (賴清德) wins re-election, the people added.
Photo: Reuters
“If that happens, I think 2028 becomes pretty sporty,” said one of the US officials, who like the other sources spoke on condition of anonymity.
The assessment, which has not previously been reported, is a significant update to the years-long understanding among US officials that Xi wanted his military ready to potentially take Taiwan by force next year, the centenary of the founding of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA). China has never ruled out using force to bring Taiwan under its control, but has never publicly confirmed a 2027 readiness order.
In Taipei, Presidential Office spokeswoman Karen Kuo (郭雅慧)said in a statement yesterday that under Lai’s leadership, Taiwan will not only strengthen its self-defense capabilities but will also continue to work closely with all international democratic allies, including the US, to maintain the status quo, deter threats through strength, and ensure peace.
"For the sake of its citizens’ freedom, democracy, prosperity, and well-being, Taiwan will not abandon its commitment to democracy and freedom in the face of any military threat," she added.
China’s US embassy and Taiwan’s representative office in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The 2027 benchmark, which analysts say is about Chinese military preparedness rather than a timeline for invasion, has for years created a sense of urgency across multiple US administrations in countering China in the Asia-Pacific region.
The US intelligence community has hinted at Chinese wariness before.
It said in its annual threat assessment in March that China did not, at least at that point, have a plan to invade Taiwan next year and still preferred to wrest control of the nation without the use of force, if possible.
US officials offered mixed assessments of the degree to which China might view the 2028 US presidential election as an important indicator for military action.
While three of the people familiar with the matter said Beijing might also want to evaluate the outcome of the US election, particularly given rising US voter antipathy toward US military action abroad, the first US official said Beijing viewed both Democrats and Republicans as largely aligned on Taiwan.
While China might have a preference in the 2028 US election, “it doesn’t become as decisive a factor in my opinion, as it might have been 15 years ago,” the official said.
US President Donald Trump has downplayed the likelihood of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan during his presidency, going so far as to say last year that Xi told him China would not invade while he was in office.
Xi has not rescinded his goal for the PLA to have the capabilities available to take Taiwan by force by next year, officials said.
However, the military did not accomplish as much last year militarily as it probably had intended because of the impact of China’s anti-corruption campaign, the people said.
Since coming to power in 2012, Xi has unleashed a sweeping corruption and discipline crackdown. Millions within China’s vast bureaucracy have been investigated, with scores of senior party, government and military officials ensnared and purged.
In the past few years, the PLA has been a target of the campaign. A string of investigations and expulsions has left just two active officials on the formerly seven-member Central Military Commission, including Xi himself, who serves as chair.
China’s military exercises last year were smaller and less threatening compared with the past several years, according to the US official.
While they bounced back a bit this year, the official suggested that Chinese military officials were dissatisfied with their readiness.
China was believed to have drawn a lesson from the wars in Iran and Ukraine, which is the need to move quickly once any invasion begins and avoid getting bogged down in a sustained conflict, the official said.
“There are way too many pieces that aren’t quite in place yet for what would be the most difficult military operation any military has attempted probably since the Allied invasion of Normandy,” the official said.

The Golden Horse Awards yesterday announced the nominations for its 63rd installment, with Arrested Memory (狂忘警探) leading the tally with 11 nominations, the Taipei Golden Horse Film Festival Executive Committee said.
Arrested Memory was nominated for best narrative feature, director, leading actor, supporting actor, cinematography, art direction, makeup and costume design, action choreography, original film song, film editing, and sound effects, the committee said in a statement.
The darkly comedic crime thriller follows a Taiwanese detective who develops amnesia shortly after being transferred to a new post and becomes embroiled in a high-profile kidnapping case as his memory deteriorates.
Photo courtesy of Applause Entertainment
Japanese filmmaker Hiroyuki Tanaka, known professionally as Sabu, directed the film.
Meanwhile, Shu Qi’s (舒淇) directorial debut Girl (女孩) ranked second with 10 nominations, while Double Happiness (雙囍) and We Are Born Good (善男信女) tied for third with nine nominations each, the committee said.
This year’s competition received 587 submissions, including 92 feature films, three animated features, 60 documentaries, 294 narrative short films, 71 documentary shorts and 67 animated shorts, the committee said.
Photo: Hu Shun-hsiang, Taipei Times
For best actor, Leon Dai (戴立忍) was nominated for his role in Kung Fu (功夫) alongside Liu Kuan-ting (劉 冠廷) for Double Happiness, Yeung Wai-lun (楊偉倫) for We Are Born Good, Ethan Juan (阮經天) for Arrested Memory and Jack Tan (陳澤耀) for Dead Tide (黑潮).
There are no Taiwanese actors among the best actress nominees, with the contenders being Angela Yuen (袁澧林) from Afterpiece (第四幕), Jennifer Yu (余香凝) from Double Happiness, Liang Cuishan (梁翠珊) from Big Little Things (謊言生活), Chung Suet-ying (鍾雪瑩) from We Are Born Good and Yeo Yann Yann (楊雁雁) from We Are All Strangers (我們不是陌生人).
The nominees for best narrative feature are Girl, Double Happiness, We Are Born Good, Arrested Memory and We Are All Strangers.
The awards ceremony is to be held on Nov. 22 at the Taipei Music Center, with the red carpet starting at 5pm and the ceremony to begin at 6:30pm, the committee said.

A debate on a cash handout is pointless
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:59 UTC
01:40:59 KST

President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration plans to distribute NT$10,000 in cash to every citizen next year, while the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus on Tuesday said it plans to propose a bill that would provide a NT$20,000 cash handout. Whether to hand out NT$10,000 or NT$20,000 has become the latest point of contention between the ruling and opposition parties, but beyond the political tug-of-war, a much more important question remains: Once the money is spent, what would Taiwan have to show for it?
Universal cash handouts are simple, direct measures that are immediately felt by the public. With prices, rent and the cost of living all rising, a cash payment might provide meaningful assistance to many households. Therefore, universal cash handouts should not be reduced to a binary choice between “handing out money is pandering to voters” and “not giving any money is neglecting people’s livelihoods.”
The problem is that while cash can ease immediate financial pressure, it does little to address structural issues such as wages failing to keep pace with the cost of living, housing affordability for young people, a declining birthrate, long-term care needs and the transformation of small and medium-sized enterprises. The amount of any universal cash handouts offers an additive effect — meaningful institutional reform is what holds the potential for a multiplicative impact.
Rather than repeatedly engaging in a political struggle over how much cash to distribute whenever fiscal conditions allow it, the government should establish a transparent and predictable sharing mechanism for economic dividends that allocates fiscal surpluses into three pots: one for debt reduction to ease the burden on future generations, one for investment in areas such as childcare, housing, long-term care and industrial transformation and one to be shared among the public, depending on fiscal capacity. Universal cash distribution would no longer be one-off handouts, but part of a fiscal system. When the economy is doing well and the government has the capacity, people can share in the gains while the government simultaneously reduces the debt burden on future generations and accumulates long-term investment.
Moreover, the fruits of economic growth do not necessarily find their way into everyone’s pockets. The robust performance of the artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors and export-oriented industries does not mean that people working in the restaurant, retail, tourism and traditional industries — or all wage-earning households — are experiencing the same benefits. True, tangible economic growth is not a mere matter of GDP, but whether wages can keep pace with the cost of living, whether young people can afford housing and raise children and whether elderly people can enjoy a secure retirement.
What the ruling and opposition camps should really be competing over is not simply who can hand out more money, but who can ensure that the benefits of economic growth last longer. Whether the amount is NT$10,000 or NT$20,000, any such policy should be guided by three basic principles: It should not increase the government’s debt burden, it should not crowd out existing government programs and it should follow lawful and constitutional budgetary procedures.
Once the cash is spent, it is gone. It is the institutions that remain and can continue to deliver benefits year after year. Rather than fighting over whether next year’s handouts should be NT$10,000 or NT$20,000, the government and the opposition should seize the current wave of economic growth to turn today’s “AI dividend” into tomorrow’s “institutional dividend.”
Chen Ching-yun is a former director of the Legislative Yuan’s Bureau of Legal Affairs.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Throughout the past decades of local elections, I have not seen anyone seriously discuss a long-term vision for urban planning, let alone with the kind of clarity and insight that Shen possesses that compels people to keep listening. He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision
If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets. Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. They end wargames when missiles stop flying and submit policy papers after the fate of a beachhead is decided. This narrow focus ignores the grim reality of “the day after.” To address this blind spot, the Irregular Warfare Center (IWC) published a seminal study on March 5, 2026, titled China’s Way of Occupation: Implications for Taiwan. Authored by Jan K. Gleiman and others, the report analyzes Beijing’s actions in Tibet, Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and Hong Kong to expose a chilling playbook

Fuel surcharge to increase amid rising costs: CAA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:59 UTC
01:40:59 KST

An international fuel surcharge for Taiwan-based carriers is to be raised for the third time this year due to the rising price of oil, the Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) said yesterday.
The surcharge for short-haul international routes is to increase from US$32.50 to US$37.50, while the surcharge for long-haul routes would rise from US$84.50 to US$97.50, the CAA said, adding that it has asked airlines to clearly disclose the changes to passengers.
The adjustment is based on a fuel surcharge mechanism established by the CAA and Taiwan-based airlines in 2005. The mechanism uses the international aviation fuel price announced by state-owned CPC Corp, Taiwan, as the benchmark.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
Under the mechanism, no surcharge is imposed when the fuel price is below US$40 per barrel. When the price reaches US$40, but remains below US$50, airlines may charge US$5 for short-haul routes and US$13 for long-haul routes.
For every additional US$10 increase in the benchmark fuel price, the surcharge rises by US$2.50 for short-haul routes and US$6.50 for long-haul routes.
CPC said its international aviation fuel price has risen from US$156.79 to US$177.89 per barrel, moving the benchmark from the 13th to the 15th pricing tier.
The latest increase follows two previous adjustments.
The first took effect on Aug. 9, when the benchmark price rose from US$133.29 to US$147.57 per barrel, moving from the 11th to the 12th tier. The surcharge was consequently raised to US$30 for short-haul routes and US$78 for long-haul routes.
The second took effect on Sept. 7, when the benchmark moved up another tier to the 13th, raising surcharges to US$32.50 for short-haul routes and US$84.50 for long-haul routes.

MOE extends partnership with University of Zurich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:59 UTC
01:40:59 KST

The Ministry of Education (MOE) and the University of Zurich (UZH) have renewed the Taiwan Studies Project, extending the academic partnership over the next five years, the Taiwan Representative Office to Switzerland said.
The new agreement, covering this year to 2031, was signed in Zurich on Wednesday in the latest addition to years of cooperation between the ministry and the UZH’s Institute of Asian and Oriental Studies, the office said in a statement.
“The renewal of the Taiwan Studies Project means that the academic partnership between Taiwan and UZH will now continue into its second decade, providing a sustained institutional framework for Taiwan-related teaching, research and academic exchange in Switzerland,” it said.
Photo courtesy of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Switzerland
The UZH and the MOE jointly launched the Taiwan Studies Project in 2017, with the latter providing funding in an initial two-year agreement, the office said.
Since then, the program has been renewed three times, with the latest five-year renewal activated retroactively on Sept. 1, it said.
Under the leadership of program director Simona Grano, who is also head of UZH Research Area China-Taiwan Relations, the Taiwan Studies supports research and scholarly exchange on Taiwan and its international environment, the office said.
Grano and Lee Chun-yi, associate professor of politics and international relations at the UK-based University of Nottingham, coedited Changing Dynamics in Geopolitics: Implications for Taiwan, published by Palgrave Macmillan last year, it said.
The volume incorporated works on Taiwan’s changing geopolitical environment and its ramifications for the intensifying US-China competition by academics hailing from Europe, the UK, the US and Asia-Pacific countries.
The Department of International and Cross-Strait Education is tasked with handling the Taiwan side of the renewed agreement, as part of its mission to support international scholarly exchanges and promote Taiwan studies programs abroad.
In related news, the UZH Research Area China-Taiwan Relations is to hold a talk on narratives surrounding Hong Kong’s sovereignty transfer in Taiwanese and Chinese-language media, the university said.
The event featuring Lutgard Lams, professor of media discourse analysis at KU Leuven’s Brussels campus, is part of the Zurich Taiwan Lecture Series and would take place at the UZH on Oct. 21, the office said.

Micron Taiwan accelerating expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:59 UTC
01:40:59 KST

Micron Memory Taiwan Co (台灣美光) yesterday said it is accelerating memorychip capacity expansion amid growing artificial intelligence (AI)-driven demand, with its accumulated investment in Taiwan reaching NT$1.6 trillion (US$50.2 billion) as of June.
The company’s investment in Taiwan has surged over the past four years, with recent spending equaling the total invested over the past 25 years, Micron Taiwan chairman Donghui Lu (盧東暉) told a media briefing in Taipei.
“The launch of ChatGPT and the outbreak of COVID triggered increasing demand for memory chips. Since then, demand has gathered pace rapidly, with only a brief pause in 2023 when a major downturn” hit the industry, Lu said.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
At Micron Technology Inc’s earnings call in Boise, Idaho, on Wednesday, the company told investors that memory supply constraints would be even more severe next year and in 2028, prompting more customers to sign long-term supply agreements with the company.
In Taiwan, Micron is scaling manufacturing capacity across its four major sites to meet demand by leveraging the region’s comprehensive semiconductor ecosystem, Lu said.
In Taoyuan, it is transforming an older cleanroom into an advanced facility (Fab 11E), equipped with extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems to produce next-generation DRAM chips, he said.
The upgraded fab is slated to begin operations late next year or in early 2028, Lu said.
The new fab’s advanced infrastructure is built to support next-generation lithography, making it fully capable of housing high numerical aperture EUV tools in the future, he said.
The company is building its second high-bandwidth memory chip packaging fab in Taichung’s Houli Science Park, Lu said.
The fab, which is expected to start volume production in the middle of next month, would be the US firm’s largest manufacturing site in Taiwan, he added.
Over the past 13 years, Micron has tripled its footprint in the Houli park and occupies 73 percent of the park, up from just 23 percent when it first established a presence there in 2013, he said.
The company also aims to commence production at its two fabs in Miaoli County in the second half of next year, he added.
As Micron expands its footprint beyond Taiwan, the company is collaborating with Taiwanese supply-chain partners — such as Marketech International Corp (帆宣), a facility monitor and control system provider — to construct cleanrooms and install equipment in Boise, Lu said
L&K Engineering Co (亞翔) is helping build a new advanced memory packaging fab in Singapore, while United Integrated Services Co (漢唐) has been tapped to construct Micron’s new fabs in Hiroshima, Japan, he said.
The company’s other key Taiwanese partners include cleanroom mechatronic engineering leader Acter Group Co (聖暉), advanced packaging equipment specialist Scientech Corp (辛耘) and automated equipment giant Mirle Automation Corp (盟立), Lu said.

Japan tightens permanent residency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:58 UTC
01:40:58 KST

Japan yesterday toughened requirements for foreigners wanting to obtain permanent residency, as part of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s push to tighten immigration controls.
Under new rules that would come into effect in stages, foreign residents wishing to stay in Japan permanently will have to prove their annual income is above average and they can carry casual conversations in Japanese.
Application fees would also rise 20-fold.
Photo: AFP
At one immigration office in central Tokyo this week, hundreds of people queued, hoping to wrap up procedures before the price spike.
“I understand that over-accepting foreigners ... might dilute Japan’s unique culture. But at the same time, given its low birthrate and aging population, Japan has to accept foreigners,” said US-born university student Yujie Chono, who was among those waiting.
He said he had been waiting for five hours to file his paperwork.
Previous guidelines did not lay out specific thresholds for income, pension or language skills. Even though Japan has a rapidly aging population and is experiencing labor shortages in many sectors, opposition to immigration is growing, prompting a push by Takaichi for tighter regulations on foreign nationals.
“As the number of foreign residents in Japan increases, the government is facing the fact that some citizens feel anxiety and a sense of unfairness,” Takaichi wrote on X, adding that she was pushing for “orderly coexistence” with foreign nationals.
Programs to attract international workers have fueled public worry. Anti-immigration sentiment has spread across social media and false claims have circulated widely, including that a significant portion of welfare payments in Japan go to foreigners and that they are making Japanese streets less safe.
Experts and many business leaders warn that Japan must welcome more foreign workers to sustain itself.
“Japan should stop viewing foreigners merely as a temporary labour force and instead promote their long-term settlement by expanding Japanese-language education and improving their treatment,” the Nikkei said.
Foreigners were a major issue in last year’s upper house election, which saw the sharp rise of the “Japanese first” Sanseito party, which describes immigration as a “silent invasion.”
The new rules for permanent residency come after the ruling Liberal Democratic Party last year pushed to tighten regulations for business manager visas, meaning entrepreneurs would be forced to leave Japan if they do not meet the new conditions.
Some foreign residents seek permanent residency to secure long-term stability, employment freedom and to earn trust within Japanese society. Those without permanent residency often have a difficult time seeking mortgages, for example.
The changes might prevent some people from applying for permanent residency, but should not immediately push anyone out of the country.
Under the regulations, the application fee for permanent residency will soar to ￥200,000 (US$1,263) from ￥10,000. Candidates must also show “understanding” of social rules and demonstrate expected pension benefits equivalent to someone who has paid pension insurance for 30 years.

Latvia expected to keep EU course as Russia looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:57 UTC
01:40:57 KST

Latvians vote tomorrow in an election dominated by the threat from Russia, and despite progress made by populist and protest parties, they are expected to confirm the country’s pro-European and pro-Ukrainian course.
The Baltic state is a key pillar of NATO’s eastern defensive flank, and experts said there is widespread support for supporting Ukraine in the war with Russia.
“The stance toward Russia is the main reason for Latvians’ Western, NATO and European anchoring,” a Western diplomat said, adding that it would be hard to imagine major political changes.
Photo: AFP
Polls predict the center-right United List, led by Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, would emerge the largest party in parliament the vote.
However, his center-right coalition, which also brings together the centrist New Unity, nationalist National Alliance and the Union of Greens and Farmers, is expected to emerge weakened from the election.
Security is at the top of voters’ minds in a country bordering Russia.
There is broad consensus on maintaining military spending at nearly 5 percent of GDP and on supporting Ukraine, LaSER analyst Roberts Kits said.
The economy is also a major concern for voters. Latvia is the least affluent of the three Baltic States in terms of living standards. Growth is sluggish, with voters pointing to the cost of living, the state of the healthcare system and the difficulties of public finances.
Complicating this are major regional disparities.
Around Riga, GDP per capita reached 101 percent of the European average in 2024, according to a Brussels report.
However, in other regions this figure does not exceed 50 percent.
As elsewhere in Europe, economic concerns have given a boost to populist parties in the run-up to the election. The Sovereign Power party, critical of aid to Ukraine and increased military spending, is polling at 9 percent — and could reach second place in parliament. Considered pro-Russian by its critics, the party emphasizes Latvia’s economic difficulties. However, the party is isolated politically and barring a huge upset has no chance of entering a future governing coalition.
Another populist party, Latvia First, is also at 9 percent, and its businessman leader, Ainars Slesers, is regularly compared to US President Donald Trump.
The party is winning support with a conservative message and promises of economic revival, and could become an indispensable partner in coalition talks.
Long rallied behind the “Harmony” party, Russian-speakers, who make up about 35 percent of Latvia’s population, no longer vote as a unified bloc.
Harmony, which won several parliamentary elections without ever entering government, disappeared from parliament in 2022 and has very little chance of returning.
“We should not look at Russian-speaking voters as a single bloc with a uniform electoral behavior,” Kits said.
While identity issues have not disappeared, a growing part of this electorate now votes according to economic and social criteria.

16:40:55 UTC

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu yesterday said that the copilot who tried to crash a passenger jet carrying 174 people on its way to Israel had undergone Islamist radicalization.
No motive has been determined for Wednesday’s harrowing near-disaster on flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, when passengers were able to subdue the attacker and a reserve crew aboard landed the plane in Saudi Arabia.
“I think it’s too early to say whether he had any connections with Iran or with any anyone else,” Netanyahu said.
Photo: Israel’s Foreign Ministry / AFP
It was clear that the copilot was suicidal, he added.
“If you couple that with the what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalization that are found in his background, I think that’ll give us the a pretty good clue,” he said. “But again, I don’t make final conclusions yet.”
Meanwhile, a passenger who helped save the plane from crashing said he knew how to stabilize a nose-diving aircraft after watching an aircrash TV show.
Yaniv Hayun is being hailed in Israel as a hero after he and three other Israeli passengers managed to subdue the copilot, who had stabbed the flight’s captain, before pulling up the jet’s steering control to right it.
A second air crew aboard helped land the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.
“We knew there was an attack, because a woman screamed ‘stabbing’ and the plane shook,” Hayun said. “At that moment I ran to the cockpit and the plane dived.”
He told Netanyahu, who met him at the airport, that the stabbed pilot managed to open the cockpit door before collapsing.
“One [pilot] was down and one was on the controls, and another person came in with me, I grabbed the assailant and put him in a chokehold, and pulled him out,” he said.
He and a few other people subdued the copilot and then he pulled up the steering control of the plane, Hayun said.
Asked how he knew what to do, Hayun said he watches Air Crash Investigation.
Tzvika Manes, an Israeli bank executive and one of the passengers who helped hold the copilot down, said they used airline earphones to tie the copilot up.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he was nominating Hayun for the Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism, along with Manes, and Manes’ wife Tali — who was first to alert the passengers of the violence in the cockpit — and Shota Musaev, a doctor who treated the wounded captain.
Musaev helped incapacitate the copilot with another passenger, Asaf Rajuan, who was also nominated.
“I’m not a hero,” Rajuan said. “It’s something you do without thinking, running to save your daughter’s life, your family’s life, your wife, and all the staff and people on the plane. You don’t think, you just act.”
The airline captain, Smit Machchhar, has also been hailed as a hero for his actions to thwart the disaster, with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi writing on X: “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valor helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy.”

Ronaldo leaves Portugal camp after he is dropped
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:52 UTC
01:40:52 KST

Portugal captain Cristiano Ronaldo on Wednesday announced that he had left the team’s training camp in Denmark after coach Jorge Jesus told reporters that the striker would be dropped for their next match.
Ronaldo had been due to train with his teammates at the Parken stadium in Copenhagen on Wednesday but left abruptly after Jesus’ news conference.
The veteran coach had said that Ronaldo, who spent the entire match on the bench against Norway on Sunday, would not start their UEFA Nations League clash against Denmark either.
Photo: AFP
“Following the national team coach’s press conference, and after having a conversation with the Portuguese Football Federation president, I decided to leave the national team’s training camp,” Ronaldo wrote on Instagram.
“In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated,” he said. “Now is time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates, without exception.”
Jesus had earlier said that there was no rift between him and Ronaldo, although the 72-year-old did acknowledge that his captain had been disappointed to remain on the bench in the side’s win over Norway.
The news sparked a wave of memes on social media and furious backlash from Ronaldo’s sister, Elma Aveiro.
“They don’t deserve to have the best of anything,” she said about the Portuguese people on Instagram. “We are envious, scornful, and ignorant, and we deserve to return to the mediocrity that defined us in the pre-CR7 era of football.”
Following the 2-1 victory in Oslo, Ronaldo went straight to the changing rooms without joining his teammates in acknowledging the Portuguese supporters in the stands.
“There was no incident whatsoever,” Jesus told reporters.
“Any player — and I was a player myself ... when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don’t get on ... no one is happy about that,” Jesus said on Wednesday.
The Portuguese coach added that he had told Ronaldo before the match that he would not be in the starting lineup, but that he might bring him on toward the end of the game.
“Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It’s nothing to make a fuss about,” Jesus said.
Jesus had said that the five-time Ballon d’Or winner would train as normal on Wednesday. However, despite arriving at the stadium in the team bus, Ronaldo did not join his teammates on the pitch in Copenhagen.
Portuguese media shared a video of him leaving the Parken Stadium alongside two members of the backroom staff just after Jesus’ news conference.
They also said that Ronaldo’s private jet was heading to Copenhagen.
Following Ronaldo’s social media post, the Portuguese federation released a statement confirming that the former Real Madrid, Manchester United and Juventus player had left the squad’s training camp.

US senators urge speedy arms delivery to Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:52 UTC
01:40:52 KST

Twenty-one US Democratic senators in a joint statement on Thursday last week urged US President Donald Trump to “immediately deliver congressionally approved defense assistance to Taiwan.”
The statement followed Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
Those commitments include US$1.3 billion in funds provided by the US Congress, existing weapons sales and a US$14 billion package of new arms sales approved nine months ago, the joint statement said.
Photo: Screen grab from Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Wang Ting-yu’s Facebook page
“[US] support for Taiwan’s self-defense is non-negotiable and crucial to preventing a cross-strait conflict that would destabilize the region and threaten the global economy,” it said. “The US must stand with Indo-Pacific allies in combating [China’s] economic and military coercion as well as directly confront [its] renewed island-building in the South China Sea and increasing aggression in the East China Sea.”
The joint statement was led by US Senator Jeanne Shaheen, ranking member of the US Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, and was signed by other senators, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer; Senate Democratic whip Dick Durbin, ranking member of the Senate Committee on the Judiciary; and Jack Reed, ranking member of the Senate Committee on Armed Services.
The Chinese Communist Party’s repression is worsening across China and expanding beyond its borders, with its Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress codifying the forced assimilation of Tibetans and Uighurs, the statement said.
The statement listed people who remain unjustly detained in China, including pro-democracy Hong Kong media mogul Jimmy Lai (黎智英), 78, who is still in prison.
“Human rights cannot be an afterthought in our relationship with China,” it said.
The senators criticized Trump for “roll[ing] out the red carpet for Xi” instead of confronting him on key issues such as “military aggression against our allies.”
Trump had traded “tough diplomacy for a ballroom tour and a lavish dinner with his billionaire friends,” the statement said.
“The American people deserve leaders who fight for their financial security and defend our national interests with purpose and measured strategy, not pageantry,” it said. “We will compete successfully with China only through sustained investment in our own strengths, close coordination with allies and an unwavering defense of our democratic values.”
In related news, the air force yesterday confirmed that the first two of the 66 F-16 Block 70 (F-16V) jets Taiwan purchased from the US are to arrive today at Taitung County’s Chihhang Air Base (志航基地).
The jets left the US on Aug. 17, but remained in Hawaii for an extended period.
Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said the F-16Vs had reached a stage where they were ready for delivery and that the Ministry of National Defense would announce their return flight once the schedule is confirmed.

FDA fines probiotic firm for 7th time this year over kidney disease ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:49 UTC
01:40:49 KST

A probiotic seller has been fined a total of NT$4.02 million (US$126,181) this year over advertisements falsely claiming that their product can "reverse kidney disease," the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said yesterday.
The Huo Hua Sheng (活化勝) probiotic seller has been ordered to remove the offending advertisements and fined a cumulative NT$8.9 million since 2024, while its endorser, nephrologist Chiang Shou-shan (江守山), has been referred for disciplinary action.
Chiang had appeared frequently on television and in other advertisements with the product promoting its purported health benefits and making exaggerated claims that the probiotic can treat or reverse kidney disease, the FDA said.
Photo: Taipei Times file photo
The product mainly contains probiotics and lactic acid bacteria, but the advertisements could lead consumers to believe that it has therapeutic effects, said Cheng Wei-chih (鄭維智), head of the FDA’s Planning and Technology Management Division.
Such claims could also cause people to delay seeking medical treatment, Cheng said, adding that the advertisements contravened regulations prohibiting food advertisements from making false, exaggerated or misleading claims or claiming medical effects.
The Huo Hua Sheng product has been fined repeatedly over its advertisements.
Authorities imposed NT$3.08 million in fines in 2024, followed by NT $1.8 million last year, FDA data showed.
So far this year, authorities have found seven contraventions involving the product on four television channels and imposed another NT$4.02 million in fines, bringing the cumulative total to NT$8.9 million, the data showed.
The FDA has also asked television industry groups to ensure that the offending advertisements are removed from their member channels.
Chiang has been referred to Taipei City Health Bureau for disciplinary action under the Physicians Act (醫師法), the FDA said.
Possible penalties include a warning, restrictions on the scope of medical practice or revocation of his medical license, it said.
The FDA reminded consumers, particularly those with kidney disease, that food products are not medicines and cannot replace proper medical treatment or claim to cure diseases.

India to face Pakistan for cricket gold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:48 UTC
01:40:48 KST

World champions India are to face archrivals Pakistan for Asian Games men’s cricket gold after both yesterday won their semi-finals with ease in Japan.
India hammered Sri Lanka by 124 runs after Pakistan beat Bangladesh by six wickets to set up a mouth-watering final tomorrow at the Korogi Athletic Park Stadium in Nagoya.
India posted a testing 169-7 on a sharply turning pitch after being asked to bat.
Photo: AFP
Sri Lanka lost two wickets without a run on the board and crumbled to 45 all out in less than 10 overs of chaos that included three run-outs.
It was Sri Lanka’s lowest total in a men’s T20 international, worse than the 77 they scored against South Africa in New York in 2024.
Sri Lanka opted to field and were given a taste of the power of 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi on his Asian Games debut.
The fearless teenager, who topped the IPL batting charts this year, smoked a whirlwind 38 off 21 balls with six fours and two enormous sixes before falling to a thick edge caught at backward point.
“He is an amazing talent,” Sri Lankan coach Ashan Priyanjan said.
Ishan Kishan was India’s mainstay with a crafted 80 not out, including five sixes.
When Sri Lanka batted, pace bowling great Jasprit Bumrah ripped out two wickets in his first over.
They were 18-5 by the end of the fourth over, with spinner Axar Patel taking two of the wickets.
Nuwanidu Fernando decided he would not wait around for a slow death and smacked two sixes off Washington Sundar only to run himself out for 15 two balls later.
The end came rapidly with the last three wickets falling in three balls.
“We don’t know anything about the final match yet,” Patel said when asked about facing Pakistan. “Especially about which wicket we will be playing on. “But all the three pitches in that square look very similar as they all have a lot of cracks.”
Earlier, Abdul Samad smashed an unbeaten 30 off 15 balls as Pakistan thumped Bangladesh by six wickets with nine balls to spare in a semi-final reduced to 13 overs by a wet outfield.
“To be honest, we don’t really care about who will win and who will reach the final,” said Pakistan batsman Saim Ayub, who scored 21 of his side’s 112-4 after Bangladesh posted 111-7.
“All we care about is winning the final, no matter who we are playing against,” he said of the prospect of facing India.

Southern science park approves Nanya Tech project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:47 UTC
01:40:47 KST

DRAM chipmaker Nanya Technology Co (南亞科技) has received approval to build an advanced 3D wafer packaging and testing plant for high-capacity and high-bandwidth memory modules in Pingtung County, the Southern Taiwan Science Park Administration said yesterday.
Nanya Technology is to focus on developing through-silicon vias (TSVs) and wafer stacking technologies, enabling the vertical integration of DRAM chips into compact 3D structures to maximize capacity and bandwidth while minimizing latency, the science park said in a statement.
Nanya Technology did not disclose how much it plans to invest in the new site, as the project is still in its preliminary stage, it added.
Photo: Grace Hung, Taipei Times
Nanya Technology said in July that it provides wafer-to-wafer bonding for customized memory chips and is developing silicon-on-a-chip-attached memory module solutions, extending its core manufacturing business into emerging advanced memory packaging technology.
The move aligns with the company’s strategic expansion into 3D IC and TSV technologies. To scale these new packaging and testing solutions, the company indicated at the time that it was considering building a dedicated manufacturing facility in Taiwan.
The science park administration yesterday also approved Fangsco Co Ltd’s (凡事可) NT$20 million (US$628,101) investment plan to develop surgical power systems and precision components used in dental and orthopedic operations, the statement said.
South Korea’s semiconductor material supplier Hansol Chemical Co also received approval to invest NT$800 million to develop and produce advanced materials in Taiwan, aiming to enhance key semiconductor material supply resilience locally, the statement added.
To date, the science park administration has approved investment projects totaling NT$108.11 billion from 21 companies, it said.

Navy vice admiral joins CGA top ranks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:46 UTC
01:40:46 KST

Vice Admiral Yuan Sheng-hua (原聖華) yesterday became the first navy officer to be appointed a deputy director-general of the Coast Guard Administration (CGA), tasked with improving coordination between the navy and the agency amid intensifying maritime pressure from China.
No active-duty navy officer had ever served as CGA deputy director-general or director-general, the agency said.
President William Lai (賴清德) presided over Yuan’s promotion from rear admiral to vice admiral and his new position at the CGA at a ceremony at the Presidential Office in Taipei.
Photo: CNA
“I expect Vice Admiral Yuan to draw on his experience to promote coordination between the navy and the coast guard, strengthen maritime intelligence sharing, and ensure that maritime surveillance and reconnaissance, as well as emergency response, are closely coordinated so that we can jointly safeguard the country’s maritime territory,” Lai said.
Recent developments around the world show just how quickly the modern battlefield is evolving, he said.
“Gray zone” operations can unfold alongside cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns, while the growing use of artificial intelligence and uncrewed systems is accelerating tactical shifts and decisionmaking, he said.
These challenges underscore the need for military capabilities that can withstand prolonged periods of attrition, he said, adding that even the most advanced weapons systems are only as effective as the maintenance and sustainment capabilities behind them — and the skilled personnel needed to keep them operational over the long term.
The armed forces and the CGA must work more closely together to respond to the rapidly changing maritime security environment, the president said.
The two sides should share intelligence on maritime activity and ensure stable command and communications under all circumstances, he added.
Ocean Affairs Council Minister Kuan Bi-ling (管碧玲) said that in the face of China’s “gray zone” activities and complex national security threats, the CGA needed someone familiar with maritime defense operations, and the transition between peacetime and wartime conditions, making Yuan an ideal candidate for the post.
Yuan became the agency’s third deputy director-general — a position created following passage in June of amendments to the Organization Act of the Coast Guard Administration (行政院海岸巡防署組織法).
The CGA said the creation of the new post addresses changes in the maritime situation surrounding Taiwan and the evolving geopolitical landscape.
It is also aimed at advancing a “sea-air integration” strategy, technological transformation and preparations for transitions between peacetime and wartime operations, the agency said.
Yuan previously served as deputy chief of staff of the navy, director of the Strategic Analysis Division under the Ministry of National Defense’s Department of Strategic Planning, commander of the navy’s 192nd Fleet, and director of the navy’s Training and Readiness Division.
Additional reporting by Chen Yun

The Philippine operation “disrupted the vessel’s unauthorized marine scientific research and compelled it to leave its loitering position,” said Jay Tarriela, Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson on South China Sea issues. The Philippine Coast Guard said the BRP Teresa Magbanua and an aircraft were deployed to counter the Chinese vessel, which it said had remained about 37 nautical miles northwest of Itbayat Island since Monday. The Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) yesterday said that threats made by one or more persons impersonating a Taiwanese documentary distributor who brought a film about alleged forced organ harvesting in China to the country in 2024 appear to be a "new method" of Chinese transnational repression.
One or more unidentified individuals have contacted and threatened people and organizations on at least three occasions while claiming to be Kuan Chien-chung (管建忠), who distributed the documentary State Organs in Taiwan, MAC Deputy Minister Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) told a regular news briefing in Taipei.
After the people who were threatened reported the matter, Kuan, head of Lion Movies Culture Co, was questioned by police, Liang said.
Photo: CNA
"The purpose is to make Mr Kuan run around exhausted," Liang said.
Someone used Kuan’s phone number in November last year to threaten a lawyer and demand money, prompting police to summon Kuan for questioning, he said.
A similar incident involving the Kuma Academy — a Taiwan-based civil defense group — occurred the following month, while on Tuesday someone again claiming to be Kuan and using his phone number threatened the Taiwan Falun Dafa Association, a local organization of Falun Gong practitioners.
With the MAC’s assistance, Kuan yesterday reported the matter to police, Liang said, adding that the council would coordinate with the National Police Agency and Ministry of Justice in handling the case.
Asked what led the MAC to suspect the involvement of the Chinese authorities, Liang said the incidents did not appear to be simple cases of impersonation and threats, but rather "systematic" operations.
"For now, we are provisionally classifying it as a case of transnational repression," he said, adding that the designation could be reviewed as more information emerges.
Authorities have not identified those behind the threats and the circumstances surrounding the cases remain under investigation by judicial authorities, he added.
State Organs is a Canadian documentary about two families searching for missing relatives and allegations of state-run forced organ harvesting targeting Falun Gong practitioners in China, the film’s official Web site says.
In late 2024, cinemas and other organizations involved in screenings of the documentary in Taiwan received dozens of threats, including bomb threats.

AI has the power to realign politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:45 UTC
01:40:45 KST

Last month, the US showed the world both of its minds about artificial intelligence (AI). The people building the most powerful systems, from Anthropic and OpenAI to Elon Musk, were asked to slow down. The heads of the two leading labs even carried that plea to the UN Security Council. The day before, at the same UN headquarters, US President Donald Trump declared that “whoever wins superintelligence wins” and signaled the US should charge ahead.
Between the builders’ plea and the president’s boast runs a fault line that could remake US politics. Big issues have done this before: slavery gave birth to the Republican Party, and civil rights turned the white South Republican. AI, one of the biggest changes in human history, could do it again, this time through a white-collar revolution.
Demand for AI has no ceiling, and no single company dares slow down alone. So the brakes would come from society. As Pope Leo XIV has said, AI’s challenge is “not technological, but anthropological.”
Nvidia Corp chief executive Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) urges the industry to “run as fast as you can,” and the chips that would train the AI models of 2028 are already leaving Taiwan. Those chips would carry a new kind of intelligence, even a new civilization, that learns, copies itself and coordinates faster than any human society was designed to absorb.
People and institutions move at human speed: a degree takes four years, a career decades, a new social contract a generation. No one can retrain every time a better model ships. The speed and power of AI would upend how we work and live together, and social stability would be among the costs that spill out, onto people and into politics.
The US has lived through this once already. For three decades, globalization shipped factory jobs abroad, while a fiat-money economy of cheap credit inflated the assets of those who already owned them. Factory towns emptied, wages fell behind asset prices and the working class that paid the bill found its champion in Trump. That was the blue-collar revolution.
AI could spark the white-collar one. Globalization’s winners, the lawyers, coders, analysts and graduates who sell knowledge, face a rival that learns faster and costs less every quarter. So do whole economies built on exporting skilled work.
This spring, graduates booed commencement speakers for praising AI. In Festus, Missouri, voters threw out every council member on the ballot after the council approved a giant data center. The people absorbing the costs want a vote on the future they are being handed.
Former White House strategist Steve Bannon now sounds like US Senator Bernie Sanders on AI, and Republican presidential hopefuls are courting the skeptics. A conservative need not change their mind about taxes to decide that their children’s future among the machines matters more.
Meanwhile, at the top of US politics, AI is starting to split along party lines. The Republican president wants to race and leaves the brakes to the builders. Summoned to the White House to talk safety, the industry’s chiefs signed a voluntary pledge to police themselves, which Trump called “morally binding.” Leading Democrats want public brakes. Former US president Barack Obama and former vice president Kamala Harris have embraced a slower pace, and California Governor Gavin Newsom has ordered work on an AI kill switch.
Pope Leo’s first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, insists that a slower pace is no enemy of progress. Flying home from France, he even took aim at Huang: The man now touting AI “guardrails,” is the same one who wants no limits and no government regulation, he said.
Catholics are part of the US’ great swing vote: They backed the Democrats in 2020 and Trump in 2024. Their Church is drawing young converts, and their pope, who has already opposed Trump over the Iran war, is at odds with him on AI, too.
Voters have yet to decide which party owns the issue, and that is the Democrats’ opening. AI would disrupt society like nothing before it, and the white-collar revolution it sparks would need a champion. Trump rode the blue-collar revolution to power. If they play it right, Democrats could be the Trump of the white-collar one.
Taiwan might be the AI race’s factory floor, but it has reason to watch where this debate is heading. Taiwan relies on the US for its security and has always needed friends on both sides of US politics. If AI proves as disruptive as this writer expects, the voices calling for safety would not stay on the sidelines for long. Taipei would do well to start building bridges.
Taiwan’s values give it a head start. A society that takes universal health insurance for granted, and expects the state to cushion ordinary people through change, already shares the safety camp’s instinct that AI should serve people rather than the other way round. That common ground is also insurance.
“Whoever wins superintelligence wins,” Trump said. The booing graduates and the voters of Festus are asking a prior question: Wins what, and for whom? The party that answers first would stand on the right side of history, and might find a new majority there.
James Lee is senior adviser at the Taiwan External Trade Development Council.
In 40 years of watching politics, I have never seen anything quite like Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) breed of politician. He has a presence that commands attention, and a combination of qualities that appear to be the result of powerful political currents. What is it that makes Shen different? Throughout the past decades of local elections, I have not seen anyone seriously discuss a long-term vision for urban planning, let alone with the kind of clarity and insight that Shen possesses that compels people to keep listening. He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision
If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets. Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. They end wargames when missiles stop flying and submit policy papers after the fate of a beachhead is decided. This narrow focus ignores the grim reality of “the day after.” To address this blind spot, the Irregular Warfare Center (IWC) published a seminal study on March 5, 2026, titled China’s Way of Occupation: Implications for Taiwan. Authored by Jan K. Gleiman and others, the report analyzes Beijing’s actions in Tibet, Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and Hong Kong to expose a chilling playbook

The use of AI in creative and academic work has become increasingly common. Coast guard’s strategic status is rising: budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:40:45 UTC
01:40:45 KST

The Coast Guard Administration (CGA) plans to significantly expand its participation in international security cooperative frameworks and its operational capabilities, a budget proposal for next year showed.
The budget indicates a transformation of the CGA from a maritime law enforcement arm into a national defense and intelligence gathering entity capable of tackling larger regional security matters.
The proposal showed that personnel from the coast guard’s Intelligence Division and Special Action Support Center are to participate in high-level national security talks with the US.
Photo: Screen grab from AIT’s Facebook page
As the CGA has dealt with China’s rising “gray zone” threats around Taiwan, it has become a valuable asset to national security agencies. Since establishing a working group with the US Coast Guard in 2021, the agency has developed mutual trust with the US through cooperation on maritime search-and-rescue operations and disrupting the smuggling of advanced chips.
As part of the transition, Navy Vice Admiral Yuan Sheng-hua (原聖華) was yesterday appointed a deputy director-general of the CGA to help prepare the agency for more complex and demanding responsibilities.
The CGA is also allocating funds to organize a “friendship fleet” next year with a large offshore patrol vessel and about 100 personnel and cadets to visit the Philippines for eight days.
It would be the first time for a Taiwanese government ship with paramilitary capabilities to sail to the Philippines on a goodwill mission since the two countries severed diplomatic ties in 1975, marking a breakthrough in bilateral cooperation in maritime security.
The visit and the donation last month of a decommissioned 500-tonne Kinmen-class patrol vessel to the Philippine Coast Guard is expected to elevate Taipei’s relationship with Manila.
Taiwan and the US are jointly building an advanced command-and-control system to coordinate in the region. The Ministry of National defense has allocated nearly NT$500 million (US$15.7 million) to National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology to develop a “common operational picture,” which is expected to be finished by the end of next year, as part of that effort.
The CGA is also planning to integrate its radar systems into the Taiwan Tactical Network being implemented in the nation’s armed forces, and invest NT$1.2 billion to buy US-based Shield AI’s V-BAT vertical takeoff and landing drones.
The V-BAT is a reconnaissance and surveillance uncrewed aerial vehicle with strong resistance to electronic interference and advanced intelligence. The drones are expected to become an important tool for countering Chinese patrol operations near Taiwan.
