Australia as an AI Middle Power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:05:00 UTC
23:05:00 KST

Australia’s role in the frontier world of artificial intelligence was the focus in Canberra last month, with two events bringing together hundreds of defense, diplomacy, development, and industry experts. The Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI) gathered the national security and defense community for an AI Masterclass on September 14. The next day, the Development Intelligence Lab’s Situation 2026 explored how AI can solve Indo-Pacific development challenges.
The events revealed a country grappling with what it means to be a middle power in the age of AI. As ClearAI founder Jisoo Kim put it, at a time when AI is developing at breakneck speed and reordering economies and societies, “Where in this ecosystem, where in this global economy is Australia going to sit?”
Judging from opinion polling, many Australians would probably prefer that AI had never been invented. But now that the cat is out of the bag, Australia needs to think about what it means for its security and prosperity, and the risks and opportunities it brings.
As a middle power, with a range of assets and resources, Australia is not powerless in the face of these changes. It has some capacity to influence the new world that AI is making.
Assistant Minister for the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton addressed this openly. Asking how middle powers manage AI, he identified four plays: alignment with a superpower, leverage in the value chain, competition through different models and capabilities, and sovereign capability. Charlton stated that Australia is pursuing all four simultaneously.
Shadow Minister for Industry and Sovereign Capability Andrew Hastie broadly agreed, particularly emphasizing the U.S. relationship as Australia’s “line to sovereignty.” Hastie suggested using Australia’s relationships in Washington to encourage a hyperscaler to invest in Australia.
Without data centers, frontier labs, and talent, Australia remains dependent on what comes through submarine cables, and this may make Australia a “supplicant state” – with Hastie using the analogy of the nuclear race, where once the U.S. convinced Australia to withdraw, it has been reliant on Washington ever since. He gave a sense of the stakes for Australia: countries with AI will pull ahead and Australia will fall further behind.
According to Minister for Industry and Innovation Tim Ayres, the government’s “aim is not to do everything, but to make ourselves the indispensable country.” That is, to find what Australia can excel at in this new ecosystem and make it the country’s comparative advantage.
Australia brings assets in policy expertise, talent, and trust. Ayres also highlighted capabilities in chip packaging, quantum computing, and specialized datasets, alongside institutional advantages such as firms and unions working together in the national interest.
Throughout the discussions, there were multiple calls for Australia to work with other countries including the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, South Korea, and India.
As the American Enterprise Institute’s Ryan Fedasiuk put it, middle powers have a path forward if they “conceive of AI as a global megaproject which everyone can contribute to.” Importantly, “Sovereignty doesn’t mean autarky. Sovereignty means being able to choose your own dependencies rather than having them foisted on you.”
Aditya Maheshwari of the Indian Institute of Management Indore outlined how middle powers could energize their own ecosystems through talent, research, joint projects, and shared computing facilities, rather than competing with the United States and China on frontier models.
Australia also has considerable opportunities to shape international standards. Australian Signals Directorate Director-General Abigail Bradshaw argued that having a place in the AI industry strengthens Australia’s sovereignty and gives it a voice in global standards.
Australian AI Safety Institute head Kate Conroy highlighted Australia’s ability to punch above its weight internationally, drawing on its experience in developing standards adopted globally.
Australia’s Ambassador for Cyber Affairs and Critical Technology, Jessica Hunter, argued that Australia has the assets, relationships, and agency to be a shaper of the AI world rather than merely a consumer.
It’s interesting that this proactivity is being actively encouraged by frontier labs, including OpenAI Vice President Ann O’Leary and Anthropic Special Envoy and former U.S Ambassador to Australia Jeff Bleich.
An important element of being an AI middle power is to think about how it contributes to development outcomes. As Minister for International Development Anne Aly put it, “The value of technologies lies in the way that people’s lives are improved.” The challenge is “to ensure the benefits of emerging technologies are shared widely rather than used to widen inequalities.”
Through this lens, Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade sponsored a competition on what Indo-Pacific development challenge AI could solve in the next five years, gathering more than 100 proposals. From disaster warning systems to healthcare and protecting Pacific maritime zones, there are countless ways Australia can use AI to contribute as a development partner.
Times of change are generally good for middle powers, enabling them to play an entrepreneurial role. These discussions demonstrated the benefits of Australia inserting itself into the AI economy, shaping global safety standards and enabling positive diffusion of technology across the region.

Excitement from a virtual reality game spills over into men’s romantic judgments, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:00:44 UTC
23:00:44 KST

A recent experiment suggests that physiological arousal, such as the excitement of playing a fast-paced video game, can make men more likely to find online dating profiles attractive. The research, posted as a preprint on SSRN and submitted to Computers in Human Behavior Reports, suggests that men may carry over excitement from an unrelated activity into their romantic judgments. Women, on the other hand, do not appear to show this same bias when evaluating potential partners.
The psychological concept at the center of this research is the arousal misattribution hypothesis. This idea proposes that people can experience physical signs of excitement, like a racing heart or sweaty palms, from a completely non-romantic source and mistakenly interpret those physical feelings as romantic or sexual attraction toward another person.
For example, in a classic 1974 experiment, men who crossed a scary, wobbly suspension bridge were more likely to later call a female researcher compared to men who crossed a safe, solid bridge. The bodily activation one feels during a scary movie or an intense ride might be incorrectly processed by the brain as a spark of chemistry with a date.
When scrolling through dating apps, users make very rapid judgments based on brief visual and textual information. In this environment, visual appeal is highly influential. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 indicated that physical attractiveness heavily dictates whether a dating profile is chosen, overshadowing other traits like occupation or intelligence. Relatedly, a 2008 study of online dating profiles found that physical appearance was one of the strongest predictors of how appealing people found a profile.
Most past research on misattributed arousal used traditional, face-to-face scenarios and older methods to trigger physical excitement. The authors of the new study wanted to see if this psychological quirk still happens in modern, digital environments where people select partners on screens. Led by Bahar Gürer and Yannik A. Escher at Leuphana University Lüneburg, the research team used virtual reality to safely and consistently create an arousing experience for participants before they evaluated simulated dating profiles.
The experiment included 130 participants recruited on a university campus (average age about 23). To begin, the researchers randomly assigned the participants to one of two virtual reality experiences. Half of the participants spent three minutes in a calm, low-arousal virtual environment, which involved looking at a peaceful forest scene. The other half spent three minutes playing a fast-paced, high-arousal virtual reality rhythm game called Beat Saber.
After the virtual reality session, participants viewed eight mock dating profiles designed to look like a dating app. These profiles were tailored to match each participant’s reported sexual orientation. For each profile, participants answered questions about the person’s attractiveness, perceived sexual warmth, and compatibility. They also rated how similar they felt the person was to them, whether they thought the person would return their romantic interest, and how likely they would be to go on a date with them. Finally, participants made a binary choice to either approve or reject the profile, mimicking the swiping mechanism of modern dating platforms.
The results showed a consistent pattern of elevated interest among participants in the high-arousal group. Those who played the intense virtual reality game rated the dating profiles higher in attractiveness and sexual warmth than those who viewed the calming forest scene. The high-arousal group also perceived the people in the profiles as more similar to themselves, felt higher levels of compatibility, and expected that the profile owners would like them in return. The only measure that was not statistically significant was the participants’ reported likelihood of actually going on a date, though the trend leaned in a positive direction.
Overall, the arousing experience boosted the probability of participants approving a profile from 17.4 percent to 24.9 percent. However, when the researchers conducted planned exploratory analyses to look at men and women separately, they noticed a stark gender divide. For men, the high-arousal condition drastically increased the likelihood of approving a profile. Men in the calm group approved only 11.3 percent of the profiles they saw, but men in the high-arousal group approved 31.4 percent of them. This means that men who played the arousing game were nearly three times as likely to swipe right on a potential partner.
In contrast, the virtual reality experience had virtually no effect on women’s dating choices. Women in the high-arousal group approved 20.5 percent of the profiles, which was slightly lower than the 23.3 percent approval rate seen in the low-arousal group. Women’s ratings of the profiles’ attractiveness and compatibility also did not shift based on their physical excitement levels. The researchers pointed to an existing theory proposing that men rely more heavily on bodily signals when judging their feelings, while women pay more attention to contextual clues.
“Thrilling experiences may enhance many people’s romantic lives,” Rui Miguel Costa, an assistant professor at the Faculty of Health Sciences at Universidade Europeia in Lisbon, told PsyPost. Costa, who is also a member of the Research Center in Sports Sciences, Health Sciences, and Human Development (CIDESD) in Portugal and was not involved in the study, noted that the findings align with prior observations. “It is consistent with other studies finding that previous exposure to arousing situations increases subsequent sexual arousal and attractiveness for opposite-sex people,” he said.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Notably, this paper is a preprint, meaning it has not yet been peer-reviewed. Peer review is a process where independent experts evaluate a study’s methods, results, and conclusions before it is officially published in an academic journal. Because this research has not gone through that formal vetting process, its findings should be treated as preliminary.
Another limitation is that the researchers relied on self-reported feelings of physical arousal rather than using objective medical devices like heart rate monitors or skin conductance sensors. Because people can sometimes misjudge or struggle to describe their own bodily states, future studies could benefit from tracking participants’ actual biological responses.
There are also a few details to consider regarding the dating profiles themselves. The researchers chose faces that varied in attractiveness, but none were rated as highly attractive, and participants’ ratings were fairly low overall. The effect might look different with very attractive profiles.
Finally, the laboratory setting meant that participants faced no real social consequences for approving or rejecting a profile. Real-world dating apps carry the potential for actual conversations, dates, and rejection. The lack of stakes in a mock environment might change how closely someone weighs their physical feelings against a potential partner’s traits.
The researchers noted that while their study partially replicates the classic 1974 bridge experiment, the effect size they observed was about half as large. The authors suggested several reasons, including the low stakes of swiping on a screen, the possibility that participants consciously discounted the arousal they knew came from the game, and the likelihood that the small 1974 study originally overestimated the true effect. Exploring these dynamics in a live dating app environment could help researchers understand how physical excitement sways romantic choices.
“I think there are problems with the interpretation in terms of arousal-misattribution hypothesis, which implies that high attraction results from misinterpretation of partner’s value,” Costa said. “In real life, outside of theoretical theorizing, people we look at and the contexts [they] are in are indissociable. In the real world, arousal elicited by other people is inextricably intertwined with the arousal elicited by contextual factors.”
According to Costa, evaluating a person’s appeal entirely separate from their environment is nearly impossible. “Absolute intrinsic attractiveness of a partner is something that only exists in abstractions and theoretical models, not in the real world, and ultimately, none of us can precisely identify all sources of arousal that affect us; the mystery of passion may lie somewhere here,” Costa added.
When it comes to future research, Costa suggested that researchers should directly ask participants about their awareness of these effects. “In next studies, it would be important to ask participants to what extent they think their attraction is being influenced by the previous arousing situation,” Costa said. “Probably, many people are actually aware of these enhancing influences. Remarkably, this type of question has not been done.”
The study, “High Arousal, High Attraction? A Virtual-Reality Experiment Testing the Arousal-Misattribution-Hypothesis in Online Dating,” was authored by Bahar Gürer, Yannik A. Escher, Hannes M. Petrowsky, and David D. Loschelder.

Labor will go after lawyers trying to 'game' the visa system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:59:54 UTC
22:59:54 KST

Labor targets migration lawyers and agents over 'futile' visa cases
In short:
Labor will target lawyers and migration agents who profit from visa applications and protection claims with little or no prospect of success.
The crackdown is part of a broader overhaul as the government seeks to reduce Australia's migration numbers.
What's next?
New rules for international students start today and follow changes to skilled visa processing last week.
Migration lawyers and agents who help people pursue baseless visa claims will be targeted under a federal government crackdown on those who profit from attempts to "game" the system.
Assistant Citizenship Minister Julian Hill will use a speech in Sydney on Friday to condemn professionals who sell "false hope" to clients with little prospect of remaining in Australia and flag plans to restrict their activity.
Mr Hill will also unveil more details of Labor's broader migration overhaul announced last month, including that new restrictions on international students will take effect from today.
Australia's net overseas migration (NOM) was 292,100 in the year to March, with the government pledging to reduce the rate to 225,000 by next financial year.
After failing to secure support from the Coalition for measures that would require new laws, Labor is pursuing its target through ministerial directions and regulation.
Spurious protection claims and visa applications lodged with the help of lawyers and agents are among the issues the government is seeking to address.
In his speech, Mr Hill will single out lawyers over some of the "worst, sharpest practice" he has seen, declaring he has "no confidence" in the current regime — operated by states and territories — governing their involvement in migration cases.
He will reveal Home Affairs has been ordered to develop options to close a regulatory gap that allows lawyers to pursue visa applications that have no reasonable prospect of success.
Legal ads 'coach people on how to claim they're bisexual'
Mr Hill will point to one case where a lawyer explicitly told the department their clients knew they were ineligible for a visa but wanted it refused so they could appeal the decision and eventually seek ministerial intervention.
In another example, a lawyer lodged a "high volume" of employer-sponsored visa applications across multiple job-types and industries that were all linked to the same address and included businesses that had previously been liquidated.
Mr Hill will also take aim at "outrageous online advertising" by lawyers allegedly coaching potential clients about false protection claims.
"Ads that appear to coach people on how to claim they're bisexual when they're not, or how to convince the department they're being persecuted when they're not, in order to support a protection claim," he will say.
"That's not legal representation. It's a misuse of the migration system for profit."
The number of people on bridging visas has more than tripled from about 130,000 in 2017 to 413,000 this year, as a growing number of people remain in Australia while lengthy appeals are resolved.
An average of 1,580 onshore protection claims are lodged each month and as of June almost 37,000 rejected claims were before the Administrative Review Tribunal.
About 90 per cent of protection applications are refused at primary stage, while a similar amount is refused on appeal.
Home Affairs coming after 'rogue' agents
Mr Hill will outline details of proposed changes to the code governing migration agents that would prohibit them from assisting with visa applications they "know, or reasonably ought to know, lack a factual or legal basis".
"People are persuaded to pursue visa pathways that offer little prospect of success," he will say.
"False documentation is prepared or misleading information is provided.
"Excessive fees are charged for services that either should never have been offered or are highly unlikely to achieve the promised outcome."
Current rules allow registered agents to proceed with a "futile" case if the client acknowledges that advice in writing.
Mr Hill will also confirm a dedicated taskforce is now investigating "rogue" operators who are unlawfully providing migration assistance.
He will say these "fake agents" are taking money from "often vulnerable people for migration advice or assistance without being registered agents or lawyers legally able to provide advice".
"In essence, if you're taking money from people and unlawfully providing migration advice, Home Affairs will be paying a lot more attention and coming after you," he will say.
Skilled visa processing resumes under new directions
New student visa restrictions taking effect on Friday will curb onshore visa hopping, limit students switching courses or providers, and bar many from bringing family to Australia.
Labor has also revised a controversial move in July to push most offshore skilled visa applications to the back of the processing queue to slow overseas arrivals.
The change left businesses facing lengthy waits to bring in workers, including nurses and teachers, prompting industry groups to warn Australia's skills shortages were being made worse.
After the backlash, the government sharpened the focus of the skilled migration program, with two new ministerial directions taking effect last week.
Healthcare, construction, teaching, resources, agriculture, aquaculture and fishing are being given priority as Labor seeks to steer skilled visa places toward areas of need.
The points test is also being overhauled to better recognise high-demand skills including trades needed to build homes.
A separate ministerial direction on character-related visa decisions is due to take effect later this month, which will put greater emphasis on family violence, exploitation, other serious offending and hate-motivated behaviour.

This giant stick insect fooled scientists for decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:59:22 UTC
22:59:22 KST

This giant stick insect fooled scientists for decades
Two new giant stick insect species have been discovered in Australia, including one with bizarre “lidded” eggs unlike anything scientists had seen before.
- Date:
- October 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Sydney
- Summary:
- Scientists have identified two new species of large Australian stick insects, including one that lays extraordinary “lidded” eggs never before recorded in the group. The discovery also revealed that a familiar stick insect had been misidentified for decades, showing how much biodiversity may still be hiding in plain sight.
- Share:
Scientists have identified two previously unrecognized species of large stick insects in Australia, revealing that even in some of the country's most closely studied environments, new species are still waiting to be found.
A University of Sydney research team reexamined Australian members of the stick insect genus Anchiale and discovered two new species. One produces unusual eggs with a distinctive lidlike structure. The researchers also restored a third species that had gone unrecognized for decades.
Their work shows that insects previously classified as just two species actually represent five separate species. Together, they occur from northern NSW along coastal Queensland and into tropical northern Australia.
Hidden Diversity Among Familiar Insects
Scientists reached these conclusions despite a large amount of existing information about Australian stick insects. More than 1000 citizen science observations have been submitted through iNaturalist and the Atlas of Living Australia, and the insects have also been studied scientifically for decades.
Even so, the researchers say much of Australia's insect diversity remains undocumented.
Lead author Dr. Braxton Jones of the Aola Richards Sydney Insect Hub at the University of Sydney said the discoveries demonstrate how much scientists still have to learn about insect biodiversity.
"Taxonomy is often a bit like detective work. Even among some of Australia's most photographed and frequently reported insects, we're still finding species that have escaped scientific recognition," said Dr. Jones, a Postdoctoral Research Associate in the Molecular Ecology, Evolution and Phylogenomics Laboratory.
Fun Facts About Stick Insects
- Many stick insects can reproduce without mating with a male. The process is known as parthenogenesis, in which a female produces eggs that develop into female-only offspring that are clones of herself.
- Some stick insects defend themselves by spraying chemicals at predators. The spray can irritate the eyes and mouth of an attacker.
- Australia's longest stick insect measures around 62cm (the world record is 64cm). Australia has 130 known species, while 3609 species are known worldwide.
- Stick insects belong to a group called Phasmatodea, a name derived from an ancient Greek word meaning "phantom" or "ghost." Their remarkable camouflage allows them to blend so effectively into vegetation that they can appear to vanish among leaves and branches.
- Some species can slowly change color to better match their surroundings. Their appearance can range from green to brown, and some can even resemble lichen as they blend into leaves, bark, and branches.
- Baby Extatosoma tiaratum stick insects use an especially unusual survival strategy. After hatching, the tiny nymphs have been observed emerging from ant nests while looking and behaving like ants. Their eggs can be carried into ant nests, where they remain dormant for months and receive protection from wasps. After hatching, the young insects use their ant-like color, shape, and behavior to move unnoticed toward the top of a eucalyptus tree.
- Some stick insects respond to threats by suddenly displaying brightly colored wings, which can startle predators. Certain species can also create a rustling noise with their wings, adding another defensive element to their wing morphology.
- If a predator catches a stick insect by the leg, some species can deliberately detach the limb and escape. This process is known as autotomy. Young stick insects can regenerate the missing leg during later molts, gradually restoring what was lost.
A Stick Insect Misidentified for Decades
One of the study's biggest surprises involved a large stick insect that had long been familiar to both scientists and insect enthusiasts.
Researchers combined DNA analysis with museum specimens, field surveys, citizen science observations, and studies of insects raised in captivity. The evidence showed that the insect had been incorrectly identified for decades.
It is now recognized as a separate species called Anchiale robusta.
The findings are published in Austral Entomology.
The researchers also formally described Anchiale mabiensis, a new species found in Queensland's critically endangered Mabi rainforest on the Atherton Tablelands.
Its eggs contain an unusual structural lid that has not previously been documented in any stick insect or its closest relatives.
Discovery Could Help Forestry and Agriculture
The revised classification may also have practical value.
One stick insect known for occasionally reaching plague-like population levels and stripping leaves from trees was found to represent more than one species. Distinguishing between those species could help researchers and land managers better understand and manage future impacts on forestry and agriculture.
The study also points to another possible new species from Cape York. Researchers believe it may be undescribed, but they need additional specimens before they can confirm its identity.
Dr. Jones said: "These findings demonstrate the importance of protecting threatened ecosystems and documenting Australia's extraordinary biodiversity before we lose species without us having even discovered them."
Funding for the research came from the Australian Biological Resources Study, through the National Taxonomy Research Grant of the Commonwealth Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water, as well as a CSIRO postgraduate scholarship.

Taiwan Can’t Fight Beijing’s History War While Erasing Its Own ROC Legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:58:00 UTC
22:58:00 KST

At last week’s summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping, the White House described the United States and China as World War II allies who “fought side by side to win the war.” It was a small phrase with a large omission. The government that represented China during the war, and fought alongside the United States against Japan, was the Republic of China (ROC). The government Xi leads – the People’s Republic of China (PRC) – did not exist until 1949, four years after Japan’s surrender. By collapsing the two into a single, unbroken “China,” the summit’s language risked allowing the PRC to inherit the legacy of a war it did not fight.
Taiwan’s government noticed. Its Mainland Affairs Council pushed back, insisting that the ROC was the “true ally” that fought with the United States during the war, and emphasizing that the PRC did not even exist during World War II. Deputy Foreign Minister Wu Chih-chung went further, calling the framing an act of “de-ROC-ization” – in which the Republic of China’s very existence is being erased from history, and replaced by the Chinese Communist Party. “We should feel very distressed,” Wu added.
Taiwanese scholars echoed the concern, warning that if Washington adopts Beijing’s version of events, the result could be a further hollowing out of the ROC’s place in the historical record.
There is an obvious irony in Taipei’s complaint, however. Taiwan’s government has been taking steps to distance itself from the ROC moniker.
This year, Taiwan’s representative office in Los Angeles sent out National Day invitations branded “Taiwan National Day.” The previous year’s cards had read “Republic of China 114th National Day.” The same government whose deputy foreign minister accused Beijing of erasing the ROC internationally was removing references to the ROC from its own diplomatic correspondence.
This trend also impacts how Taiwan’s government speaks about World War II. In August 2025, marking the 80th anniversary of Japan’s surrender, President Lai Ching-te referred to the occasion as the “end of the war” (終戰), rather than using the more traditional ROC-centered formulation, “victory in the War of Resistance” (抗戰勝利). Lai’s message emphasized the broader lessons of aggression, unity, and victory. Opposition lawmakers criticized the omission of the ROC’s wartime role, interpreting the terminology as part of a broader shift toward a more Taiwan-centered historical narrative.
The term “end of the war” is not new to Taiwan’s official vocabulary, nor does its use prove an effort to erase the ROC. But the choice of terminology in a major 80th anniversary commemoration illustrates a broader evolution in how Taipei frames the war and Taiwan’s place in it. The “Republic of China (Taiwan)” formulation associated with the Tsai Ing-wen era, together with Lai’s subsequent emphasis that the ROC and the People’s Republic are “not subordinate to each other,” has produced a more Taiwan-centered conception of ROC sovereignty. Critics argue that this can weaken the salience of the ROC’s pre-1949 history, the period when it controlled mainland China, even as Taipei continues to invoke the ROC as a sovereign state distinct from the PRC.
Successive Taiwanese governments have had domestic and diplomatic reasons to soften the ROC’s historical claims: a citizenry that increasingly identifies as Taiwanese rather than Chinese, a desire to avoid unnecessarily entangling Taiwan’s future with the mainland’s history, and a preference for language that does not appear to revive a rival claim to “all of China.”
The argument here is not that Taiwan’s evolving democratic identity is morally equivalent to Beijing’s historical revisionism. One is the normal evolution of a pluralist society’s self-understanding; the other is a state-backed effort to shape historical memory in ways that support a broader political narrative. But the two are not unrelated, either.
Taiwan’s own retreat from ROC symbolism complicates its ability to contest Beijing’s framing of “China.” It can narrow the space in which Taiwan is willing to defend the ROC’s history and identity, leaving more room for Beijing to present its own account of China’s wartime and postwar history.
Taipei has repeatedly emphasized that the PRC has never ruled Taiwan, and it has invoked the ROC’s historical continuity, as well as postwar arrangements including the San Francisco Peace Treaty, in making its case against Beijing’s territorial claims. These arguments depend in part on Taiwan being understood internationally as a political entity with its own historical trajectory – including a wartime and postwar history distinct from that of the PRC.
That creates a strategic paradox. The more Taipei reduces the visibility of the ROC’s historical identity in its own diplomatic and commemorative practice, the less salient that historical continuity may become internationally. This does not automatically strengthen Beijing’s legal case or alter Taiwan’s sovereignty. But it can give Beijing greater narrative space to portray the wartime “China” as an uninterrupted predecessor of today’s PRC, while making the ROC’s alternative historical continuity harder to communicate.
I have argued elsewhere that Taiwan’s assertion of sovereignty in its own waters suffers from a similar underlying problem: not insufficient assertiveness, but the absence of a coherent doctrine explaining when and why Taipei invokes its own claims. The same logic applies here. Beijing is contesting the historical identity of “China” itself, using the Trump-Xi summit as one more venue in which to do so.
Taiwan is right to object to historical formulations that erase the ROC’s role in World War II. But an objection becomes harder to sustain when the government’s own recent practice – from diplomatic invitations to commemorative language to evolving formulations of national identity – makes the ROC’s historical identity less visible.
None of this means Taiwan must reverse its democratic evolution or resurrect a mainland-centric ROC identity that most Taiwanese people no longer want. It does mean that Taipei cannot simultaneously retire the ROC as an inconvenient historical label and rely on it as part of the foundation of its case against Beijing. If Taiwan wants the ROC’s history to remain a live argument against the Chinese Communist Party’s claims to sovereignty over Taiwan, someone has to keep making that argument – including, consistently, the government in Taipei itself.

The True Story Behind Netflix's The Widower and the Many Wives of Thomas Randolph
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:55:45 UTC
22:55:45 KST

On the night of May 8, 2008, Thomas Randolph called Las Vegas police with a disconcerting alert. “My wife’s been shot,” he told the 9-11 dispatcher. “There’s a guy in my house and I shot him.” That night, Randolph and his sixth wife, Sharon Causse, had gone out for a Mother’s Day dinner. But once they returned home, Randolph stayed in the car to listen to the radio, letting Sharon go inside by herself. Minutes later, an intruder wearing a ski mask and carrying a bag of jewelry fired a couple of fatal shots at Causse.
Upon hearing the gun discharge, Randolph later said, he entered the house, relaying to police in a walkthrough that he’d found Sharon lying on the floor bleeding out. At that moment, after seeing a moving shadow, he grabbed a gun from a nearby room and reactively shot the intruder multiple times, killing him with a bullet to the head, before clearing the rest of the house and calling authorities.
The initial layout of the case was shocking, but it also seemed cut and dry. At least until detective Dean O’Kelley began examining the chain of events a little more closely. Why was the intruder’s ski mask on the garage floor without any blood on it? How were multiple rounds shot in the hallway but no bullet casings were left there? Why did a neighbor hear gunshots at 8:33 p.m., but Randolph’s 9-11 call didn’t occur until 8:45 p.m.?
The next day, veteran Dateline NBC producer Dan Slepian heard about the murders from O’Kelley’s colleague, who offered an intriguing message: “You might want to pay attention to this one.” Slepian had previously worked alongside the LVPD homicide unit, filming real-time investigations, so he was accustomed to documenting cases as they unfolded. This seemed like another prime opportunity to do just that.
Except when Slepian and O’Kelley teamed up, neither realized they were embarking on a 15-year journey—one that would eventually expose the truth about Randolph, a former paralegal who received life-insurance payouts after three of his previous wives all died under suspicious circumstances. Over the years, Randolph, known as the Black Widower, would escape two death penalty convictions, repeatedly finding ways around the legal system for as long as he could.
That lengthy investigation, along with Randolph’s sinister history, is the subject of a new Netflix documentary, The Widower: ‘Til Death Do Us Part. Directed by Chris Smith, the executive producer of Tiger King, the documentary leans on Slepian to tell the complete story, featuring his real-time footage of interviews with Randolph, witnesses across the country, and family members of his victims, as authorities worked to eventually convict him of murder, put him behind bars, and keep him there.
“Normally, the more you investigate, the closer you get to an answer,” Slepian tells TIME. “This investigation did the exact opposite. Every answer widened the frame. Another marriage, another state, another death, another witness. And that's when I realized that what we were covering wasn’t just a single murder case, but a pattern that had been unfolding over decades.”
As Slepian and O’Kelley began digging more into the Mother’s Day murders, the pair found more alarming circumstances and reasons to believe Randolph had been lying about the sequence of events. Causse's daughter Colleen told them that Randolph had become the beneficiary of her mom’s will three months into their marriage. He’d also taken out a $350,000 life insurance policy on her—raising Colleen’s suspicions even further.
The pair also traveled to North Carolina to interview family members of the intruder, Mike Miller, with whom Randolph had developed a working relationship. According to his brothers, Miller had become Randolph’s handyman and was constantly on the phone with him about various things—inlcuding one call in which, according to Miller’s friend, Randolph asked Miller if he’d be interested in killing his wife. It was juicy hearsay, and key context, but the prosecutor’s office declined to issue an arrest warrant. They’d need to do more digging.
The rest of the documentary unfolds much like O’Kelley and Slepian’s real-time investigation, criss-crossing the country and unearthing new information about Randolph’s past that eerily informs the Causse case. “That kind of documentation as things unfold adds a value to not only the journalism but to the storytelling itself,” Slepian says. “There's a layer of suspense because the viewer understands that neither we nor the detectives have any idea what's about to happen.”
The reality was more vast than either Slepian or O’Kelley could believe. It started with a visit to Randolph’s first wife, Kathy, who shared that after marrying Randolph in 1975, he’d taken out a life insurance policy on her. After having two kids with him, Kathy filed for divorce and remarried to Steve Thomas. Unbeknownst to her at the time, Thomas told O’Kelley and Slepian that Randolph had previously tried to groom to kill Kathy, but he refused to cooperate. Then a larger trend emerged.
In 1983, on the same day his divorce to Kathy was finalized, Randolph married his second wife, Becky Gault. Three years later, Slepian and O’Kelly would find out that Gault had died of a gunshot to the head inside her Utah home. Her death was initially ruled a suicide. But in 1988, her death was reclassified and Randolph was put on trial for murder, after he’d collected a $500,000 life-insurance payout.
It didn’t help his case that his friend and handyman, Eric Tarantino, testified that Randolph had hired him to kill Gault and had been planning her murder for six months before Tarantino eventually backed out of the plan. A year later, Randolph was acquitted after his lawyers convinced the jury that Gault had died by suicide, though Randolph was convicted of witness tampering (which would later be expunged) after he was found guilty of offering an undercover cop money to kill Tarantino.
Three more marriages ensued, each culminating under strange, sometimes fatal circumstances. There was Gaynal Allmon, who was “stupid enough to marry him,” she says in the doc, after admitting he’d also taken out a life insurance policy on her. They divorced before anything nefarious happened, but Francis Randolph wasn’t as fortunate.
Throughout their marriage, Frances had a heart condition that required surgery, so Randolph himself selected the doctor to perform the operation. She made it out to the recovery floor, but then Randolph called her family and indicated she’d taken a turn for the worse. “He insists she died from malpractice,” Slepian says in the doc. “He ends up not only collecting on her life insurance money, but he sues the hospital for wrongful death.” And this occurred after Randolph had recorded Frances reciting her will on videotape. Not long after her death, he married Leona Stapleton, but she died of cancer soon after their nuptials.
“I went to 10 states and was embedded with [investigators], but what was surprising to me was when I told everyone we met that I was with NBC News, almost every witness in every state said, ‘Oh yeah, you can film this,’” Slepian says, suggesting to him that they all believed Randolph was guilty and wanted to help catch him. “The extraordinary thing is that as we traveled digging into his past, it felt like we were walking into the present.”
The pile of evidence and statements was finally enough to take Randolph into custody. He was arrested in January 2009, effectively hiding out at his mother’s home in Utah, where police had to drag him through the snow to their vehicle, an incident Slepian recorded on camera. By then, Slepian had developed a rapport with Randolph over the phone, gleaning insight into his behavior throughout the investigation. But his access only deepened once Randolph was detained and Slepian obtained his permission to keep the camera rolling.
Over the next few years, Randolph became convinced he could sway public opinion. He repeatedly delayed his 2008 murder trial, fired lawyers at the last minute, and tried to keep Gault’s case from the ‘80s out of the court. “It was just all kind of a big challenge or game for him,” Slepian says. “He turned suspicion into entertainment and would use his charm and the uncomfortable charisma to camouflage the suspicion.”
Looking back, it became clear to Slepian that Randolph had learned from his first murder trial. Given that Tarantino tried to burn Randolph on the witness stand, Slepian came to believe Randolph had killed Miller to eliminate loose ends. Still, he never felt confident that a jury would see it the same way. “The more the facts around him grew darker and more absolute,” Slepian says, “the more he seemed to grow confident in his ability to shape the narrative.
Throughout this time, Slepian had struggled to tap into Randolph’s impenetrable psyche and cocky personality. The Dateline producer worked to remain unbiased, in part to keep Randolph talking throughout his stay in Clark County jail. “We’re going to become infamous together,” Randolph tells Slepian in the documentary, further creeping him out. “The things that he said were so unsettling so often,” Slepian says. “But the unsettling part wasn't what he was saying, it was how comfortable he was saying it.”
Slepian had spent much of his previous work fighting for inmates who had been unjustly imprisoned. The irony of taking on this case was stark. “My focus normally is on people who are screaming into the wind from a prison cell who have had an injustice done to them and they can't get anybody to listen. They feel like the system has manipulated them,” he says. “This was kind of the same, except that Randolph was the one manipulating the system. He played the bureaucracy like a piano and kept winning over and over again. And that to me speaks volumes about the system as a whole.”
In June 2017, eight years after Causse’s death, Randolph’s case finally went to trial, where he was found guilty of conspiracy to commit murder and two counts of first-degree murder and was sentenced to death. But that wouldn’t be the end. Three years later, the Nevada Supreme Court reversed the conviction and death sentence, ruling that the trial should not have allowed evidence from Gault’s case—just like Randolph had told Slepian. “I put nothing past him,” Slepian says. “It really is because of him that the trial was delayed for nearly a decade. And I think he was waiting for witnesses [to die].”
But during his retrial in 2023, Randolph couldn’t pull any more strings. O’Kelley, who, according to Slepian, had “encyclopedic” knowledge about the case, testified and laid out all the inconsistencies in Causse’s case. His testimony, combined with Randolph’s performative reenactment video the night of the murders, convinced the jury of his guilt. “Had it not been for Dean O'Kelly, Thomas Randolph would likely be free today,” Slepian says. “I think Randolph saw the camera as giving him a stage. But it also gave detectives a record.”
Randolph, now 71, was sentenced to 60 years to life at the Lovelock Correctional Center in Nevada. And, as noted in the documentary, he’s had multiple appeals denied, including one in early September. Slepian, who still calls Randolph in prison, notes that the Black Widower continues to claim his innocence and has people on the outside handing out flyers around the courthouse about his case.
At this point their conversations remain strictly about his legal case, but Slepian is glad that he’s kept his word and remained objective throughout the years. Otherwise, he never would have gotten to share this story. “I had to keep my footing, just listening, knowing why I was there, and using the archive of him over time to create a record,” he says. “The archive itself became a witness to him over time. Now, the whole world gets to know who he is right now.”

ynet Global to broadcast Awake Jerusalem live as Christian leaders from 51 nations gather in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:53:09 UTC
22:53:09 KST

More than 550 Christian leaders from 51 nations have arrived in Israel for a major gathering of international faith leaders, culminating this week in Awake Jerusalem, a night of music, prayer and solidarity at Jerusalem’s Tower of David.
ynet Global will broadcast Awake Jerusalem live on October 3 on its website and social media channels, bringing the event to audiences in Israel and around the world.
The concert is part of a 10-day delegation organized by Eagles’ Wings and led by its founder and president, Bishop Robert Stearns. Taking place during Sukkot and in the days leading up to the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks, the visit brings Christian leaders, dignitaries and officials to Israel for meetings, briefings and encounters with Israelis directly affected by the past three years.
For Stearns, who has been coming to Israel since 1992, this visit feels markedly different.  “I feel that nationally there is a greater sense in the nation of dependence on God for help, and a spiritual component that has renewed,” he said on an interview ahead of the events. But he said the change he sees is not only spiritual. He has also noticed Israelis taking greater personal responsibility for explaining their country and experiences to the outside world.
Stearns recalled having lunch with three Israeli businessmen who had nothing to do with politics, yet each was thinking about what role he could play in Israel’s struggle over international public opinion. Israelis, he said, understand the military battles being fought by the IDF, but increasingly recognize another arena as well: what he describes as an “eighth front” - the battle over Israel’s story.  “I sense a tremendous level of personal responsibility that Israelis are taking for telling the story and being a ‘shaliach’, a messenger,” he said.
‘Come and see for themselves’
That idea lies at the heart of the Eagles’ Wings delegation.
Among those participating are senior Christian leaders whose churches and networks collectively reach tens of millions of people worldwide, including Bishop Dr. David A. Sobrepeña, founder and senior pastor of Word of Hope Christian Church in the Philippines; Rev. Ricardo Castillo Medina, general superintendent of the Assemblies of God in Costa Rica and president of the World Hispanic Assemblies of God; and Brazil’s Rev. Dr. Reinaldo dos Santos.
Delegations from Kenya and Nigeria are also participating. They include Kenya’s First Lady Rachel Ruto; Ogiame Atuwatse III and Olori Atuwatse III of Nigeria’s Warri Kingdom; and Nigeria’s Minister of Defence, Gen. Christopher Gwabin Musa.
Stearns said the delegation represents networks reaching some 100 million people globally. “We are here to pray. But to act,” he said. “We are not just here to sing. We are here to become educated, empowered, and go back to our nations.”
During their stay, delegates are scheduled to meet Israeli leaders, IDF and Foreign Ministry officials, faith leaders, returned hostages and bereaved families. Strategic briefings are also intended to give participants a deeper understanding of Israel’s security challenges and the impact of the past three years.
Stearns believes there is still a significant gap between the support Israel receives from evangelical Christians and Israelis’ understanding of that community. “There’s very little bridge of connection,” he said, noting that Israelis sometimes approach evangelical support with uncertainty or suspicion.
His answer is direct engagement. Eagles’ Wings says it has brought some 45,000 people to Israel over the years, including thousands of pastors and influencers. Stearns said that when participants are asked afterward about the most memorable part of their visit, the answer is often surprisingly simple: Shabbat.  “When we saw women lighting candles, fathers blessing sons and daughters, when we saw the phones go off, traffic die down, and the beauty and power of the simplicity of family and friends coming together,” he said, describing what visitors tell his organization.
Such experiences, he argues, can have more impact than political arguments. He recalled speaking recently with a German businessman visiting Israel for the first time. His reaction, Stearns said, was straightforward: “This place is nothing like the media says.”
“That’s just a human being experiencing the land,” Stearns said. “Israel tells its own story.”
Prayer - followed by action
Asked what prayer can accomplish at a time of war, division and rising antisemitism, Stearns said prayer without tangible action is insufficient. “Prayer is everything. And prayer must have with it action,” he said, citing the Bible’s teaching that “faith without action is dead.”
“We must pray, but we must become the answer to the prayer that we are praying.” For Stearns, that means participants returning home better equipped to speak about Israel, confront antisemitism and engage their own communities.
He also sees the current moment as an opportunity to deepen Christian-Jewish relations while acknowledging the real differences between the two faiths.  “We have genuine theological differences, and they should be respected, mutually,” he said. “But we are united in 95 percent in our view, and we must build this gesher for the sake of humanity, so there is a brighter future.”
Music from the Tower of David
That bridge will take a musical form on October 3. Awake Jerusalem will bring Christian artists from around the world to the Tower of David for an evening centered on Jerusalem, faith and solidarity with Israel.
According to Stearns, public interest was immediate. “We opened to sell tickets, and we sold out in four hours. Gone,” he said. The vision, he explained, is deliberately youthful and joyful, using music to rise “above the noise” at a moment dominated by conflict and political division.
“David was not only a warrior, he was also a musician,” Stearns said. “So the City of David should put the music” at the center. He hopes Awake Jerusalem will continue to grow, with ambitions for an even larger event at Sultan’s Pool next year.
Engaging younger Christians is becoming an increasingly important part of that effort. Stearns said Eagles’ Wings recently brought 100 college students to Israel, part of a broader attempt to expose a new generation to the country beyond what they encounter through social media, campus activism and international news coverage.
Many evangelical Christians grow up with a strong connection to the biblical Israel, he said, but often know far less about the complexities of the modern state and the conflict surrounding it.
Bringing them to Israel allows them to encounter that reality themselves. “You shape people’s views by telling stories,” Stearns said. “Israel and the land of Israel tell a story that the nations can learn from.”
For Stearns, the events of the coming days are part of something larger than a single delegation or concert. After more than three decades of bringing Christians to Israel, he believes the challenge now is turning affinity into meaningful relationships,  and relationships into action. “It’s time for tachles,” he said, using the Hebrew and Yiddish expression for getting down to practical matters. “We have to stand together shoulder to shoulder.”
And on October 3, that message will begin with music in the heart of Jerusalem.
ynet Global will broadcast Awake Jerusalem live from the Tower of David on October 3 on our website and across its social media channels.

'Terror-Free Türkiye' initiative has brought new momentum to region: Erdogan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:46:20 UTC
22:46:20 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has said the "Terror-Free Türkiye" initiative has already created new momentum in the region.
Speaking at the Turkish parliament on the opening of the new legislative year on Thursday, Erdogan said the initiative has strengthened Türkiye's position amid regional turmoil.
"In an environment where our region has turned into a ring of fire, the 'Terror-Free Türkiye' efforts have already had a deterrent effect on Türkiye's adversaries, have further strengthened Türkiye's power, and ushered in a new momentum in our region," he said.
"On matters concerning Türkiye's national interests, politics must be able to reach a full consensus," Erdogan said, referring to the recent initiative as the "Great Türkiye Consensus."
Erdogan stressed that the "Terror-Free Türkiye" process is aimed at building this "national consensus."
Economic growth
Speaking on the Turkish economy, Erdogan said: "Despite the wars and crises that have erupted one after another in our region, we have managed to keep Türkiye on a path of development and growth."
Türkiye's economy grew 2.5 percent year-on-year in the first half of 2026, he said, adding that annualised national income exceeded $1.7 trillion.
The country's exports hit a record $280.3 billion on an annual basis in August, he added.
"Following the agricultural frost and drought last year, our agricultural sector has made a rapid recovery," he said.
Türkiye maintained a strong performance in tourism despite regional conflicts, Erdogan said, adding that tourism revenues reached $25.7 billion in the first six months of the year.
"We strengthened our national defence industry with new products while also becoming a country that exports defence products to the world," he said.
Erdogan said Türkiye's defence and aerospace exports increased 16.2 percent to $6.3 billion in the first eight months of the year.
"We are at a sustainable point in terms of our external balance. We expect the current account deficit to remain at 2.6 percent of GDP this year," he added.
Ongoing fund investigation
Turning to an ongoing fund investigation in the country, Erdogan said: "We are also successfully overcoming the issue that has emerged in a certain segment of the funding markets."
"In accordance with the capital market regulations, we are swiftly resolving this matter while upholding fairness and justice and ensuring that no one's rights are infringed upon," he said.
"We will not allow this issue to turn into a threat to our economic security and social peace," Erdogan added.

New “plant armor” more than triples strawberry yields
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:43:15 UTC
22:43:15 KST

New “plant armor” more than triples strawberry yields
- Date:
- October 1, 2026
- Source:
- North Carolina State University
- Summary:
- A new protective fabric boosted strawberry yields by as much as 3.56 times while blocking insects and still allowing sunlight, rain, and airflow to reach the plants. Originally inspired by research on military clothing, Plant Armor could also help farms reduce pesticide and water use.
- Share:
A newly developed textile covering helped strawberry plants produce more than three times as much fruit in tunnel field trials, while showing no harmful effects on plant health. Researchers say the technology may also offer a way to reduce water use and reliance on pesticides in strawberry production.
The fabric, called Plant Armor, is designed to be placed directly over strawberry plants. Its three dimensional structure creates a barrier that keeps insects from reaching the plants, while the layered material still allows sunlight, rain, and air to pass through.
In tunnel field tests, strawberries protected by Plant Armor produced yields as much as 3.56 times higher than uncovered plants. The fabric did not reduce light availability or negatively affect relative humidity.
A Fabric That Protects Without Blocking Sunlight
"To produce fruit, plants need sunlight," said Gabriel Olawuyi, a graduate research assistant at North Carolina State University and lead author of a paper on Plant Armor. "We expected that Plant Armor's seemingly opaque fabric would lead to an increase in vegetative biomass at the expense of fruiting -- because reduced sunlight would trigger a 'shade-avoidance' response, making the plant divert energy toward stem and leaf growth rather than fruit production. However, we found the fabric did not impede access to light at all, and fruit production increased significantly."
Researchers also found that Plant Armor created a steady warming effect throughout the three growing seasons. According to Olawuyi, that extra warmth helped covered plants reach the fruiting stage earlier than plants grown without the textile.
"Plants require a certain amount of accumulated heat, calculated as 'growing degree-days,' to progress through developmental stages including fruiting. Our plant cover has proven to enhance these," Olawuyi said. "The plants were in a condition whereby the warmth they need to go through each phenological stage to their production was given to them optimally, and they produced far more than the uncovered plants."
Because Plant Armor physically prevents insects from feeding on the plants, Olawuyi said the technology could also reduce the amount of conventional pesticides needed in agricultural fields.
From Military Textiles to Strawberry Fields
The idea behind Plant Armor did not begin with farming. The technology emerged from research focused on making military uniforms more resistant to mosquito bites and improving comfort for soldiers wearing body armor.
That unexpected path from military clothing research to agriculture demonstrates the value of collaboration across scientific fields, said co-author R. Michael Roe, William Neal Reynolds Distinguished Professor at NC State.
"The path to Plant Armor started with trying to make a cloth to go on a soldier's chest to make body armor more comfortable," said Roe. "Then, through trial and error, we arrive at a product which could triple the output of strawberry farms here in North Carolina.
"We couldn't have predicted that when we started. Without all these people here doing research and following the science, we wouldn't have arrived at this product."
Study Details and Support
The paper, "Knitted 3-D, Porous Textile Cover to Enhance Strawberry Fruit Production and Prevent Insect Feeding," is published in the journal Agriculture. Co-authors include James Clothier, Matthew Bertone, Grayson Cave, Reuben Garshong, Andre West, Loganathan Ponnusamy and Clyde Sorenson of NC State University.
This project was supported by a grant from the North Carolina Agricultural Foundation (grant number AG00463770). The work was also supported by the Research Capacity Fund (HATCH), project award no. 02853, from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's National Institute of Food and Agriculture. The Plant Armor Gen 2 fabric studied in this paper was patented by North Carolina State University (US Patent No. 11,582,968 B2; 21 February 2023) and is licensed for commercial development by the University. This work was a collaborative project between the NC State College of Natural Resources, Wilson College of Textiles and College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.
Story Source:
Materials provided by North Carolina State University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Gabriel Bamidele Olawuyi, James Clothier, Matthew A. Bertone, Grayson L. Cave, Reuben A. Garshong, Andre J. West, Loganathan Ponnusamy, Clyde E. Sorenson, R. Michael Roe. Knitted 3-D, Porous Textile Cover to Enhance Strawberry Fruit Production and Prevent Insect Feeding. Agriculture, 2026; 16 (19): 2084 DOI: 10.3390/agriculture16192084

Trump’s energy chief asked Europe to release more than a third of its diesel reserves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:38:55 UTC
22:38:55 KST

U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright attends an announcement made by President Donald Trump at the White House in Washington on Sept. 28, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
BERLIN — The Trump administration has circulated a proposal to European governments asking them to release a large portion of the bloc’s strategic diesel reserves to ease soaring fuel costs, according to four officials in European and U.S. governments.
The plan, put forward by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, was pitched as an alternative to President Donald Trump's threat of a blanket ban on diesel exports from the U.S.
Under the proposal, EU governments would release 120 million barrels of diesel from their national strategic reserves over 180 days, a government official from a European country told POLITICO. The official, like others in this story, was granted anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the proposal's details publicly.
Advertisement
That would account for well over a third of the approximately 315 million barrels of diesel EU countries held in reserve as of June this year, according to Eurostat figures. Among EU countries, Germany, France, Italy, Spain and Poland hold the largest reserves of the essential transport fuel.
POLITICO reported Tuesday that the White House was floating the idea of asking the EU to use its diesel reserves to bolster global supply and thus lower prices. A German government official on Thursday confirmed that the United States had contacted Berlin in the matter.
Multiple countries in Europe were approached for a coordinated release, according to a person familiar with the Trump administration's plans. One major EU member was approached bilaterally in the U.S. last week, according to a senior European energy official.
"It was very hypothetical: ‘What do you think about Europe releasing some of the reserves in order to decrease prices, put pressure on supplies?'" the official said. "'It could also help our government not to continue the discussion on the export ban.'"
Wright, along with the U.S. oil and gas industry, opposes an export ban on one of the world's most in-demand petroleum products, and the proposal is seen as an attempt to find an alternative to such a drastic measure.
At a press conference Thursday, Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen wouldn’t confirm whether the EU had received Wright’s request but said that any stock releases would only be agreed through the International Energy Agency, a Paris-based institution which coordinates energy policy among rich countries and oversaw an earlier stock release this year. She added that the Commission was in close contact with EU member countries and Washington.
Advertisement
Meanwhile, President Trump on Wednesday confirmed that a diesel export ban by his administration was still on the table. “I’m thinking about it,” Trump said of the export ban at an Oval Office event. “I speak to [Energy Secretary] Chris [Wright] and [Interior Secretary] Doug [Burgum] about it a lot — they sort of think it’ll help diesel, but it might raise the price of other things.”
Trump declined to rule out restricting diesel shipments. “It’s something that we think about and we talk about every day,” he said. “But it just seems that it would have a negative impact on gasoline, so that would go up a little bit, and diesel would come down a little bit.”
Wright, who was with Trump in the Oval Office on Wednesday, said the administration would soon announce measures aimed at bringing down diesel prices. Europe would also be announcing moves to add supply to the market, he said.
“You will hear announcements from our friends in Europe about new diesel supplies that’ll come to the market that’ll meaningfully push diesel prices down,” Wright said.
Ben Lefebvre and James Bikales contributed reporting.

Afghanistan condemns Pakistan as U.N. mission says airstrikes killed 10 civilians, "most of them children"
Islamabad — Pakistan launched new airstrikes in Afghanistan overnight, killing at least 10 people, most of them children, the United Nations mission in the country said Thursday.
Islamabad claimed the attacks targeted militants with Pakistani insurgent groups who have mounted attacks on the country, but Afghanistan's Taliban government accused the neighboring nation of aggression, saying the strikes hit civilian homes, killing women and children.
"UNAMA has confirmed that at least 10 civilians were killed, most of them children, and 9 people injured in airstrikes," the United Nations Mission in Afghanistan said in a statement shared on social media. UNAMA did not attribute the strikes to Pakistan, but no other nation has claimed recent aerial attacks on Afghanistan.
The strikes targeted areas in Afghanistan's Kunar and Helmand provinces, and chief spokesperson for the Afghan regime Zabihullah Mujahid said three civilian homes were destroyed.
He condemned the Pakistani bombing as an act of aggression.
Pakistan's Ministry of Information presented a sharply different account.
In a statement sent to CBS News, the ministry said the strikes were intelligence-driven, "well planned and calibrated" and hit militant hideouts and camps at two locations, and that "initial reports suggest the killing of 22 terrorists."
The ministry claimed "large quantities of weapons and ammunition" were also destroyed in the strikes.
"The threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan," Pakistan's information ministry said. "Our action precisely targeted the terrorist hubs."
"Maximum precautions were taken and it was ensured that no collateral damage occurs," it said, adding that its attacks would "continue at full pace to wipe out" alleged terror groups operating in Afghanistan.
Videos circulating from the scene of strikes in Helmand province, near the Pakistan border, showed people searching through the rubble of a destroyed mud-wall house, finding remains.
Ebad Khan, a resident in Kunar province, told CBS News one of the strikes hit a home belonging to a family that had moved in only a day earlier.
"They had children and livestock. They had just moved from another district," he said. "Unfortunately, all six members of the family were killed, including children."
Repeated cross-border clashes between the neighbors have escalated this year, with Pakistan carrying out airstrikes inside Afghanistan on multiple occasions. The countries have long accused each other of allowing terrorist groups to operate along their shared border, plotting attacks on civilians and security forces.
According to UNAMA, the clashes have caused more than 1,100 civilian deaths and injuries in Afghanistan this year alone.

Denmark Launches Largest Volunteer Guard Exercises Since Cold War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:32:02 UTC
22:32:02 KST

On October 1, the large-scale military exercise Blåtand began in Denmark, involving more than 6,500 soldiers from the Danish Home Guard (Hjemmeværnet).
This was reported by the Danish Ministry of Defence.
Organizers describe them as the largest exercises for this unit since the Cold War.
In addition to the land component, representatives of the Naval Volunteer Guard (Marinehjemmeværnet) and the Air Force Home Guard (Flyverhjemmeværnet) are also participating in the exercises, which has roughly doubled the total number of participants.
The exercises will take place from October 1 to 4 in Jutland and on the island of Funen. In certain areas, participants are conducting training exercises in close proximity to critical civilian infrastructure.
In total, activities are planned at more than 70 locations in one of Denmark’s regions. According to the commander of the Danish Home Guard, Major General Hannar Arpe Nielsen, the military must make training as close to real-world conditions as possible and operate directly in those areas where problems could arise in the event of a crisis.
In addition, according to Esben Salling Larsen, a military analyst at the Royal Danish Military Academy, the tasks of the Danish Home Guard today differ significantly from those the unit carried out 20 years ago.
He cites the Guard’s ability to rapidly deploy a significant number of forces to strengthen the country’s defense as one of its key advantages.
The Danish Home Guard performs a wide range of tasks in support of the Armed Forces, the police, and other government agencies. The main functions of the land units include guarding military facilities, patrolling, surveillance, and protecting critical infrastructure.
The Naval Home Guard monitors shipping in Denmark’s territorial waters, reports suspicious activity to the Navy, guards ports and other critical facilities, and participates in search-and-rescue operations and the escort of foreign military vessels. The Air Force Home Guard is responsible for guarding air bases, aircraft, helicopters, and radars; controlling access to military airfields; and assisting the Danish Air Force during training exercises and in crisis situations.
Some of its units also carry out aerial surveillance and search missions. In addition to military tasks, volunteers assist the police in searching for missing persons, secure crime scenes, control traffic, and help government agencies during floods, storms, snowstorms, and other emergencies.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that in August 2026, 1,600 Danes were drafted into military service as part of a new 11-month program.
