Former Employee Arrested in Connection with Killing of Bulgarian Businessman Iliyan Filipov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:09:54 UTC
17:09:54 KST

A former employee of Bulgarian businessman Iliyan Filipov, who was shot dead in Plovdiv overnight, has been arrested in Sofia in connection with the killing, according to Bulgarian media reports.
The suspect is a 51-year-old man identified by the initials S.M. He reportedly has a police record and worked for one of Filipov’s companies until several months ago. According to 24 Chasa, he is believed to be the man whose image, showing him wearing a hooded sweatshirt, was released earlier in the day. The image was reportedly taken from security cameras in the area where Filipov was killed.
Filipov, 53, was shot dead shortly after midnight at a property he owned in Plovdiv’s Hristo Smirnenski district. A criminal investigation has been launched under the supervision of the Plovdiv District Prosecutor’s Office.
The emergency services received the report of the shooting at around 1 a.m., according to Plovdiv District Prosecutor Vanya Hristova and senior police commissioner Vasil Kostadinov. Investigators said Filipov died from a gunshot wound and that all possible motives and lines of inquiry were being examined.
Authorities said the shooting took place in a parking area in front of a residential building at a complex behind 134 Peshtersko Shose Boulevard. Police cordoned off the area and continued forensic examinations, while investigators were pursuing various possibilities, ranging from a contract killing to a crime linked to personal circumstances.
Prosecutors said witnesses were continuing to be questioned and a forensic medical examination had been ordered. Physical evidence has also been collected as part of the investigation.
Bulgaria: Botev Plovdiv Owner and Businessman Iliyan Filipov Shot Dead in Plovdiv
Security Measures Intensified
More than 12 hours after the killing, police continued checks at the exits of Plovdiv, stopping vehicles and checking their occupants. A national coordination headquarters was established, with security measures tightened not only in Plovdiv and neighboring regions but also along the border, according to the director of the National Police General Directorate, Chief Commissioner Emil Parmakov.
Deputy Interior Minister Emil Ganchev, who was also at the scene, urged against drawing comparisons with organized crime-related killings in Bulgaria during the 1990s.
Investigative and forensic work is ongoing. Residents living near Filipov’s property reportedly said they had not heard anything at the time of the shooting.
Interior Ministry Orders Review of Previous Reports
Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev ordered a full review of whether the Ministry of Interior had previously received information, complaints or reports from Filipov concerning concerns for his safety. According to the ministry’s official records, there were no such reports.
The ministry also said it would examine whether authorities had taken appropriate action following publicly circulated information in March 2025 that Filipov was concerned about his safety. The review will also assess whether any important circumstances or information were overlooked by law enforcement in 2025.
Killing Draws International Media Attention
The killing quickly attracted attention from international media outlets. By Wednesday morning, the case had reportedly been covered by more than 15 foreign media organizations in over 10 countries.
Reuters was among the first international agencies to report the killing, describing Filipov as a prominent Bulgarian businessman and president of a top-flight football club. The agency identified him as the owner of construction and transport company PIMK and majority shareholder of Botev Plovdiv.
Other international outlets also reported on the killing, including British football publication Inside World Football, Romanian media, Greece’s Proto Thema, Poland’s RMF24, Russia’s Sport-Express, Serbia’s Glas Srpske, North Macedonia’s Libertas and Euronews Albania.
Who Was Iliyan Filipov?
Iliyan Filipov was a businessman from Plovdiv and the owner of PIMK, a major Bulgarian transport and construction company with interests including rail transport and real estate. He also owned Botev Plovdiv football club.
Born in Plovdiv on March 31, 1973, Filipov was one of the two co-founders and owners of PIMK. The company operates through numerous subsidiaries involved in construction, freight forwarding, rail transport, concrete production and quarrying.
Filipov took ownership of Botev Plovdiv in June last year. PIMK is described in the source as one of Bulgaria’s largest transport companies and among Europe’s top 10 in the sector.
The company has also expanded into construction. In 2020, PIMK won a tender to reconstruct Plovdiv’s Hristo Botev Stadium for nearly BGN 44 million, according to the source.

U.S. Air Force buys 40 electronic warfare kits for F-15EX
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:09:09 UTC
17:09:09 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded BAE Systems a $146.7 million sole-source contract for 40 EPAWSS hardware sets for F-15EX Lots 7 and 8.
- Work will take place in Nashua, New Hampshire, through August 2030, with $58.8 million obligated at award.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded BAE Systems a $146.7 million contract for 40 sets of the electronic warfare suite that protects the F-15EX Eagle II, covering jets in the fighter’s seventh and eighth production lots.
The sole-source contract, announced by the Department of War, buys 40 production hardware sets of the Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System, known as EPAWSS, along with magazines and retainers for the jet’s countermeasure dispensers. BAE Systems will do the work in Nashua, New Hampshire, and expects to finish by Aug. 31, 2030. The U.S. Air Force obligated $58.8 million in fiscal 2025 and 2026 procurement funds at the time of award, and the full value works out to roughly $3.7 million per set.
EPAWSS is the F-15’s built-in self-protection system. It warns the crew when enemy radars are tracking the jet, works out where those radars are, jams them, and controls the release of chaff and flares to decoy incoming missiles. Every F-15EX is built with EPAWSS installed at Boeing’s St. Louis factory, and the U.S. Air Force is also retrofitting the system into part of its older F-15E Strike Eagle fleet, where it replaces an analog electronic warfare suite in use since the 1980s.
The award follows a U.S. Air Force move to add a capability EPAWSS does not cover. On Sept. 29, the F-15 program office asked industry for an already-qualified missile warning system that could be fitted into six sensor locations built into the F-15EX for that purpose, The Defence Blog reported. EPAWSS focuses on radar threats, while a dedicated missile warning system looks for the heat or light of an incoming missile’s motor, including heat-seeking missiles that give off no radar signal.
The F-15EX is a two-seat, heavily modernized version of the F-15 that the U.S. Air Force is buying mainly to replace its aging F-15C and F-15D fighters. The order for Lot 7 and Lot 8 hardware means EPAWSS supply is being lined up for jets that will be built over the next several years, and the service’s fiscal 2027 budget request asked for 24 more F-15EX aircraft.
EPAWSS cleared full-rate production in early 2025, and the U.S. Air Force has since opened a dedicated installation line at Warner Robins Air Logistics Complex in Georgia to speed upgrades of F-15Es outside their regular depot maintenance.

A New Lens on Modern Heritage: ArchDaily Partners with World Monuments Fund
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

What makes a building worth preserving? Age is the most common answer, but not always the best one. A building from the 1950s or 70s may carry as much historical significance as a medieval cathedral; it simply demands a different framework, one that weighs political context, cultural meaning, and architectural innovation over the mere passage of time. This is especially true for modernist architecture across the so-called Global South, where the movement took on unique forms of expression.
It is precisely this conversation that ArchDaily and World Monuments Fund are now opening together. WMF brings on-the-ground conservation expertise across the world, and ArchDaily brings the editorial capacity to contextualize that work and connect it to a global audience. The goal is to do both at once: preserve places and tell their stories, shaping how modernist heritage is understood far beyond the field of preservation itself.
To mark the start of this collaboration, we spoke with Javier Ors Ausín, Director of Thematic Programs at World Monuments Fund, and Christele Harrouk, Editor-in-Chief of ArchDaily. Read the full conversation below.
Related Article
United Nations’ Africa Hall Restoration in Ethiopia Receives 2026 World Monuments Fund/Knoll Modernism Prize
Romullo Baratto [Managing Editor]: What does this partnership mean to World Monuments Fund and ArchDaily? Javier, would you like to begin?
Javier Ors Ausín: This is a new partnership for World Monuments Fund, and we are genuinely exploring what it means as it unfolds. But what strikes me as particularly special is how complementary our roles are. At WMF, we engage directly with sites, implementing conservation projects, advocacy initiatives, and documentation of heritage preservation work. We work with governments, communities, local NGOs, and professionals in the field. Having ArchDaily as a partner — a platform that communicates architecture to an international audience through a broad network — means we can both engage with sites and preserve them, while also explaining why this work matters and why these places are globally relevant. The ability to pursue preservation and narration in parallel is very valuable.
Christele Harrouk: I really like what Javier said about this complementarity. We represent two complementary forms of responsibility toward architecture. WMF works with communities, places, and physical conservation. We work on narration, giving the world access to these stories. What makes this collaboration so meaningful is that it brings both capacities together and makes the work accessible to a global audience, while also contributing to safeguarding it.
 Because talking about something, documenting it, is itself a form of conservation. For ArchDaily, this partnership is particularly significant because we see ourselves as active participants in architectural culture. This collaboration gives us a chance to reflect that — to help shape what conservation is, what heritage is, and how people understand and engage with it.
JOA: Exactly. By doing the editorial and communication work, you are making communication itself part of the conservation process. In the conservation field, we sometimes limit ourselves to before-and-after photographs. But communicating the work from beginning to end is also conservation; it builds visibility, awareness, and ultimately support for the initiatives and field projects we undertake.
RB: Christele, why World Monuments Fund, and why now?
CH: ArchDaily has been around for 18 years. Almost two decades documenting and doing more than what a platform typically does. Our role goes beyond documentation and narration: we contextualize, connect information, make knowledge available, and we explain why it matters. Over those years, heritage has been a recurring thread. So when WMF came along, the timing felt exactly right — we had, in some sense, built everything toward it. They brought conservation knowledge, on-the-ground expertise, and active projects. We brought our editorial team, our global audience, and our archive. It was the best timing.
JOA: When I joined World Monuments Fund as an architect, almost ten years ago, I realized how segregated our field was. A lot of experts working in heritage preservation were not really part of the broader architectural conversations and discourses. Partnering with ArchDaily is a way of reconnecting the specialized discussions happening in the heritage field with the broader architectural discourse. There is no better partner for that: ArchDaily is genuinely shaping and actively participating in the global architectural conversation.
CH: I'd add one more dimension: what World Monuments Fund and ArchDaily together make possible is not just ensuring that the architecture that matters survives physically, but that the knowledge around it also survives. That, for me, is the core of this partnership.
RB: One of the defining features of the partnership is the focus on modernist architecture, with a particular emphasis on the Global South. Javier, why do you think that is the right frame for this collaboration?
JOA: What initially drew me to the field of preservation and documentation of modernist architecture was the opportunity to tell a larger story about 20th-century architecture. In my experience as an architect, the established narrative around modern architecture heritage remains quite narrow, focused primarily on the United States and Europe.
 But modernism was not confined to those regions. It took different shapes in South America, Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and the Middle East, adapting to different climates, materials, and technologies. Since joining WMF, part of my mission has been to tell that larger story through our sites and projects.
To give concrete examples: we developed a conservation management plan for the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Stadium in India, a brutalist structure designed by Charles Correa and Mahendra Raj during the post-independence period. The urgency was heightened after the demolition of modernist sites in India, but also because these buildings are aging and require expert conservation management. In Africa, we are currently working in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, in a remarkable and relatively unknown example of modernist architecture deeply grounded in the local climate and vernacular construction traditions, using earthen materials and natural ventilation. The partnership with ArchDaily is an opportunity to expand that global narrative while also addressing the real technical challenges these buildings face.
RB: Christele, you've mentioned ArchDaily's coverage on heritage throughout the years. How do you see WMF's work fitting into ArchDaily's agenda?
CH: Being global is foundational for ArchDaily, but what we've been working toward is becoming more intentional about what "global" actually means. It is not just about publishing projects from many countries. It is about understanding architecture in its full context: shaped by climate, culture, politics, materials, economies, communities, and histories. That applies directly to modernism. We have long questioned the idea that architectural movements radiated, unchanged, from one center outward. We know that they were transformed, became hybrid, were appropriated, and challenged. Africa, the Middle East, Latin America, Central Asia — all of these places produced distinct histories of modernism.
 When we choose what to publish and how to contextualize it, we are participating in the construction of architectural history. We are adjusting the narrative. That has been central to our work for at least a decade.
With WMF, we have the opportunity to take it further: to discover more places, more contexts, more projects, and to push forward the idea that preserving modernism also means shaping what becomes visible and what is taken as a reference.
RB: When we think about heritage, modernist buildings don't enjoy the same prestige as, for instance, a Gothic cathedral or a medieval town when it comes to preservation. Javier, how do you build the case for this kind of work? How do you approach governments, communities, and other stakeholders?
JOA: That is the fundamental challenge. A medieval building, a castle, a cathedral, a mosque, is automatically recognized as a place of historical value and significance. A building from the 1950s, 60s, or 70s has to constantly prove that it embodies heritage values, historical significance, and architectural innovation. That is frustrating for anyone working in this field, but it is also the central challenge we all contribute to overcoming.
 Our approach is grounded in interpretation and education. We work to show — to communities living near these sites, to governments, to the broader public — that the value of these places is not based solely on age, but on the political and historical context in which they were built and the architectural innovation they represent.
Take the United Nations' Africa Hall in Addis Ababa, recognized by WMF in 2026 for its restoration project. Its importance is not that it dates to a particular decade. It lies in what it represents: decolonization, institution-building in Africa, the creation of a continental platform for political discussion. The fact that it was built in Ethiopia — the only African country never colonized — is, itself, a layer of historical significance. There is also remarkable architectural innovation in its use of reinforced concrete. Much remains to be done in terms of interpretation and knowledge dissemination to overcome the perception that these buildings are too recent to be preserved. In fact, many of them are approaching a century of age. Interpretation, ultimately, is where the opportunity lies.
RB: Many of the cities where these buildings are located are facing rapid urban growth. How do conservation and urban development coexist? How do we balance civic interest, land value, and the preservation of buildings that, as you've said, are not measured by age alone?
CH: I don't see them as opposing forces. We tend to forget that cities are living systems, and that heritage, the buildings we're discussing, was always part of those systems and evolved alongside them. The question we should always be asking is how we allow our cities to change, to grow, to evolve, while also understanding what they already carry culturally, socially, and in terms of heritage value.
And not just what that value is, but who gets to define it. That question is crucial. WMF is doing important work in redefining which buildings can be considered to carry value, not necessarily because of specific construction techniques, but because of their place in the urban fabric, the stories they hold, and how they are embedded in the lives of the communities around them. In rapidly changing cities, the communities living in these places must be part of determining their future. Heritage cannot be defined only institutionally or architecturally, without understanding its collective and lived value. It is not a question of conservation or urban growth — it is a question of how our cities can evolve with a greater awareness of what already exists, what we need to preserve, and what we might lose in the process.
JOA: I agree entirely. People tend to see conservation and development as opposing forces, but they shouldn't. The question for me is: how can architecture and conservation serve as vehicles for informing the decisions we make about how our cities grow? Cities have always changed — and modernism itself was a force of urban transformation in the 20th century. So the question is not conservation versus growth, but rather how heritage preservation can provide the tools to ensure that when cities change, those decisions are informed by community needs, by the cultural and historical places embedded in the built environment.
 Conservation, rather than being imposed, should be one more tool in the toolkit — helping us make informed, sustainable decisions. I prefer to see it as a tool to manage change, not resist it.
This is also why I advocate for architects to be more actively involved in government, in institutions like WMF, in platforms like ArchDaily — because that is where these ideas need to be present to have real impact.
CH: That's something I say constantly: architects need to be in decision-making positions, especially in politics. Change happens faster, and with greater impact, when it comes from there.
RB: What will ArchDaily readers find on the platform that they wouldn't without this partnership?
CH: We're digitizing WMF's projects and creating an online library that will document them through project features, narratives, interviews, stories, and accounts of specific conservation processes. What we want to do is turn WMF's archive into active architectural knowledge and situate it within ArchDaily's ecosystem of architectural knowledge.
JOA: This is a genuine opportunity for WMF to present our work in a completely different way: to tell a comprehensive story about what we've been doing in modern architecture since the early 2000s, not just through completed projects but through new material we'll generate together. We will speak about projects currently underway and begin working on a new project next year, with ArchDaily as a partner. What excites me most is the idea that the editorial angle can be an integrated part of our work — not something that happens after the fact, but something that runs alongside the conservation process from the beginning.
RB: Could you tell us more about this new project for next year?
CH: This is the most exciting part. We always say architecture matters, and this is our chance to demonstrate that in practice. This will be the first ArchDaily-supported conservation project, and the financial commitment matters because it marks a shift from documenting value to actively supporting it.
 We'll follow the process from beginning to end, showcasing how the project evolves — the stages, the phases, the story behind it. It's an educational process in itself. It extends what ArchDaily is already doing; I see it as the next step, a natural continuation.
JOA: Absolutely. This is really an opportunity to go beyond a conventional communications partnership and put everything we've been discussing into real practice. WMF is constantly engaging new sites, and the scope varies enormously — from physical restoration to conservation planning, adaptive reuse, advocacy campaigns for sites under threat. We don't yet know exactly what shape this project will take with ArchDaily, but that's also part of the excitement: exploring how editorial and communications expertise can be integrated into a project from the very beginning. Knowledge sharing and visibility are also forms of advocacy — and many of these sites urgently need that.
CH: What I find most compelling is using an individual site as a reference point for larger questions. How has modernism been transformed across continents? How have political and social histories shaped architecture, and how do they continue to shape it today? How have communities changed these buildings, and what can those transformations teach us? How might all of this change our contemporary practice? Using this site to answer larger questions — about heritage, about modernism, about the world, about the narratives we tell — that is what this is really about.

Russia’s state arms giant claims a new drone-missile class
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:59:51 UTC
16:59:51 KST

- Russian state conglomerate Rostec said its S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T jet-powered strike drones perform the role of cruise missiles at lower cost.
- Rostec said the weapons are already used in Ukraine and should become standard weapons for Russian frontline aviation.
Russia’s state defense conglomerate Rostec says three of its newest jet-powered strike drones, the S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, can now do the job of cruise missiles at a fraction of the cost, and that all three are already being used against Ukraine.
Rostec made the claims in comments to the Russian Defense Ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda published on Sept. 30, describing the weapons as a new category that sits between attack drones and missiles. The company did not give prices, production numbers or performance figures for any of the three, and its claims about accuracy and combat results could not be independently verified.
“In fact, a classic cruise missile is already a fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle. However, not every UAV of this type is a cruise missile. Nevertheless, in the new S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, this line is being erased,” Rostec said in its statement.
The company said the drones have the accuracy, maneuverability and range of cruise missiles while being significantly cheaper than conventional missiles, and that the gap between the two kinds of weapon will keep shrinking as drone production matures. Rostec said it expects the new jet-powered drones to become a standard weapon for Russian frontline aviation in the near future, alongside the glide-bomb kits that Russian jets have dropped on Ukrainian front lines in large numbers since 2023.
The S-71M and S-71K are designed to be launched from fifth-generation fighters, including the Su-57, Rostec told the state news agency TASS. Both are sized to fit inside the Su-57’s internal weapons bay, which lets the jet carry them without spoiling its radar-evading shape, and Russia’s arms exporter Rosoboronexport displayed them next to a Su-57E at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt in September.
Ukraine’s military intelligence has examined debris from both. It says the S-71K, known as Kovyor, carries a 250-kg (550-pound) OFAB-250-270 high-explosive bomb as its warhead and lacks terminal guidance, and that the S-71M, called Monokhrom, contains an NVIDIA Jetson Orin computing module, a small U.S.-made computer built to run artificial intelligence software on board, Militarnyi reported. Some published reports have swapped the two designations, so details tied to each name should be treated with caution.
Rostec told TASS that the smaller Dan-T has been confirmed in hundreds of launches against Ukrainian targets and can be fired from aircraft and helicopters, including foreign-made ones, which suggests the company is aiming it at export buyers. Accounts of where the Dan-T comes from differ: some analysts describe it as the export name for the S8000 Banderol, a small jet-powered cruise missile built by Russian drone maker Kronshtadt, while Ukrainian experts have described it as a strike version of the Dan-M jet target drone that Russia used for air defense training.
Ukrainian estimates put the Dan-T’s range at roughly 500 km (310 miles) with a 135-kg (298-pound) warhead, The New Voice of Ukraine reported, citing Ukrainian intelligence officials who said Moscow wants the weapon built entirely from Russian components.
That goal follows Ukrainian findings about the Banderol, which first appeared over Ukraine in spring 2025 and is launched mainly from Su-30/34 combat aircraft, Orion drones and Mi-28 attack helicopters, often from occupied Crimea toward the Odesa region. Ukraine’s military intelligence says the Banderol contains a Chinese-made jet engine, a Japanese battery and mostly U.S.-made electronics, Euronews reported.
Cheap jet-powered weapons that fly like missiles force Ukraine to spend scarce and expensive air defense interceptors on targets that cost Russia far less to build, the same logic behind Russia’s mass use of Shahed-type drones.
Rostec placed the new drones in a wider family of guided weapons that includes the Iskander ballistic missile system, Tornado-S rocket launchers with guided rockets, Krasnopol guided artillery shells and the Kalashnikov Group’s KUB loitering munitions.

Türkiye captures suspect in 2013 Reyhanli attack
Unknown

16:58:02 KST

Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization (MIT) has captured Omar al-Khatib, a Syrian suspect accused of helping plan the 2013 Reyhanli bombings near the Turkish-Syrian border that killed 53 people.
Al-Khatib, who was wanted under an Interpol Red Notice, was intercepted while attempting to flee to Europe by sea and brought to Türkiye, security sources said on Thursday.
The sources said he helped plan and organise the attack and coordinated contacts between its perpetrators and intelligence officers loyal to ousted regime leader Bashar al Assad.
MIT had been monitoring his activities in Syria as part of efforts to track down those responsible for the bombings in Türkiye’s southern Hatay province.
Planning and preparation
According to the sources, al-Khatib arranged meetings in 2013 between Yusuf Nazik, another planner of the attack, and Syrian intelligence official Kifah Melhem, during which details of the operation were decided.
Al-Khatib and Nazik entered Türkiye through Hatay in February that year to identify targets, subsequently obtaining approval from Melhem, who was based in Latakia, the sources said.
In May, before the attack, al-Khatib accompanied Temir Dukanci to the Latakia branch of Syrian military intelligence to collect materials for the explosive device, they added.
The sources said Dukanci and Nazik transported the bomb-laden vehicle to Reyhanli, where it was detonated remotely.
After the attack, the pair fled to Syria, where al-Khatib took them to the same military intelligence branch in Latakia. The sources alleged that the ousted Assad regime rewarded al-Khatib and the other perpetrators with money.
Efforts to track down suspects
MIT began tracking those responsible immediately after the bombings and closely monitored al-Khatib’s activities in Syria, the sources said.
His capture follows the arrests of Nazik in 2018, Cengiz Sertel in 2024, and Muhammed Dib Korali and Temir Dukanci in 2025.
Melhem, whom the sources identified as the major general who ordered the attack, was appointed head of the National Security Bureau by Assad in February 2024.
He fled abroad after the fall of the Assad regime, according to the sources.

Russia sentences founder of exile news outlet Astra to seven years in absentia. Her lawyers say she was convicted of violating ‘foreign agent’ regulations despite never being designated one.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:40:11 UTC

Russia sentences founder of exile news outlet Astra to seven years in absentia. Her lawyers say she was convicted of violating ‘foreign agent’ regulations despite never being designated one.
Ulyanovsk’s Zavolzhsky District Court has sentenced Anastasia Chumakova, Astra’s founder and editor-in-chief, in absentia to seven years in prison.
Chumakova was charged with spreading “fake news” about the Russian army and violating “foreign agent” regulations.
The court also barred her from running websites and other online platforms for four and a half years and fined her 200,000 rubles.
According to Astra, witnesses in the case included neighbors of Chumakova’s relatives who did not know her and had never seen her.
The prosecutor had sought a nine-year prison sentence for Chumakova.
The “fake news” charge concerned both posts on Chumakova’s personal Telegram channel and Astra’s March and April 2022 reports on the killings of civilians in Bucha, in the Kyiv region, during the Russian occupation.
Responding to the allegation of “failure to comply with foreign agent obligations,” Chumakova’s defense told the court that she did not have “foreign agent” status. Astra itself had been designated a “foreign agent,” but Chumakova had been added to a registry of people affiliated with a “foreign agent.”
The defense asked the court to acquit Chumakova and recognize her right to redress for wrongful prosecution.
Russian authorities designated Astra’s Telegram channel a “foreign agent” in 2024. In October 2025, Chumakova was added to the list of “terrorists and extremists.” In November that year, it emerged that she had been placed on a wanted list in connection with the “fake news” case. In January 2026, authorities opened another criminal investigation into her, this time for allegedly failing to comply with “foreign agent” requirements.

Christa Pike in critical condition after Tennessee botched execution, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:48:27 UTC
16:48:27 KST

Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
A condemned female murderer who survived two lethal injections during a botched execution by the US state of Tennessee is in critical condition and receiving "life-saving care," her lawyer said on Thursday.
In an extraordinary chain of events, Christa Pike, 50, was whisked from a prison execution chamber to a hospital on Wednesday night, still alive despite two deadly doses of pentobarbital.
"What we have been told is that she is in critical condition, receiving life-saving care," Randy Spivey said in a virtual news conference on Thursday afternoon, declining to provide further details.
He urged Governor Bill Lee, who had denied a clemency request earlier in the week, to scrap Pike's death sentence.
"After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa's sentence now."
Experts on the US death penalty said the case was unprecedented.
"This failed attempt is the worst we've ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," said Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre.
The centre counts seven inmates whose executions could not be carried out because medical staff were unable to establish IV lines, but "Pike is the first person to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs."
Late on Thursday, US President Donald Trump questioned how an execution like Pike's could fail, telling reporters that it "shouldn't be very difficult."
'Loudly snoring'
The case had already attracted scrutiny as Pike would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Kim Chandler, a media witness with the Associated Press, told CBS News that "Pike appeared notably awake as the execution began" at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.
"A couple of times she looked around the room. At one point she looked towards prison officials and asked if it was supposed to feel that way," Chandler said.
Pike later began snoring and witnesses listened from the viewing area for about an hour before being ushered out.
The condemned woman was "loudly snoring, clearly very alive" as journalists left, Chandler told CBS.
Pike's legal team had previously objected to the execution IV protocol, saying it would have caused needless suffering due to her small veins and a blood condition.
"I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt" to start an IV line, Spivey said.
Lawyer Stephen Ferrell said medical experts had warned of needles becoming dislodged or piercing through the vein, causing lethal drugs to flow into Pike's arm instead of the bloodstream.
"It sounds like that is likely to have occurred," he said.
Media witnesses said Pike told execution staff her arm felt like it would "burst open," and Spivey said he saw her right arm turn purple, especially after the second lethal injection.
Pike had not been scared to die, Ferrell said.
"It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death, and that's what happened, minus the death."
'A mess'
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol," adding that Pike was subsequently taken to an "off-site medical facility."
Governor Lee called for a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the failed execution.
The state's remaining scheduled execution, convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton is scheduled to die on 3 December, would not be carried out this year, Lee added.
Pike's case had sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals. She was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer's body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, told NBC News the botched execution was "a mess."
Pike's lawyers had argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of Slemmer's killing. They also cited her history of childhood sexual assault and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Following a flurry of legal filings that delayed the execution by several hours, the US Supreme Court on Wednesday night cleared the way for the punishment to go ahead.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
UN rights chief Volker Turk urged Tennessee not to make a new attempt to execute Pike.
"The case of Christa Pike lays bare multiple reasons why the death penalty should be abolished," his office said on X.

U.S. Air Force buys weather data from smart balloons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
07:45:18 UTC
16:45:18 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded WindBorne Systems a sole-source contract worth up to $48.7 million for global atmospheric data through Sept. 30, 2033.
- Only $1.7 million was obligated at award under the first task order, meeting the contract's required minimum purchase.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded WindBorne Systems, a California startup that flies a fleet of self-steering weather balloons, a contract worth up to $48.7 million to supply atmospheric data for military weather forecasting and mission planning.
The contract, awarded on Sept. 29, covers continuous, global and targeted vertical profiles of the atmosphere, from the surface up to the stratosphere, according to the Department of War. The work runs until Sept. 30, 2033. The U.S. Air Force obligated about $1.7 million in fiscal 2025 and 2026 research and development funds under the first task order, which meets the contract’s required minimum purchase, so the rest of the $48.7 million ceiling will only be spent if the service places more orders.
The contract was awarded without competition by the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Hanscom Air Force Base, Massachusetts. The notice does not say how much data the U.S. Air Force will buy, which regions it will focus on, or whether it will cover WindBorne’s own forecasts as well as its raw measurements.
WindBorne, founded in 2019 by Stanford University graduates and based in Redwood City, builds what it calls Global Sounding Balloons. Each weighs less than 1.4 kg (3 pounds) at launch and carries solar-powered sensors that measure temperature, humidity, pressure and wind. Unlike standard weather balloons, which rise for a couple of hours over their launch site before bursting, WindBorne’s balloons stay aloft for weeks and repeatedly climb and descend between about 1 km and 20 km (12 miles), sending data back by satellite.
The balloons have no engines. They steer by changing altitude to catch winds blowing in the direction they need, which lets the company send them toward specific areas. That is what the contract means by targeted profiling: measurements over places the U.S. military cares about, including oceans and remote regions where few weather stations exist and traditional balloons cannot be launched.
The company says it keeps about 600 balloons in the air at any time from 20 launch sites around the world, TechCrunch reported in August, when WindBorne raised $37 million in new funding at a $250 million valuation. It also runs WeatherMesh, an artificial intelligence forecasting model trained partly on its own balloon data.
WindBorne has worked with the U.S. military for several years. The U.S. Air Force gave it a contract in 2021 to help build its balloon constellation and feed the data into the service’s weather cloud, and the Defense Innovation Unit and the U.S. Air Force picked it in 2022 as one of five companies for a commercial weather data prototype project. The company has also had research contracts with the U.S. Navy, and the National Weather Service buys its data, which feeds into NOAA’s main global forecast model.

Heat deaths in Western Europe top 34,600 during warmest summer ever

Heat deaths in Western Europe top 34,600 during warmest summer ever
- More than 34,600 heat-related deaths occurred in five Western European countries during the hottest summer on record, with Spain, France, Germany, Britain, and Belgium all severely affected.
- Spain recorded 5,805 excess deaths with 61 heat wave days, while Germany saw about 16,000 heat deaths, the highest in a decade, including a record June wave.
- Western Europe experienced temperatures 2.5 deg C above average, with 52 per cent of the continent facing extreme heat stress, surpassing previous records and challenging healthcare systems.
AI generated
MADRID – More than 34,600 people died in five Western European countries due to heat this summer as the region posted its hottest June, July and August on record, according to a Bloomberg compilation of mortality estimates from different agencies.
Spain saw its deadliest summer since records began in 2015, with 5,805 excess deaths attributable to heat between May 15 and Sept 30, according to data from the Instituto de Salud Carlos III that was made public on Oct 1.
In France, three heat waves led to an estimated 7,824 deaths, the highest toll since at least 2015, according to provisional figures from the national public health agency. Germany, Britain and Belgium also recorded elevated heat-related mortality.
“Spain has recorded 61 heat wave days over the summer, with four heat waves, a fifth in September and extreme heat episodes in May,” said Diana Gomez, head of the mortality monitoring system at ISCIII. “All of that has resulted in an increase of deaths attributable to heat.”
Heat can exacerbate existing illnesses and is particularly dangerous for vulnerable people including young children, the elderly and workers exposed to high temperatures over long periods of time.
Western Europe faced extraordinary heat throughout the summer, with average temperatures for the region 2.5 deg C above the average between 1991 and 2020, according to the latest monthly report by Earth observation program Copernicus.
European data indicate temperatures over the summer were the highest since at least 1979 across virtually all of England, Wales and Belgium, as well as most of France, Spain, Italy, Switzerland and Austria.
The previous record was set in 2003, when countries including Britain, France and Germany recorded tens of thousands of heat deaths, and healthcare services struggled to cope with cases of heat stroke, forcing authorities to improve emergency responses and hot-weather services.
On 17 days in 2026, at least 60 per cent of Western Europe experienced temperatures above 30 deg C, according to a Copernicus report released on Oct 2. That compares with 11 days under the same conditions during the summer of 2003.
A record 52 per cent of the European continent experienced temperatures of 38 deg C or higher during the summer, which qualifies as “very strong” heat stress under the Copernicus ratings system.
In Spain, the 2026 summer’s heat deaths exceeded the previous record of 2022 by more than 1,000, the ISCIII found.
The worst day was July 10, according to the public health research institute, which calculates excess mortality by comparing the daily total of deaths to average mortality rate in previous years and factoring in temperature thresholds for each of the country’s 50 provinces.
“Thresholds have been surpassed in every province for many days,” Gomez said. “Ours is the only system that issues daily estimates and, since we have a lot of experience in this field, several European countries have been in touch with us over the past few days.”
In Germany, deaths reached the highest level in at least a decade, with about 16,000 heat-related deaths between April 6 and Sept 13, according to the Robert Koch Institute, the federal government agency responsible for disease control. About 9,600 people died as a result of the heat wave at the end of June, which was the worst on record for Western Europe. The country’s previous record was about 9,000 heat deaths in 2018.
Preliminary data from Sante Publique France indicate heat deaths in France this summer hit the highest number since at least 2015 due to three major heat waves in June, July and August. The government agency is expected to publish a definitive mortality report in early 2027.
That compares with 5,700 estimated deaths in 2025. In 2003, researchers at the University Paris 5 found that devastating temperatures that year led to 14,800 excess deaths in August alone.
In Britain, heat waves caused an estimated 2,877 deaths in May and June, according to the British Health Security Agency, which is due to release a final mortality report covering the whole season in 2027. In Belgium, 2,112 people died between June 18 and July 12, according to Sciensano, the country’s public health institute. BLOOMBERG

Ukraine's budget revenue lags plan by UAH 49.5 bln in 9M
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:02:52 EEST
16:02:52 KST

The general fund of Ukraine's state budget fell UAH 49.5 billion short of plan in January-September 2026, almost two-thirds of it (UAH 32 billion) in August-September, Budget Committee head Roksolana Pidlasa said in a Facebook post.
"Budget 2026 execution for nine months: the state of budget revenue is deteriorating… The main reason is constant Russian strikes on business," she said.
Revenue from import VAT fell short by UAH 35.7 billion, or 6.8%, VAT on goods produced in Ukraine by UAH 32.9 billion, or 11.4%, domestic excise by UAH 19.1 billion, or 16.5%, and dividends and part of net profit of economic entities by UAH 10.8 billion, or 16%, Pidlasa said.
At the same time, there was overperformance in corporate profit tax of UAH 29 billion, or 12%, and in personal income tax and the military levy of UAH 6.6 billion, or 2.6%, which offsets the shortfall in other taxes, she said.
According to preliminary data, UAH 1.9 trillion was credited to general fund revenue in January-September 2026, excluding international grants, she said.
The biggest sources were import VAT at UAH 491 billion, corporate profit tax at UAH 270 billion, personal income tax and the military levy at UAH 266.3 billion, VAT on goods produced in Ukraine at UAH 255.2 billion, National Bank of Ukraine funds at UAH 146.1 billion, import excise at UAH 134.6 billion, domestic excise at UAH 96.5 billion, dividends and part of net profit of economic entities at UAH 57.1 billion, import duty at UAH 48.4 billion and rent payments at UAH 42.6 billion, Pidlasa said.
About $22 billion in international aid was used to cover general fund spending in January-September, and another UAH 350.6 billion was raised from domestic government bond placements, she said.
The biggest spending categories since the start of 2026 were defense at UAH 2 trillion, or 61.3% of all general fund expenditure, debt repayment (domestic and external) at UAH 427.9 billion, social protection and veteran support (excluding public investment projects) at UAH 342.6 billion, debt servicing (external and domestic) at UAH 275.2 billion, the medical guarantees program and health screening at UAH 144 billion, school teachers' pay (education subvention and top-ups) at UAH 116.7 billion, and basic and additional grants at UAH 48.5 billion, she said.
"Until the second tranche of EU macro-financial assistance ($4.26 billion) is received, the budget situation will remain critical," she said.
The Ukrainian state budget for 2026 was initially adopted with revenue (excluding grants) of UAH 2.90 trillion and expenditure of UAH 4.77 trillion, including UAH 2.61 trillion and UAH 4.38 trillion respectively in the general fund.
In June, parliament raised revenue to UAH 5.20 trillion and expenditure to UAH 6.41 trillion, mainly on the back of a EUR 45 billion EU loan, including UAH 3.38 trillion and UAH 4.50 trillion respectively in the general fund.
Under the International Monetary Fund's Extended Fund Facility program, updated in July, general government revenue is forecast at UAH 6.78 trillion this year, compared with UAH 5.06 trillion last year, and expenditure at UAH 7.94 trillion, compared with UAH 6.63 trillion.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky and representatives of the ruling Servant of the People faction said another increase in defense spending of $27 billion was needed. In September, the government stopped financing capital expenditure because of a funding shortfall.
Total cash expenditure of the general fund reached UAH 2.7 trillion in January-August 2026, compared with UAH 2.23 trillion in January-August 2025, while revenue was almost UAH 2.3 trillion, compared with UAH 1.71 trillion.

Hearings in the case are ongoing.
Regarding Ukrainian assets belonging to Usmanov and his business partners, the Skoch and Streshinsky families, the HACC already ruled in 2024, following a Justice Ministry lawsuit, to seize them in favor of the state. This involved more than 165,000 tonnes of iron ore products worth an estimated more than UAH 2 billion, as well as 100% of the charter capital of Peter-Service Ukraine LLC, an IT company previously controlled by Usmanov, according to then-Deputy Justice Minister Inna Bahatykh.

Ukraine secures 20mm ammunition for F-16 jets to counter jet-powered drones – Sybiha
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:07:14 EEST
15:07:14 KST

Several partners, including Spain, Belgium and Poland, will soon deliver 20mm rounds for F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine, which are effective against Russian jet-powered drones, Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said.
"We spent the whole day (Wednesday – Interfax-Ukraine) working on the 20mm caliber issue. And we succeeded. I believe we've secured a solution on this caliber for a significant period ahead. I thank all our ambassadors. The president was calling leaders from the front line. The defense minister was calling his counterparts. I was calling foreign ministers. This is critical. Given that we haven't yet built up sufficient capacity to shoot down jet-powered drones, and with new strikes being prepared, it was critically important to help our military bring these drones down. Right now, aside from air defense systems, which are too expensive to use constantly against drones, the most effective tool is the F-16 fighter jet. That's why we're now using them extensively," Sybiha said.
He separately thanked Spain, Belgium and Poland, which has already begun the delivery process, adding that Ukraine will have the necessary ammunition very soon.
"And this is very important, because diplomacy right now is about concrete things — above all, defense capability. I think this is one of our success stories, bringing things together across many levels and sectors. And for all of us, it means fewer hits on Kyiv and other cities," the foreign minister said.
Bloomberg earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that Ukraine wants to purchase tens of thousands of 20mm rounds for F-16 jets to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones. According to the news agency, intercepting one drone takes about 150 rounds on average, with daily demand potentially reaching around 10,000 rounds.

North Korea’s recent economic growth and leader Kim Jong Un’s repeated nods to addressing a widening regional “wealth gap” suggest the time may be right to build a new bridge linking the country’s main port city on the west coast to the southern provinces.
There are currently no bridges across the Taedong River between the main port city of Nampho and Pyongyang, meaning deliveries through the port must make a 65-mile (105 km) detour up to the capital or an even slower route across the West Sea Barrage to reach the closest southern city.

President Stubb names Finland's first F-35 'Sisu'
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:42:17 EEST
16:42:17 KST

Finland's Air Force officially introduced its new F-35 fighter jets on Thursday at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi.
The jets represent the country's most expensive procurement ever, at approximately 10 billion euros. In total, Finland has ordered 64 of the high-tech American fighters.
President Alexander Stubb gave the first aircraft a very Finnish name, 'Sisu'. There is no direct English equivalent to the term, but it is generally understood to mean extraordinary perseverance in the face of extreme adversity.
Commenting at the ceremony, Stubb shared details of a conversation he had with US President Donald Trump about the jets' capabilities.
"'Alex, they are great! You just press the button and they fly by themselves,'" Stubb recalled Trump saying.
The US-made aircraft can fly nearly autonomously, identify threats, communicate with other fighters and evade radar detection. They are expected to excel at spotting small, low-flying drones — a growing necessity after months of Air Force drone surveillance over the Gulf of Finland.
After poor weather conditions initially delayed proceedings, the ceremony featured a Hornet jet's air display and a peek at the F-35's first manoeuvres in Finnish skies.
Two F-35s have arrived so far, with Lapland Air Command expecting to receive more of the fleet next year as it phases out its ageing Hornet fighters. The first F-35s should be ready for air combat duties within a year.
The jets' total costs cover the aircraft, weapons and airfield construction, with expenses set to rise as systems are upgraded over the aircrafts' lifecycle.
